Hollow Knight is a must buy for fans of Metroidvania platformers and/or the Souls series.
Pros:
+Unique aesthetic.
+Great visuals and soundtrack.
+Fluid and precise movement.
+Surprisingly interesting and diverse cast.
+Well paced for a Metroidvania game.
+Optional upgrades make exploration feel rewarding.
Cons:
-Gameplay can feel tedious at times (comes with the territory of being both a Medroidvania and Souls-esque game).
-Trial and error (will annoy some more than others).
-Some enemies are essentially clones of others.
-Some areas lack bosses, feeling dull as a result.
-Combat can feel repetitive.
Most of my cons are a bit nit-picky, especially considering the game's price.

Some adventure games are light on the gameplay in favor of going hard on the adventure. Tick Tock Isle is an interesting case because it goes light on both the gameplay AND the adventure. That might not sound too appealing, but the whimsical, off-beat story really works to bring this one together.
You play a young Tintin-looking fellow by the ridiculous name of Strike Mainspring, called out to a remote island to fix a busted clock. Ascending the one towering building on the isle, you encounter a time machine that sends you back to the heady year 2009, when the island was still inhabited by its eclectic cast. Your adventure, then, is to repair the time machine and get back to where you belong.
Accomplishing this is going to take a lot of running around, opening doors, picking up stuff, and talking to people. The family that resides on the island includes an elderly couple at imaginary war, a workaholic wife and her useless husband, a firey seductress, and a luchador. They each have their problems that you can help address, and often must help with to progress. The dialog is plenty charming between you and the strange players, though it's all kooky and irreverent without a lot of depth.
As for the rest, it's as simple as can be. The controls are left and right to scoot around, up to jump, and down to interact. Enter opens your notebook with your inventory, map, and to do list. The map isn't terribly important as the game world is quite small, just a circuit around the island and a bunch of interconnected rooms in the building that you'll get used to soon enough. Your inventory is more helpful, with a slot for every item in the game, an indication of when it's been used, and a cutesy description that hints at its purpose.
That's the game, running around fixing crazy people problems, scooping up items, and using them where they need to be used. I can't really say there's much in the way of puzzles, because items are used automatically when interacting with a point of interest. That means you can solve just about every puzzle by picking up an item and trying all the interaction points, which can also mean a lot of backtracking. There are a few brief platforming interludes but they're very much the exception and not at all challenging. The time travel theme at least is used to great effect, I won't spoil how but it gives a hint of cleverness to the simplistic puzzles.
Once you grok the layout of the island and start digging into the tasks at hand, you'll be able to speed through the game in about an hour. That's not long, but it's an hour full of charm and levity. The excellent pixel graphics help keep things interesting, and the sound design fits the atmosphere well all the way to the adorable ending. You won't find much depth or story here, but Tick Tock Isle was a short and sweet experience that kept a smile on my face the whole time.

This game, like Morphopolis, is a collecting game. However, more functionality is present in this game vs Morphopolis.
The principle is simple: Eat a number of a certain colored orbs, and you gain some traits related to that color. There are three colors: Blue, Green, and Red. Different ratios of orbs results in different appearances. You are able to die, so you have to be methodical with how you play, but can be played casually without issue.
I don't believe it's worth full price, but the game is known to drop below $1 during sales. For trading cards and achievements, it's not a bad game for sale price.

Just completed a run-through of the Tick Tock Isle. In brief, I would describe it as functional, but forgettable in pretty much every regard. The graphic are sharp enough for a 2D title but the music, SFX, character and world design is uninspired, both in terms of aesthetics and mechanics.
Gameplay comes almost entirely from the old adventure school of ‘use item x on spot y’, except the game automatically prompts you at interactive spots, and automatically selects the correct item to be used. This effectively removes what little engagement this style of gameplay can bring to the table, meaning that most of the game just has you running systematically from room to room and hitting the down key whenever it tells you to do so. There is minimal thought involved, and after about 20m or so, it just felt like a chore.
While character interaction is serviceable, the writing really isn’t strong enough to carry the game either. I didn’t feel particularly engaged either in the story or any particular plotline, and it seems that they didn’t really make much use of the potential their setting had to offer. You could probably call the dialogue mildly humorous, though it’s in the random/non-sequitur/pop-reference sort of  way.
On the positive side, gameplay length is about 90 minutes, which, given the amount of content is just long enough not to wear out its welcome.
It’s not a bad game, but Steam has better to offer, even at this price point.

In short, Hollow Knight is a 15$ "Gift that keeps on giving" game with simple gameplay mechanics complemented by a vast amount of content, beautiful soundtrack AND free Extra Content. One other way I would describe the game is that it is similar to a "2D Dark Souls-esque" game.
An interesting element that drove me whilst playing the game was that it compelled me to achieve a near 100% before I even get into the "boss" fight. I had all the charms, fully upgraded the Nail, saved all Grubs, get 2400+ Essence, and even get all the Mask Shards and Vessel Fragments! I first bought the game at full price, expecting a maximum 2 hours indie game and I was so wrong. In fact, I purchased the official soundtrack for an extra 10$ because I felt the 15$ price tag wasn't equivalent the game, and also I liked the soundtrack, so win-win. If my research is correct, Team Cherry, the developer of Hollow Knight, consists only of 2 or 3 members. That is mindblowingly impressive, considering that this game is an easy 8/10 or 9/10 from me. I hope Team Cherry does well in the future and hopefully create another great game. Credits to the people who helped Team Cherry with this game as well, you guys truly did a spectacular job.
However, no game is without flaw, such applies to Hollow Knight as well. Around my 8th to 9th hour of the game, the game started to feel like a chore, that is, but this feeling was later diminished by playing more and achieving more.

This is definitely one of the best games I've played in a very long time. The controls and platforming are very tight, and the combat is so satisfying. The music is absolutely phenomenal, and never feels out of place. The cast of NPCs is interesting, and I actually found myself seeking out more dialogue. The atmosphere is perfect. The gameplay is also superb. It's a metroidvania, so a bit of backtracking is to be expected, but it never becomes tedious. The difficulty is also in a great place, and provides just the right amount of challenge without being cumbersome.
For only $15, this game will provide a minimum of 15 hours of gameplay, and thats if you don't go off exporing anything. You will more realistically get ~20 hours out of it, and could easily get 40 hours out of it if you were going for 100% completion.
Do yourself a favor and drop the $15 on a solid 2017 GOTY contender. You will not be disappointed.

Sometimes you come across a game where within seconds of playing you know you are going to love it. Hollow Knight is not only this kind of game, but you are also treated and surprised by a deep and interesting story,  stunning scapes, wonderful characters, beautiful music, intricate mechanics, tight controls, and the flexibility to play the game the way you want to play it. All of this drawing you in more and more as you carve your path through this enormous unique world set out before you.
I could really go on about the beauty and fun of this game for ages, but honestly the best part of this game is the challenge. Your hand is not held and yet the punishments for mistakes are fair. This is enough challenge to get your heart really pumping as you close in on the end of a boss encounter, yet you are not devastated as you fail. Instead you are excited as you learn and feel eager to try again!
If you are on the fence about Hollow Knight I urge you to give it a chance. Embrace the challenge, explore the secrets, read the dialogue, immerse yourself in the world, and play it with a controller!

Never written a review on here but I felt it necessary as most of the glowing reviews on here are very misleading.
The game is not difficult in the sense most people would think. It requires very little thought to find the optimal solution with the information you have, and then it is simply rolling the dice a few times to beat the combat. The "difficultly" is the game punishes you for things you have no way of knowing will happen until they happen, but they happen the same way every time, so you reroll with the new information.
The game thusly becomes basic pattern recognition and trial & error. The patterns are very simple, the options are few. It is almost like a long series of multiple choice questions. If you put in the wrong answer, try the other one until you can proceed. You keep this up until you either beat the final boss or run into a wall. You will likely run into many unbeatable walls, and reroll many times, before you even see the final boss.
For me, the final straw was getting to the last boss only to be utterly destroyed by him. It took around 7 reloads to land one hit, and another 20+ reloads to give up, as he never went below the first "slightly wounded" state. The most I ever got was 2 rounds of combat.
If the above sounds like a good time to you, then definitely buy it, but to me this game is incredibly niche and I can't in good faith recommend it to anyone.

The primary issue with FF13 is that it is a horrible port.
PC gamers have some basic expectations when it comes to their games.  Being able to tweak graphic settings and change the resolution are one of them.  To release a game in 2014 with no graphic settings of any kind and a fixed resolution of 720p is inexcuseable. Very Fun card game revolving around the deck you build, there are almost unlimited choices you can make with the decks that are already given to you right when you enter.The decks that you build require you to have a minimum of 40 cards but its maximum is unlimited, you can have anyamount of cards if you have the requirements for them to be in your deck. Some people say its a Pay To Play, but the game it self rewards you with cards, booster packs, and the 2 types of points used to buy the booster packs or even Deck packs for just logging in for a few days straight!
There are 3 ways you can win if you choose to play this game, by reducing your opponents health from 100 to 0, or doing the same with there Moral from 100 to 0, or by accomplishing the requirements from certian cards that you play when you have them in your hand. And unlike Hearthstone or Magic the Gathering, this game has alot more original and creative aspects to a card game that i have seen. There is a market DURING the games you play to Draw a card, Swap a card out for a random one, or To increase the Maximun resource counter you have. There is even a commander out post for 3 creature cards of your choice (which can be immediatly played if you have the resources) and thoese creatures can have amsome abilities, like " Pay 2, Summon a 3/2 minion in to your safe zone". Most creature and character cards have that awsome aspect to them that make this game alittle bit complicated but still fun in the end.
To just simplify, its a really fun game that is original and should have some time in the spotlight for its amazing gaming concepts.

Pros:
- IMO the best FFB customization of any racing game out there right now.  It's a blessing and a curse, because it can be super daunting to get dialed in when you aren't sure what the million different tweaks and settings mean/do, but once you've got it dialed in, the feeling is incredible, especially with a direct drive wheel.
- Unbelievable sound engineering.  Again, top of its class and absolutely thrashes every other sim out there in this space.
- VR Support--while not 100% there yet, it's definitely coming along very nicely and the UI is done well for the medium.
Cons:
- It's pretty much all pay-to-play content.  This doesn't bother me, as I'm quite happy to buy the entire bundle to save some cash, but if you were to buy pieces by themselves you'd probably go broke pretty quick.
- Online mode is a bit of a crapshoot with who you'll be racing with, leagues would help, but I don't think they want to get into a space being a direct iRacing competitor, so it seems to be a bit in limbo.  I generally race offline, so take all of my online criticism with a grain of salt.
- Speaking of offline racing, AI tends to get a bit smashy-smashy when the difficulty goes up.  Whereas in rFactor2, the AI can be quick but also conscious, in Raceroom they're pretty prone to bumping.
Overall:
- Currently my go-to sim for the feel and polish of the game.  While overall I've paid more for this game than my other racing sims (not counting iRacing), I like that everything that's _in_ the game works well and feels great.  I'm not relying on third-party mods with wildly varying age and quality like with Assetto Corsa and rFactor2.

The short of it is:
Performance wise, I've heard there are some glitches, but never saw anything that stood out. I never had any real problems aside from the usually odd jump mechanics, which are better in this title than the title that came before black flag, and easy to adjust to anyhow. It plays smoothly, has decent enough graphics and unlimited baddies to wack if your feeling blood thirsty.
It can be a little grindy for some folks, but with so much to do, I didn't really notice. Also, no serious gamer is a fan of U-Play imo, but otherwise I really have no complaints. Even then, U-Play at least allows you to share rare finds with friends, which is an interesting feature.
Black flag is an atmospheric AC game that won't feel very linear, as there is tons to do and it makes use of it's rather open world quite well. I've had loads of fun with it and I highly reccomend it.
Long Verision:
Ever played an Assassin's creed game and got frustrated with with the limits of the asassin code? I did. Thank god for black flag!
AC games can be a hit or a miss, but even in the good ones sometimes you are left going "for crying out loud! I'm an assassin! What care I about the common folk?!" In older titles, it seems like for every enemy its okay to kill, there seems to be 20 civillans in the way and well, mistakes happen. Mistakes that would cost you because the commoners tend to get in the way.
Well, you might not get to stab a bunch of innocents in this verision of AC ethier.. but for once, you won't notice. Black flag is definitely a title for those who want to cut loose. The civillans rarely get in the way here. They are spaced out nicely while still feeling kind of like a dense population and there are baddies a' plenty.
The hero character of the hour, Edward, is also not your typical assassin from the order. He cares a whole lot less about all that honor talk, perferring the sound money makes. He has no qualms about killing for some coin and he gets away with it. Why? In AC:BF you play as a pirate who is pretending to be one of the assassins and therefore is not fully bound by the code.
And when I say your not bound, I mean by the assassin's code or anything else. Black flag isn't just about hunting that templar scum. Sure, it's in there, but as a sailor, you soon will find you have wide swaths of ocean to travel with plenty of side actitvies to do.. some of which are locked behind story missions, yes, but the game gets rolling quickly and everything is open fairly early on without ruining progression.
Want to upgrade your weapons? Go for it.. but you'll want to hunt that animal down to do it.. after all, you need it's skin.. and different animals means areas of travel and tactic. Want to hunt a whale? Well, are your harpoons up to snuff? What about your rowboat? For that matter, what about your main ship? Is it strong enough to face the might of the sea?
You do want to loot miltary ships of all that heavy gold, sugar, cannon shot and metal don't you? Or were you just after boarding the scuttled enemy ship so you could fight them hand to hand, walking amongst them like the god of death your feared to be? Well, then you better buy a decent sword and cloak to look the part!
And did I mention the songs your crew will sing as you sail the ocean, which you have to chase down to unlock? What about the forts you can wage battle against, or the ability to dock into a town and go hunting for soliders or raiding stock houses?
What about a trading mini-game that allows you to capture ships and make them work for you in real time? It's a good way to make some coin while your working that 9 to 5 job that paid for the game in the first place. But then, maybe your just a landlubber who likes to gamble on british checkers. Yeah, it has that too.
All the while, the usual AC goodies are there in the missions with a decent story and some fun sneakiness if you want it. Yes, if you want it.. most of the missions don't require you to be sneaky. It's a bonus, nothing more.. but might make things easier on you if your smart about it.  Black flag typically lets you play your way.
Plus.. did I mention treasure hunts? Because what is a pirate without some buried tresure maps?
On the modern day side of the story, your a promising intern at Astergo Entertainment. So when you want to step out of the animus (your simulator) and go back to  modern day, that's fine too. It has it's own little story to tell, which leads to several easter eggs from the older AC titles.. making black flag a great game to start on if your a little behind or even new to the assassin's creed games.

I've just finished this game. In one word, it's a gem.
It's been a while since I've been motivated to actually 'finish' a game, and I must say this game is worth finishing. The story is very good, with a nice twist at the end, and the art in it is exceptionaly good, I'd say it's one of the most beautiful games I've played, ever. This game has 3 VERY strong points: visuals, audio, and story (the script).
~ Pros ~
- Visual/Graphics: this is one of the strongest points in this game, the only word I can use to discribe it is 'beautiful'. The scenarios are very well achieved (kudos to the guys in charge of this), and the level design goes along with it, gorgeous yet very functional and entertaining.
- Audio/Music: another great aspect of this game, the music is brilliant, suits the game perfectly, and has been carefuly chosen to strike a great balance between cultural references to old Japan and modern bits here and there.
- Story/Script: the writers did a wonderful job here, at first the story is a bit tricky, it doesn't show right away where it's heading, you discover the story arch as you play the game, which is exactly what I like, I don't like knowing beforehand exactly where the game is taking me. There are a few nice twists along the way and at the end, something I particularly enjoy.
- Voice acting: I decided to make this a point by itself because of how good it is. Lo Wang's voice actor (the main character) has done a perfect job, seriously, it's believeable, enticing, entertaining, funny, and feels like a real person. The guy who voiced Hoji also did a great job, those two are voices you'll listen to throughout the entire game, and it's a welcomed performance because of the chemistry they achieved.
- Fun: sometimes we play games and we forget this is an important thing, this game is entertaining yes, I've said that before, but it's also 'fun'. The game has some very good and fun bits all over the place: funny comments, hidden secrets, fortune cookies with phrases that will make you crack, and it all has been included in a very fitting manner, it keeps you in a good mood and makes you actually WANT to keep playing. The intro video is actually your first experience with this, just see it and you'll know exactly what I'm taking about (also check below about this).
~ Cons ~
- Intro video: it's a bit old graphics-wise, which is weird because the rest of the game has exceptionaly good graphics and other videos that look much better. Trust me, don't let yourself be fooled by the quality, I even think it may have been done that way on purpose, but I'd have liked it to look a bit better, just a personal preference. The rest of the game looks great so don't worry.
- Story: although this is one of the best aspects of this game, it does have a few moments where it falls under cliches and old formulas. Most of the time it works, so I can't really blame them, and it adds to the game being a 'classic' in a way, so perhaps it's not truly a bad aspect, just be aware of this.
~ Conclusion ~
That's it, several Pros and a couple of Cons that aren't even that important to be honest, I've had a lot of fun playing this game, and I can't believe it had been sitting in my game list all this time without me paying attention to it. Shame on me.
As for the price, if you can grab it on sale don't even think about it, just buy it, I'll even say it's worth its full price, so if you can afford it go for it, you won't regret it.

As with every platformer, a lot more is needed than just "jump to this platform" to make the game exciting. INK doesn't offer an explicit narrative. What INK has going for it is your ability to spray multi-coloured ink droplets around you (in random size) to reveal the landscape to you. Yes, every level starts out as invisible. Ink (either sprayed, or tracks left by the player and enemies) works as your guide through each of the 75 levels.
However, that is it's only real "original" leg to stand on. You'll see a lot of industry standard mechanics (spikes, wall jumps, double jumps, moving platforms). Some levels also seem to be re-used but with different enemy placements. Speaking of enemies, they require one jump on before destruction (hello, Mario).
INK has a very gradual learning curve -- the first 5 or so levels acting as a tutorial, and gradually increasing in difficulty all the way to the end of the game. The final "level" is definitely the most difficult.
INK does not contain checkpoints. You die, you start the level over. However, the level remains uncovered after each death (i.e. it doesn't become fully invisible again). This is pretty brutal coming to later levels, especially when the "secrets" hidden in each level require risk to reach, and they get reset if you die before completing the level.
A minamalistic approach, INK isn't strong in its visuals, if that's what you consider important. The main character is literally a white square. Enemies are colour changing rectangles. Keys are key-shaped. Levels are chunky and cubic. Bosses -
. Backgrounds - consistently black void.
There are seven tracks - title screen, tutorial levels, world 1, world 2, world 3, bosses, credits. Considering that each 'world' is about 20 levels, you'd better get used to looping 3-minute tracks if you sit and play in a long session, like I did. The music does suit the overall feel of the game however.
If it's there, I don't see it. Maybe the dev went for an "interpret this as you will" approach, but either way, there's no explicit storyline. If story is important to you, you'll feel lost in INK.
Bosses offer no explanation either. Enemies have no name or lore. The ending is
.
Sometimes, you can perform triple jumps if you land and jump on nearly the same frames.
As well as this, the game crashes at a consistent point every time in the credits roll. The music continues, a window pops up, and the game ends. Not great.
INK is worth a go if you don't mind a lack of story, you want familiar concepts and solid platforming. The game did only offer me about 2 hours of gameplay before I finished it. I wasn't in awe playing it; there is no real reason for me ever to go back and revisit.
I'd give INK a 5/10. Nothing spectacular, nothing abysmal; it's OK for what it is. It's a dislike because there's not enough in the game making me want to like it. Oh well. Hopefully this can be an experience to improve upon.

This was a very charming game, short and sweet. I highly recommend it if you enjoy pixel art, which the game tackles beautifully, and simple puzzles. The music, while not particularly memorable, is also handled very well; I played this game on a lazy Saturday afternoon and it was so incredibly relaxing to explore the clock tower, sipping coffee and listening to the calming melodies.
The game is, of course, very short, so this game may not be the best for those who would rather sink their teeth into meaty adventures. Mileage will vary slightly, but if you plow through everything at once, Tick Tock Isle will more than likely take you around an hour to complete. Despite the short play time, though, the characters leave an impression. They're all facing problems that are in many way familiar, yet these problems are expressed and/or solved in unique ways. The family musician, Melody is uninspired; Rod and his wife clash over his laziness; Rivet and Brazo, two other residents, lament their lack of skill in certain areas. Solving their problems are satisfying and the conclusion of the game, if somewhat abrupt, feels earned.
Some other quick notes:
1) It was lovely to see small references to other time travel-based stories in the game; I'll leave the matter of what's actually referenced a surprise, though.
2) There's at least one secret/easter egg that I managed to catch on my game, which added an interesting little tidbit to the backstory (keep an eye out, near the very end of the game, of an area to use the cheese). And based on one item I ended up not using, I think that there could be at least one more. Just something of interest to mention for the completionists out there.

You're not playing the way you want to in this game; you are playing the way you must do to succeed. That is, you're not role-playing your character, rather you're manipulating your character's stats once you've found out through trial and error what stats your character needs to have to progress.
For example. One scenario for the thief is to ambush a caravan. If you want to avoid a fight you need to convince your boss to trick the delivery into rerouting. But if you take that option, you, the lowest member of the thieves guild, has to have enough lore to personally forge the papers. So, to do your job, you need at least level 3 in sneak, theft, lock-pick, persuasion and now lore. You need high thieves skills to steal the signet ring later on but you have to dilute your skills to pick up lore, which is way out of your skill set. Advanced level thieves might also be forgers but not the guys working the street for goodness sake. What you end up doing here is repeatedly restarting this scenario with different skill arrangements to find the one that actually works. This is not an RPG, this is a trial and error, skill-search mini-game.
The alternative, the combat scenario, requires you to have high enough combat skills to take on five mercenaries in full armor, with shields and military grade weapons while you're in a T-shirt attacking them with a knife. Granted you've got four friend with crossbows, but you've at least got to take on one of these guys; maybe two or three at once. Reload, reload, reload hoping for a string of lucky rolls is how this scenario is done.
This is why this game is frustrating rather than, say, difficult. You either do the skill-search mini-game or the RNG combat lottery. Neither one of which is fun. Granted, the combat is skill-based, but with these sorts of combat scenarios, it is the RNG that will determine the overall outcome. Apparently, if you get really good at it, that is not true. But getting to that level, it sure is.
On top of this, there are actually very few quests. There are a bunch of alternatives, but any given character type has only a few that they can reasonably do. A smooth-talker, for example, cannot do the heavy combat scenarios. Nor vice versa. And aside from the quest givers, some merchants and a few thief targets, the rest of the population are mannequins. Exploration is minimal and the game is on rails.
Clearly, a lot of people think that this game is great, but be warned: to have fun in this game you have to fit that niche.
Not recommended.

A well designed, fairly well balanced game.
* It IS very similiar to Civ V, in appearance and some of the cores. However, there a number of departures, and it does an excellent job of highlighting the things that make it unique.
*Compared to Alpha Centauri, the narrative is rubbish, Not a sticking point for me personally, but a little disappointing none the less.
*Alien creature AI is phenominal, and I enjoy the fact that, unlike barbarians in previous CIV entries, they don't just murder-death-kill everything in their sights, unless provoked.
*There are a number of subtle touches to the game, such as leader appearance, that make the affinity system actually immersive.
*Health is a HELL of a thing to manage on higher difficulty settings. Jebus, Marty, and Bro-seph it's hard.
All in all, combat is good, balance is good, ultimate units made me feel like a god, I highly encourage picking up this game if you like turn-based strategy. But despite similarities, DO NOT go into it expecting CIV V or Alpha Centauri.

The short of it is:
Performance wise, I've heard there are some glitches, but never saw anything that stood out. I never had any real problems aside from the usually odd jump mechanics, which are better in this title than the title that came before black flag, and easy to adjust to anyhow. It plays smoothly, has decent enough graphics and unlimited baddies to wack if your feeling blood thirsty.
It can be a little grindy for some folks, but with so much to do, I didn't really notice. Also, no serious gamer is a fan of U-Play imo, but otherwise I really have no complaints. Even then, U-Play at least allows you to share rare finds with friends, which is an interesting feature.
Black flag is an atmospheric AC game that won't feel very linear, as there is tons to do and it makes use of it's rather open world quite well. I've had loads of fun with it and I highly reccomend it.
Long Verision:
Ever played an Assassin's creed game and got frustrated with with the limits of the asassin code? I did. Thank god for black flag!
AC games can be a hit or a miss, but even in the good ones sometimes you are left going "for crying out loud! I'm an assassin! What care I about the common folk?!" In older titles, it seems like for every enemy its okay to kill, there seems to be 20 civillans in the way and well, mistakes happen. Mistakes that would cost you because the commoners tend to get in the way.
Well, you might not get to stab a bunch of innocents in this verision of AC ethier.. but for once, you won't notice. Black flag is definitely a title for those who want to cut loose. The civillans rarely get in the way here. They are spaced out nicely while still feeling kind of like a dense population and there are baddies a' plenty.
The hero character of the hour, Edward, is also not your typical assassin from the order. He cares a whole lot less about all that honor talk, perferring the sound money makes. He has no qualms about killing for some coin and he gets away with it. Why? In AC:BF you play as a pirate who is pretending to be one of the assassins and therefore is not fully bound by the code.
And when I say your not bound, I mean by the assassin's code or anything else. Black flag isn't just about hunting that templar scum. Sure, it's in there, but as a sailor, you soon will find you have wide swaths of ocean to travel with plenty of side actitvies to do.. some of which are locked behind story missions, yes, but the game gets rolling quickly and everything is open fairly early on without ruining progression.
Want to upgrade your weapons? Go for it.. but you'll want to hunt that animal down to do it.. after all, you need it's skin.. and different animals means areas of travel and tactic. Want to hunt a whale? Well, are your harpoons up to snuff? What about your rowboat? For that matter, what about your main ship? Is it strong enough to face the might of the sea?
You do want to loot miltary ships of all that heavy gold, sugar, cannon shot and metal don't you? Or were you just after boarding the scuttled enemy ship so you could fight them hand to hand, walking amongst them like the god of death your feared to be? Well, then you better buy a decent sword and cloak to look the part!
And did I mention the songs your crew will sing as you sail the ocean, which you have to chase down to unlock? What about the forts you can wage battle against, or the ability to dock into a town and go hunting for soliders or raiding stock houses?
What about a trading mini-game that allows you to capture ships and make them work for you in real time? It's a good way to make some coin while your working that 9 to 5 job that paid for the game in the first place. But then, maybe your just a landlubber who likes to gamble on british checkers. Yeah, it has that too.
All the while, the usual AC goodies are there in the missions with a decent story and some fun sneakiness if you want it. Yes, if you want it.. most of the missions don't require you to be sneaky. It's a bonus, nothing more.. but might make things easier on you if your smart about it.  Black flag typically lets you play your way.
Plus.. did I mention treasure hunts? Because what is a pirate without some buried tresure maps?
On the modern day side of the story, your a promising intern at Astergo Entertainment. So when you want to step out of the animus (your simulator) and go back to  modern day, that's fine too. It has it's own little story to tell, which leads to several easter eggs from the older AC titles.. making black flag a great game to start on if your a little behind or even new to the assassin's creed games.

Blockstorm is an awesome fps voxel game that I definitely recommend. The environment is almost 100% destructable (with the exception of just a few specific types of blocks that need to be indestructable so that you aren't falling through the map or something annoying like that). There is a built-in editor at the main menu, enabling you to make your own maps and customize weapons and character skins. There is also player made skins you can find on the Steam community page for Blockstorm, available to individually "Subscribe" to, which then will be in your game ready to use (and furthermore, edit and customize with the editor if you desired). Blockstorm is an enjoyable game and worth paying for.
Compared to free-to-play voxel shooters like OpenSpades for example, this game feels, and in my opinion, is all-around better; which probably has a lot to do with Blockstorm being a game you have to purchase. The characters in this game also look much more unique, distinguishable, and detailed than any other voxel game I have come across. In addition to just having these unique asthethics, playing the game is also more enjoyable because of it. Seeing all the detailed and complex custom character skins other players are using when you are in a server, just adds to the experience and appeal. And of course, the extremely destructable environment will always add diversity to each match you play. Even not using your weapons and, for example, just building a defensive structure or using your shovel (which each player automatically has) to dig through blocks and tunnel around the map, is a rewarding experience all on it's own.

This review was done on game version 1.0.1
Ink is a short and simple platforming game, which relays on its ink spreading mechanic and a it's very colorful setting to standout from rest of the platformers.
A quick list of pros and cons:
+Charming colorful look of the game
+Thight controls
+Inking mechanic is nice and working well
+Overall solid gameplay
-Very short (I completed game in under 1-hour)
-Lack of enemy variance (3 differrent enemies)
-Not really that challenging game overall
-Boss fights are nothing special or memorable
-Lack of options and 30fps lock (Developer is currently working on that)
Core elements of the game are working well, which is the reason I recommend this game. Controls are tight and level desing is interesting enough to keep you playing throught the game. There are three bosses you have to defeat, but these boss fights aren't anything special or that memorable.
The world and atmosphere stays the same throughout the game. Calm ambient music and the same look of the world follows you the whole game. I would have loved to see a little more variance in music and atmosphere between the games three differrent worlds.
Ink doesn't have any kind of options or settings and is locked at 30fps, which is a shame, but the game is simple enough so there really isn't that big of a need for any of those. Developer is currently working on adding an option for keybindings and 60/30fps toggle so that is a big plus.
Overall I liked this short charming game, although it had potential to be much better. It is not that memorable or super unique, but the core gameplay is solid enough and it is pretty cheap, so I would recommend this for those who like simple platformers and don't mind the short length of this game.

Where do I start? I'll get the worst part about this game out of the way. The came is about 2-3 hours too long. There are a lot of parts to it that serve no purpose but to make the game seem longer. Now that's out of the way, I'd really recommend this game. The humor is great, it may come off as a shallow hack and slash game at first, but the lore and story is actually pretty decent, and I really love how they handled the ending of the game.
The game mechanics themselves are pretty awesome, and it is very satisfying to use the sword and the shotgun (which through uprgrades can fire 4 shots at once!). The characters are pretty well written. The only character arc that was left incomplete were those assassin sisters, I'd have loved to drive my sword through their annoying faces.
In conclusion, this game qualifies as a classic, it's a very "gamey" game, they haven't really tried anything new apart from the sword mechanics, the mission design is pretty mediocre and with the same tiring puzzles that require next to no brain use ( which means that they were not there to entertain, but to just increase the length of the game). I think this game would have been an all time classic with a lot more fans if it was about 7-8 hours now, so that would have been a breath of fresh air, but because the game is so long, the fresh air gets pretty stale. (Too much of a good thing, I guess).
At least you can never say you didn't get your money's worth!

I recommened Beyond Earth, but with the caveat of: Wait till it goes on sale. The basic core mechanics from Civ 5 are all there (construction, units, combat, diplomacy, trade, etc), however this is Civ 5 core without some of the strategic depth that game brought to the table (ex: no religion). It's been greatly simplified down (where are the charts?) and some aspects are broken right now (you can keep plugging away without any messages telling you that you are ready to win the game, you have to hunt through sub-menus to find those).
The biggest reason to wait is they took out every mechanic from all of the DLCs. So everything that already exists (advanced trade, additional content, better religion) all gone. I'm sure they'll all be added back as DLC.
So essentially it's Civ 5 with an alien theme and few extra mechanics. The research web isn't really that interesting since in order to take advantage of your affinty's full powers you need to research everywhere anyway. In the late game combat is essentially the same thing regardless of whta you look like. Evernote has the same basic units (couple of uniques, modified and some other bits).
So the game is fun, but I suggest you wait till either a lot of Workshop mods are published, or till the DLCs are out and discounted.

As others have said, it's a bit trimmed down.  Missing are luxury resources, any real interaction with "city-states", great persons of any sort.  What you have instead are interesting choices that actually affect how your buildings and units function (similar to the bonuses you'd get from religion or great works).  The game itself is very pretty so long as you don't mind the tilt-shift perspective.
On the negative side, the auto-unit-focus is still present and impossible to disable, so the game will wrench you away from whatever you were looking at to whatever it thinks you must witness.  There are some graphical glitches, especially enemy unit frames.  It is very difficult to tell what each unit actually is and which faction it belongs to (though there are the faction flags above them).
All in all I would say this game more immitates Civ 5 rather than improves on it.  It feels like a game inspired by it, not a true successor.  I'm sure it'll have lots of DLC to improve upon most of the above for your extra hard-earned dollars.

Truly, I like this game as An F2P, definately the best simulation that is free. but it does have it's flaws.
I'll be going into the Pros and Cons of RaceRoom Racing Experience by Sector3Studios.
The Pros of the game weren't exactly hard to guess, were they?
The First pro is definately that it is free, sure, there are clearly better ones than this one, but alot of the "Free" games that are better for me are mostly Demos of said racing games. It feels nice to have a simple racing simulation that is free to the community.
The Second Pro is clearly going to be all the different setups, there are so many options in the game, affecting the car and the game itself.
The Third will be all the different modes, you can play Time Trials, race against other players (Never done it, but I swear you can), and race against bots.
Now I will list the obvious cons of the game.
The First one is probably: You guessed it, the terrible Pricing and DLC Maps and vehicles.
While you still get all of the gamemodes, the DLC stuff pretty much destroys the entire purchase of the game, I have absolutely no need to complain over a free game, but having only 3 cars and 5 race tracks, seems pretty awful for the better free ones out there, like Victory: Age Of Racing, or Trackmania: Nations Forever. The DLC Pricing is terrible, costing a whopping $160.1 to unlock all DLC for the game, and wanna know the biggest cut out of that? The most expensive DLC pack, "Oh, you can get 4 cars and 7 maps!" for $35, seriously? $35 dollars for 4 cars and 7 maps, not to mention, A SINGLE DLC PACK. And all the others are far, far worse like the two 20-25 dollar DLC Packs, for more cars than the 35$ but with way less maps, so 7 maps are worth 10$ more?
The Second Con is how you have to create a RaceRoom Racing Experience account, sort of like Roblox, Trove, or Robocraft. Which would obviously create some problems for the game, an example would be servers crashing constantly, people leaving the game forever (Uninstalling) but had to go through the process.
the Second Con I can tie my experience with, I had to create an account on this, which was not hard at all, but then had to Confirm my E-mail after, which apparently was troubling for Sector3 since I had to resend the email 6 times before actually getting the Confirmation. a long time after, probably a couple months, I had sent a report to Sector3Studios through G-mail about how all servers were down during the summer, according to the response, from Hannes Wallstedt of Sector3 Studios, there is a period as to which the staff are away for the studio for weeks or months. Here is the text I can quote from Hannes' Response:
"Hello,
Very sorry for the late reply. We're returning from a period where many of our staff have been away from the studio.
The game has not been shut down. Are you still experiencing issues?
Best regards,
Hannes Wallstedt
Sector3 Studios"
This is definately the wrap, while I can still recommend the game for some people who are looking for a free racing simulation, this could be it, but it definately needs some more Renovating, Sector3.

For anyone totally new to any kind of CIV game who likes sc-fi themes, I can recommend it when it goes on a sale.
It is a very solid complex turn-based strategy game which offers different kind of winning conditions. If you don't read guides and etc, this game will offer you hundreds of hours of fun trying to find out what is best under different circumstances. You progress and keep progressing by learning from your mistakes on different difficulty levels. This stands apart from the sci-fi theme which you can like or, like me, dislike.
However...
Build on the CIV 5 engine and the 100 turns pre-release video you'd expect this game to be CIV 5 in a different theme. A reskined and renamed game. And pretty much that's it! It is easy to relate resources, textures and names back to what they are in CIV 5. Really a somewhat 1:1 copy. I wonder how long it takes before workshop items appear that restores all to what they are called and look like in CIV 5.
As BE is being sold as a stand alone game and not as an expansion package to CIV 5, you'd expect the game to progress in terms of bug fixes, system resource hungryness, gameplay and etc. But no progression on that.
Random events are back from CIV 4 (or was that a mod?) and is the only additional thing. You can choose between two benefitting event options and that is the only gameplay that has been added in comparison to CIV 5. They claim to have worked on the multiplayer part, but it functions just as bad as CIV 5. Resync in turn 1, free techs being given to your opponents...
Sad enough it is build on the same engine as CIV 5, but they removed the dx9 and touchscreen executable. Dx9 offered way less desync issues while playing multiplayer and the touchscreen executable in CIV 5 let you play the game without the game crashing while touching the screen.
On the other hand they added mantle support to improve multicore performance, but hell i prefer a better functional product above mantle or a dx12 low level kind of api support.
Looking further into the game there is some unbalance, unfinished work or too cheap reskinning ruining the gameplay.
Playing on marathon in turn 75 ~ 150 and I have to put my city production to work on energy or research as I already literally build every building that I researched. This is the first time in a CIV game that I can't build anything anymore in a city so early in the game. Ofcourse I can put effort in researching tech so I can build more buildings, but w00t so early in the game and nothing to do.
The cityproduction advisor tells me to build a building which improves the energy (gold for civ 5) output by +1 for each desert tile. But, I don't have a single desert tile anywhere near any of my cities so this building is going to cost me energy for each turn instead?
Than the developpers crafted some awesome tile add-on called miasma (a marsh for civ 5) which gives you negative health for each turn you stand on it. By researching the correct stuff you can regain health when standing on it. A very neath idea, BUT... they did not change the code of the AI players when attacking defending. The AI idles in miasma losing health or attacks you from out miama... If they declare war you can just do totally nothing and wait for them to die in miasma!
They should have made this an expansion to CIV 5, should have worked on the multiplayer desyncs and should have added mantle support to CIV 5 instead of this unlogic split. As a standalone BE is standing in the shade of CIV 5 as it offers less content, more unbalance and the very same bugs that CIV 5 today offers.

One of the most underrated racing games on steam.
After playing project cars for a while I wanted to have a step up in simulation and force feedback in racing games. Raceroom cars really drive much more intuitive and predictable in my opinion. The force feedback is really excellent and easy to setup. The car and track selection is top notch, but it will cost you a bit.
I think the fact that the game is "free to play" actually hurts the opinion of this game and perhaps also their sales. The publisher has opted for a "microtransaction" system where you buy cars and tracks individually or in groups. What a lot of people will not know is that you can buy everything for about €65.- But you will have to buy VRP from the site
and with that ingame currency you can then buy the premium package (or if you want to safe some VRP buy the starter pack first and then premium). You then still have left a little VRP to buy future content. You will not have a season pass, instead you will buy all the content that is currently available.
This convoluted / confusing system probably scares away quite some customers and hopefully eventually they will go to a different approach.
There are many different car classes available including: WTCC / DTM / GT2 / GT3 / GTO / group 5 / GTX. Within each class there are many cars available to have some variability on the grids. Most popular classes are probably GT3 / Group 5 and the '92 DTM cars, but since I don't play multiplayer I can't vouch for how much they are played online.
The AI in this game is quite good, despite being a bit overaggressive. It really is nice to see cars have actual battles and fight for their places. The AI does not divebomb you like they do in project cars, but if you are a bit slower than them they do have a tendency to touch your rear, which can be quite frustrating and it is advised to practice with AI and set the difficulty accordingly. There is also an automatic difficulty setting, but you will need to do a lot of training with AI before this works well and you will have to do this separately for each class, making it a pain. I typically test the AI and adjust the difficulty myself.
There are unfortunately no day / night transitions and there is no weather. All this is promised to come when the game will go to the unreal engine, but this will take a long time, probably not earlier then late 2018. Now you only have 5 different time settings in the day which can be chosen by you or random.
What really sets this game apart from games like RF2 / AC / Pcars is the sound design. This game is the benchmark in great sound for racing games. Hitting the kerbs, changing gears, roaring engines, all sounds absolutely amazing. I urge you to watch gameplay footage of the Ford Zakspeed Capri on youtube. Although it was pretty good in Pcars, Raceroom really sets the bar very high. For me personally immersion is what matters most and sound is a very important aspect of that. Assetto Corsa or Rfactor 2 are said to have better physics, but since I will not be able to judge this, for me what is most important is how believable the cars feel and sound to me to make it feel realistic.
Recently I purchased an Oculus Rift and tried the game in VR. This really works very well, but there are still some issues. The menus are a bit frustrating to navigate, since I still use the mouse for this. Navigating the menu with my T300 does not work well enough. However, the racing itself works great! With some supersampling (>1.5) the game looks great and performs well on my 980 card. However, you will need ASW activated to achieve constant smooth gameplay, since it is very difficult to keep stable 90fps in VR. If you hate ASW artifacts, then you really need a 1080Ti to have ok settings with high enough framerate and preferably a skylake or newer processor is required. My i5 2500k @4.8 manages quite well with ASW enabled though.
The game might not be as polished as Project Cars, but it is an absolute dream to drive cars in this game. With a nice setup with a play seat + steering wheel + VR the immersion is fenomenale. It is unfortunate that so may people here on steam with <1 hour gameplay rate this game negatively, because given some time with setting everything up and buying some packs the game is really, really worth it!

Unfortunately the middling-to-negative isndustry review of Civ:BE should be taken on board; most of the design decisions are more miss than it, for me at least.
# Tech web #
Quite awful; not because it is confusing (though it is) as techs can be learned, but because BE techs are so very soul-less and homogenous.
Without the anchor of real-world context, 99% of the web is just technobabble unlocking equally soul-less and homogenous build options or passives.
By late-game I was developing & stealing technologies at a rate of knots, but honestly it wasn't even worth the effort looking them up - just checked to see if a new build option appeared in my capital.
Future Civ verdict: Dear goodness no!
# Build options & wonders #
Swing & a miss here for the above mentioned homogeny, but also functionally the standard is extremely low - most the building never get beyond the level of Civ starter buildings (1 upkeep for 1-2 of whatever), and a fair few are stinkers relating to +1 for whatever rare resource tile you might have 1 of in your civilization.
Wonders are bottom of the barrel stuff even allowing for tourism, religion, United Nations & other civ mechanics being stripped away; expect a lot +1 culture and a 5% military buff, often without any kind of accompanying 'cinematic'.
What is fun is the introduction of "quest decisions", which basically mean a few turns after you construct the first of each building you get the choose between 2 perks; most are incredible snoresome (building produces +1 whatever), but there are a few gems e.g. choosing between expanding alien-repelling-effect to 3 squares from your cities or making your trade caravans alien-immune.
Future Civ verdict: "quest decisions" would be very welcome.
# Geography & aliens #
I'm afraid the geography is a big disappointment, beyond the initial 'headstart options' (see coasts, advanced resources, choose staring tile); resources aren't intuitive or interesting, there's far too many usueless valleys (aka mountains), and ocean tiles are complete non-entities in BE...
Since you don't explore to actually meet other civilizations/city-states, there's only one ship unit and there're barely any ocean tile resources nor (crucially) improvements oceans are dead tiles compared to land tiles and the various things that can pop up on them throughout the game.
The aliens are initially fairly interesting, but like miasma you can outclass them quite soon (or just stand on an alien repellant tile and gunt hem down with impunity) and they serve little purpose beyond XP fodder for your military.
You can develop alien themed units with sufficient Harmony, but they are nothing special and it's still best to simply eradicate wild aliens to free up your land.
Future Civ verdict: Don't see anything to take away from this, though if subbed beasts for aliens in a prehistoric Civ age it could be fun!
# Affinities & culture trees #
Affinities seem to be an attempt to reinject some of the more interesting effects that buildings or wonders would normally supply in Civ, and they are fairly fun but let-down by the fact that whatever tech you pick & once you begin stealing technologies (which is so easy you should!) all your affinities will be rising rapidly anyway.
In my latest go I went pure Purity in all my decisions but am right now sitting on 7 Purity, 4 Harmony & 4 Supremacy anyway because affinity points are thrown at you regardless.
Culture trees are a bit regressed, since you have them all available at once and can reach the 'top' unlocks in no time at all - a lot of blah +1's, military +5's and 10% health/happiness bonuses (ooh; +1.7 science - you're spoiling us!).
The slightly more substantial bonuses are for putting x points into a particular tree or tier, which relegates actual upgrades to the filler portion.
Personally I did not find either mechanic allowed me to imagine any kind of 'feel' to my own civilization; you're pretty much always going to be an empire human-hybrid-cyborgs with a taste for farming, art & high-powered laser-cannons.
Future Civ verdict: Please no - would be a tremendous step back, in this form at least.
# World building #
Far too sparse to be interesting; you basically know nothing about your own civilizations leader but 4 lines on the load screen, and the only character other leaders have is in their oft-repeated greeting phrase.
Some of the technologies have characterful and/or amusing intro lines (e.g. the internet "was the sieve of human stupidity"), but after a while they bland together because there's only so many ways to comment on a dozen varieties of bio[whatever] - wonders have less lore, and many have no pop-up what-so-ever.
The BE planet itself is uniformly drab, and you'll see all breeds of alien in short order - anything that looks at all interesting (e.g. floating rocks or hers of not-troop aliens) will be +1 whatever on a tile and go completelty uncommented on in-game, so hard to get invested in.
Future Civ verdict: Thankfully shouldn't be an issue, since Civ has it's own setting.
# Overall verdict #
It's not a badly constructed game (though there are some cut corners e.g. wonders, unit upgrade descriptions), but it has most the parts of a Civilization game with little of the character or soul.
A reasonable way to pass the hours, but I do regret pre-ordering.

Originally, I gave this game a negative review due to the sheer awfulness of the opening experience.  You buy a game for which you exceed recommended specs, you expect it to run well out of the box.  After playing for a while, I'm changing this review to a positive one with caveats.  Everyone's talking about port quality, so let's get that out of the way first:
PORT QUALITY:  It's pretty obvious that Square Enix is just getting back into the PC market- out of the box, this port is *dreadful*.  You're going to have to tweak settings for this game on your graphics card in order to get it to run well, and if you have a minimum spec computer, you should probably pass on this game entirely.  You'll also want to use a controller or VJoy- the game checks constantly to see if there's a controller plugged in otherwise, which will kill your frame rate.  Settings for this game reset every time I open it, and before loading I have to manually select Controller Input from the menu.  There are no in-game graphics settings, but it's not the end of the world- the "omg 720 peeeeee" people seem to have been expecting a complete remaster of the game for their $16.  If it's important to you, get GeDoSaTo.
GAMEPLAY:  It took Square 20 years, but they *finally* nailed the ATB system.  I've never been a fan of the gameplay systems which use the ability to navigate menus quickly as a core game skill.  FFXIII requires you to make decisions under time pressure, such as which Paradigm to pick and when you should eschew the Auto-Battle command for manual input of abilities, but there is never a point where you have to dive three menus deep to find the particular item you're looking for.  Your decisions are always within a couple of button presses away, making the core skill the ability to make good decisions in a quick fashion.  FFXIII may have the best battle system yet in the Final Fantasy series.
One negative is the insane degree of linearity.  You spend the first thirty hours of this game running down hallways.  Want to get off the hallway?  Run into a short cranny, fight the optional encounter, pick up a treasure chest and get back on it.  It's something I hated about FFX, and it's something I hate about FFXIII.
PLOT:  I'm firmly convinced that most of the people who have reviewed the plot in this game played for five hours before forming their opinion.  One of the frequent comments you'll hear is about how Lightning is an emotionless character trying to act cool, which.... what?  She drops that schtick during the third chapter.  Perhaps people were expecting an overly gushy character like Luna, but I rather prefer strong female characters who aren't written as stereotypical females.  The same goes with comments as to how confusing the plot is, and the only way I could understand that is if people skipped all the cutscenes and ignored the Datalog.  If there's anything that's confusing, it's the supporting characters who get little screen time, such as Cid Raines, Jihl Nabaat, and Yaag Rosch; without reading the Datalog, you will have little idea who these characters are or what their role in the story is.  Try not to build an impression of the plot for this game through the first hour of gameplay, because there is some absolutely dreadful dialog going on there.
GRAPHICS/MUSIC:  You expect awesome graphics and a stellar soundtrack from any FF game, and FFXIII delivers.  I'm not talking about pixel count (and if that's more important to you than game experience, why do you play games anyways?), I'm talking about how graphics/soundtrack work to serve the story.  Locations aren't pretty for the sake of being pretty; in each chapter, the scenery serves the emotional context of the plot.
If you do buy this game, you're going to have to do some work with your graphics settings to run it the way it was intended, but you'll ultimately be rewarded with a very positive experience.

Like the earlier installments of Hitman, Abosolution is a fantastic stealth sandbox. Where many stealth action games reward purely the quick and silent kills, the Hitman series has rewarded players for sitting and watching as much as quickly killing things and Absolution is no exception.
The difficulty is far more forgiving than the earlier games allowing players who wish to just blow through the story or experiment with the environment can do so with ease on the easiest difficulty and those who seek perfection can do so on the higher difficulties.
Story is not the strong point in this game, rather the interesting environmental kills setting up a cascade of death and watching it unfold without having to pull the trigger yourself. Or for those who like to get their hands dirty, weaving in and out of the patrolling guards or even going guns-a-blazing. The Red Dead Revolver like deadeye mechanic works well with gunplay and for the stealthy, the instinct system allows for some improvised stealthing and adds a lot to the feel of being a Hitman.
There is a slew of funny and/or interesting dialogue for those patient enough to hide in the shadows eavesdropping on conversations and that's where a lot of the content is. Sadly those who wish to blow through the main story alone will likely miss out on a lot of the often off the beaten road gems.
This is a game for gamers who have the patience to sit and watch every once in a while, experiment, and replay levels to get the most out of it. Those looking for a strong main story will be disappointed.
Well worth giving it a go if you have the patience.

I first spotted Tick Tock Isle on Greenlight, and because it looked so cute, charming, and nostalgic, I supported it.
And I'm glad I did because the game has turned out to be much more than I had originally anticipated!
~.~.~.~.~.~.
+ Pros:
*Pretty environments, cute character graphics
*Relaxing soundtrack
*Short and sweet story
(Up to 1-3 hours gameplay, great for casual play)
*Simple control scheme
(Arrow keys, Enter, and Esc)
*Low price
*Replayability
(There's quite a bit to do, some of it is optional, so there's still enough to explore and enjoy)
- Cons:
*Platformer puzzle difficulty
(In my opinion, the two last platformer stages - in the guise of children's imaginary forts - were rather frustrating, and the one-hit death felt unfair; there should've been a health bar. But, it's a small aspect)
*Fixed window mode
(It's better to play in window mode since all the graphics are sharper and nothing is cut off at the edges. But, when attempting full-screen by pressing Alt+Enter, the graphics were a bit blurry and at least the main menu was out of focus)
*Continuity itch
(It's a sweet, short, standalone game. But, there are a few aspects left unexplained, and it's such an enjoyable setting that I'd be very open to playing future entries if the developers decide to turn it into a series. Some may feel that 'continuity itch' in the end.)
~.~.~.~.~.~.
I really enjoyed the colorful pixel art (Unlike some other indie games, the colors aren't too bright or loud, they're very even), the relaxing soundtrack (flutes in an island setting, along with telltale tick-tock sounds are very fitting), and the endearing characters - each with their own personality and brief backstory - that change over time the more you interact with them in the hopes of improving their futures.
In a way, I guess it could be compared to classic adventure games like Monkey Island meets Back To The Future, it was a delightful and fun experience!
I'm actually a little saddened that it wasn't a little longer, because I wanted to keep exploring and know more about the characters - especially Strike, our time traveler, I'd like to know more about him and his world.
Overall, it's a charming game and it's priced at an incredible bargain, it's a win-win!

That said the game doesn't have the largest player base anymore (only a few hundred people at a time now a days) and there are some noteworthy issues with it.
Rating of IW:
Mechanics: 9.5/10 (and I don't think I'd give anything a 10)
Strategic Depth: 9.5/10
Balance: 6 (it's not horrible and the margin by which it tends to favor certain builds isn't actually that big. But the meta has felt pretty similar for a long time).
Welcoming to new players: Game 1/10; Community 7-8/10. This game takes a lot of time to really get into. It's a great game but expect to put many hours into it to get a feel for the mechanics, tricks, meta, etc. (To give a rough idea I'd say you need to spend about 20hours on this game just to get a decent feel of it).
Developer Responsiveness: 6/10
Bugs: 5/10 (They aren't horrible, you can still play the game and most often don't run into them, but do expect to lose matches occasionally (around 1 in 50?) due to bugs that aren't going away anytime soon).
F2P: 9.5/10
So with regards to the mechanics/strategy. This game uses simultaneous turns and resources automatically increase up to 10. The resources thing is nice (particularly if you are coming from magic, no getting land sc***ed or mana glut) but it's really the simultaneous turns that make this game stand out. Both players que there turns at the same time, on a given turn one player has priority and priority switches player each turn. The order of play is as follows: upkeep and comes into play effects, premeptive abilities, regular abilities, attacking and the other player defending (each of those resolves for the player with priority and then the other player and each player gets to que the order in which their cards happen within those phases) - although it's a lot more streamline when playing it than what I just described sounds.
Since both players turns are qued at the same time and resolve without either player being able to react to them this introduces a lot of bluffing into the game. For example "Which zone is this character going to be in? One were they can attack or defend or back in support where they are safer from my opponents removal cards?" A lot of the game has to do with correctly and consistently anticipating your opponents actions and winning a game has as much to do with deck construction as it does with accurately predicting your opponent (depending on the match the second one of these can be more important.. especially in draft formats).
Cards: Cards are quite diverse and comprable to magic the gather in terms of the range of their mechanics. (Noting that magic has something like 20 years on this game, so more like magic back in the mercadian masques block).
Welcoming to new players: The community is pretty friendly and will generally be pretty nice to players (well, maybe not if a player is complaining to them about something that they aren't really the person it should be taken up with, but in general). That said the campaign and challenges (a.k.a. tutorial/single player) is pretty short and it takes a very long time to build up ones card pool. So starting out you will probably lose a lot. Try rift runs because at least then the card pool is statistically the same for you and your opponent, but you won't have the experience with the game that they do and still don't expect to win that much for awhile. Harsh I know, and lots of players (both new and old) have given feedback on how to improve that aspect but,
Developer Responsiveness: This is a game by a small indie company. They have a community manager and player support person (a different person for each of those). Both of those people are pretty on top of it and I do feel like the developers work pretty hard on the game behind the scenes. Also generally they do actually look at player feedback and address it... eventually. I've made several different suggestions (on rewording particular cards, new card ideas and various other things) as I've played the game and I've usually seen something addressing what I've mentioned (text being fixed to make it more clear, cards to fit slots that certain factions were lacking, etc). That said don't expect a quick response to anything that requires input on the devs side of things. My general feeling is that between coming up with new cards and fixing stuff that their small dev team is a bit overwhelmed and while they will get to stuff eventually it might take a few months - really pressing stuff is faster, but don't be surprised if this thing you feel like is really pressing isn't pressing enough to get addressed quickly.
Bugs: The game is peer to peer, meaning that desyncs will happen and when they happen lots of things will get screwed up and sometimes the match will just freeze (in game this is refered to as the endless turn bug/glitch). Most often this doesn't happen, but expect it to happen about 1/50 matches on average and when it does happen expect it to either cost you or your opponent the game. This might eventually get fixed, but from the communty managers responses/how long people have been complaining about it, I wouldn't expect it to happen anytime soon (maybe in a couple of years?).
That aside the game isn't that buggy, usually there are a few issues after a patch but they tend to get resolved within a few weeks and aren't too major (things doing a little bit different things than what the cards say, UI scrolling being a little off, etc).
F2P (free to play): You get IP (in game currency for playing dependent upon how long you play (ip gain for a match caps at 5minutes into the match)) and eventhing in the game can be bought using IP. Also IP works out to being something like $3-4/hour in terms of spending real money on packs. Which is a pretty good rate considering that your getting that for just playing the game. That said, when starting out you will run into people who seem to have all the cards and be able to do these decks that you don't feel like you'll ever have the cards for. In general those people have been playing for a long time. It requires a lot of time and/or money in order to get a good card pool and whether or not the person has been spending money or not if they have a good card pool they have probably played for quite some time (notice my almost 1300hours on the game and I didn't start until this game was advertized on steam). The game does favor more experienced players, honestly less in the card pool issue (since there is a built in draft format that is a lot of fun and honestly better than ranked play, at least in my opininon), more in the fact that it's a deep strategy game and it takes time to learn how to play and then a lot more time to learn how to play well.
Overall it's a great game, with some notable drawbacks, but I'd still strongly encourage checking it out if you have time. It's more one of those games to play for awhile, get a good feel for and then come back to it now and then (I strongly encourage long breaks from it when you get bored with it).

Read this review first. Also, I started playing this game two weeks ago from the post date of 8/11/15, so everything I'm saying is current.
This. Game. Is. *Awesome*.
I played Magic The Gathering my entire childhood, MTG Online, WoW TCG, Hearthstone, and Hex, and they all pale in comparison. I've heard nonsense in these reviews ranging from matchmaking issues to.... "ths game sux cuz not nuff dbl xp wkends".... (seriously? lol)
At the end of the day, TCG's (or CCG's *shrug*) are *all* about the cards, and mechanics of the game. This game is So much more fun, complex, and strategic than *any* other game in the genre, bar none. Anyone who tells you differently is lying, an idiot, or rage-quit because they lost their first battle and got angwy.
I'm not just some fanboy. There are a couple of glitches, and from what I hear, there could be a better matchmaking system I guess (though I find I win a completely reasonable amount of matches, regardless of being new). However, the game itself just can't be beat. Try playing this game for a few days and going back to Hearthstone. Go ahead, I just did it. I was literally *bored* to tears. It doesn't have one tenth the depth or strategy that Infinity Wars has. It's just a fact, guys.
The cards are *beautiful*, *all of them are animated*, and...you...can... *trade* with your friends... (or enemies, or strangers... whatever). For those of you who have actually played other online TCG's, I'm sure you can appreciate putting the 'T' back into the acronym. I don't know about you guys, but that was half of what it was about when I was a kid.
There are *8* incredibly distinct and well-designed factions to choose from, each with their own goals, combos and strategies that make sense, and carry a personality of their own. You can *combine* them into a deck of your choosing, and the combinations really let your own deck designs shine.
The game has 4 zones during play. One of which is the 'Commander' zone, which is a set of 3 characters of your choosing that start on the board from turn 1. While I, myself, found it a bit 'too much' when i first started, it's come to be one of the most amazing and distinguishing mechanics this game has to offer, bringing a new level of customization and gauranteed strategy to your deck.
Don't listen to the nay-sayers. If you're here on this page because you're bored of what little Hearthstone has to offer, download this, and thank me later.

An overall neat and clever game that hits a few rough patches along the way. The presentation is fantastic; the art and the music are great, the way the story is told works effectively enough as well. The puzzles are generally very well crafted though there is the occasional slip into tedium, but not very often, though often enough to be noticeable. The puzzles never really repeat themselves over the 3-4 hours it takes to complete the main game, so there's plenty of variety even if the end result is a tad on the short side. I also wish there was a bit better way to navigate around the map, as the central tower helps but can still result in a fair bit of time spent getting back to some rooms when looking for the secrets. The secrets themselves are also generally well-handled, never overly challenging though a few of them rely on luck due to the physics.
If I had to call out one especially weak part of the game though, it's certainly the boss fights. They're not really that hard, no, but the problem is that you end up dying repeatedly trying to learn what all the boss does, because if you don't know what's coming often you won't have the time to react. The final boss is probably the only exception to this but replaces this instead with tedium; one phase is hard to figure out but trivial once you know what to do; one phase basically exists to kill time with attacks that are incredibly easy to dodge; and one phase can get you stuck in an impossible situation the third time it repeats if you're unlucky enough. The flaws of the game aren't enough to bring it down entirely as the majority of the game is quite an enjoyable experience, but it does knock the game down in my favor a small degree. Still, pretty good game, maybe a bit short for the price tag though I can't truly be the judge of that.

I'm sure there's nothing I can say that hasn't already been said, but I'll throw a few more words of praise on the pile.
Short version: Metroidvania Buge Souls
Longer: Incredibly well-designed, interconnected world that drips with atmosphere that is usually somber, often ominous, and always beautiful. That isn't to say that there aren't plenty of lighter moments, but the levity is provided most often by the charming art style, varied cast, and tremendous soundtrack. Still, it feels first and foremost like a delve into darkness, and the Knight's progression reflects that very well, both in setting and in available abilities. And boy are there plenty of abilities to find. And yet, they all feel useful and usable in an extremely tight and fluid way that almost exclusively eases navigation of the many treacherous zones. Actually, 'ease' probably isn't a word you want to associate with this game. It's not shy about ramping up the difficulty in the later sections, and some of the optional boss fights had me yelling some choice obscenities after my 12th attempt. That's kind of the beauty of it, though, because practice will generally get you through it and leave you feeling accomplished. Very much like the Souls games in that way.
Flaws?... I, um, honestly am having a hard time coming up with any. Maybe you'll get tired of trekking across the map to get to the more isolated areas? That's probably about it. And even those treks would often yield some secret item or area that I had missed on a previous pass.
