Alright, bought it and beat it in a comfortable single sitting. The game is very short. It will probably take an hour and a half to beat even with finding most of the collectibles. The game controls fairly close to Super Meat Boy with double jumps and wall clinging, except in this game your character has a bit less inertia/accelerates quicker and ungrips walls faster if you hold off of them. The jumping is also a bit quicker. Meat Boy gets lots of air time but ink-square falls pretty quickly. Ink also has a double jump which allows you to change your velocity much more than just holding a direction. It's all a bit less easy to control than Meat Boy, but it is serviceable. The visuals were nice. All very clean and colorful, and it is fun to see layers and layers of ink cover the environment. All the characters are basic geometric shapes such as square, triangles, and circles, but they fit the aesthetic fine. The sound is super basic, and the soundtrack wasn't memorable, but I didn't tire of it (or notice it at all really).
For me the biggest issue of the game is that the whole paint the level mechanic really doesn't matter very much. Every double jump makes Ink-square "spit" ink drops all around him, blotting bits of obstacles all around him. I feel this mechanic is supposed to be more interesting than it actually is. Each level you can't see any ground except what you're standing on and areas with enemies (which also leak ink onto the environment), but after a few double jumps your path is clear. When I got to a new level I would just try to complete it blind which do to the predictable placement of ground isn't very difficult to do. As I went through I'd cover large swaths of the stage in one life so by the time I died it pretty much became just another platformer. Your paint stays after each death (in fact, dying makes a huge splatter all around you to cover objects) so just throwing yourself around a few lives will almost completely paint the level. Sadly, by the third act of the game, the developer also started running out of ideas it seemed. Most levels at that point put the whole challenge on dodging little homing projectiles like those annoying homing monsters in the Hell part of Super Meat Boy. They weren't fun in that game either. All stages are relatively small, either confined to a small square space or presented in a line. I think this is what made the ink mechanic fall apart a bit. Even without being able to see anything you know where you're supposed to go. Being able to grip walls makes it even easier to blindly barrel through levels since if you don't make a jump (because you can't see it!) you'll probably just stick to the wall of the platform anyway.
There's also collectibles you can find by squirting ink in inconspicuous and out of the way portions of some levels. I got around 12 out of 20 on my first run, so they are at least decently hidden and some require you to go off the main path to find them. The other part of the game were the 3 boss fights. They kind of reminded me of Super Mario Brothers boss fights where they basically amount to dodging an attack and jumping on its head a few times, but they were at least well designed. They are all kind of pretty looking and the last one was particularly cool (he's in the trailer if you look).
Overall, it was okay. It's a platformer and it's cheap. I had fun.

Strata, plural for
, is a Latin word which means layers. Its game machanics are very simple. A block can only be crossed twice, from the diagonal left and the diagonal right. However, only the second line that crosses which matches the colour of the block is valid. You just need to know which block comes first.
If you haven't played Lyne (which deals with patterns) I recommend that you do that first, as a warmup, because this game takes another step further (deals with colours). It should not be rushed, just take your time.
Difficulty is determined by the types of colors and the size of the grid (from 2X2 to 6X6). In 2X2 systems it is fairly easy to predict the flow, and if you gained more experience through the game, you will notice there is an algorithm to the solutions, but from 5X5 onwards it will twist your mind a lot. At that point it was literally impossible for me to figure out which goes first without using the hints as the sequence is too complex.
However, there are some bugs which the developer is not around to fix anymore, but it's easily fixed by quitting the game.

After finally beating this game after playing it for over 20 hours, I feel it is necessary to update this review.
I originally gave it a negative review, mainly due to the jump frustrations found early in the game. After grinding through the game, I will change my review from negative to positive, but just barely.
The story is interesting, the puzzles are very creative. The humor is appreciated for a chuckle here or there. Overall, with one exception, this game is excellent.
The one exception, is 'almost' a deal breaker. The jump frustrations. I enjoy a good puzzle game, and finding out how to solve a problem is very rewarding. I do not mind making the puzzles more difficult to solve, but the jump frustrations almost made me quit, 100x over. Some puzzles are very long, and if you mistime or miss a single jump, you have to start all over. I would spend literally hundreds of tries on certain rescue or escape missions.
I kept dying, and dying, and dying. I died some more. But I fought through and told myself, I just need to beat the level once. And I did.
All of this could have been avoided if the developer added a quicksave feature. This feature can be enabled for adventure mode only, and would help a lot of players. In fact, with a quicksave feature, I would not even mind the jump frustrations since I just need to do it once.
The main difficulty of this game is not necessarily the puzzles, although some are very creative and difficult, but the perfect jumps requirement. This is a very challenging game, and should have been given a quicksave feature.
Original Review:
I really had high hopes for this game. I am a huge fan of puzzles games, from Portal, to Talos Principle, to Swapper, to the Turing Test. I was able to solve all those puzzles, including some of the most difficult star ones from Talos. I also enjoy platformers, so I thought, this must be a great game for me.
Unfortunately, after giving it a fair shot, it just is not so. The puzzles are interesting, and they alone would have captured my interest. However, the frustrating controls are irredeemable.  You touch lava in the slightest, you die. You touch an ice platform, you slide off and end up in lava. You cannot see further ahead, so you end up having to jump (and die) just to figure out what is beyond the screen.
This is not a puzzle game, but more of a jump frustration game. If the game was based more on puzzles, instead of skill jumps, I would have wholeheartedly endorsed it.

Beyond Earth is a game that can and will be compared to both Civ 5 before it and Alpha Centauri, being its "spiritual sucessor" or whatever.
Compared to both of them, this game is trash.
It plays more like a vanilla Civ 5 with a stripped down tech tree and half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥new features.
The tech "web" is still so small that you end up researching the same things as everyone else, just in a different order.
The lack of specific units, buildings, or truly lasting bonuses for sponsors make every leader play even more similar than they did in Civ 5, instead of having the more varied gameplay options of AC.
To be honest, the only things this shares with AC are basic themes of landing on a planet with modern technology (hey you can do that with modded Civ 5) and having a bad UI for 2014. Civ 5 + G&K + BNW had a good UI, but despite recylcing the same engine and gameplay they couldnt just make everything neon blue squares, no, they had to throw everything all around the screen and make you hunt for all the buttons and waste time constantly moving the mouse around to do basic things like activating a production queue.
Back to the leaders, they're so similar they're forgettable. Nothing in this game ever refers to factions by the faction names, they always use the leaders' names, which, due to he fact they're forgettable; and they dont even have their own unique VOICES; I found myself declining invitations to wars not because I wanted peace but because I had no clue who "Elonda" or whatever was." And this is made even worse by the fact there's only 8 of them in the base game! Eight! I know SMAC didnt have dozens of leaders but they were all unique and had different gameplay based on separate ideologies. Here the Ideologies are instead handed out as "be Hitler, be robo-Hitler, or be space hippie."
And then there are the gameplay issues. Health (happiness with another name) is the real difficulty. 150 turns in on an easier difficulty and you'll still have trouble staying positive. And then the only real solution to this is the completely broken virtue (social policy) available to people who main the Industry (Currency+Production) line.
The Affinities (Gameplay-based ideologies) are also way too open. You can get the unique units of all of them in the same game, again being dependent on the fact the tech tree is so small you end up researching techs that give you exp for different affinites regardless.
Trade is broken, the spy program should just be wiped entirely due to the horrible "chaos" mechanic that requires you to keep doing actions over and over to destablize a city in order to do something better.
Not only that but the actions they do are absurd and contribute way too much to gameplay instead of just being a passive hand of guidance that interferes once a blue moon instead of stealing a new tech from Indian space hippie chick every 20 turns.
TL;DR= This is more like an "overhaul mod" for Civ 5 or a beta version of an actual game.

So I can't say I'm one of those hardcore Civ players who has been around since the beginning. My major experience with civ was Civ 5. I love Civ 5, but even when Civ 5 came out it lacked a lot of things. After sitting through several long games now of Beyond Earth, I can say with certainty this game is incomplete, and I'm not really looking forward to the inevitable DLC that goes back and adds in the things that should've been part of the core experience.
I hear a lot of 'it's just a reskin of Civ5' and honestly I wish this were true. It's not even that. There are only 8 civs and they are all one incredibly pointless decision away from being the same thing.
- Unique civs gone.
- Religion, gone.
- Tourism, gone.
- Artifacts, gone.
- City states, gone.
- Artwork throughout the game is gone, replaced by crude sketchy designs for wonders and single color icons for units.
- The UI is blocky, basic, and for many people difficult to see.
- All that great themed music you loved about your favorite civ, gone!
Literally on every possible level from gameplay to graphics to sound this game has absolutely nothing on it's predecessor, but I don't want you all thinking I'm living in the past though comparing this to what Civ5 had and this doesn't though. It's time to discuss the new things!
- barbarians (aliens) which can randomly instantly kill units with no warning
- tech scattered randomly about a web instead of organized in a tree
- nearly invisible death clouds on random tiles
Well... that's about it. Hey did you notice how I used random there in each one? Cause random lack of control = fun right? The developers who came up with this need to take a toboggan down a rocky cliff and we'll see how much random fun they have on each random rock.
Don't buy this now, wait until the DLC is out and it's being offered as a 'game of the year edition' on some Steam sale.

I want to start off by Saying this is a civilization game. Of course there is some fun to be had here. I also want to say that this is a rather long post. For that i'm sorry so i'll give a brief verdict to those who want to do the quick read
(Abstract: game has a great design and intriguing basis to start a civilization game. Ultimately its held back by its lack of substance and civ diversity. Meaning..... Low replay value in my opinion. )
I also want to say that this is not CIV 5! i'm sick of seeing it.....yes it used the predecessors engine, but other than that this is clearly a different game.
I've been a long-time fan of the series and there have been some high and lows along the way...some would argue that civ 5 was a major step back from 4, others enjoyed the change. Sadly in the case of beyond earth I'm disappointed
I wanted to love this game; I think it has a fantastic basis to grow into something that is wonderful and unique on its own.
The game has been given a fantastic starting narrative and the alien planet is intriguing, I found myself deeply engrossed in this aliend worlds discovery.... however thats where my wonder stopped.
What unfortunately holds this game back is its lack of substance and diversity.  The joy of researching that new unit to lay waste to your enemies is sadly stripped away as your units upgrade over time. They upgrade depending upon what affinity you choose to follow.
The tech web is bland and the UI is horrid. When unlocking a new tech I didnt always know what was unlocked as units, buildings, and wonders are displayed by foreign symbols which don’t differentiate one from the other on quick glance.
Civs tend to play more or less the exact same as each other as there are no unique buildings or units..... yay???? Whose idea was that?
Currency has simply been replaced by energy.....
And then theirs health
I found Civ 5's most irritating feature was its hugely penalising happiness mechanic which prevented massive growth of civilizations. However in that game it could be curbed by bringing in luxury resources to make your population happy.
In this game they have imported the exact same flawed mechanic from its predecessor and called it "Health." your Civs health will steadily decline as your citys grow and expand, to curb this effect there are no longer luxury resources to make people happy. Instead the only way to keep those Civs happy is to invest heavily in Virtues (Like social policies) that grant your Civ health bonuses or build health producing buildings...... so guess what I was building most of the time yes even before important economic and buildings and defences.
I suppose the alternative would have been to stay small and only have 3-4 cities....... once again yay????
One quick rant on diplomacy thanks for adding favours that’s a really neat new feature. Except well what do i need them for?  Without the need to trade for luxury resources, and since no research agreements are available anymore,  truth be told what do I need other civs for then.  Really because well they don’t have anything i'll ever need or want apart from their land.  Has it been reduced to this? Oh and covert ops.....cool.......at first.....except my agent has been caught 3 times.....and no diplomatic fall out????? is that working correctly. Just checking so no incentive to not steal research from my best ally.....cool....steal away
I know I’m carrying on so I’m going to wrap this up. I really really wanted to like this game. Civilization is one of my all-time favourite franchises, however their just isn’t a whole lot of substance here to keep me interested for those hundreds and thousands of hours I would normally pour into a game like this. And that’s so disappointing...
I’m really surprised that Firaxis would release this game so "naked"...then again I guess it’s the way of modern games to ship incomplete and make you pay through the nose for those necessary "expansions" that actually make the game interesting and playable.

I recommend this for its unique elements, story, and combat. I played it for over 40 hours, and could probably play it for another 20-30 without seeing everything. Totally worth the price, sale or not.
This game took me by surprize. There is a depth to character creation, and how your character fits into the story. Fetch quests are pretty much non-existant as it will give you the option to travel instantly in dialog very often. (wish more games would do that)
Much of the game can be played WITHOUT COMBAT, if you like that kind of thing, and build your character right. But combat can be very fun, even if the randomness can sometimes be aggrevating. Thankfully, there is a save/load feature that is pretty quick if something really bad happens. I found myself using it a lot just to experiement with various choices (do I let someone die or do I save them) both in and out of combat.
PROS:
Complex characters and story (most things have prerequisite skills or attributes)
Simple character building with enough options to warrant replays
Fast and convenient quick save and quick load
Good UI
Unique combat (some weapons are really unique, and dodge vs block+armor mechanic)
CONS:
Just 1 real CON in my opinion, and that is the shortage of skill points and a lack of difficulty option to help alleviate it. That brings in these related cons:
Save and load happens A LOT, unless you want to replay the entire game with one point difference in some skill
Often don't spend my reward points in case I need them for some future quest, increasing the amount of reloads
Hard to figure out what skill level is needed for many quests (save and reload, increase by 1 each time, etc)
TL;DR: TRY THE DEMO!!!! Note the complexity of chapter 1's design (many ways to beat), and know that it continues to grow. Lore skills in particular gets very interesting and surprizing.

Farming Simulator 15 is an ok game. The gameplay is credible. The physics are very much incredible. Although the person who designed the physics lives on the moon it is a rather good game. It is (except forestry) well balanced and enjoyable to a farming enthusiast. If you are willing to buy the game for it's multiplayer. Don't. You have to have friends who are willing to play for a fun multiplayer. The graphics have been improved to a high level from Farming Simulator 2013 and the content with it. The map feels small if you are driving across it at high speed. You'd probably be able to fly where you want to go with the physics. The forestry feature is OK to some extent. Trees never fall the way you want them and sometimes glitch and either fall into the ground or fire off into the stratosphere. (I have had both events occur in 24 hours of gameplay.) If you were to go straight into forestry and ignore the farming aspect of the game it would be a rather short and easy experience as you get 6x the amount of money for 2 hours of forestry than you would for 2 hours of farming. The farming aspect is almost the same as 2013; the same plants to grow, same method but with a couple new harvesters and many new tractors. The livestock feature also seems to be exactly copied over. A couple of the other new features include: tyre tracks that will follow exactly where your vehicle has been and dirt, your tractors may get dirty and grubby, but you are able to wash them with a power washer that costs £4,500. In the options, there aren't many. Although you can reset the key bindings for every key, but by default they are all the same as Farming Simulator 2013's which is a nice touch.
Overall I think it is a good game and I would recommend it. If you ignore the physics and the small map then it is quite a good game. If you are unsure about getting Farming Simulator 15, buy 2013 first as it is cheaper and the only real difference is forestry. Everything else is cosmetic.

Taking place a couple of months after the events of Dishonored 2, Death of the Outsider puts you into the shoes of Billie Lurk, a minor character from the previous game upgraded to a supernatural blood-spiller. She reunites with her old mentor, Daud and is given one of the most daunting missions in the entire series: Kill the black eyed, exposition obsessed MCR fan, The Outsider.
This standalone includes five missions and will take as long as you want it to. Being someone who went completely ghost throughout the entire game and did most of the contracts, my playthrough took around ten hours. That being said, it might take you less time than that because going undetected in the last mission is more difficult than I ever imagined it being. The enemy A.I. at times can be a little random in what they can see, whether you be above them on a chandelier or hiding beneath a desk. This feels somewhat more pertinent than it was in the previous game so hitting quicksave and quickload is a bit more common than it should be. On normal difficulty, it felt like the amount of time it took for an enemy to spot you was inconsistent as well, especially in the last level. There was one section where just peeking around a corner would immediately set off someone at least fifty feet away from me.
Those annoyances aside, I do recommend Death of the Outsider if you like the Dishonored formula and enjoyed the expansive levels and cathartic combat possibilities. The expansion takes over some of the better qualities from Dishonored 2 and changes the formula up in a few interesting ways. The most notable change is that there are no mana potions anymore. Your "void energy" recharges on its own so you don't need to worry about using powers in quick succession and reducing your mana pool until you drink a potion. The second change related to this is that you don't hunt for runes to upgrade your abilities. The abilities you get at the beginning will stay the same throughout the entire game and you can only improve yourself by using bonecharms and upgrading your gear at a black market. So for those who hated hunting for runes in any Dishonored game and felt like it took up half your playtime, rejoice! Another change is the inclusion of "contracts" which are little side missions that will reward you with money and bonecharms. It can be as simple as a fetch quest or it can be as elaborate as making the main mission much more difficult if you choose to pursue it. Oh, and one more big change: NO KARMA SYSTEM. Your body count does not determine the ending at all, yet there are two outcomes. Your ending will be determined by one choice in the final level and like the previous games, the outcome isn't entirely satisfying or cathartic but the journey there was interesting at least. If you enjoy the lore of the series, Death of the Outsider does add a lot of interesting details to existing characters and factions. Just felt that was something worth mentioning.
New Game+ has been carried over from Dishonored 2 but it’s not nearly as interesting as the system present in that game. In NG+, abilities such as Displace, Semblance and Foresight get replaced with a mishmash of Corvo and Emily’s abilities: Blink, Dark Vision and Domino.
A couple of little side notes before going to the final verdict:
I liked Billie Lurk as a character because she’s capable and ruthless while also having a sense of humor. She never begs for sympathy and is always just doing what she thinks will help her out. She might tell you of nightmares and the people she’s lost, but she doesn’t cry and expect things to change. She’ll find the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s responsible, slit their throats and call it a day.
I thought that elaborating on the Outsider’s origins would ruin his mystique and rule out any possible Dishonored sequels, but I think Arkane did just good enough of a job to avoid those pitfalls.

While this does use some of the environments (Karnaca) from Dishonored 2, they’re used just differently enough to not make the experience feel stale. The 3rd mission, The Bank Job is probably my favorite level and is one of the best designed in the entire series.
So overall, if you liked Dishonored 2 and don’t mind some gameplay tweaks, give Death of the Outsider a shot. The port isn’t garbage and it has just as much replay value as the previous games. If I had to give an arbitrary score, I’d say 7 / 10 would fit it the best. While I do enjoy this series immensely, as time goes on, I feel a bit more critical towards the aspects that don’t work as well as they should. The sometimes unrefined mechanics can bog down perfectionist runs and make save scumming more reliable than it should be.  I have faith that Arkane can improve the series if given another chance, but for now, it’s a good if flawed stealth series with supernatural elements.

Right off the bat, Teslagrad impresses with a wonderful art style and animations that immerses the player in its steampunk world. Rain falls in torrents, molten steel glows ominously in the depths of the tower in which you explore, and electricity crackles and hums. It's a world of mechanical beasts that can destroy you in a moment, of dangerous traps and puzzles, of strange gadgets and weird machinery, and at the heart of this world is you and the Tower
Fleeing into this mysterious Tower, you'll work your way through its many rooms and floors, each offering new and inventive puzzles and obstacles to surmount. The game doesn't waste any time in throwing complex platforming puzzles at you; within the first 30 minutes or so, you'll already be equipped with a gauntlet able to reverse an object's polarity and blink boots that allow you to teleport a short distance. The puzzles and platforming all revolve around utilizing and switching between magnetic fields, causing objects to attract or repel. In this way, you turn platforms into barriers or elevators, move along ceilings or float over gaps, and more. Surviving the challenges require both puzzle solving and tight platforming as you time teleports between moving hazards or switch your own polarity to navigate around electric barriers. Hard to reach batteries offer replay value, as there's usually an optional extra challenge between you and the collectibles.
I'm only about two and half hours in at the moment. If there was one minor flaw, it would be the lack of checkpoints in boss fights. But the boss fights themselves are fun and varied and use the mechanics in cool ways. Controls are responsive and simple, WASD to move, Space to jump, arrow keys to use your abilities. But from those simple controls, Rain Games has crafted a fun and challenging puzzle platfformer that not only offers exciting gameplay but a fantastic art style as well

Yay this is a kids' game super funny :)
And for 0,99€ - which means way less on sale or with a coupon - can entertain you or your kids for many playthroughs :)
The game itself is quite simple and unfortunately suffers of a quite common issue on Steam, a machine translation of the game hub store that makes the text (and there's a lot of text for such a tiny game) quite unreadable.
It's quite sad, but let's go on XD
The game as usual lets you choose from windowed and full screen modes and the graphics quality (it doesn't really affect the game xD) and well, I'd suggest you to play it windowed since you don't need a wide game screen.
Maybe, the only bad thing I found is that there's no tutorial at all, which made my first trip with the van end in a big crash at the first intersection xD
Well, you can just click with the left mouse button to make a turn :)
The game consists of an (almost) infinite race in which you control a van that goes forward automatically - you have to time every click in order not to crash and to make the right curves, turning when you have to.
Plus, you will find lots of money on the course and the cash is often positioned on one lane or on the other one, so since you can't move your van laterally well, you'll need to time the turning point so that you'll ben in the same line with the cash.
With your earnings, you'll be able to unlock eight different vans in the main menu! They also have some references to pop culture, but I think they refer to American TV shows or similar things 'cos I didn't recognize them ahah :)
Of course, as you go on the track course will be more difficult with more close turning points and the velocity will also increase a bit but everything works perfectly and I've never experienced a single time in which my click (ok, you can also use the space bar to turn but I found the mouse a little bit more suitable but anyways you can use the control you like the most!) didn't respond well. For every click I always had the perfect curve and the hitboxes are also really good, you'll never crash by going close to the wall or similar things.
The downside of the game of course is that, presenting only a desert track and just some different vans unlockable thanks to your earned money, it can become monotonous after an hour or two and this is one of the main reasons why it's best suitable for kids that look for a nice casual and light game to play whenever they feel like, since there's not a real challenge apart from the scoreboards and the achievements!
Ok, I said "almost infinite" 'cos actually the race eventually finishes, and it takes some time; being randomly created, it's based on the money counter and not the actual length (so if you don't collect money you'll go forever xD); more precisely, every 500$ earned you'll get a step up in difficulty and finally on reaching the 5000$ mark you'll finally get to the game end (of course the packs of banknotes are from 20$ onwards, not 1$ at a time ahah).
And yeah, after the 2500$ mark actually the van will start going quite fast, trust me! :)
The Z in the title by the way stands for the zig-zag road you'll be onto xD
Ok, everything said, for some cents it's a really nice game with no bugs whatsoever and especially if you've got kids or children at home they'll enjoy this little game I think, as I enjoyed them back in the '90s on the C64 ahah :)
I've just got one thing to point out: the game store page says that lots of languages are supported, but actually in game there are only few lines in English and there are no subtitles at all, at least I tried everything but I just came up with the Italian store page which is translated by some bad online translator I think. But don't care about this: no language skill is needed for this game ahah :) It's completely Unity-made and graphic-related so only your reflexes or your kids' ones will be necessary to get through it and maybe to finish it at the 5000$ mark :)
Have fun with this one :)

INK is a platformer where you use paint to uncover the level and make your way through it as you would any other platformer. There are several ways to spread paint, such as simply moving, double jumping, defeating enemies and... Dying.
Yep. Dying.
I absolutely adored INK for its very fast-paced gameplay and the whole concept of using paint to find the level. It is a very interestin ceoncept which was well made. Very, well made.
The game starts you off on very simple and easy levels but at a certain point, the difficulty of the levels suddenly shift and it becomes extremely hard to complete even a single level. You may spend possibly 30 seconds on one level, and then the next, you'll be stuck on it for about 15 minutes at the max. It does get a little frustrating, as after just being on a level for about 1 minute or so, the entire level is uncovered and it becomes a simple platformer, with just the colours of the area changing.
This needs to be pointed out, the soundtrack for the game is extremely well made and simply beautiful. It keeps in with the tone of the game but not when you're screaming your lungs out after dying for the 50th time on the same level. Still, lovely soundtrack.
The game is stuck at 30FPS which I honestly did not like very much, but that is just a matter of opinion and what you're used to.
The game is a little short, so be warned. It took me about 2 hours to finish all 75 levels, and that's it. You can go back to collect all the coins, and get 100% completion, but just the minimum of finishing the levels is approximately 2 hours. It does leave me wanting a bit more, but I can say I am very satisfied.
Overall, the concept of using paint to find the level is well made, the levels are good as well (including the rage inducing ones), music is amazing, and, though short, it has left a very strong impression on me. I would easily place it up there with many other great platformers. I highly recommend buying it just for the concept itself.

At first glance this game seems to have a lot in common with Super Meat Boy (which I consider to be the greatest platformer released in the last 20 years or so). And while INK may not have the ultra-polished controls and level design of Super Meat Boy, it's still a fun game that's worth playing.
I did have a bit of trouble with the double jump mechanic - if I jumped off of a ledge at the last moment, it would often count me as having already left the platform, and I'd only get the second jump of my double jump.
Small issues aside, I thought the whole ink gimmick was pretty cool, and it's a surprisingly pretty game for being so lo-fi. If you enjoy games like Super Meat Boy, Electronic Super Joy, 140, Love, or VVVVVV, there's a good chance you'll like this one.

This game blew away my expectations. The map is massive, the secrets are endless, the customization for play style is diverse, and it's probably the least linear platformer I've seen. What could be a simple cracked wall can lead to an entirely new (optional) section of the game. It's rare to explore a path and not feel rewarded. If you find nothing, come back when you can explore it a bit more thoroughly. Most importantly, prepare to be frustrated. You will agonize as you make dumb mistakes, or throw yourself endlessly at a boss that you haven't learned the patterns to yet. It's all the more gratifying when you make it through.

Hollow Knight is a good 2d Dark Souls inspired game that has a good story and good music. However it fails to adapt one essential key aspect of Dark Souls, and that is in Dark Souls you will always learn from any mistake or death. You may learn a different enemy attack pattern or realize that there is a specific sound or movement cue. In Hollow Knight once you get far enough the bosses stop giving you a cue and it starts to become a game of reactions. Where deaths to bosses become frustrating due to seemingly RNG deaths or where an early mistake has you simply resigning yourself to die and try again.
That isn't to say that the game is without merit or that bosses shouldn't always just have a sound or movement cue, but when all of the bosses abilities can be used combined with any sound cue it can easily create confusion when you tried to learn the cues from a previous fight.
TL:DR - Instead of buying Hollow Knight just replay Dark Souls and pretend that it is in 2d.

INK is a good game. Not perfect, but it is very fun. :)
PROS
------
- Great clean aesthetic. Reminds me of '140' (not in terms of its music, but it's 'abstract platformer' design).
- Excellent controls. This is a big one. If a game like this didn't control well, that'd be a deal-breaker from the start.
- Pleasant background music.
- Fun boss fights and just a great 'chill and play' vibe. I dig it a lot.
CONS
------
- Lack of rebindable controls. This doesn't bother me much (since I prefer playing on a controller - and the only button you use is 'A' to jump), but I can see how this would be a hindrance to some.
- Lack of an 'Options' menu of any kind. You either play the game or you don't play the game - that's it. Volume, Resolution, Screen Size - none of that can change. This is a bummer because...
- I suffered from horrendous lag/slow-down - especially on the later levels. Maybe there were too many paint particles on the screen at one time. I dunno. The fact is - the game became so slow that it was unplayable. I reached level 74 of 75...so I may stop there. With such a clean, simple aesthetic this shouldn't be a problem.
Granted, I don't have the most powerful computer in the world, but games like 'Shovel Knight', 'Oniken', 'Shantae and the Pirate's Curse' - and virtually every other 2D game I own - play perfectly fine. So, such laggy performance is a bit of a shock. Perhaps this can be addressed in a future update.
- Also, the pacing is a little weird. After introducing a few gameplay mechanics, there's level after level after level where nothing seems to change - and then projectiles are introduced, which was appreciated. Good ideas are here, but I think it would have been better to see more of them. Thus, the game does not play as smoothly as it could. Also, the boss levels seemed too few and far between. Just my opinion. >_<
FINAL THOUGHTS
-------------------
- Overall, it's a really fun game. Except for some technical issues, it really plays quite well. No story or characters to speak of, but great arcade-like platforming action. A great way to spend an afternoon if you ask me. :)
Final Score: 7.5 out of 10

Dungeon Defenders 1 is a Tower defense game. It follows the tale of four young heroes, who due to their heroic parents recent disappearance; have taken it upon themselves to go investigate it as well as the sudden increase in monster activity. This takes place over 20+ stages of normal activity and a (DLC) 5-mission campaign to save your parents, with a bunch of cool stuff inbetween.
Right off the bat I will mention:
If you are the type of person to sit around comparing gear numbers for stats you want; you'll find yourself right at home here. Especially if you don't trust the auto-evaluation system on the game. But once you are all geared up, its all a matter of who you geared up. Which brings me to the classes.
You got 4 (With about 2-3 as DLC, and 4 as genderswap DLC with slightly different abilities?): Apprentice, Squire, Huntress, and Monk (With Jester, Summoner, and EV as DLC). Apprentice places a variety of projectile towers, Squire places a mix of Melee Range and projectile towers; Huntress places AOE floor traps; and Monk places AOE Auras. All have their uses, I'm sure you can google it to look into each ones usefulness. (Jester can summon any of the classes towers at random, Summoner can summon Crystal minions on a whole other Defense points Pool, and EV can summon hi-tech laser walls and the ever useful "Tower buff beam")
The goal is as simple as any other tower defense: Protect your goal. Each map has one to 4-5 crystals, and you gotta make sure enemies don't destroy them. From kamikaze kobolds to giant ogres, to even Land sharks and flying goblin copters. It's a hectic mess that can sometimes be super easy, or force you to stay on your toes. The rewards are pretty nice though, some maps giving special weapons and equipment. In the storyline there are about 4 bosses total, maybe 5.
Dungeon Defenders 1 is a pretty solid Tower defense game, If you have time to spare and enjoy the chaos and sometimes struggle of winning a hard defense, go for it! But do it only on sale, cause 9/10 the game is usually dead. DD2 hasn't lived up to anywhere near my expectations, but lots of people go to it now.

“Strata” is a 2D puzzle game which players are asked to create the correct pattern using different colored ribbons. Its artistic textures create a soothing gameplay.
The game starts with 2x2 tutorial puzzles. Tutorial is nice and easy to understand. It shows the player what his/her goal is, and how the ribbons are used.
In the puzzles, the player is given a set of different colored ribbons. These ribbons can be placed on rows or lines of the diagonal puzzle ground. Puzzle grounds have colors in intersection of rows and colors. As expected, when ribbons are placed on rows and lines, they intersect. Puzzle logic comes from this intersection. Whichever ribbon is placed later, its color occupies that intersection. Players’ goal is to create the same pattern on the puzzle ground.
This game has a static logic for its puzzles. That means there are no new additions when player advances to later puzzles. Logic is always the same. Only things that change are size of the ground and number of the ribbons’ colors. Smallest puzzles’ grounds are 2x2 and largest ones are 6x6. If I calculated correctly there are 485 puzzles (excluding tutorials) separated into 7 sets and each set is separated further into 4 waves. It is worth noting that this static logic may be a deal breaker for some people.
Puzzles’ difficulty is tricky to talk about. There is a trick to solve the puzzles. This trick can be used to solve even the most-complicated-looking-level. If player can figure it out then very few puzzles are challenging and rest is easy. So it is safe to say that unofficial puzzle goal in this game is to solve the trick. Levels can be considered as tools to figure it out.
During my gameplay, I came across some minor bugs. These bugs did not affect actual puzzles; they were all in main menu. The game has a menu that resembles a navigation system instead of standard button menu. And this menu can sometimes act weird. Luckily the game can be restarted in a few seconds so even a restart doesn’t make player loose anything. Regardless, they should be fixed.
As a final note, games achievements are all easily achievable. So this is a good game to get a “perfect game” status if you are interested in such things.
The game has nice textures and uses pastel colors, which makes it easy on the eyes.
Art style and realistic instrument (piano, classic guitar and bell) notes that play after almost every player action create a relaxing environment.
Puzzle logic looks really unique.
Because this is a puzzle game, it is not necessarily a bad thing. Also it is a little expected. That said, using the same logic throughout the game results doing the exact same thing again and again.
The game has some minor bugs that don’t affect actual puzzles. Still they should be fixed.
It was nice to play a game that actually made me relaxed for a change. These kinds of games show that games are not all about action or achievements; so I recommend it. Still it is worth noting that this puzzle game is mostly recommended to people who care “solving puzzles” more than which puzzles they solve, due to its static logic.

Puzzle platformer that uses the good old gravity switch mechanic to pack tons of content into small areas (or to hide lots of content in large areas). Gameplay comes in 2 flavors: small discrete puzzle levels that you'll have to get intimately familiar with to plunder completely, and "run from the lava" esque sequences where you'll have to memorize the layout for some precise moves as it kills you over and over again. In general, the game is totally unafraid to kill you, but you just instantly respawn in a Super Meat Boy fashion. This might be a turnoff for some because the controls aren't quite precise enough to warrant the level of precision the game sometimes expects, but you do get to try again in 2 seconds anyway. If anything's a dealbreaker it'll be that last bit.
On a more positive note, the level designs are pretty good and the use of "biomes" works pretty well. Each biome has a discrete set of mechanics that don't just accumulate, meaning that, say, there's lava in the first area but the second area relies on deadly grass for a hazard, even though the designers could have easily said "ok lava does literally everything we need in a hazard it can be everywhere". Each new biome reimagines the game, so that instead of figuring out obscure interactions between two dozen mechanics, you get to master the interactions between the mechanics that were deemed to belong in a given biome. (This also means that there's a reasonable limit on the number of ice levels, and even though ice was actually used in a smart way unlike most platformers, I appreciate this on principle).
All in all not a perfect game (and you may find yourself loudly insisting that during the running segments) but it works and I found it to be one of the more interesting things I've played this year.

This game is great if you're a Civilization fan. Make no mistake, this is not an Alpha Centuari remake. It's mostly Civ V in space, but Firaxis made some great changes to it to make this feel like its own game. The new questing system is awesome. You get things ranging from tutorial-like missions to actual story-based stuff. Nothing too crazy in depth, but still pretty cool to see things happen as a result to your actions on a plot-level.
The Affinity system is pretty cool, too. You can choose between three different affinities based on the technology you research. This opens up new units (upgrades), new buildings, and victory conditions that you can only access if you have a high enough level in a given affinity. And this leads us to win conditions. Each condition has a specific affinity attached to it that is required to attain a specific win condition. Not only that, but each one has lore behind it you can read in the quest log that ties into the views of each specific affinity. These range from things like building a gate to bring humans from Earth to the new planet to ones like discovering an alien signal to decrypt.
Overall, if you like the Civilization series and enjoy a SciFi setting, you'll love this game. It's just as addictive as the mainline series with some unique twists and it unshackles itself from history settings to really let Firaxis go in new directions with things like technology. You can have flying units very early on in this game.

I got hooked on this game, which was quite unexpected given the blocky graphics and frustrating combat.  It takes place in a Roman-era setting where several great houses are all vying for power, and there's a couple of guilds and factions that are egging them all on to advance their own agendas.  There's a very cool story underlying this about techno-mages and Gods that you can delve more into if you want to play archeologist in the ruins, but this is really up to you.  The charm of the game is that there are so many different story branches that you can influence.  My second playthrough was completely different than my first!  The game relies heavily on skill and stat checks.  I almost see this game as more of a puzzle game because it will take a few playthroughs to familiarize yourself with what skillchecks you need to pass at what times so that you can earn more skill points.  The challenge is that no character can pass EVERY skill check, so you have to be very careful in how you build your character.  As all the other reviewers have pointed out, you're going to have a much more enjoyable experience if you make either a pure combat character or a pure diplomatic character.  Your first two playthroughs should be with each of these, in fact.  Once you start mixing it up, you end up with a character that can't pass any speech checks, which results in having to fight, and you won't be able to win any fights because the combat, which is heavily reminiscent of the early Fallout games, is brutally unfair unless you put every single point into your weapon skills (and even then expect to spend a good amount of time staring at your reloading screen).  I think the biggest payoff is that after you've played through a couple of times, you MIGHT be able to piece together how to get the hidden best ending!

Rather than a typical RPG, its more like a very complex choose your own adventure storybook, with a well integrated combat game attached to it.
The overaching mystery is rather stunning and satisfying, its masterfully woven into the underlying story, with tons of different perspectives and snippets.
The human stories beneath them, however, start strong but falter towards the end (too many choices to be accounted for, too drastic and hasty a push towards the end).
The writing is also impeccable, not too long as to be boring, not too short as to leave you clueless, generally appropiate tone to each character, with a suffocating atmosphere of despair (fitting with the setting), and with enough black humor to prevent the story becoming crushing.
Its also not too long, a playthrough is around 10 hours, and two playthroughs can be achieved with very little repeating content. Even more is possible if you happen to love it, I tried 4, though the latter two were sped up using cheats to skip the 'already seen' parts.
Shockingly, the game has superb combat for such a melee based rpg with no magic, all 6 weapons are genuinely distinct and viable, with multiple attack styles making you question your tactical choices all the time. Strategic investments into alchemy and crafting can be extremely impactful as well.
The game has good music, good artwork (if sparse), though given the lengthy development of this game, the 3d world looks like the typical budget unity rpg, Its tolerable but certainly not pleasing to the eyes.
Overall, would definitely recommend if you like stories, this one definitely branches in many many ways, not just the mainstoryline but also every possible sidequest. But if you want a more casual or combat oriented RPG, go play divinity 2 or any of the three mainstream RPGs (TES, Fallout and mass effect).

Age of Decadence is a difficult game to review and describe. It's fun, interesting, thought provoking and challenging, however the things that make it this way run counter to what nowadays are expected RPG conventions. Thus it's a game that has both potential to amaze and frustrate depening on who's playing and what they're expecting out of it.
For instance you wouldn't expect an average RPG to be willing to throw challenging fights at you practically everytime you enter combat. That careful distribution of skill points isn't a tacked on system but your main means of survival and that you get to make choices that matter with consequences that can throw you into difficult battles your character might not be built for.
This is what AoD is in a nutshell, its an RPG from an earlier era, for players who don't want to play another chosen one master of all combat styles and savior of the weak, but instead its a game focusing on integrating the player character into the game world. The game is fairly text-heavy with most of what happens outside combat explained through the dialogue window. In that sense it feels like an attempt to bring the experience of a tabletop roleplaying game onto a computer screen.
For it's good sides speaks the great writing, variety of skills, challenging and thought out combat system, unique setting and lots and lots of choices along the story.
As for negatives, the skill system comes across as bit arbitrary with the dialogue skill checks, some skills might seem redundant (like a bunch of dialogue only skills for persuading people that have no use outside conversation), combat can be frustrating and takes time to figure out and commit to, and it's possible to get stuck in the game through poor decisions on how to spend your skill points. Also game can be fairly short for just one run, with most of the game being there to discover on subsequent playthroughs when you gear up to meet a skill check that stumped you last time to try a different path.
But don't get me wrong, AoD isn't a bad game. It's just not a game for everyone. It's highly replayable and I'm surprised by the sheer ammount of thought put into the way your choices along the story can change it along the way, there's seven factions to join but even within one faction's questline you get choices to take sides in internal disputes, options to switch sides in conflict. Can't win a fight your quest giver gave you and don't have the skills to pass the dialogue check? Maybe there's a way to cut a deal with the other party and get yourself a cozy position in their ranks instead.
It's that kind of game and honestly, you don't see this level of freedom of choice often. If you think you're not one to be easily frustrated by the game's difficulty, I'd recommend you give this one a go.

I was a hardcore FS2013 fan, for that reason I love this. New graphics of course, and cutting down trees. The best part is being able to cut down trees blocking fields and workers in the equipment. This was the biggest problem for me in FS2013, you can cut trees that tractors are hung up on. The maps are huge, plenty of room to stretch your legs. Also lots of farming fields, you'll never run out.
Bugs are the only drawback, there aren't any show stoppers though. Very minor stuff. The physics work much better than FS2013, though is still buggy at times. Bumping a rock for example can (rarely) send your machine across the map. The automated workers at least attempt to fix from getting stuck at the edge of fields. Don't make them too large, also. The missions are given out at job boards. You can set the frequency (mine is set to 2min), and multiple jobs come in. FS2013 put the machines on your screen, was annoying. I keep a cheap tractor at the job board to check missions constantly.
For whatever reason, a massive bonus of several hundred thousand dollars comes with the farming missions. The payout would be 10,000 ish, and the bonus could be 400,000 dollars.. what? The drawback is these missions may or may not pop up often. Once I got 3 missions at a time, other times I had to wait several days. I expect this to be fixed? who knows, it's the only true way to get money quickly.
The job board is almost always pallet missions, that is, pickup a pallet and drop off to said location. Those get old very quickly.. Grass cuttng mission is painfully slow until you get both front and back mowers. There is no longer the useless riding mower, also.
As with FS2013 farming, farming the largest fields with the largest/quickest equipment is the key to success. The tractors are the same, maybe a couple new here or there. But the graphics overall is such a huge improvement. You can wash your equipment for kicks, or if you are really, really bored.
The starter equipment is much better as well, the very basic tractors go 42mph. No more rust bucket putt putts. They have high maint cost of course, the sooner you get rid of them the better.
Overall, they thought BIGGER with FS2015 as an improvement. There is rarely flat terrain. Everywhere has hills, sometimes road going up very steep terrain. Improperly powered tractors have no chance of pulling trailers up steep hills. The way things are laid out, you are sometimes better off taking the roads. Versus FS2013, you would bee line towards your point, plummeting down the sides of hills.
Other thoughts:
The reset button needs some kind of timeout. It's too tempting to reset your tractors and equipment constantly. Maybe a minute or so, nothing silly.
Picking up trees is hard, period. I've spent a good amount of time picking up tree trunks, sometimes it takes several minutes PER log, you need to gather hundreds of them.

Death of the Outsider is another great entry to the Dishonored series with so far the most engaging story, concluding the entire Kaldwin story arc. Billie Lurk, the new playable character, is really well written. Her motivation to finish off Outsider is making the story feel really personal, therefore I was really looking forward to how it all ends. This is how main characters in Dishonored games were always suppose to be like, but they never managed to transfer their motivations to player as good as they managed it with Billie Lurk in Death of the Outsider.
Game itself is just as good as all previous Dishonored games. Gameplay stayed mostly the same with just a few minor tweaks (I really like regenerating mana, instead of drinking potions all the time) and two (out of three) brand new powers, level design still enables you to play however you like with a lot of different ways to complete each mission and the art style is still out of this world.
They also managed to optimize it this time around, so you don't have to worry about terrible performance from Dishonored 2. While Dishonored 2 was dropping to 40's with a lot of settings lowered, DotO was running stable 60 FPS 99% of the time with everything maxed out.
Death of the Outsider is also surprisingly lengthy (16 hours with completionist play style and reading most of the books/letters), so you also shouldn't be worried that you won't get enough bang for the buck with this game. Not to mention the great replayability...
So stop reading, go buy it.

I'm really loving this game. It feels like Dust: An Elysian Tail, but with money drop on death. Not to fear though, you can corpse run and regain your lost money!

*The games art work is beautiful and the characters all seem to have a fair amount of thought and time put into them.
*The game seems to be pretty open for exploring and doesn't force players  to go straight to doing story related tasks although doing so will unlock abilities that will be needed for collecting items and things that are hidden through out the world.
*Most of the gameplay is underground with a main hub town being placed on the surface (I just beat Hornet a little while ago and now I'm back to exploring, so I'm not too far in).
*You can upgrade your gear later on and collect mod items that can boost your character in different ways like increasing spirit gain.
*Some bosses require trial and error along with learning their moves and when its best to move in for a strike.
*Corpse running involves finding your spirit and slaying it, which in turn, saves time grinding to re-earn lost money (Usually takes about two hits with your melee weapon)
*Theres a sort of stag beatle fast travel for moving between major areas, which I love the visuals for. It looks great. ;)
*Just found a money bank, this will come in handy later
*you don't start off with much, but you can gain money and gear fairly quickly/ easily. Thats not to say bosses will be easy, they can be a bit tricky and tough to take down.
*Try not to die while corpse running, your dropped money will be perma lost.

ATTENTION: This review was made from a casual gamer's point of view. My opinions may only be relevant to those who are novices to racing simulators.
Overall, it is a poor game that is not enjoyable at all. After a while, my head starts to hurt because of the unrealistic engine sounds. It might be a good game if you are just looking to test your driving wheel. I rate it a 5/10.
Main Menu - 2/10 - I don't know why, but it takes about 1-2 seconds to load after pressing a button in the main menu. This might be poor optimization by the developers. The main menu is also bland in style and not user-friendly.
Tutorials - 0/10 - There is no tutorial whatsoever.
Controls - 3/10 - I would not recommend playing this game with a keyboard.
Physics - 8/10 - The game's physics seems pretty realistic. The only problem, however, is that you don't feel like you are moving at your speed. Driving at around 150 km/h feels like you are just casually driving on your local highway.
Gameplay - 8/10 - This is a racing simulator, therefore it has to feel like you are actually racing. This game does so in a good manner.
Graphics - 6/10 - The racing simulators in the arcades probably have better graphics than the graphics in this game.
Sound - 8/10 - Each car has its own unique engine sound. However, it does not consider the fact that racers wear headphones so the engine sound must be muffled. Because of this, it sounds like you are actually listening to the engine itself. Also, there is no communication between the pit crew whatsoever.

You are a bully and you hit everyone who comes near you. That´s the essence of the game.
I´m just kidding. I have to recommend this game but with a big but. I really like this game, is fun, it´s filled with so many things, great aesthetics, works perfectly, the control system is great (I´m playing it with a Xbox 360 control), it´s an amazing game.
BUT, and as I said, it´s a big but, the game has some big flaws that make me think about giving it a bad review, but it´s too good to do that. First, the difficulty is really high, sometimes frustrating and that happens a lot. This game should have a diffiulty level system because it´s really, really hard sometimes, not all the time but often. Add to that a terrible saving system where you can only save if you find a chair that is not all around but in specific points. So you die, and you have to repeat sometimes a huge space to fight a boss again, for example, that becomes boring pretty soon. I have played around 30 hours (I played before with a friend) and the game keeps me coming, that´s why the recommendation, but I´m starting to lose the joy of the game.
Another big flaw, you don´t know where to go, sometimes you just have to repeat some place you did just to find a new place, and the game is pretty big, so you could spend hours just wandering around trying to find something new, and that can become boring really fast, the game should have missions that give you clues of where to go.
It´s a good game, apart from that. If you like a challenge and like this kind of Mario games, you should try it right now, it´s well made, fun, huge, you will spend several hours in it and you will be happy. But if you get frustrated with games that make you repeat something over and over, don´t get this game.
I just wish the producers read this reviews and fix what it needs to be fixed. Just the save system. If it´s hard but you can repeat fast a hard part, well, I would try that, I already are doing it with this awful save system. Don´t get me wrong, I like the chair system, I just wish there were more chairs and chairs just before bosses, so you can try 100 times until you pass.

Dungeon Defenders 1 is a Tower defense game. It follows the tale of four young heroes, who due to their heroic parents recent disappearance; have taken it upon themselves to go investigate it as well as the sudden increase in monster activity. This takes place over 20+ stages of normal activity and a (DLC) 5-mission campaign to save your parents, with a bunch of cool stuff inbetween.
Right off the bat I will mention:
If you are the type of person to sit around comparing gear numbers for stats you want; you'll find yourself right at home here. Especially if you don't trust the auto-evaluation system on the game. But once you are all geared up, its all a matter of who you geared up. Which brings me to the classes.
You got 4 (With about 2-3 as DLC, and 4 as genderswap DLC with slightly different abilities?): Apprentice, Squire, Huntress, and Monk (With Jester, Summoner, and EV as DLC). Apprentice places a variety of projectile towers, Squire places a mix of Melee Range and projectile towers; Huntress places AOE floor traps; and Monk places AOE Auras. All have their uses, I'm sure you can google it to look into each ones usefulness. (Jester can summon any of the classes towers at random, Summoner can summon Crystal minions on a whole other Defense points Pool, and EV can summon hi-tech laser walls and the ever useful "Tower buff beam")
The goal is as simple as any other tower defense: Protect your goal. Each map has one to 4-5 crystals, and you gotta make sure enemies don't destroy them. From kamikaze kobolds to giant ogres, to even Land sharks and flying goblin copters. It's a hectic mess that can sometimes be super easy, or force you to stay on your toes. The rewards are pretty nice though, some maps giving special weapons and equipment. In the storyline there are about 4 bosses total, maybe 5.
Dungeon Defenders 1 is a pretty solid Tower defense game, If you have time to spare and enjoy the chaos and sometimes struggle of winning a hard defense, go for it! But do it only on sale, cause 9/10 the game is usually dead. DD2 hasn't lived up to anywhere near my expectations, but lots of people go to it now.

It's hard to decide whether or not to recommend this game.  It's pretty cheap, looks fine for it's basic style, has some funky menu music and okay sound effects, and it runs smoothly.  But it's also very basic and doesn't offer much in the way of replay value.  Maybe adding a few more maps, maybe some objectives, something along those lines to spice it up a bit.
I think I'll settle on recommend just because it does run fine, is cheap (though could be cheaper...), achieves it's goal, and it has achievements.  Who doesn't like achievements?

This old-school style RPG succeeds brilliantly at creating a series of vignettes for the player to interact with. The system is heavily based on your skills and attributes, and the wide plentifulness of content is gated by skills which makes the player constantly guess what they're missing.
The problem is that everything else--and I do mean
--is mediocre to bad. The setting is unimaginative and the characters are intentionally made flat and unlikable, which means that for all it's success in creating a game with mystifying and challenging goals, both the background, pulp, and the payoff of these goals feel completely hollow. Dialogue is extremely uninteresting and nearly all of it has the same literary voice. There's a conversation with a certain character that has very strict requirements to initiate, but once you do initiate it, they basically end up spelling out every single secret the world has to offer. Once you get to this conversation, you have no reason to ever pay attention to any of the dialogue except for your own options. This is drilled into your head by the fact that there is a skill check in nearly every dialogue menu and there are only 2-3 instances where you can do anything meaningful without a skill check.
The combat system is acceptably mediocre, but the way that encounters and combat skills are managed is truly awful. The developers favored realism over feasibility, except in cases where realism would ever favor the player. For example, during the first act, you are tasked with taking on a bandit camp. True to what would be the case in a realistic scenario, these bandits travel in packs (5 people), and have poor equipment, but are roughly as good in combat as an inexperienced imperial guard. The problem is that the player *physically cannot* reach a point where they are better than an imperial guard. Consequentially, this means that the player is facing five opponents equally as strong as they are.
The intricacy of the vignettes wears off quickly when you realize what you have to do to meaningfully interact with them. Because the world is so boring and the game is so skill check heavy, all you're doing is unlocking meaningless content. The whole game is a glorified excel spreadsheet.

I'm going to preface this review by saying the I absolutely love Civ5. I've put hundreds of hours into it, and still play it fairly regularly. When people began saying that Beyond Earth was going to be a reskin of Civ5, I was actually okay with that (although for a full priced game? Maybe not for everyone, but I would've still been happy with it). The problem is that Beyond Earth is worse than Civ5. Given that it took two incredible expansions to get Civ5 to where it is now, perhaps one could say that it's excusable for Beyond Earth to be in a similar Vanilla state. No, as of right now, I have no reason to play Beyond Earth instead of more Civ5 with Brave New World.
As for my problems with the game, I'll just cover my biggest ones:
- The colors of the terrain itself are awful. There's a total of maybe four or five different shades of green, purple, and brown that get meshed up into all of the terrain features, making it often impossible to tell what kind of terrain each tile has, or if that tile contains miasma or something.
-The UI is in many ways much, much worse than Civ5. In addition it being, in my opinion, fairly unattractive to begin with, it is completely unintuative at times, in particular on the tech web where it is very difficult to tell what kinds of benefits each of the little identically colored circles are that you're unlocking. Furthermore, it seems like the changed things just to change them, which resulted in some pretty poor changes. On the city screens, the clean menus are gone and have been replaced with garbage screens that are very difficult to use.
- Trade routes are incredibly tedius, and overpowered to the point where you need to rush anything that benefits them to min/max properly.
-The late game is awful. Apart from domination, all of the victory types are glorified science victories (research this, build this, wait for this). The first game I played, I spent the last third of my game sitting and waiting for either techs to finish, or waiting for some artificial timer to finish so I could win. I ended up deleting all my trade routes so they wouldn't pop up every other turn, and hitting the auto-end turn button so the game could just finish itself, as there was nothing left for me to do. Mind you, this was over the course of about 125 turns or so.
All in all, this game might be good with expansions, but it shouldn't have to be. I don't forsee anybody playing this instead of Civ5 in a few months, and this is definitely not a game worth full price.

There are plenty of things to enjoy about Sid's newest entry to the Civilization franchise.  Right from the beginning, you see the influence Civilization V had on this installment's UI. Beyond Earth attempts to streamline the large amount of individual information into easily accessible tabs at the bottom of the screen. City screens and building queues remain largely the same from Civ V but retain the ability to have a city product science, production, or culture from Civ IV; this means you do not have to wait to research a specific technology midway to late in your game to help boost production values.
Tile improvements function the same way they did in Civ V, with strategic resources and valuable resources that you build improvements on to add them to your civilization. Every type of tile improvement is done with the worker robot, including the ones done in the water (as your robot can hover on the water)j. This way, cities that aren't on coasts can still benefit from water based tile improvements without having to build a specific unit. Also, with the lack of Great People in Beyond Earth, unique tile improvements are done with the worker robot.
The map layer stays the same but has a new orbital layer that allows you to see the locations of the various types of satellites and orbital units that you can build; these units, once built, are placed over an area of the map that the player specifies (within their borders) that provide bonuses over time. New building improvements provide boosts in effectiveness and orbital time.
The new resources on the map layer function exactly as they do in Civ V, with specific technologies needed to be researched in order to reveal them on the map and allow the workers to improve the tiles. As Beyond Earth takes place on alien worlds, the resources are given a new skin and name but function the same as their Earth-bound counterparts; the best example of this is Titanium, which is bascially the alien equivalent to Iron.
Now, while production, science, and culture remain unchanged in their functionality in Beyond Earth, there are two new statistics that the player must keep an eye out: Energy and Health. Health is the collective happiness of the player's colonies as acts the same way Happiness did in Civ V including having specific buildings that can increase its value. You want to keep your colonies healthy, for the player gains bonuses to their production based on the happiness score. Energy works exactly like gold did in Civ V, with unit and building maintenance costing energy to keep up.
Next up are the Affinities and Virtues. There are three types of Affinities and four types of virtues that benefit the player in some way. Affinity points are gained by researching technologies that have an Affinity bonus attributed to them. As you gain points in an Affinity, you unlock higher levels of that Affinity. Affinities are beneficial in that they unlock unique units that you can build and allow the player access to better versions of the units they already have. In effect, the Affinities of Beyond Earth function like the Ideologies in Civ V, but the player has access to all three at the same time. Virtues function the same way Social Policies functioned in Civ V but more condenced. Each of the four Virtues have three tiers that require the player to unlock to gain access to the higher tiers. Once all the bonuses in a Virtues' tier have been unlocked, the player gets a Synergy bonus that does a variety of things (boost production, free tech, better combat, etc.)
Victories are handled much differently than in previous Civilization titles. As the player progresses, quests will appear that, if completed, give the player a reward of energy or resource. When different buildings are complete, there will usually be a choice quest that affects its function (one example is that a building could either give a +10% bonues to Food production or Science production). Each victory requires you to complete specific tasks that decide which type of victory you achieve; the progress for each victory is tracked within the quest menu under the victory tab.
Aliens and Miasma: Just typing those two words gives me a headache. Aliens are the bandits of Beyond Earth with "nests" popping up in unclaimed territory and moving about the world. The difference from bandits is that players don't have the option of turning off aliens. It is their planet and the player is stuck with them. There are various types of aliens (melee, ranged, sea, air) and eliminating a nest provides you with energy much like bandit camps did in Civ V. Miasma, on the other hand, is a map condition that works like nucler fallout from Civ V. Random tiles will have miasma on them that cause damage to the player's units that end their turn in that tile. There are technologies to research that allow you to remove miasma or make it beneficial to it so it really is a nuisance in the early game only.
The Tech Web is easily a confusing entity in its own right. As Beyond Earth does not have Ages that the player's colonists go through, the technologies that can be researched are not broken up into individual categories. Instead, the technologies the player can research are arranged in a circular web the gradually expands outward meaning that entire sections of the web can be ignored in favor of specific technologies depending on the Affinities the player wants or the player's individual playstyle. The web itself is composed of "branches" and "leaves"; the branches are the types of technologies you can unlock and the leaves are improvements to that technology. Some branches aren't unlocked until you complete a connecting branch, so it is important to plan which technologies you wish to research rather than just going down in sequential order.
Overall, my recommendation is that if you enjoyed playing Civilization V, then you will enjoy the new flavor that Beyond Earth gives. Sid Meier's Civilization: Beyond Earth does not vastly improve upon its predecessors; but rather, takes the best from those that came before and provides a new landscape for players to mold. Beyond Earth stays true to its Sid Meier's namesake.

This is what Dishonored 2 should have been.
Sneaking is an actual possibility without reloading every five seconds because of guards having godlike awareness - also thanks to an interesting "changeling" ability of Billie and just flat out better level design.
It doesn't overstay its welcome. By mission 6 in Dishonored 2 I just wanted it to end. Death Of The Outsider might be a bit too short, but it is "just" an expansion, so that's excusable.
The ending doesn't suck. Dishonored 2's ending was a hastily created slap in the face of anyone interested in the story.
Death of the Outsider brings a better closure to the previous game (including some of the sub-plots left open) as well as offering a good ending on its own.
The game still has some problems:
- You get absolutely flooded with whale bones. No idea what to do with all of them, way too much for crafting.
- The ability to listen to rats is pretty pointless (at least it is funny to listen to them).
- If you do not go for the stealth approach, the game will be extremely easy. Combat is really, really easy if you have ever played a proper FPS in your life and have the reaction of something faster than a snail.
- Way too many items are handed to you - I finished the game on hard without ever using most of them. You're totally fine just using your abilities and sword (or hands if non-lethal).
Nonetheless, I can recommend this - though at a sale. 30€ seems a tad bit too much for a 12 hour expansion.
