Now this is my first review, so don't expect to much from it. It will also be pretty Biased.
Let's start off by saying that i am a HUGE fan of Civ V, and have clocked atleast 80 hours into it (on a different account) and I fell in love with all the things it had. Civ V was also very easy to learn, which made me love it even more, even after i  had so much more to learn. Now that i got my introduction to Civ done, lets talk about Beyond Earth.
Beyond Earth is a very Civ V like game, those who didn't like Civ V most likely will not like Civ:BE. For some of those Die-Hard Civ V lovers, some may hate this aswell, paying 50$ for almost the same game. Now, dont take that statement as "DO NOT BUY THIS GAME." I fully recommend this game to Civilization Lovers aswell as new people into the Civilization Fanbase. Civ BE has a lot of new stuff that i have come to like and hopefully you aswell. They now list all the Victories you can acheive, aswell as telling you how close you are to completing them, and tell you the other Sponsers way to completing them. It also adds new unit types, and a entirly new thing; Supremecy (I probobly misspelled that), Purity, and Harmony. You can work on all three at once, but i recommend working on one at a time. These new options to run your Civ are very nice and add more variety. Civ:BE also adds a new way to gain Tech. Remember that old tech tree? Well forget about it. You know how it wasnt very hard to gain every tech in the game then just sit there building the spaceship? Well Civ:BE adds a new Tech Web. The Tech Web consists of Branches (main tech) and Leaves (side tech). Leaves come off of branches, adding a few more things concerning the technology. As far as i know, you cannot gain every tech in the game. You can get close, but currently its impossible. The game maxes out at 500 turns, allowing you to have a chance at victory. Civ:BE also adds a new way to personalize your Civ/Sponser. You now have the ability to choose which Planet you want to colonize, aswell as choosing what type of settlers you want, whether you want ones that will give you more science, food, etc. You also have Cargo, which you can choose to give your Sponser a boost (more food at beginning of game, more science, etc.), There are no more barbarians. Now you have aliens that have multiply unit types at once, not just sticking with the base game unit types like Civ V. They have alien *camps* known as hives which will spawn aliens, but they can also come out randomly. There are also Sea Aliens, like the Kraken, and Sea Dragon (dont attack these early game, you will get REKT.). There is also a new terrain modification called Miasma. Miasma is like a poisionous gas that if you stand in, every turn you have a unit in there it will lose 10-20 health (you can get rid of miasma later in the game.).
Now, i think Civ:BE is a great game. I will fully recommend this game, if you want to try it out, or your a hardcore Civ fan. I also think Civ:BE has a lot going for it, of course, since it onlt just released there are bugs and crashes, i experience only one so far, playing through an entire game in 7.1 hours, only one crash. I do recommend saving a lot, just incase you do crash and dont want to lose progress.
And with that, i will conclude my first review. I hope this review is helpful for new/old players that are looking for details on Civ:BE. 80% recommended from me. Hope i helped your decision, and Happy Civing!

The Age of Decadence is a home-brewed role playing game(unique setting) that rewards multiple playthroughs and experimentation. The setting can best be described as a blending of many containing legionnaires, magic, an extinct ancient civilization, medieval themes and much more. Different starting options provide different content and ways of approaching the game which provides much of the games content, as one path alone will only provide a few hours of content once you become familiarized with the game-play.
In regards to game-play this is where it excels as a role playing game. Depending on the character you wish to play you can be as diplomatic or as savage as one would please, leading to different situations in almost all playthroughs. Its combat though does have a bit of a learning curve and is rather brutal, and I can only suggest that if one would like to partake and excel in combat at all they must focus on it character development wise as you will quickly fall behind and die otherwise.
Overall  I would suggest this game to anyone looking for a rpg with an incredible amount of replayability, interesting story, and brutal combat.

Sometimes every now and then a game comes along that surprises you - renewing faith in a genre and reminding you exactly why you liked it in the first place.
With expectations low thanks to the prolific consolization and emphasis on creating cinematic experiences to the detriment of the game-play, Shadow Warrior benefits greatly from being a game that understands, first and foremost, a first person shooter is about combat.
A reboot of the 1997 game of the same name, aside from a few references, it's decidedly different style shooter. While the original had no story to speak of, with protagonist Low Wang, much in same vain as Duke Nukem acting as a pop culture spouting archetypes of 80's and early 90's action heroes, Lo Wang in the reboot, while retaining much of this is more fleshed out by virtue of having a personality - and a sense of purpose.
The story motivation itself is relatively simple. Low Wang must recover several blade parts, while a mystical story of demons from another realm unravels around it. Comparative to another FPS revival such as the New Order, with continual interruptions to game-play, long monotonous mumbling of self-important up it's own♥♥♥♥♥♥nonsense, Shadow Warriors story-telling never feels like it's a detriment to the gameplay or taking itself too seriously, remaining concise with an appropriate tonal shift towards the end the game - that sort of becomes poetic, without being Bioshock Infinite levels of pretentious, it's surprisingly moving considering the game is about a man who repeatedly makes♥♥♥♥♥♥jokes.
The story is there, if you want it - never over stepping the mark into obnoxious.
Much like Kurt Russell in Big Trouble In little China, (which was a clear inspiration for the first game), Low Wang is a goof, a legend in his own mind while paradoxically tripping over himself on a continued basis. An avid collectors of comic books, at one point the player will enter his weapon laden Batman cave, as he shaves his head in a self aware reference of the alpha male figures he aspires towards - it's both a reverential acknowledgment to the genres influence, while directly relating to the player, who probably isn't the coolest dude in the world.
Expecting old school shooting may lead to a huge disappointment for fans of the original, gone are maze like levels, replaced by Painkiller style arena battles. While old school elements are retained, such as rewarding exploration, simultaneously carrying a multitude of weapons, item pickup's in the form of health and armor and minimum plot, it carried over elements from Flying Wild Hogs previous game, while expanding upon it with action RPG elements - in many ways, it shares more in common with a game like Diablo or Devil May Cry than the original Shadow Warrior.
Essentially, player enters area, kills creatures, progresses, rinse and repeat.
This may sound repetitive, and towards the end of the game it can be - much like Diablo it's alleviated with a constant stream of crums in the form of upgrades, new enemies and sporadic bursts of narrative as well a changes of scenery to give the player just enough momentum to continue playing.
It doesn't seem hyperbole, to call the combat, sublime. On the lower difficult, spamming a few shots, or a few sword swings will quickly led to redundancy. On the higher "insane" difficulty, the context changes entirely.
In a similar games like Serous Sam - it uses huge environments with much of the combat at a distance, when enemies reach the player, it's almost entirely a case of pushing the backward key with largely inept weapons, Shadow Warrior on the other hand uses tighter environments to minimize downtime - implementing a dodge keys to make any direction viable, encouraging the player not to retreat but to actively move around mitigating crowds using their head on the fly. Very rarely will the player be still, or monotonously pushing the backward key, even healing itself can be done while going on the offensive, simultaneously shooting at the same or upgrading KI attacks to act as direct healing - respectfully limited .

Borderlands boasted very much about it's touted millions of weapons, yet all arguably feel the same without in anything other than a minimal alteration, comparatively, Shadow Warrior has half a dozen, with upgrades significantly changing both the damage output and play-style of the weapon.
To alleviate the problem of swinging disconnected melee synonymous with other games i.e. Bethesda titles - rather than spamming light and heavy swings as the primarily means of combat, Shadow Warrior focuses on double tap charge ups with single hit bursts minimizing the sense of disconnection and using the KI as a means to justify non connected attacks.

No, it won't blow you out of the water, and there is some anger warrented for the lack of upgrades and powers, BUT for 30 dollars it's well worth the price, and a must play on sale if you are itching for more Dishonored.
I haven't finishe it yet, but so far the story isn't absolutely stellar, but very interesting anyway. It gives a deeper look into the Void and the Outsider, as well as how deep corruption runs in the south. Seeing Daud again is wonderful, his character is lively (not literally, he's old and dying) and believable. Billie is an interesting character but doesn't strike me with the same wow or aw that is to be had with Corvo or Daud. (side note: look into Corvo's past, it's VERY interesting!)
Billie's writing and voice acting is top notch, so while her character isn't super intriguing, she is enjoyable.
The game is more difficult, and the way you're supposed to complete your objective isn't as obvious anymore. There is *slighty* less hand holding (thank the Outsider) and certainly less obvious comments from Billie. (seriously, Emily and Corvo had to state the obvious every 10 minutes in D2)
Gameplay does have some odd changes, such as your mana (Void Energy) is refilled infinitly and has 3 charges, rather than a bar. It's not a bad change, but not a good one. It makes powers less spammable, which doesn't bug me as I don't spam powers anyway. I think it was unneeded, but it is what it is so whatever.
Power! The three you get are very interesting, but it's a shame it's only 3. I love them nonethelss.
Gear! Also interesting, with some funny tropes like upgrading to shoot pens are people.
Length varies, if you only do the main story and skip side quests (contracts) you are cutting your playtime in half. The contracts do actually dove tail into the main story at times so they are worth  your time on that front. On top of that, they are interesting, new, and varied. To top it off they can get pretty difficult, too. I think they really are worth your time.
Overall, I'd say this game is worth the price and worth a play IF you want more lore and gameplay because you love the series, like me. If you're not incredibly interested in more gameplay and story, that doesn't massively change anything, then I'd say skip it.

This game is awesome! Really great mix of platforming and action.  Very, very polished game.  There is tons of things to do without it stretching thin or feeling dragged out. Quite the contrary, it's very consistent experience from start to finish, if not getting better and better.  There is a real sense of progression from start to finish.  New abilities that unlocks previously inaccessible areas (which also increase platforming variations), new moves, new spells.  There's no leveling in this game, only power-ups.   There's no grind at all.  In fact the resource you collected can feel useless late game (my only minor complaint).
The map is intricate, large, and interconnected.  There are so many hidden areas without them feeling absurdly hidden.
You can always find 99% of them if you are paying attention.  You don't really need guide, but chances are you'll need it if you want to 100% it.  But it's not really necessary.
The game is rather difficult.  But it's fair and reasonable, and you'll see yourself getting better and better at it. There are some high-difficulty optional late-game areas.  Some platforming challenge, some combat challenge, and a mix of both.
The story is told in a similar fashion to dark souls.  Sparse, disjointed pieces of information here and there without any handholding or exposition.  I'm not sure i understand it, but the atmosphere and art told a story by itself.  A dreamlike story of a desolate civilization below earth.
There's no weak point in this game.  I can't recommend this game enough.

First and foremost, I am a huge Final Fantasy fan and this is my first review of a Final Fantasy game! To this day Final Fantasy remains my favorite game franchise.
With that said, Final Fantasy XIII is in my opinion, one of the weakest installments in the series. The visuals are stunning, the music is utterly fantastic, the voice acting is pretty decent, but the characters kind of suck. The story, when combined with the characters really blows. However, I think the story could be much more appealing by simply having better quality characters to go with. And then there are my issues with overly linear gameplay and arguably highly simplified combat system.
Moving throughout the game feels like sitting in a cart in a theme park following a track. The freedom to venture off, sight see and explore is missing for most of the game. When you finally do get to explore, it’s just in one massive field. In previous FF games you can pilot an airship around the entire planet. But not in FFXIII. And personally, that is my biggest disappointment in the series since FFX was released.
The combat system is a cool idea, but I think it would be better suited for a mobile spin off version of the game. FFXIII deserves so much more when it comes to combat. No longer can you give your characters commands and masterfully build a strategy around their every move. Much like in XII, your characters are automated and basically play the game for you. I understand this is a solution to being able to make the fights have more movement in a shorter amount of time, but to me, having the game play for me just is not as fun. I do enjoy it a bit, but when compared to the older combat systems in previous titles, it does not hold up.
As far as the port to PC, it’s great that they did it, but they obviously do not understand their PC audience very well. They should have known how upset we would all be upon finding out the game is locked at 720p. There are seriously zero PC settings beyond “Windowed or Fullscreen?”. Thankfully, on day 1 a kind gentleman created a mod that unlocks the resolution and allows you to customize.
Despite my complaints, I hear good things about the sequels and plan on playing them as (if) they release on Steam. I am glad I played XIII, and even though it does not feel like a Final Fantasy game anymore, it has it’s moments that trigger feelings of nostalgia from previous titles. If you are already a fan of FF, jump into this expecting something completely different. If you are not, jump into this and enjoy, but do not judge the entire series through this game alone. The older ones are better.

This a great little game, you could say it's one of those hidden gems.
Although the playtime isn't that long, the visuals and music is incredible for a game that (most of the time) only costs 1$
You play as a small microorganism climbing the evolutionary ladder by eating one of three microelements:
-Red which makes your Sparkle (as your species is called) faster and more manouvrable, however at the cost of eating speed.
-Blue which makes your sparkle more balanced in the way of movement and eating speed but sadly looking quite uninteresting.
-Green which makes your sparkle incredible at eating with the highest eating speed and a skill that makes your mouth about 5x bigger, however it isn't very fast and his turning speed also ins't too great. However the green sparkle is in my opinion the best looking sparkle.
As you grow more and more instead of eating stationary microelements you start encountering species, most of which have ways of stopping you eating them often in the form of a slow trap. others take a long time to be fully eaten and until they are they will keep pushing you a level upwards if you touch their head, and others are relatively peaceful but require you to find a way into their body to eat their guts and finally decapitate them.
Each stage of evolution your sparkle evolves visually, at first growing longer and developing a type of sac to show you its road to the next level by the size of it, after that it will grow jaws or in the case of the omnivore it will grow even longer, after that evolution truly branches and  every sparkle will go it's own way, i will not spoil this because they look too beautiful to explain.
Though the levels are few (there are only 14) there are 2 optional boss battles, The Squid-Worm and the Octury.
The Squid-Worm is a large worm that requires you to eat all of his segments before eating his head, not too hard but it looks great and it's a fun way to show yourself how far you've come in your mad dash to become the top species in the sea.
The Octury is a humongous octopus that will make you eat all the glowing orbs on it's tentacles before entering it's head and devouring it from the inside out, though -once more not very challenging it's a huge monster that is great to look at in comparison to your little sparkle.
This is a great game and if you like Flow or need something relaxing in your library i definitely reccomend you to pick it up, it's very cheap and there are even trading cards to be gained.

The visuals in this game are very well done, varying from cute to creepy with surprising finesse. While I wouldn’t say Hollow Knight is on the same level as Ori and the Blind Forest in terms of its sheer wow-factor, it’s rendered in a unique art style that is always captivating to look at and works well for the precise sort of gameplay the game strives to achieve. Animations are smooth, and the developers did an excellent job of making the characters come alive in a fully 2D setting. Speaking of characters and animations, there are a shockingly large amount of both (in a good way!). In one particular area, after you’ve completed a certain objective, the animation for each enemy in the area changes to a completely new one; a change so appropriate and unexpected that it left me grinning with appreciation. That’s great! And it really shows the amount of work and care that went into this game.
Combat and platforming are, for the most part, very good (more on this later). Your offensive options in Hollow Knight are simple, and in the beginning stages of the game they feel limited and dull. Once you start encountering some tougher enemies and bosses, however, it becomes clear that the simplicity of combat is by design; success against the enemies is determined primarily by movement and timing, not flashy maneuvers. You’ve got spells and special abilities called Nail Arts as well, but the former use up the same pool of Soul that you use to heal and the latter and usually pretty situational. I didn’t use either very often, but that’s alright. There are a number of equippable charms in the game which affect your character in different ways, and a number of them improve the efficacy of spells or the practicality of Nail Arts. If I wanted to I could have used these charms, but the standard nail attack was satisfying enough for me so I stuck with that.
Many of the platforming segments are difficult, but usually this is because the game has a good item hidden away at the end of the section and you’re sufficiently rewarded upon completion of the segment. There are a few stinkers, though; I remember at least one difficult platforming section only rewarded me with a chest of geo (in-game currency), which wasn’t at all worth the effort as I already had too much geo. My main problem with the platforming sections is that each time you’re hit by a spike or pool of acid, you take damage; in order to heal, you’ve got to use some of your limited Soul pool. This means that you have a limited amount of attempts at a given platforming segment before you need to take a break and go grind enemies in order to get back your soul. This feels clunky, and after playing Ori and the Blind Forest it feels like a step backwards that doesn’t improve the game at all. I think there’s a charm you can get later that makes your health slowly regenerate, but this would still require you to wait after failing a jump too many times.
Exploration is wonderful! The world in this game is very big, and you’re not given a map until you find the map maker in each area. This makes each new area feel mysterious and dangerous, and it makes finding the map maker an excellent reward. You really feel like you’re trekking new ground and making progress as you explore and your world map expands, which is a great feeling and very satisfying. There are secret areas galore, and you’re given every reason to go back and revisit previous areas once you’ve got new movement abilities. Unfortunately, you can only fast travel from certain benches (basically checkpoints), and shopkeepers are spread across the map, which means you’ll be going through areas you’ve already fully explored very often. I don’t actually like this; I think the game would have been improved by allowing fast traveling from every bench, because a lot of the traveling to fast travel stations is just down time that isn’t particularly engaging. That’s an issue, but it’s certainly not game-breaking, and a lot of people probably prefer that sort of hands-off approach to travel.
So I’ve mentioned a couple of small issues up to this point, but aside from that it sounds like I really enjoyed the the game -- so what gives? Why have I given it a thumbs down? I know that many people are going to disagree with me on this one, but I feel a certain obligation to relate my opinion as accurately as possible for a game that left me as mixed feelings as Hollow Knight.
It’s the difficulty. There’s a strong taboo in the gaming community against saying that you think a game is too hard, but I don’t even think I’m necessarily trying to say that. I think what I’m trying to say that the game is too frustrating; I don’t think I’ve ever seen a game as simultaneously well-polished yet strictly anti-player as Hollow Knight. During my exploration of one area, I fought some really tough enemies and climbed high up a series of platforms. I reached the top, found an optional area that I wasn’t interested in yet, traveled left, and then found a shortcut back down to an earlier area. Great! The last bench was a long while ago, so I could use a shortcut. I hopped down the long hole and landed at the bottom shortly after. To my horror, this “shortcut” wasn’t a shortcut at all; it simply plopped you down in an earlier area with no way of climbing back up to where you were. In order to get back to where I was, I had to go through the entire difficult area again and complete the same series of platforms. Dying wasn’t an option; I had too much geo, and the vendor who could help me with that was a long ways away. I was very frustrated because of this.
Sure, I got back to where I was, and it didn’t take me that long admittedly, but it left me with an unpleasant feeling. This was a trick put in by the developers that didn’t lead to any reward or new challenge; all that happened as a result was my having to repeat an area. When I finally got back to where I was, I didn’t feel rewarded; I felt relieved, and that’s not what I want out of a video game. I’ve finished all three Dark Souls games and Bloodborne and loved them all; what those games usually do is present a negative stimulus (a hard boss or area) that you’ve got to overcome, and when you do, you’re presented with a positive stimulus as a reward (a new item, lots of souls, a new area) that overcomes the negative stimulus. In Hollow Knight, often times the games merely presents a negative stimulus (having to repeat an area) without bothering to give you a sufficient reward. That’s where that sense of relief comes from; the negative stimulus is removed, and that’s all you get. That’s all an oversimplification, but I hope you can see what I mean.
Additionally, a few of the bosses feel cheap and unfair. One boss has an attack where he dashes at you from across a dark room. That’s fair! That’s fine, I just jump over that attack, and it’s telegraphed by a running noise. Cool. The problem is, sometimes he stops his run in an instant, and starts shooting projectiles at you; so you judged your jump and dash based on the boss’s trajectory and momentum, but since the boss somehow lost all momentum in an instant without a telegraph, you end up landing right on top of him instead of to his side. Touching enemies deals damage, so you take a hit. All things considered, this boss still isn’t affirmatively too hard, but in fighting it I did die a few deaths that I felt were not my fault, and when I finally beat it, I didn’t feel like I had overcome a challenge. I felt like I lucked out, and that this time the boss didn’t use his instant stop attack too often.

This game has got a lot going for it, and I’m sure that some people will appreciate the hyper-difficulty and anti-player nature of some areas. There's plenty of content here, though; 28 sets of puzzles altogether, and the size of each set is based on the size of the boards within (3x3 boards have 9 puzzles, 4x4 boards have 16, up to 6x6 which have 36 each). I don't think it's the kind of game that you can play a lot of in one sitting, though, but as a game to occasionally come back to to keep your mind sharp, I'd definitely recommend it.

A surprising game that caught me by surprise with pricing and alleged content, Hollow Knight is a refreshing sight to behold with it’s visual designs, great OST, excellent atmosphere and fun (albeit a bit frustrating) bosses. The gameplay itself seems to be a “harder” version of the Metroidvania genre and despite a few gripes with the movement, it still handles very well. Still it does have a few flaws, such as the back-tracking (that can consume a lot of your time, but it’s being resolved by the dev team), a few questionable level design with a few areas that aren’t more varied (Greenpath is an example) and the game starts too slow at the beginning, then it increments the pace with each ability acquired (before acquiring a few abilities, it was a tiresome experience, then it speeds up considerably).
The game in it’s current state is a pretty complete experience and with 40 hours or less, you should be able to obtain the desirable “100%” completion of the game, yet there are more content then what it informs and the new updates that have been received and are still coming to the game will surely prolong the experience.
For the price i paid, even if discounted, was on par with the content you would find on more pricey games. I can surely recommend this game for those that like the genre and for the different aesthetic with a theme that involves insectoids. If you are not suited for quick-paced games and/or higher than average difficulty, then this might not be the game for you.

This is a great game.  I've always loved TCG's (mostly MTG and Yugioh back in the day) and they were fun but I've always known that they could be done better on a computer.  An online digital card game can do so many things that a physical TCG can't (like animated cards, auto match-making, zero rule disputes) and Infinity Wars totally nails it.  If you've ever played MTGO *shudder* then you'll be dumbfounded by how poor an it is in comparison to IW.
Solid excecution aside, Infinity Wars also succeeds on the artwork side of things.  Any collector/player would probably agree that card art is an important part of getting involved with these games.  The artists for IW know what they're doing.  The cards look fantastic and they're animated to boot.  It's dark/gritty comic-book feel and just looks awesome.
Finally, and most importantly, we have gameplay.  Here is where I think the game should really take off.  It's completely original and operates totally different from any TCG I've ever playeed.  One of the most interesting things about it (going back to what a digital game can do that a physical one can't) is that people plan and execute their turns simultaneously.  Nobody gets to go "first" and you're generally not having to deal with a lot of the annoying "priority" issues that you find in games like MTG.  This completely changes the dynamics and tempo of the gameplay and it's a lot of fun.
I would recommend anyone who likes TCG's to try this out.  It's free to start and you can actually get a lot of gaming in without buying anything.  So far I've spent about $25 and I'm holding my own in the ranked queues pretty well.

The game difficulty raises slow and usually it becomes harder with more colors. It starts at 3x3 fields and 2 colors, later it goes up to 5x5 and 5 colors and 6x6 and 4 colors.

I'm not playing this for long but i was suprised how much of a copy of MTG it seems to be, positively. Surely it looks different but if you know MTG well enough you will notice that its basically the same with slight changes. You will declare attackers and defenders aswell, just not in the form of tapping but in the form of moving the cards to specific areas. Cast creatures cant be moved to any of those areas instead they are resting in the Support area whey they cant attack or block.
The biggest Changes to MTG are:
No mana cards - You get +1 Mana every turn
Mana is colorless
Players make their moves at the same time
Monster HP does not reset at the end of the turn
And the most weirdest part, 1 Monster can block every attacking Monster if it has enough HP and propably destroy every attacker.
So basically it feels like a slightly easier MTG and fans, just like me, could enjoy it.

There is a store available just like any other free to play game where you can buy booster packs, decks, and aethetic changes such as icons, card backs, and battlefields (the area in which the cards are played). While at first, I was having a lot of fun with this game, it became a little too grindy for my tastes.
The first half of the missions straddle the tactics/tower placement/hero skill tree perfectly, and I was enjoying exploring the various classes and their skill trees to change up my tactics, or find ones best suited to the maps I was playing.
However, the second half of the game is far too frustrating because it always feels like not matter what you do, it's not enough. The best way for me to explain this game is that it feels like a F2P game that had in app purchases to "quick buy" skill points and the better items, except, even if you wanted to do that, that option is not there and time is the only investment.
Again, a mostly fun experience that got really frustrating. After 19 hours I've had some fun with this game, but it's time to move on. A "no" rating from me, unless you're looking for a squad/skill upgrade tower defense game AND you've already played the excellent Defender's Quest.

It's exactly what it says on the tin -- tower defence, and an over-the-top one at that.
Good for laughs and some gratuitous carnage. It boils the genre down to the bare minimum; but then hand-waves most of the negative aspects of that decision with its sheer level of over-the-top chaos and comedy.
You can't set targeting priorities, the tower locations are limited and predetermined (so it's a challenge of filling the limited space with the right combo of towers in the right order), the hero units become very powerful very early (they have progressive levelling so you can grind out early missions to unlock their higher upgrades before moving on) but at this rate will probably fall away in the later game... in short, if you're a die-hard enthusiast of the more traditional tower defence genre then this game may be too simplistic for your tastes; but if you want a straightforward game that *feels* like a modern tower defence game then OTTTD fits the bill.
And it's a big bill -- HeroCorp's services don't come cheap, apparently. Fortunately the game price is down the low end of the scale; plus you'll get all the sushi you can eat. This game takes "paint the map red" to a whole new level.

I really like this game. Why? Because I came to it without hoping it to be a DLC to CIV5 nor a sequel Alpha Centauri. It's its own game. Basically the game comes down to this: take the engine and main concepts of CIV5, set it in space so it plays like the end game of CIV5 with even the melee units using guns, take some concepts from Alpha Centauri like alien life that can be used in a multitude of ways and a tech tree that isn't linear and is full of branches, throw in some other amazing mechanics and you have this game.
Could you say that this is somekind of frankenstein project? Yes, but when it takes the better of both worlds it's hard to complain. But I will still make my points based on CIV5
Breaking down the systems:
Units: there's way less units than in CIV5, but that's easily overcome by the amount of customization you get for each unity. The level up of the units doesn't give you those branching choices from CIV5 (that in the end didn't matter much because you choose them depending on your current situation) but now you have the upgrade system that's based on your affinity, for each new level of affinity you get to choose between 2 bonus for the unit. There's even some unitys that are multi affinity (the Xenoswarm is the unity you get from harmony, but at the second level they can get a different perk if you also have a little of purity or supremacy). Units go from melee, ranged, siege, naval and flying. Flying has been changed from what I remember from CIV5, they can't leave the city they are currently attached to, wich makes them a very powerful unit that is limited to their range.
Cities:
Instead of just settling a new city you first build it as a outpost, in theory this sounds different from CIV5, but it isn't, you will only have a little delay before getting the city to work, 5 turns more or less. City management is exactly the same as in 5 from what I see. You can build tile improvements, buildings, assign specialists, create wonders, convert a resource into another and so on. The one thing that is different is how the game was nerfed regarding resources. In CIV5 I would build roads in every tile in my cities, now the money (it's called energy like in AC) is a lot more hard to come by, basically because the whole game is more slowed down, it takes more turns for workers to create things. And that's amazing to me, makes you think more. And now instead of happiness you have health in your city, so there's no more luxury resources.
Diplomacy:
This is the part that made me feel frustated, it's same as CIV5. It's actually worse if you take into consideration that now there isn't anymore luxury resources, only strategic ones. So you can only trade for strategic resources. The rest is exactly the same, even the text in the buttons are the same.
Tech:
Now we have a tech web instead of a tree. It has branches and leafs. To reasearch a leaf you must first reasearch the branch. Some leafs give you affinity points, so you will probably get some affinity from another path at some point. But it works so wonderfully well that I feel that going back to a game of CIV5 will be painful. Because it's a web you can ignore certain techs, you don't need to reasearch everything, it's so open I find myself forgeting to get some units because I was focused in another area. It looks like there's less techs compared to CIV5 but they all feel more useful.
Orbital layer:
A very nice new addition, you can launch satellites to give you temporary bonus or even attack enemies. This helps when you see that you are starting to lose money and don't have time to create more tiles to produce it, just launch some solar sattelites to give a little more time to fix the situation.
Covert ops:
I wouldn't say this is a upgrade to the old spionage system, this is a new system. You use your spys much more actively in this game. You can ask them to steal money, steal techs, attract huge alien worms to cities and so on, but unlike in CIV5 where you just wait, here they can get killed by the other faction spies, they can suceed but get caught in the process. And you can't just go to a city and begin stealing techs or troops, you need to raise your threat level first, set a network and begin stealing things from the first levels until you can do more important things.
Quests:
This is nothing like I thought it would be, it's actually meaningful. It gives you great bonuses for completing them. Some of them have a good backstory too. I got one where a ship crashed in the planet and when I went to investigate there were heavily modified humans from another planet settled before the one I was. I got the choice to either accept them in the planet or kill them on sight, I let them stay, them another quest showed so that I could either give them shelter (+1 population in the capital) or let them be on their own (a station appears, more on that later). Beyond this there's building quests, (that aren't really quests, I think they need another name). Every building that you construct for the first time gives you one, and you need to choose between two options. The outcome will affect every other building of the same type. You can get bonus like more hit points from a defense system or make them have no maintenence cost.
Stations:
The replacement of city states, but instead of being min civs they are now only trade routes. You can destroy them, the AI love to, but I don't see a reason to do it, it only gives you some money and another resource, they are better working as trade hubs.
Trade routes:
Since resources seem to come slower, trade routes are something you will not want to miss. But they are the worst thing in the game. Why? Because when you trade convoy is back from a route it will ask again wich route you want it to do, and they come back fast, so you will spend a lot of time searching through countless trade routes wich one was the previous, the game does show it, but it's very hard to notice.
Fighting:
The same as CIV5, move, attack, kill, level up, die.
Miasma:
A hurtful alien poison, that plagues almost 50% of the map. With harmony you can actually be healed by it after you get a certain level or a certain tech. You can even use it in your favour. Pretty straight forward but a nice addition nonetheless.
Starting a game:
We no longer have a wide range of civs to choose from, but this is made up for the amount of customization the game has and the beginning bonus you choose: sponsor (basically the civ), colonist types, spacecraft, cargo.
take a look at it for yourself. This really impact the early game. And mid game you get to choose the affinity wich is what change the game the most.
Final verdict: if you want a sequel to Alpha Centauri, don't get this game, you WILL be disappointed. If you come nitpicking for CIV5 elements you get a lot them, because for ♥♥♥♥'s sake this is a civilization spin off game. Buy the game if you want the same CIV you already know how to play set in a futuristic world with some very good twists. Only buy it if you can get behind these facts.

After 15+ hours invested in this amazing platformer I have finally finished the first playthrough. Man, was it:
- Tough! Many of the levels pushed me to my platforming limits, sometimes because of the controls being imprecise (although you get used to them) but more often than not because the game asks you to make a lot of difficult jumps.
- Logically challanging/puzzles are well designed. Many of the levels especially later in the game are complete brain twisters. Each new mechanic adds a new dimension (sic) to the complexity. Usually you can squeeze by with a few orbs but collecting them all more often than not requires a much different attack plan on where to go and how to approach the level.
- Frustrating! No save points in levels means you will be starting from scratch every time you die (and you will die a lot my counter ended up at 1200 deaths or so). The biggest frustration came from the wall of doom levels, but arm yourself with patience they are doable you just need to slowly progress through deaths to know whats around the corner, and keep track of the whole level in your mind until you master it.
- Beautiful. Really digging the art style and the tiling engine here (and especially different worlds) provides a lot of good variety.
- Funny! The story is nothing amazing but the way its communicated had me chuckle quite a few times. The lines can be super cheezy but given the setting they are intentionally so and it mostly works. Ariel can be super annoying at times though, you will learn to ignore it until the end :) I did wish for a mute button a few times, but it passed momentarily
- Addictive! No matter how many times you die, or you get mad, you will be back. Usually once I got stuck, taking a break and tackling the level fresh allowed me to uncover the path forward. Levels being difficult are extremely rewarding when finished and you will be coming back for more.
- Adaptable! There's "Easy mode" if you want it, although I really haven't tried it. If the difficulty is too much for you, as I understand, it provides a lot less repetition should you die with save points and gives you a lot more time in racing levels.
- Joy to navigate! Next to no backtracking needed due to clever teleportation system in the menus (which are great overall)!
- Cross platform! Nuf said.
The negatives I have are mostly centered on:
- Repelants in the last world and water bouncing. They are super hard to predict if your jumps are going to make it or not, or in what direction you will be flung. I felt like this boosted the difficulty for no good reasons.
- Difficulty curve spikes very fast in the first world after level 4-5. More gradual introduction would have appeased less experienced players.
- Most mechanics are introduced properly but not all. One example if pushing blocks in the desert, or gaining speed off of ice scating/gravitational shifts to do large jumps. You do discover those on your own but only after a lot of experimenting.
- The soundtrack is ok, I love the main theme, but it seems prevelant in every song in different flavors and as such gets a bit dull over time.
My initial experience was little shaky, but the more I played the game more I really enjoyed it. Give it a go if you like difficult puzzle platformers I doubt you will want to miss this masterpiece.

So I'm having a blast with the game so far.  The improvements over FS13 are pretty dramatic in a lot of areas.  The vehicle modeling is vastly improved, showing far more detail and complexity in various areas.  The cabins now have fully-functioning side mirrors and all the dashboard dials are fully animated.  Combined with the new lighting engine, the collection of vehicles and equipment are far more gorgeous than they have any right to be in a mere Sim title.
On the downside, the environments look largely the same as FS13.  You can notice sharper texture work all around (buildings, stone walls, etc.) but harvest-ready wheat, canola, corn, etc. seems carried over from the last game.  The biggest offender is the draw distance, which hasn't changed much.  I know it can be difficult to render natural environments with expansive, flat planes that stretch on forever, but the graphical fill-in render distance feels way too short.
It's not all bad on the environmental front.  There's been numerous upgrades as well.  Vehicles leave tire tracks behind them and kick up dust.  Harvesting fruit is now fully animated (instead of simply disappearing when collected, it's now cut-down and pulled through the rotating header blades).  Similarly, treated soil is now animated when plowed and cultivated, showing churning dirt under the blades instead of a simple texture swap in FS13.  Vehicles now get muddy with prolonged use.  A handy high-pressure sprayer allows you to manually wash them off.  I do think the dirt accumulation happens way too fast though.  I like effect, but your equipment can get completely covered in mere minutes.  I'll be looking forward to a mod that stretches out dirt accumulation over a longer period.
As advertised the physics engine has undergone a full overhaul.  Vehicles now have weight to them.  You can feel it when you're pulling heavier equipment and your speed pulls back when riding up inclines.  Equipment is now power-rated, meaning low-rpm tractors can not pull larger loads as there's a minimum threshold they must meet.   Overall, the machinery feels heavier and more substantive, like they stick to the ground vs. flying off on the slightest whim in FS13.  There's also been an upgrade in the audio dept. as engine sounds are deeper and more guttural, adding to the sense of authenticity.
Side missions are handled more intelligently in the new game.  Instead of having them pop up at pre-set intervals, you instead travel job boards located around the map and pick from a list of job opportunities.  You still have lawn-mowing and pallet delivery missions, but they've also added 'great demand' requests for various grains.  Picking when and what you want to do makes you feel more in control of collecting extra coin when needed.
So all in all I'm really enjoying my time with Farming Simulator 15.  It's just as Zen & relaxing as ever, only this time out if feels entirely Bigger, Better, & More Bad♥♥♥♥♥  The game feels like it's come into its own and is finally in the Big Leagues.  It's met all my "upgrade expectations" that were set in motion during the initial media rollout and info dump regarding new graphics and physics engines.  Honesty, when standing FS13 and FS15 side by side, I can't help but think about the all-around qualitative leap from Euro Truck Simulator to Euro Truck Simulator 2.  ETS2 was a breakout hit for SCS Software that had enough crossover appeal to even help legitimize the oft-stigmatized Mundane Vehicle Simulator (tm.) genre with the masses.  I'm now wondering if it's FS15's turn to make a similar leap in awareness and appreciation.  Seeing it sit at #1 on the Steam Top Sellers chart every day since release has been a positive nod in that direction.
Side note: Been playing for over 7 hours and I haven't even touched the new Logging feature set, so I have no feedback in that regard.  I've never been into money-cheat mods, opting instead to build my empire up from the ground floor, adding to my fleet piece by incremental piece.  I'll get there in due time.  I'm in no hurry.

At the release price, I can't recommend this game to anyone unless they have not purchased civilization 5. I tried to tell myself that enough stuff would be changed that it was more than a reskinning of civ 5 with a sci-fi theme, aliens instead of barbs, a reorganized/different take on the tech tree/social policies. I was wrong. After playing it for a while now, I can't help but feel cheated that this was sold as a standalone new IP and not a standalone civ 5 expansion (cheaper). I also feel like they left out NEEDED content with plans for DLC/expansions.
Positives
- webbed tech tree
- orbital units - the only real addition vs mod of civ 5
- core civ 5 gameplay mechanics (unit types, combat, economy (every resource is merely rebranded)) - which made that a great game, but also a negative when viewed as part of a BRAND NEW game (see below)
- quests, allow you to customize your experience, but with a caveat - see below
- tweaking of espionage system
Negatives
- much of the core game has been borrowed from civ 5 - this is only a step beyond what a creative modder could do with civ 5 - a very small step - the orbital units just sit on a different layer and provide various area of effect modifiers (maybe some attack, I have not used all). This was possibly beyond a modder in Civ 5, but as one of the only REAL additions to the game, is it enough to justify the game? re-organizing a tech tree is also not very hard for a huge triple AAA company...
- eight starting "sponsors" ----civilizations - really, only 8 really??? Yes, there are other customization options when you start, but the bonuses that made each civilization feel unique have been removed. No custom units based on your start choice.  There are overall less interesting choices, and you can just customize a few options as to how you like to start a game (start with a worker vs a building in town for example, or bonus to culture vs bonus to energy (gold)).
- the aliens, TOO few:       Wow, I mean they at least have unit variety (some melee, some melee with extra movement, some ranged, a few tough wandering melee, a few ocean dwelling aliens), but that runs it's course rather fast. Ask yourself this, with all of the borrowed assets from Civ 5 - which the game engine and core mechanics are arguably the hardest to develop - why is there only one set of aliens? This game is bone-jarringly terrible and it's not what it claims to be.
There is no meaningful amount of freedom in this game.  You're allowed a few starting choices such as which guild you want to start with and which faction you want to ally with.  From there, you're often railroaded through scenes without even the illusion of choice.
For example, I wanted to play a persuasive assassin for my first play-through.  A rogue who uses poison and guile to perform their vile tasks.  No, that's not possible.  Spoiler alert: you're going to kill your first mark with a crossbow whether you like it or not.
From there you'll notice the terrible writing.  It's awful.  The content is like something from a Jerry Springer script.  Which is disappointing, because story was advertised as one of the highlights of this game.  For example, certain NPCs swear because this world is 'edgy'.  That would be fine, but for two reasons.  1) They swear like they're disgruntled teenagers from the modern world.  The language used and the way it's presented clash with the setting.  2) The profanity is a placeholder for actual content.  I have absolutely no idea why half of these people are swearing so much because there's nothing in the script illustrating why they feel the way they do.
The combat is half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥  It's dull.  Simply not good.  There's no dynamism.  You select from a lame, text-based menu which attack you'd like to perform, then you run away.  You keep doing this until one side dies.  And yes, the combat is balanced to present you with a fair chance of dying.  But it's not difficult because it takes skill.  It takes no skill.  It simply requires you to have built your character to be a combat character.  If you're not a combat character, you're simply going to die if you get into combat.  There's no way to talk your way out of it, either, once you're in it.  And some setups throw you into combat with no warning.  It's punishing, but not at all made with any sort of an eye for gameplay.
Without freedom of choice, a good story or good combat, I find there's just no reason to play this game.  Which makes me very curious about all the positive reviews it's received.  If you look at the negative reviews, the majority of them seem fairly well-written.  However, they're heavily downvoted.  All of them.  And all of the positive reviews are heavily upvoted.  To me, this says that these guys either have a rabid fan base, or they're paying for positive reviews and favorable up/down-votes.  Either way, it feels like there's some seriously dirty false advertising going on.

Civilization: Beyond Earth may not break any boundaries, but it is still an enjoyable new addition to Sid Meier's legacy. Certainly nowhere near SMAC - which the devs have been trying to highlight for some time - Beyond Earth changes the formula up enough to make it feel more than just a reskin.
Beyond Earth puts you in control of a set of colonists sent into deep space in order to find a new Earth. At the start of the game, you are given several choices to make regarding your sponsor, space craft, and initial colonists – besides the choice for sponsor, which is like choosing your Civ, every other choice directly affect your early game, which plays a bigger part in this iteration of Civ.
Once your colonists land and set your first city, you are given an explorer unit plus any bonus unit based on your choices at set up. Like Civ, early exploration is key in getting an early advantage; however that is more emphasized in Beyond Earth, with the presence of resource pods and excavation sites. Resource pods are exactly the same as ancient ruins in Civ, giving a random bonus when you pick it up. Excavation/artefact sites are very much like the excavation sites in Brave New World, except that you gain a random bonus from them without losing your explorer, although it would have to go back to one of your cities to gain back an excavation module.
One key area that the game tries to emphasize are the aliens on the planet. Aliens are present from the very moment you make planetfall, and are quite hard to face head-on without upgrades, but become nearly a non-issue after you grab a few upgraded units. These aliens are mainly docile when left alone, but they can turn aggressive if you step too close to a nest, which spawns new aliens. In time, and, depending on your affinity, you can train your own alien troops to fight for you.
Unit progression works differently than in Civ – you have a few base units to work with initially, which improve as your gain levels in your affinity, your moral alignment of sorts which also leads to certain victory conditions depending on which affinity you choose. Once you level up your affinity, certain units get to be upgraded – all units usually receive a combat boost, but you get to choose side-upgrades, such as additional movespeed, bonuses for attacking with friendly units around, bonuses for flanking, and so on – while nowhere as deep and complex as SMAC’s custom unit set up, this gives a twist to the way units work in contrast to Civ V.
Along with unit upgrades working differently, Beyond Earth adds a 4th unit type - orbital units - which occupy their own special layer, the orbital layer. Orbital units have a limited life span, and crash down as salvage as soon as their lifetime ends. Placing them is also tricky, as orbital units cannot have any overlapping areas, thereby forcing you to plan ahead in plopping them down. They accomplish various things, from removing miasma, to generating resources, and bombarding enemy units and cities.
The tech tree has been replaced with a tech web – each major research area has a “leaf” research which costs more to finish, but gives a bunch of benefits. Culture remains present in the game, but gone are social policies – you have three virtues, which give you varying bonuses, along with bonuses for choosing x amount of tier 1, 2, and 3 virtues from each branch.
Graphically, Beyond Earth is not so different from Civ V – the interface feels wholly the same, and, while the units, buildings, and landscape have changed a bit, it is still most certainly running on the same engine as Civ V. Leader screens are a bit of a letdown, as there is no special backdrop to negotiations – just a blur filter passed onto the map while you talk to a leader.
Victory conditions have changed in Beyond Earth – you have to fulfil goals and objectives towards each of the victory conditions, which require you to be on certain affinities. Domination is still present, however, if you wish to go about global conquest. The victory conditions are interesting enough, although some are a bit tedious, particularly the Promised Land condition.
Overall, Beyond Earth changes enough to be interesting, and more than just a reskin of Civ V, although barely. It lacks a certain personality to it, perhaps largely due to the leaders being very bland. If you’ve been looking for a mix-up to Civ V’s formula for a change, this brings that along. A good game that would’ve been better with much more, but is still worth checking out.

The Final Fantasy fanbase is a bunch that cannot make up it’s mind. With each new installment, you have a faction of the fanbase who wants the old, classic ATB battle system back. Then you also have the faction that wants something new and edgy. Anytime Square-Enix delivers one or the other, the fanbase causes an uproar….wanting the other! With this in mind, know that with Final Fantasy XIII….you will either love it or hate it, depending on which faction you belong to.
Final Fantasy XIII is a great game.
It's fairly linear though, but that doesn't hinder it in a bad way. It actually brings the story to the forefront of the game experience. Final Fantasy X was exactly the same, but is praised by fans as being one of the best FF titles to date (very close to VII), while FFXIII got a lot of hate after it’s initial release. Why is FFXIII different?
That's the thing: It's not!
Final Fantasy XIII takes place in a society called Cocoon, which exists in a large sphere that hangs in the sky over the world of Pulse. The citizens live in constant fear of invasion from the surface after an attack centuries earlier cracked open the shell of their world, and rely entirely on the fal'Cie, godlike creatures that provide Cocoon with everything it needs to exist — food, weather...even light. While Cocoon's fal'Cie are revered as benevolent protectors, the fal'Cie of Pulse are feared and demonized, to the point that anyone who comes in contact with anything from Pulse is considered tainted. When a Pulse fal'Cie is discovered in their own society, a chain of events leads the government to purge an entire city of civilians, and leads six strangers to become l'Cie, servants of the Pulse fal'Cie who must complete their appointed task or suffer a fate worse than death.
The story is fast-paced and filled with mysteries that unravel as the game progresses, and it's paced perfectly, with cutscenes popping up as you move through each area. The characters are also fantastic, each presenting themselves as a typical JRPG archetype in the beginning, but quickly showing much more depth. Furthermore, each character is tied to the story of the game; there are no incidental characters filling out your party, and likewise there is no main character. Final Fantasy XIII is about the overall group, and this is further emphasized by dividing them into separate groups on separate paths before they join together again for the second half.
Final Fantasy XIII's weakest link is unfortunately the beginning. The first few hours of the game see keywords like Pulse, l'Cie, and fal'Cie thrown at you without any context or explanation to their meaning. The characters also lack any kind of development for the first few hours, and the result is a confusing plotline with uninteresting characters that leaves a terrible first impression.  The combat system is completely stripped of the depth is shows later on. The player barely needs to pay attention for these early battles, and coupled with some extremely linear level design, the first three hours are unquestionably a low-point for both the game and the series.
And then Final Fantasy XIII really begins. The Crystarium, the game's answer to leveling up, becomes available, and likewise so does the Paradigm system, the meat and potatoes of Final Fantasy XIII's combat system. When this all becomes available, it becomes readily apparent why you've been spamming "Auto-Battle", and why you'll continue to spam it for the next fifty hours. The combat isn't about the nitty-gritty details of individual spells, it's about the overall strategy. Just as Final Fantasy XII gave you control through gambits, Final Fantasy XIII lets you play the general in the same way by rapidly changing between sets of classes in the heat of battle, altering tactics to suit the ever-changing situations that come up. The AI is extremely intelligent, and can select appropriate skills faster and with as much efficiency as most players, anyways.
Each character has access to three primary classes, and the Paradigm system allows you to create customized class set-ups that you can switch between at any time during combat. If you're on the offensive, a Commando and two Ravagers can effectively decimate an enemy. If you're looking at a longer fight, a Saboteur/Synergist team can drastically increase your fighting power. Facing a powerful foe? Bring out a Sentinel and let them tank while the other two lay the hurt on. Each class has a unique and important purpose, and while most fights can be completed with different strategies, many of the boss fights require rather specific ones in order to be successful.
The environments aren't the only amazing visuals Final Fantasy XIII boasts; the character/enemy models should not be sold short. The characters easily have some of the most realistic and believable facial expressions ever produced in a video game. Every emotion the characters experience is mirrored flawlessly on their face, and while the designs retain a hint of anime influence, they are still shockingly realistic.
Of course, this realism would be marred without solid vocal support, and for the most part Final Fantasy XIII delivers it. While not quite approaching the level of quality seen in Final Fantasy XII, the vocal cast of XIII nonetheless perform admirably, and this in spite of the lengthy monologues each character performs on a regular basis, true to form for a JRPG. The only weak point in the vocals is Vanille, which in the early parts of the game is rather grating. To her credit, the performance improves dramatically.
The musical score is also excellent. The main battle theme is similarly exciting and gets stuck in your head easily. While wandering dungeons, the music gets a bit more eclectic. Other tracks deviate from the usual, melodic Final Fantasy style and delve instead into techno and other styles.
Like Final Fantasy XII before it, Final Fantasy XIII has unquestionably caused cause a rift between those who love it and those who don't. As long as you don't judge the game on its beginning, Final Fantasy XIII is a game worthy of the series, and a terrific game.

I would never have thought that there'll be any games that will rival my love for Dark Souls, but here it is, a game made by technically a 2-man studio with the help of a few extra hands. Easily 40-60 hours of worthwhile content if you 100% the game and explore everything.
Great progression, fantastic attention to detail, beautiful hand-drawn everything and magnificent music. Team Cherry have a great developer's attitude that I wish more indies had; not overpricing their game, not being blinded by "industry standards" or trying to comform to a specific genre.
The added detail in places where only the most vigilant will ever find it makes exploring very rewarding. The NPCs you meet are interesting and have a story, most you will meet in several places in the world as they are also travelling and doing their own missions. There are a ton of extra dialogue depending on what actions you've taken or what items you have in your inventory or equipped. The amount of content for such a small dev team is truly astonishing.

I'd say that for the full $30 price, it might not be worth it as it is quite short depending on how quickly you play. If you can get this during a Steam sale then I would highly recommend it. It definitely feels less like a full game and more like a DLC/Expansion for Dishonored 2.
With that in mind, it's a nice addition to the Dishonored series. It expands the lore and provides and interesting new perspective to the mysterious deity, The Outsider. The voice acting is solid and the game plays as great as the other installments. The graphics are on par with Dishonored 2 with a few improvements and the realistic/painterly style looks as good as ever. I've read some people complaining about the story but I didn't have any real problems with it with the suspension of disbelief you've already have going into the Dishonored universe.
There are some welcome additions to the Dishonored gameplay in this installment, such as regenerating "mana" used to power your supernatural abilities instead of going around carrying vials of potions. Only 3 of these supernatural abilities are usable by your character in this game, but I didn't find that to be an issue becauseI usually just stick to a few of the abilities in any Dishonored game anyway. The Displace ability is familiar to players of the previous games, being just another permutation of the Blink ability albeit with some interesting modifications. Semblence is useful for gaining access to areas that are otherwise difficult to access via stealth by essentially stealing a persons likeness. Finally, the Forsight ability becomes extremely useful for recon and to plan out your route of attack. You can also use Foresight to remotely plant Displace markers for teleportation which allows you to get into some places earlier than you normally would or to otherwise go places that you wouldn't be able to go. The upgrades are fairly limited, mostly focusing on the equipment you carry with a few upgrades available for your character. A NewGame+ mode allows you to play throught the game with abilities from Dishonored 2 but I have yet to do a playthrough that way.
All in all, I would say that this game is Dishonored gameplay boiled down to it's most basic elements and it thrives within that. It's an excellent expansion to Dishonored 2, not exactly a full game. If you're a fan of the Dishonored series then you will definitely enjoy this game.

Molded after classic FPS that occasionally misses the mark.
You are Lo Wang (which gives you a pretty good idea what most of the humor is going to be like), a mafia hit-man sent to get a sword. But as typical with such transactions, you don't get the sword, kill a few dozen people, and betray your boss to join forces with a demon.
You blast your way through several demon filled chapters, picking up weapons, skills and powers, all of which can all be upgraded via money, karma, and ki respectively. You also have a sword giving you ammo saving options. Combat typically consists of being locked in an area a mowing down various demons (often with reinforcements spawning in). Clear the area to move onto the next and repeat with occasional boss chapters. The story is more fleshed out than your typical shoot em up (though not by much) and hoji (your demon ally) occasionally chimes in with commentary. They graphics are fine, though there isn't much scenery and the music is solid.
I've completed 2 runs of the game and have no interest in heroic mode (insane difficulty without saves). But managed to get about 50 hours of game play. Ultimate mode comes with the soundtrack, 2 re-skins, and a digital art book.
The combat, is, a bit complicated. Mouse fires and alt fires (RMB) your weapons. However, the powers require double taps of directional keys and mouse (forward, forward, RMB for example). This makes using your powers in conjunction with your weapons tricky. So you can't charge a power while alt-fire or reloading. Also, your dash/dodge is the shift key so avoiding attacks while shooting and charging up a power can be cumbersome.
The guns feel a bit underwhelming. You have a pistol, uzi, cross-bow, shotgun, flamethrower and rocket launcher. Each can be upgraded 3 times. There isn't much range in combat and AoE damage is powerful, as long as you don't catch yourself in the radius. Your sword is an important tool. It can deal a lot of damage, can attack multiple enemies even at range (with upgrades) and heal while not using ammo.
Skills are just passive improvements to damage, stamina, and increasing item drops. There is no reset function to this, and making poor choices can make combat difficult. Karma can be found in drops or gained during combat so higher scoring combat results in gaining skills faster.
Powers give you healing, a shield, and 2 ways to incapacitate enemies (which feels redundant). Healing is you main source of restoring hp (though it doesn't do it to full). Dragon Scales reduces damage. Flux lifts a row of enemies into the air for easy kills. Shockwave will knock down enemies that around you.
There is a decent variety of enemies that come at you in hordes. There are lesser demons which can be enraged (due to greater demons empowering them or you using powers) making them tougher versions. There are 3 greater demons which provide their own challenges. The boss fights are very similar. A large being with armor that has to be broken to temporarily reveal weaknesses. It's worth noting that hit boxes on some of the weaknesses seem off.
There are some notable bugs. Dashing on stairs may cause you to spontaneously explode and die. Seriously, don't run down the stairs. Knocking enemies down has weird animations. Sometimes there is a delayed reaction to the knock down and often heads can clip through walls. I've also had enemies just ignore knock-down.
If you find hordes of demons in locked arenas repetitive or don't have the dexterity to deal with the controls this isn't the game for you. But if you want some solid mindless rampaging to rock out with your Wang out, give Shadow Warrior a shot when it's on sale.
EDIT: Heroic Mode
So I decided to play heroic mode and it's pretty brutal. All the fire arms save the cross-bow feel incredibly underwhelming. There is an heavy reliance on the sword to make this mode viable. The game isn't particularly fair at some points. Warpers can full surround you and drop you quickly. After finally making it through chapter 8 on 5 attempts, I watched a few other playthroughs and they all got downed during the last arena fight and required demon soul to save them. And then there are the bugs.I already mentioned how using run on stairs kills you, but some times your drain soul fails to proc. I've fallen through the floor on chapter 9. Also a level on chapter 9 wouldn't highlight and required a restart. Mothers can 1 shot you from 120+ health. And some levels take an hour or longer with the obligatory massive fight at the end which maybe the only challenging part of a level. While skill and builds play a large roll in combat, I can't help but feel luck plays a large factor in one's ability to survive this challenge. It's little surprise so few people have earned this achievement.

OTTTD is your standard tower defense game, but somehow it's
.  It features a few gameplay tweaks and lovable artstyle that make it different from traditional TD titles seen before.

There's essentially one control source (mouse, arrow keys are optional and I didn't find them useful), which makes the gameplay really simple, right? Another note is that the early game is far too easy, while the late game's difficulty is based on who you've been leveling up.  I got to one of the later stages, and I've still been there after 4 hours, because I levelled up the wrong mercenaries.  I understand how the mercs are supposed to be varied, but I almost feel like there's a set of mercs that are

This is my favorite game of all time.
Dungeon Defenders is a tower defense-ish game. I hate tower defense games because they are rigid in where you can place what towers. Everything is in a grid & only certain types of towers are allowed in certain slots. DD is not at all like that. You are trying to prevent the mobs from destroying your crystal & you use towers and your hero to stop them. That's about where the similarities end. You can place your towers anywhere on the map, facing any direction, in any combinations. You can switch between characters to use towers from the Apprentice & the Squire, for example, but then play on your Monk. You cannot stack towers, but other than that you have nearly complete freedom in how you place towers. You have a maximum number of "defense units" with each tower using a particular number of DU to build so you need to be strategic with what towers you'll use where.
Unfortunately the later levels are unplayably laggy. The other drawback is that the terrain appears to disappear on the latest waves in the large maps if you have a large group & the host's upload speeds aren't obscenely fast. For my purposes there was still plenty to do in the game other without hitting these bugs.
Still, there is a ton of replayability and many, many different goals to work towards depending on your preferences. Increasing the difficulty doesn't feel like you're just doing the same map over & over as the mobs change as you increase difficulty which makes you change your build to handle the new mobs. The story is brief, but fun. The combat is intuitive. The menus are not at all intuitive, until you get used to them. I have never enjoyed a game even half as much as this one.

As I work full time, I'm not able to have camped on this title for forty hours in the first two days, but nine hours is probably just more than enough to chip in my two cents.
The graphics -are- good, but the art direction is bad.  And I think that same pattern resonates through the rest of this title.  All the game's advances from Civilization V are somehow compromised by negligent design. For every step forward we've fallen back two.
The Tech Web notion wasn't a bad one - other 4X have done this to addictive success - but in BE it seems disjointed and uninteresting.  I found myself wanting a tree list of techs to order them in terms of "earliest benefit" but, alas, I had to roll around the tech map each time to find my way.  For a Sci-Fi title I was hoping they'd really stretch their creative limits but everything in the tech is completely uninspired.
"Unit Customization" is another major letdown (but not a major surprise).  Your units basically get morphed by whatever ideology you've espoused earlier on, and you can choose to boost their defense or offense.  Each singular unit can still level, but they only get to choose between "Heal up by 50" or "Boost attack + defense +10%".  Every time.  Been a while since "customization" has been this narrow.
If you were looking forward to quests - yep they're kinda neat but you also have to go hunting for them in the UI and scroll your way through the jist of things.  They'd be much more compelling if they weren't hamstrung by the game's lacking (but likely to improve) UI.  They'd also be more compelling if they were given due emphasis, instead of being almost exclusively text blurbs, or regular choices of benefits on a new building.
The biggest letdown to me - the biggest obstacle between myself and Beyond Earth's fun - is its lack of rationality.  The Health quotient of your civ (an inexplicable replacement of Happiness) is completely out of whack - nearly impossible to master, and a burden that far outweighs Civ5's "Courthouse Problems".  Money is silly in that you can earn it easily but your various improvements (tile and city) will gobble it up in roller-coaster patterns the more you expand.  Build times (unit and structure both) are frustratingly -off- as well.  The worst offender of this irrationality is actually Miasma.  Miasma looks vaguely like pollution but it's just a damage cloud that sits on the map tiles indefinitely.  You can't ever seem to get rid of it.  You can spawn an orbital vacuum cleaner to temporarily neuter it (10 turns, then the unit dies, by default).
If they fixed the Miasma, Health, and Building Times in the game - adjusted the ratios at least - I'd say this game is as good as Civ5 at launch.  (In particular I had a lot more stability issues with Civ5 on launch than with this one.)  The game would still be uncharacterized and a little too clunky in the UI, but it would at least be more comfortable of an experience.
I don't recommend it.
