A rush-job title that is basically a mod for Civ5 but with a $50 asking price. 
Its buggy, unpolished, imbalanced and feels incomplete. 
If you liked Civ5 you will probably enjoy this game, but ultimately you'll probably abandon Beyond Earth and hed back to Civ5 after a few games. Its just not up to the task of walking in Civ5's footsteps (or Civ4 or Alpha Centuri for that matter).
The alien-scape maps look good, but don't function all that well in terms of actually playing the game. Miasma is a new hazard in the game, damaging your units for sitting in it. However, visually in the game it is a faint green mist that's very difficult to notice at a glance on the map. Likewise plains, tundra, desert and grasslands tiles all look similar are are difficult to tell apart without relying on the UI to tell you what they are, and the tiles sometimes look like hills, but aren't. Canyon squares are new impassible terrain features but its often difficult to see exactly which tiles are the impassible ones, since the graphic for the canyons is larger than the area that can't be walked over. Taken together the map is just difficult to distinguish visually.
The aliens that inhabit the lands of Beyond Earth are generally very passive and content to wander around doing nothing as long as you don't go near their nests or attack them. They appear in much larger numbers than the barbarians in Civ5 and are more organized, but ultimately they are content to stay neutral unless you aggro them. They also don't scale in strength at all during the game, once you've levelled up your units a few times they become incredibly trivial to kill off and don't pose any threat.
The quest system rewards you with rewards for completing certain objectives, but unfortunately feels like some of the quests are just a hamfisted tutorial system, telling you what you should do next. The randomly generated quests, when they occur, are a cool addition to the Civ formula but they are bugged and can sometimes give you quests that are impossible to complete (such as, build a costal-only building in a landlocked city). Broken quest don't occur too often but they contribute to the overall feel that the game is sloppy and untested.
The 'health' system that replaces Unhappiness from Civ5 feels unpolished. Its unnecessary punishing in the early game when you'd normally want to be expanding and incredibly trivial in the late game once certain technologies are researched. The main problem though, is that capturing enemy cities can cause massive penalties to unhealthiness with no real way to mitigate it efficiently (there's no equivalent to the Courthouse improvement in from Civ5). The result is that capturing enemy cities is often crippling to your economy outside of the late game where unhealthiness is less of an issue. This results in most of any given game being quite passive and solitary, with only occasional skirmishes against the aliens to keep your soldiers busy.
Trade Routs from Civ5 return, but they're even more important and more powerful in Beyond Earth. Trade Routes provide massive amounts of resources compared to how easy they are to create and overall feel imbalanced. In addition you're forced to manually re-issue your trade convoys new orders every 10 turns or so and since every city can have 2, 3 or even 4 trade routes it quickly becomes an irritating chore once you've built a colony of any decent size. Again, Beyond Earth feels poorly balanced and unpolished.
Finally, several of the victory conditions aren't working properly. The Contact victory (requiring you to unearth alien artifacts and make contact with an intelligent alien life) sometimes becomes possible far too early, allowing victories as early as turn 150 in some cases or it can simply be impossible because the required artifact will not appear. Several of the buildings that are supposed to accelerate the transcendence victory don't function at all and (although I didn't experience this myself) there are reports of the Emancipation Victory's earth-gate being impossible to destroy even when you deplete its life to zero.
With all that said, there is the fundamental basis for a good game in Beyond Earth but the game feels unfinished, not properly tested and overall rushed. I also feel as if this should have been a mod for Civ5, at least 70% of the gameplay is unchanged from Civ5 and I feel a little cheated paying $50 for this game when I already own Civ5, especially when it has so many obvious problems that could have been fixed without too much hassle.
Overall Verdict - Maybe once the game is heavily patched it will be worthwhile but for right now there's just no point in playing this game instead of Civ5.

Having played Beyond Earth for a few hours now, I still had a hard time deciding whether to recommend it or not.
It definitely is fun and I'm glad I bought it, but it is also woefully underwhelming in exactly some of those new areas where it should have excelled.
The initial customization of your expedition has next to zero impact on how the game plays out.
The tech web is difficult to navigate and the placement of improvements on the web seems random at times.
The espionage system is neat but most operations take so long to complete that you'll hardly see it.
None of these issues are particularly painful, but they also don't live up to my expectations.
There is, however, one flaw I cannot so easily forgive: The endings.
After playing close to 20 hours and getting ever closer to one of the (nicely varied and well balaned) victory conditions, I was really looking forward to winning my first game.
I had chosen "Contact" - the path to making contact with sentient aliens for the first time.
Throughout the game, the narrative of the victory quests is compelling and I was really waiting to see what would happen.
Unfortuately, this and all the other victories are a complete letdown.
A text card with an ambiguous, "will we ever know?"-style message is all that heralds your win.
No cinematic, no resolution.
It's almost as if the makers of Beyond Earth did not anticipate that anyone would actually ever want to win it.
This is such a big deal because after staring at those three lines of text for a while, I started to realise that it makes the whole experience leading up to this point feel cheap in retrospect, as if it was not quite worth the effort.
I hope that the inevitable DLC will maybe fix this.
So, why did I still recommend the game?
Because as long as you know what to expect from your victory, the journey is still great fun.
Gameplay is smooth for the most part, combat is satisfying and city management just as you would expect.
It's a solid game, unfortunately just not quite what we all were hoping for.

Age of Decadence is a fantastic RPG that easily puts to shame many AAA releases from the past few years. It is one of those games that truly lets you roleplay however you wish, and this gives it great replayability value through all of its factions, multiple ways of building your character and different stories to be experienced. Age of Decadence takes it one step further with all the possibilities it offers and is a must play for any gamer that misses the "golden era" of CRPGs.
Pros:
+ Interesting and unexplored setting
+ Lack of a clicheic main story, playing as a nobody
+ Multiple factions with individual and completely different storylines
+ Challenging and complex combat system
+ Plenty of ways to build your character and solve quests
+ Best replayability value in ages
+ Great writing
+ Beautiful soundtrack
Cons:
- Visually unappealing
- Lack of content in the last city
- Combat is partly based on luck
- Crashed a lot at launch (improved now)

This unique isometric RPG opens with a quote from Glen Cook’s
, and fans of Cook’s dark military fantasy novels will feel right at home in this gritty and grimy setting. The Age of Decadence drops you into a crumbling empire teetering on the brink of chaos, with several major guilds and noble houses vying for power while the general populace struggles to survive amidst gangs of thugs, mercenaries, and religious fanatics. It’s a harsh and brutal world with very little magic outside basic alchemy and very few monsters, though your fellow humans fill the latter role quite admirably.
Unlike most RPGs, The Age of Decadence emphasizes story and character interaction over combat as the player gets caught up in various schemes and power struggles. In many events throughout the game, the player is confronted with meaningful choices which alter the direction of the story in meaningful ways, opening new possibilities while closing off others. There are multiple paths through the story and the player can choose between allying with the Commercium (merchants guild), the Imperial Guards, the Boatmen of Styx (assassins guild), and several other factions. Each path provides a different perspective on the overarching story while the player’s decisions and actions help shift the balance of power between the various factions. This lends the game excellent replay value as each playthrough with a different character type creates a distinctly different experience.
Skills are split between Combat Skills (e.g., Swords, Bows, Dodge, Block, etc.) and General Skills (e.g., Sneak, Streetwise, Crafting, Lore, etc.). Building different skills unlocks different options throughout the game, allowing the story to progress in different directions. Of course there are never quite enough skill points to go around, so you’ll need to make some choices in terms of what to focus on, and those choices will impact which options or paths are available as you work through the story.
While combat isn’t the primary focus of the game, the turn-based combat system makes for some challenging conflicts. There’s a good variety of weapon types with poison, potions, and other items like nets and bolas supplementing your character’s abilities. Fans of traditional RPGs should be advised that The Age of Decadence takes a slightly more realistic approach to combat; you’re not likely to become an unstoppable killing machine but focusing on combat skills will allow your character to progress quite a bit. Or you can focus more on non-combat skills, leveraging skill-based alternative options which allow you to progress through the game with minimal combat.
The game’s fairly heavy on text, drawing inspiration from Cook’s noir-flavored narratives to build a broken and decaying society filled with shady characters. The world design follows suit with lots of yellows and browns, crumbling ruins and scrabbly flora. All together, it builds a cohesive world with a very distinctive feel.
Bear in mind that it isn’t an open world RPG, each area is broken up into zones and the paths to navigate those zones are somewhat limited, so you don’t get the kind of free range exploration found in open world RPGs. It also isn’t a terribly long game, though what’s there is plenty substantial enough to be satisfying, and the variations when playing through it with different characters lends it a lot more life.
Despite those limitations in scope, The Age of Decadence accomplishes what it sets out to do extremely well, delivering a unique and challenging RPG experience in a dangerous world echoing the spirit and tone of Glen Cook’s landmark military fantasy series. Just as Cook challenged and subverted the fantasy genre’s conventions in the 80s and 90s, The Age of Decadence flips around many of the conventions common to modern RPGs, offering meaningful choices and branching story paths while focusing on street-level characters with limited abilities rather than gods and kings.
Highly recommended for fans of isometric RPGs who'd like a change of pace emphasizing story and meaningful choices over endless combat.

Quick Summary: First person shooter/slasher from the makers of Hard Reset and Serious Sam. I’ve never played the original Shadow Warrior games so I don’t know if this is a remake in terms of story, but it’s fully entertaining, with a likeable ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ main character dropping one-liners like Duke Nukem. There is an RPG-like upgrade system allowing you to power up as you progress through the game, and an EX mode (new game plus) so you can replay the game with all your upgrades.
Your character is a modern day mercenary/samurai/badass named Lo Wang who’s on a job acquiring an ancient katana with mystical demon killing powers. Unfortunately, evil forces are afoot, both human and demonic, so the fate of the world is in peril and you really need that sword. Lo Wang is no ordinary♥♥♥♥♥kicker though. Due to some demonic help you gain along the way, you can use “ki” to bolster your fighting style and smite down demons with a variety of guns, spells, and even demonic body parts.
You control Lo Wang in first person perspective, and while you will find various guns along your travels, your first weapon may be your best.  The katana you start with is strong, fast, and can use ki skills such as whirling slash or a powered up forward thrust (you choose which skill you use by entering button combinations). Very similar to Hard Reset and Serious Sam, the enemies in the game tend to come at you in small groups, but they have enough life that it takes a bit of focused fire to kill each one, by which time the others will be all over you. Fortunately, (just like Hard Reset) there are a ton of destructible environmental objects that can be blown up (barrels, cars, etc.) to soften the enemies before they get close to you. Be careful because in big firefights, there will be a lot of♥♥♥♥♥♥blowing up.
There are 3 main upgrade “trees” for Lo Wang: Powers, Skills, and Weapons, and all three trees use a different type of upgrade currency. There are a number of collectibles in the game as well, some of it pretty well hidden. You’ll be rewarded for using different fighting styles and environmental kills, so you’ll want to master the various skills that Lo Wang has at his disposal. The spells/skills that he uses involve combinations of directional keys and the mouse buttons, for example D, D, right-mouse casts a heal spell, or A, A, left-mouse is the whirling slash. These powers will save your♥♥♥♥♥ so make sure you use them all the time.
Pros:
+A lot of (wang) humor and a decent story. You have a smartass companion for most of the game, so the 2 play off of each other for comedy.
+There are some huge firefights where you’ll be running away from enemies in large arenas, casting your heal spell, trying not to get pinned down. Every level has a bunch of mini bosses as well, adding to the chaos.
+Because of the unusual upgrade system, there is a lot of re-playability in the game. You need to play through the campaign more than once just to unlock all the skills and weapon upgrades.
Cons:
-On the higher difficulty, a lot of the enemies (especially mini bosses) are bullet sponges. It takes a ton of firepower to bring them down while their minions bite at your ankles. The big bosses of the game are the same way, in that they have so much life that even if they stand still it takes a long time to kill them.
-Compared to Hard Reset, Shadow Warrior has superior gameplay, but the graphics actually look worse. This might be because Hard Reset is a futuristic cyberpunk environment with lots of pretty lasers and exploding things, while Shadow Warrior purposely incorporates a lot of retro graphics.
-While I like the assortment of guns, you’ll end up not using some of them very much. For example the shotgun, crossbow, and flamethrower are nice for adding some variety to the game, but they have practical drawbacks. The shotgun only holds 4 shots in a clip, enemies move in unusual lurching ways that make the crossbow difficult to aim, and enemies have too much life for the flamethrower to be very effective. Just stick with the sword, and power up your ki attacks for maximum carnage.
Overall Shadow Warrior is an awesome game if you like retro first person shooters (Doom, Quake, etc., NOT Call of Duty). If you’re going for Steam achievements, you should know that a lot of the achievements in this game are ‘tiered’ just like Hard Reset. This means that most of the achievements are separate for all 4 difficulties (One achievement for easy, one for normal, one for hard, and one for insane). Or you can play the game in insane difficulty and unlock them all at once. If you’re the kind of player (like me) that likes to play games in Normal difficulty, you’ll only get about ½ of Shadow Warrior’s achievements. First playthrough took me about 14 hours because I was searching for all the secrets.

The Final Fantasy fanbase is a bunch that cannot make up it’s mind. With each new installment, you have a faction of the fanbase who wants the old, classic ATB battle system back. Then you also have the faction that wants something new and edgy. Anytime Square-Enix delivers one or the other, the fanbase causes an uproar….wanting the other! With this in mind, know that with Final Fantasy XIII….you will either love it or hate it, depending on which faction you belong to.
Final Fantasy XIII is a great game.
It's fairly linear though, but that doesn't hinder it in a bad way. It actually brings the story to the forefront of the game experience. Final Fantasy X was exactly the same, but is praised by fans as being one of the best FF titles to date (very close to VII), while FFXIII got a lot of hate after it’s initial release. Why is FFXIII different?
That's the thing: It's not!
Final Fantasy XIII takes place in a society called Cocoon, which exists in a large sphere that hangs in the sky over the world of Pulse. The citizens live in constant fear of invasion from the surface after an attack centuries earlier cracked open the shell of their world, and rely entirely on the fal'Cie, godlike creatures that provide Cocoon with everything it needs to exist — food, weather...even light. While Cocoon's fal'Cie are revered as benevolent protectors, the fal'Cie of Pulse are feared and demonized, to the point that anyone who comes in contact with anything from Pulse is considered tainted. When a Pulse fal'Cie is discovered in their own society, a chain of events leads the government to purge an entire city of civilians, and leads six strangers to become l'Cie, servants of the Pulse fal'Cie who must complete their appointed task or suffer a fate worse than death.
The story is fast-paced and filled with mysteries that unravel as the game progresses, and it's paced perfectly, with cutscenes popping up as you move through each area. The characters are also fantastic, each presenting themselves as a typical JRPG archetype in the beginning, but quickly showing much more depth. Furthermore, each character is tied to the story of the game; there are no incidental characters filling out your party, and likewise there is no main character. Final Fantasy XIII is about the overall group, and this is further emphasized by dividing them into separate groups on separate paths before they join together again for the second half.
Final Fantasy XIII's weakest link is unfortunately the beginning. The first few hours of the game see keywords like Pulse, l'Cie, and fal'Cie thrown at you without any context or explanation to their meaning. The characters also lack any kind of development for the first few hours, and the result is a confusing plotline with uninteresting characters that leaves a terrible first impression.  The combat system is completely stripped of the depth is shows later on. The player barely needs to pay attention for these early battles, and coupled with some extremely linear level design, the first three hours are unquestionably a low-point for both the game and the series.
And then Final Fantasy XIII really begins. The Crystarium, the game's answer to leveling up, becomes available, and likewise so does the Paradigm system, the meat and potatoes of Final Fantasy XIII's combat system. When this all becomes available, it becomes readily apparent why you've been spamming "Auto-Battle", and why you'll continue to spam it for the next fifty hours. The combat isn't about the nitty-gritty details of individual spells, it's about the overall strategy. Just as Final Fantasy XII gave you control through gambits, Final Fantasy XIII lets you play the general in the same way by rapidly changing between sets of classes in the heat of battle, altering tactics to suit the ever-changing situations that come up. The AI is extremely intelligent, and can select appropriate skills faster and with as much efficiency as most players, anyways.
Each character has access to three primary classes, and the Paradigm system allows you to create customized class set-ups that you can switch between at any time during combat. If you're on the offensive, a Commando and two Ravagers can effectively decimate an enemy. If you're looking at a longer fight, a Saboteur/Synergist team can drastically increase your fighting power. Facing a powerful foe? Bring out a Sentinel and let them tank while the other two lay the hurt on. Each class has a unique and important purpose, and while most fights can be completed with different strategies, many of the boss fights require rather specific ones in order to be successful.
The environments aren't the only amazing visuals Final Fantasy XIII boasts; the character/enemy models should not be sold short. The characters easily have some of the most realistic and believable facial expressions ever produced in a video game. Every emotion the characters experience is mirrored flawlessly on their face, and while the designs retain a hint of anime influence, they are still shockingly realistic.
Of course, this realism would be marred without solid vocal support, and for the most part Final Fantasy XIII delivers it. While not quite approaching the level of quality seen in Final Fantasy XII, the vocal cast of XIII nonetheless perform admirably, and this in spite of the lengthy monologues each character performs on a regular basis, true to form for a JRPG. The only weak point in the vocals is Vanille, which in the early parts of the game is rather grating. To her credit, the performance improves dramatically.
The musical score is also excellent. The main battle theme is similarly exciting and gets stuck in your head easily. While wandering dungeons, the music gets a bit more eclectic. Other tracks deviate from the usual, melodic Final Fantasy style and delve instead into techno and other styles.
Like Final Fantasy XII before it, Final Fantasy XIII has unquestionably caused cause a rift between those who love it and those who don't. As long as you don't judge the game on its beginning, Final Fantasy XIII is a game worthy of the series, and a terrific game.

I was seduced by Blackhole due to its narrative similarity to the incredible platformer VVVVVV. You're a spaceman who needs to find the other members of his crew in a place where gravity works in strange ways. In Blackhole, DOWN changes depending on when you step on a glowy white platform. You need to use these platforms to solve individual puzzle-levels that are distributed over across an overworld.
I finished the third overworld (the Library) before I realized I just didn't care anymore. None of the characters you are saving are sympathetic. Your constant AI companion is annoying. The mystery of "the Entity" and the Endera crew is dulled by the overbearing "HA-HA AREN'T WE FUNNY?" tone.
OK. The graphics and art style are great. The different worlds bring a sense of awe when you first reach them, but there is no exploration or adventure, there are simple overworlds and the twleve puzzle-levels per overworld. And I wish I could enjoy the puzzle levels but I just cannot. Maybe I'm wrong, but the game expects you to beat each level in ONE specific way, without alternatives. Even still, for the most part I figured out the solutions to the puzzles relatively quickly. The true difficulty in this game comes from its physics and control scheme.
The jump physics are wonky and movement is imprecise Oh! You wanted to hang on that ledge you're jumping to? Well, since you held the joystick for 40 milliseconds too long, how about you climb up top into a laser, instead? And then that AI character chimes in, "How about thinking where you jump next time?" when you didn't even die from a miscalculated jump.
This becomes maddening considering this game is a precision platform-puzzler. I've read that the controls work minutely better on keyboard, but alas, I just don't care. And it's belittling to play Easy Mode (in a game where you're constantly belittled by every character) for a game whose problems come from its physics and controls. There are better platformers waiting in my library...
If you have more patience than me (do remember, I did beat VVVVVV, so I'm no noob), and this game is on deep sale, maybe try it out.

If you have a tower defense itch you need to scratch, Over The Top Tower Defense likely has you covered. It's the future, and the world is at peace. What are the meatheads of Hero Corp to do? Why, open portals to alternate universes and pre-emptively defend Earth, of course! OTTTD mixes up the standard tower defense formula by giving you a team of three Warcraft 3-style heroes with active and passive special abilities, and tasks you with defending your headquarters from an oncoming swarm of either the aquatic, blunderbuss-toting Steamcrusties or the undead hordes of the Horror dimension. I was somewhat disappointed by the fact that there weren't any other dimensions to fight in, and just the two seems odd- you'd think there'd have been three or something. I am enamoured of OTTTD's varied hero classes and their equipment, the ludicrous gibs in-game, and pervading comical air, in particular, the Schwarzeneggar-knockoff, head-sticks-out-from-the-center-of-his-chest Assault and his one liners. However, the towers themselves very quickly become useless as you progress, not being subject to the same RPG-style progression as the heroes. The game is also extremely grindy, and stands out for this even in a genre known for brutal slogs, perhaps due to its origins as a cellphone game. The difficulty ramps up steadily over the course of the many levels, but your characters' progress quickly falls behind. I was forced to replay earlier levels many, many times to get enough experience and money to complete the grueling final waves, and by that point my heroes had long since run out of canned quips. Despite this, or perhaps because of it, actually finishing the game was immensly satisfying.

This game is awesome! Really great mix of platforming and action.  Very, very polished game.  There is tons of things to do without it stretching thin or feeling dragged out. Quite the contrary, it's very consistent experience from start to finish, if not getting better and better.  There is a real sense of progression from start to finish.  New abilities that unlocks previously inaccessible areas (which also increase platforming variations), new moves, new spells.  There's no leveling in this game, only power-ups.   There's no grind at all.  In fact the resource you collected can feel useless late game (my only minor complaint).
The map is intricate, large, and interconnected.  There are so many hidden areas without them feeling absurdly hidden.
You can always find 99% of them if you are paying attention.  You don't really need guide, but chances are you'll need it if you want to 100% it.  But it's not really necessary.
The game is rather difficult.  But it's fair and reasonable, and you'll see yourself getting better and better at it. There are some high-difficulty optional late-game areas.  Some platforming challenge, some combat challenge, and a mix of both.
The story is told in a similar fashion to dark souls.  Sparse, disjointed pieces of information here and there without any handholding or exposition.  I'm not sure i understand it, but the atmosphere and art told a story by itself.  A dreamlike story of a desolate civilization below earth.
There's no weak point in this game.  I can't recommend this game enough.

Lock, load and let the gibs fly in OTTTD, a Tower Defence/RTS game with RPG elements that pits you against some of the weirdest creatures in the multiverse.
OTTTD stands for Over The Top Tower Defence, and you'll see why when you're blasting 9 kinds of hell out of a Cactus Ghost that's making a beeline for your battlefield HQ. You play as a commander for HEROCORP™, the 4th largest private military organization in the galaxy. A long period of peace has left the company coffers a little bare so the science division developed Trans-Dimensional Rifts, opening up lucrative opportunities for war in other universes. It's like Starship Troopers meets Stargate meets Spaceballs, with way more explosions!
Features
• Ridiculously definitive edition
Prepare your eyes and ears for incredible deluxe-ness! Featuring crisper sound and high resolution graphics, the PC release of OTTTD will leave you feeling like you've actually stepped into an alternate universe and started blasting everything to smithereens.
• Deep RPG Mechanics
OTTTD lets you choose from 7 hero classes to make up your squad of 3 battlefield employees. The more action they see the more XP they earn, giving you the chance to level them up through custom skill trees, including powerful combat abilities to unleash during the fight.
• 30+ active abilities
• 40+ passive skills
• 30+ equippable weapons
• multiple armor options with stats to suit your play-style
• Weapons! Weapons! WEAPONS!
With 12 tower types to build and 6 different firearm classes, HEROCORP™ has got the hardware to ensure you can wreak havoc in your own personal style.
• Disgustingly varied foes
The range of enemies in OTTTD is wide enough to soothe even the itchiest trigger finger. Floating eyeballs? Check. Gunclams? You know it. Giant armored Wartoises? Of course. You'll even go toe to fin with a giant flying shark, and show the mythological Kraken who's boss!
The Story
The year is 2136. You work for HEROCORP™, the universe’s 4th largest private military force. Your job is to “preemptively defend” the Earth against alien dimensions. As long as you complete the missions under budget and fill out the TPS reports in triplicate, everything goes smoothly.
Is pre-emptively defending Earth ethical? Who cares when the money’s good!

I don't understand how all these reviews do not label the game as Pay-2-Win.
Don't be mistaken, this game is absolutely pay-to-win, and worst off, its pay-to-win in a game with a playerbase in the hundreds.  If you spend money on booster/decks/singles, you will have an advantage over non-paying players.  That is pay-to-win in my book.  Granted, it isn't pay-to-play.
There are ways for non-paying players to earn packs (5250 IP for a pack, you gain 150 IP per 5 minute win, 75 for a 5 minute loss.  That means anywhere between 30-40 games for 15 cards.  Did I also mention that there are 9 factions (colors/classes)?  So yeah, good luck building a deck in a short amount of time without spending money.
I would have enjoyed this game a lot more if it were still Early Access, but this game has been out for 2+ years and still has many problems.
Card interactions are buggy and the text isn't standardized across cards.  Morale values are not balanced, and card costs/purities aren't balanced either.  Many games end because of bugs or because it is just a death race or a coin flip.  There is some strategy there, but the results often boil down to luck because of the simultaneous turns.  You'll find yourself in draws very often.
There are also so many board wipes, its ridiculous.  Wrath of God/Armageddon used to mean something, but in IW prepare for Mass Death, Heat Wave, Yuanshi's Wrath, The Calamity, Shikana, MU, the list goes on.  There are many many cards capable of clearing the board of all creatures, and many decks built around those cards.
Low playerbase, no matchmaking system, so newbies are forced to play against pros, wasting their currency (it costs 1000 IP to enter a draft -- if you lose 3 games you're out).  There are separate queues for ranked/unranked but its meaningless because you don't get anything for playing ranked.  The only reason to play unranked is for the EXP and the only reason to get EXP is for the cards (assuming you're non-paying).  So you have to grind this treadmill for weeks just to be able to play the game in a meaningful way if you don't want to pay money to a game that is basically still in beta, but released for the public.
TL;DR:
Just another Pay-2-Win card game with lower playerbase than other games and worse player incentives.  The reward structure will make you scratch your head, as the game itself is a bit of fun, but the MMO treadmill they expect us to run is ridiculous.

Firstly, if you're in doubt, just try the demo. If it appeals to you, buy the game because the game is more of the same.
Now, real review time:
One of my favourite games from the last couple of years. It's not perfect, but it has strong design that very much appeals to me personally. I think it's the only game on Steam where I have all achievements and specifically went achievement hunting because most achievements represent different story paths/endings and I wanted to see everything on offer.
Overall, this game is the most fun I've had with an RPG since the ones released in the 90s and I thoroughly recommend it.
Performance and graphics are not ideal. I've had some technical problems, but nothing that broke quests or anything. Mostly odd graphics problems that could be fixed by restarting or the occasional crash. But that's also rather unimportant in my opinion, considering what the game does. Technical problems are annoying, but never stopped me coming back even for a second.
The game is not that difficult once you understand what's going on in the systems, or at least can be made relatively easy by placing your skills right.
Some general tips if you want to try it out:
Don't skimp on learning the ropes. Do the tutorial, read the help menu etc.
Save up skill points. Don't place them until you need them. This is especially useful in combination with the next point:
Save and reload a lot to see what options are available to you. Almost every single quest in the main questlines has branching points, options for betrayal etc. Make hard saves when you enter/leave major cities or hit major branching points. Feel free to set the number of quick/auto save slots higher than the default of 3.
For different playthroughs, I recommend starting by completing the game as a pure talker with no combat skills or physical attributes, following the Merchant questline (aka easy mode). This gives you a good general overview of the game without any challenging combat. Then try a pure fighter with focus on combat and crafting/alchemy, following the Imperial Guard questline, to get a grip on the combat. After that, you should have enough of a grasp of how the everything works to try your hand at hybrid characters.
For combat skills, focus on one offensive and one defensive combat skill. Never take both dodge and block. Critical strike is useful, but not necessary if you've other skills to focus on.
For non-combat skills, persuasion and streetwise are the bread and butter of talkers, along with impersonate and maybe trading. Lore is very good and opens up locations otherwise inaccessible. Crafting also has many non-combat uses in combination with lore.
For your very first playthrough, I'd recommend going through completely without guides/spoilers if you can (well, except the general tips like in this review). However, once you've completed the game in one way or another, don't be afraid to use google to check out some of the things you couldn't figure out (e.g. how to get into the Tower Of Zamedi or The Abyss)
Look in every nook and cranny of each map. There's a few things that are unfortunately rather easy to miss, even with highlighting of interactable objects turned on. And unfortunately NPCs don't have indicators (above their heads or similar) for when you can talk to them.

Hollow Knight captures something beautiful about the modern gaming experience, not just looking at the game itself but also the development team behind the game in how they handle the updates to the game. Hollow Knight is a relatively simple Metroidvania style game, which traditionally is something I'm not a fan of, however the world that Team Cherry have built, creating a cute bug environment that is somewhat haunted by a deep past referred to throughout the story of the game. The world itself feels lived in, and not just built around the protagonist.
The music of the game, composed by Christopher Larkin, is evocative and perfectly suits the themes and tone of each environment or character. The most striking moment of both sound and music, for me, was the catacombs area which ruined my whole day, due to the excessive creepiness portrayed.
Team Cherry have also been incredibly active with the community and have constantly been introducing updates with both new content and fixes to any small issues within the game.
100% recommend!

This is the only Assassin's Creed game I've played to date so that might set a bit of context. I just heard it was the best one from a friend and so jumped straight in at number IV. Well I'm half way through a second play through and decided to give this game a BIG thumbs up review. I just love it; the theme, setting and ambience created in this game is brilliant and I can't help myself but to sing along with the shanties as I pirate around on the salt seas.
Things I like;
- Sailing and pirating mechanics are masterfully achieved; simple enough to get to grips with quickly but engrossing enough to want to do for hour upon hour. Boarding enemy ships is great fun and the shanties really give a depth of experience to sailing the waves.
- The parkour is very well executed with only a few issues such as unrealistic snapping to certain edges and rocks that should be scalable but aren't. Sometimes farting about in the rigging and platforms of big ships results in an annoying death fall. Overall a great job with some occasional annoyances that any mature gamer should look past.
- The characters are fantastic and I love the protagonist, I won't say too much to spoil; I found them all entertaining and interesting plus I really like the nod to real people from history of the era.
- Stealth mechanics are easy to master so within a few hours of play you'll be performing awesome ninja death stunts. Perhaps it is a little too easy in some respects, such as AI stupidity, but that's just taste. All stealth games are like that.
- The legendary ships provide amazing battles that are hard won, even with all upgrades for your ship. I love the Man o' War with the naval ram, El Impoluto; probably the hardest ship battle in the game.
- Love the powder shot pistols; when you get to having a full set of four with two strapped to your chest and one on each hip; what a badass.
Things I liked less;
- I feel that the throwing knife is a great weapon so it surprises me that you can only get it from certain enemies and only one of them. It's easily retrieved and you can always get another, but still; why not have a set of 5 or so knives available in shops? Just a bit of an odd choice.
- Fighting mechanics could have a hard mode; it's like in the movies (think Kill Bill) when the protagonist is surrounded by gyrating opponents (to give the illusion of action) who attack one at a time. I've got to the stage where dying in battle is just not on the cards; no valhalla for me!
- A little more depth in the story would be nice but I still enjoyed the story immensely. I came away feeling I wanted more but I guess that's just how it feels upon completing a great game; can it ever be enough?
- The fleet system is a good idea for a long distance trade mechanic to bring in the Reales but it just gets a bit wearisome after unlocking all sea routes. You wipe them clear to free up the routes for trade then a day or so later you have to do it all again. And again. And again. Tedium.
- REALLY don't like the cuts to the modern era in the Abstergo Entertainment HQ or whatever it is. I get that they're trying to push the genetic memory idea into the story but it feels contrived, weird and doesn't seem to add to the game experience. I have no interest in hacking computers for emails and vids that try to add depth to the genetic memory thing and it just breaks the story up.
Amazing game. Combines pirating, ninja-ing and a historical context to create a vibrant world to be a double hard bast$%d in. Ignoring the modern era scenes, which can be breezed fairly quickly, I give it a 10/10 for sheer delight in piracy. I did pay for the game however.

What constitutes a masterpiece? What makes a game a defining work within its genre(s)? These things are subjective, but I can surely say that Hollow Knight made me ask these questions so that I might give it such labels. It is a game that nails (pun intended) the quintessential aspects of what a souls-like, a metroidvania, a platformer, an RPG should be.
The story is mysterious and elusive, told not only through cryptic dialogue, but by the beautifully drawn world surrounding our, though tiny, intrepid protagonist. Mute in the vein of Links and Samuses, he wanders through the sprawling Hollownest, a character in its own right, driven to complete an unspoken mission with no purpose given. Who are you in a world neither lost or forgotten but twisted to ruin?
I can't even begin to coherently present why this game may be one of greatest of my time. I can only hope that a few words and my 37 hours of play-time may convince you to give yourself the opportunity to experience what this game has to offer. Even if you end up hating it, I'd rather you gave it a shot than miss a work of art. That doesn't do it justice. Team Cherry painted their Mona Lisa on the first canvas. I can't overstate enough how profound this game was for me.
Pros:
- The controls are tight and responsive. When you press buttons, the character reacts. The protagonist isn't floaty and input is responsive.
- The art is gorgeous. Every single asset is hand drawn and animated, reminiscent of Skull Girls. Even if you don't like the art you have to appreciate the skill and beauty of what was done here.
- The soundtrack is appropriately melancholy as you explore the derelict depths of Hollownest. The boss music is intense and adds character where it should.
- The story, while vague, is presented wonderfully as I've stated above. You will be left with questions at the end of the game, but they are intended. What better excuse to explore the world more and decipher answers?
- The progression is solid. You collect abilities and powers via metroidvania exploration, and you buy upgrades and other abilities via a souls-like currency system.
- The difficulty can be challenging. I like to believe, for the majority of the game, not overwhelmingly so. It seems enough so that I always feel like my mechanics are being pushed. This is something I hope anyone playing metroidvania or souls-likes is looking for.
Cons:
- Due to the game's cryptic and vague nature, figuring out what to do and how to do it can be challenging at times. Beyond what may be desirable. It may get to the point that you find yourself looking something up online or backtracking unnecessarily. I'm listing it as a soft-con.
- Out of the two faults I have with this game, this one would be the dealbreaker for some people. There is a STEEP difficulty spike towards the end of the game. Some of the bosses will make you want to rip your hair out, but even those are a common staple of souls-likes and pale in comparison to my main qualm. There is a REQUIRED platforming section nearing the game's conclusion that unlocks the path for the "true" endings. This platforming section is of the lowest circles of hell. Super Meat Boy is the only comparison I can give. Be prepared for that torture when the time comes. If it wasn't that bad, I wouldn't put it in a review.
PRO TIP (NO REAL SPOILERS): There are ONLY 3 endings. 1 you get from following the standard path, and the other 2 hinge around a pivotal decision at the end of the final boss. You HAVE to complete the platforming section I mentioned above to have access to that pivotal decision. There is a 4th bonus "ending" scene that requires a chain of NPC interactions through the game. I'm putting this here, so you don't sweat yourself too much worrying if you missed something or screwed something up. SLIGHT CRYPTIC SPOILER MESSAGE THAT WOULD HAVE HELPED ME AT THE END:
If you consider yourself a fan of metroidvanias or souls-likes, you owe it to yourself to give this game a shot. That's really all I can say. The ratings tell the same story, but this is my personal invitation to you to try it. Even if you end up disliking it, it was worth finding out.

Games like this I wish there was a so-so rating.
To start, the game is actually pretty fun, cute graphics on a Kingdom Rush type of tower defense game. The major departure is that they have added permanent heroes that level up between missions. I found that the game was not really that strategic and there wasn't enough difference between the various towers.
The major issues are as follows:
1) This is a mobile port - better than 90% of the garbage ports out there, but still very evident in UI and gameplay; they did bother to add hotkeys so that's a small positive
2) The later missions are not "tower defense" levels, you place zero or only one or two towers. They are based purely on your heroes effectively.
3) That would not be an issue if heroes leveled up properly, but you will probably have to grind to get your heroes to an appropriate level to finish it. This falls back to the grindy mobile aspect.
4) You want to level up faster? Ok, pay $25 for the super deluxe edition with armor that lets you get XP faster - really? Pay to win = lose in game design.
5) The above is exacerbated if you are a trophy collector since you need to hit level 99. For context, a normal player can probably beat the game between level 30-40, so you will spend a minimum of 5-10 hours grinding (that is if you want to do pure grinding by doing 30 second level clears and not actually playing). Of course you can work around this by buying the super armor... $$$
6) The 'gore' is out of control with random fish guts and stuff covering everything including where the enemy path is. I didn't figure this out until later - but there is a setting to reduce this.
7) The price - it is twice the price as on the Android store. Why? The devs say that redid some textures and because "PC gamers can appreciate gaming art more."
Overall, while this is a solid tower defense game, I just can't accept that they have PC gamers as an afterthought and will gouge us for the privilege of playing a port. They have only added salt to the injury by keeping the grindy mobile aspects and pay to win aspects.

Got this after having finished QUBE, Naissancee, Antichamber and attempted Disoriented. I was not let down and I want more of the 'series', tho Antichamber seemed the best of its kind.
It's got small cons compared to all the pro points, only cus I can nitpick the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of everything: like being so cryptic and abstract and letting you walk through areas that are actually puzzles, not knowing you're supposed to solve stuff there. Without the hints telling me an Nth room is NOT part of the hub puzzles, I would've quit right there in the first hub, instead of going back to solve the transition room. And it's not that oh boi I had to go back, cus I did go back to places on my own accord after finishing the game, np. It's more about going 'Oh, this IS a puzzle!', in a frustrating way, instead of in a really happy, revelating way (like I experienced in Naissancee after finding the moving parts in a section).
But I got over it and was glad that there are more and better puzzles that were waiting for me.
Another small con is the feel of the game taken as a game like any other. It took me a while to get used to walking even, as you feel heavy and starting to move is like slowly accelerating from 0 to your normal walking speed, and actual movement is like sliding (like lowered friction and gravity), while running is not really a speed boost. Oh and some block collision pushes you backwards, making walking up certain stairs rather... funny. But no movement skill puzzles in the game, so this uncertainty of my position only added to 'oh no ima fall' when going towards an edge to look down. So this 'feature' worked out ok.
Which brings me to some other pros: Falling isn't punished, neither failing a puzzle. I mean sometimes you do need to fail as you first try out the room and see what it does, but I don't see it as a design mistake, specially if you're not punished and can start over or actually reset the room - neat feature!
The visuals have both pros and cons, the architecture overall is boxy but well planned and drawn out, with plenty of griebling and nice optical effects. Some structures/objects could've been made with custom models, like the made up coffins, which makes the game feel unfinished or poorly funded, but it really looked bug free (I couldn't pick up 1 of the beads on the string or w/e, and that's it, can't remember any other bug), which reveals a lasting, high quality finished product.
While the abstraction is used in telling the story and drawing a conclusion, to me it wasn't needed as a drive to move on, so I didn't complete all the hidden puzzles nor read the hidden meanings. For my soul it was enough to simply go from hub to hub and room to room, open area to another, solving them GOOD puzzles like a happy camper.
So yea, fkn play this.

The thumbs down on the recommendation is for the current game at the current price. This game is essentially a Civ 5 reskin with a few added features, and should be priced more as an expansion dlc rather than a ful, unique game in its own right. With the exception of 'favors,' the diplomacy system is exactly the same, and I mean EXACTLY. Firaxis was apparently so lazy they used the same exact dialogue from Civ 5 in the diplomacy screen.
Now, granted, the game is built on a very fun and strong foundation (that of Civ 5), and so I'll be playing it for a long time. However, anybody looking for a new and exciting entry into the Civilization francise should delay their hopes for whatever Civilization game comes later. If you think paying full price for a game that is basically a reskin of an old game is worth it, then you will think this game is worth it; if you think expansion dlcs to games should be priced accordingly lower than the actual main game, then you will be disappointed with this buy. Wait for a half-off sale or something, and then it will be worth it; right now charging $50 for this game is actually a little insulting.

Dishonored: Death of the Outsider is a standalone expansion and first and only major DLC content towards Arkane's Studios' Dishonored 2. Taking place after the events of the main game, the player takes control of Dishonored series regular Billie Lurk as she tries to rescue her former mentor Daud on the island of Karnaca and work with him to find a way to kill the Outsider and contain the threat of the Void once and for all.
While this expansion offers the same engaging gameplay of the other Dishonored games and is mostly a very entertaining ride, it also fails to reach the narrative and technical quality of the original game's main DLC content, The Knife of Dunwall and The Brigmore Witches.
The best features of Death of the Outsider are the following:
1) Billie Lurk has her own set of gadgets and powers which help set her apart from the previous protagonists and make playing the expansion its own unique experience. Furthermore, her powers are integrated flawlessly into the plot, in the measure that you can solve various main and side quests in unique ways by using them in creative ways.
2) The missions featured are very sandbox-ish in design, as you can approach them and their objectives in a variety of ways and the environments are large enough to accomodate your own playstyle.
3) The contracts mechanic. Basically at the beginning of each missions you are given some extra objectives you can pursue while you are on your main quest: these range from killing someone undetected or steal something without being noticed. At the end of each mission you'll recive money (and sometimes some charms) for every contract cleared. While some contracts may end up being extremely counterproductive towards your playstyle, they are a nice way to increase the longevity of the expansion.
The places where Death of the Outsider however falls short are the following:
1) The main structure and new content offered by the expansion in comparison to the base game. The package is only five missions long: the first one is spent into a rather anonimous Karnaca's street without any powers: the second and third take place into the same district, which doesn't look any different from anything else you've seen in the main game; the fourth mission is spent into a slightly modified and smaller map from the main game (the Royal Conservatory); the fifth takes place into a rather bland mineshaft. Also, this expansion doesn't introduce any new enemy or hazards, save from its very final sequence.
2) The story and lore angles feel played out incredibly hastly and with very weak twists, and don't quite live up to the cool premise of the whole expansion. In particular, the portrayals of both Daud and Billie are very odd and sudden, to the point we may as well talk about totally different characters.
3) Since the whole chaos mechanic was pretty divisive in the past games, this expansion just removes it entirely, so indulging into killing frenzies now doesn't hold any kind of consequence. Depending on your own opinion, that could had been either a terrible or a great idea. It's also worth mentioning that the tone of the ending is changed by the single choice you'll decide to pick at the very end.
In short, if you can't get enough of Dishonored's gameplay, setting and atmosphere then Dishonored: Death of the Outsider is most definitely a standalone expansion for you. However, if any of the above may cause you some concern or issues you may think about actually buying it for the time being

I haven't played much of it so far, but i can tell i'm going to love it. The game has awesome graphics, great story and lots of action. There are dozens of ways to kill each target as you go through the story; either stealthily or with force. The game has 2 modes. Absoluion, which is the main story, and contracts, where you compete with friends to get the highest rating and kill the selected target. The point system in the game is another awesome feature. You lose points for killing civillians and blowing your cover, and at that point you have to change your disguise by taking the clothes off of a killed target. this is a good feature because it adds to the stealth feeling of the game, and also helps you by giving you special advantages (ex. Cops can go into places civilians cant) but if someone else in the same type of clothing as you (another Cop) sees you, they begin to get suspicious, at which point you have to either take them out or leave the area to lower their suspicion. The game also has awesome fast paced gun combat when you are caught, and a cool feature called Point Shooting that can be compared to Dead Eye in red dead redemption. If you stay undercover, the combat isn't very fast paced, but still very fun to see all the creative ways to kill  (there are bonuses for things like making it look like an accident). Overall i would say this is a great game and it's worth its price. It has lots of replay value because of the endless ways to kill and it's got a great story.

This is a game that is meant to be played "casually".  While the game has multiple z-axis "planes", it is a game largely played on a 2-dimensional field, where you basically just guide your little critter to eat things until you grow up.  There are three "paths" to go down, which you traverse through eating colored blobs of three colors.
There are two modes.
In the non-competitive mode, you basically just get dumped on a map, and get told to eat everything of one color to go to the next map.  There's essentially no way to lose, but to quit, which I suppose is what makes it "casual", and it's not like games need to be hard to be enjoyable, but there's no particular story, here, to make the world more compelling without it.  There's some "exploration", just to see all the different critters, but once you have seen every level, you've seen everything the game has to offer.
In the "competitive mode", you have an AI-controlled critter competing with you for food, where victory is measured in hogging more food than the other guy can get.  While hypothetically, this means challenge and desperately trying to hunt creatures for food faster, regardless of color, in practical effect, you can just stay green and vacuum up everything far faster than your opponent, since the extra bits of food from dividing food pieces all count to your total, and you can consume more food from critters than the game expects to count. In general, I could eat several times more food than the opponent, and never once seemed like I was in trouble unless I completely abandoned attempting to eat for a while.
The big choice in the game about which critter to be is somewhat defeated by the imbalance in the practical use of the different criters.  The "carnivore" red is quick to accelerate, and gets a "dashing" skill to "attack" other creatures.  The "herbivore" green (and I put "herbivore" in quotes because you still hunt and eat other animals, you just want to eat the green ones) has faster eating time (making it so you can eat as fast as you ram through food, rather than skipping over food for a second or so) and has a super AoE suction attack that consumes all food in the area.  The "omnivore" blue (which, somehow, eats a different food entirely from both carnivores and herbivores, rather than just eating both in roughly equal measure,) gets a better turning radius and a defensive sound skill that makes creatures flee from it.
Hypothetically, in a game where combat mattered, the difference between an attack skill, a defense skill, and a resource-gathering skill might mean something, but since all you do in this game is eat, the herbivore skill is fantastically useful and makes the game significantly faster and less frustrating, while the omnivore defenseskill is useless since you need to hunt critters, rather than have them flee you, and the carnivore dash attack is pointless since the only enemies that run from you do so across the z-axis, which the dash will not go across.
Ultimately, I recommend this game only on sale for the sheer color and fascination of it.  It's odd and interesting, and worth looking at, and on sale, you can get it dirt cheap enough to justify buying it for aesthetics alone, but there isn't enough actual gameplay to keep you in it.  This is a game you can completely "play out" and feel you've experienced everything it can offer in just a half-dozen hours.

Overall: 6.5/10 (Mac version)
This is an a gaming tragedy.  Hollow Knight is almost a perfect game, but the failures that hold it back are near intolerable.
Pros:  The atmosphere, immensity, dark tone, storyline, mechanics, and painstaking detail put into the levels are all 10's.  It has an amazing depth that is self-revealing through gameplay.  Before I bought this game, I had gone back and replayed Super Metroid and Castlevania: Symphony of the Night just by happenstance.  Compared to its parent material, this game really progresses the genre.  It uses those two games as a skeleton and fleshes the game out with it's own new ideas.  There is a much much heavier emphasis on platforming than the Big Two though....
Cons:  Overemphasis on perfection combined with stuttering framerate issues.  If there is a busy screen (such as during a tricky platforming section, the trials, boss fights) the framerate will stutter and you will almost always take damage as a result of the overemphasis on perfection in gameplay.  If when you double-jump and the game skips, it is probably during some task that requires the jump to be performed near perfectly.  The framerate stutter will get you killed.  The game is difficult, which is not a real issue as that is true to the parent material and the genre.  The need for massive computing resources in a 2d platformer like this is potentially gamebreaking for people who are playing just above required specs.  If you have a high end gaming computer, buy this game.  If you are between the required and recommended specs, save yourself some fury and don't buy this game.  Normally these games get easier as the game progresses because your skill as a player increases as well as the abilities of the character, and this would be true of Hollow Knight also if the bugs (no, I mean software bugs) didn't become more evident as the screen becomes busier.  This happens more often in the late game, meaning some tasks might not be completable without endlessly repeating them and crossing your fingers.  For someone interested in delving into the story and picking up as much lore as possible it is at times prohibitive of having fun.  The strange thing about the framerate stuttering is how the game engine prioritizes the chain of events that happens during the stutter.  For example, during a double jump you will often see the animation, hear the sound, but not actually move.  If you were swinging your sword at the same time, it might pass directly through your enemy with the sound and animation but not deal damage.  However, if you managed to get caught up in touch-damage during the stutter, that damage will be applied 100% of the time.  It seems that the game engine emphasizes the edging and animations over the player actions, which can be a real bummer during freezes.  The options let you turn down the particle effects to "low" which helps a lot, but there are no further performance options.  I don't want to make it seem like it is a constant issue, it only happens sometimes.  When it happens though, it forces you to consider whether you enjoy playing enough to ignore a design issue that prevents you from fully having fun.  This could probably *easily* be patched by changing how the game deals with memory, and if we see a patch that fixes it I will gladly take back every negative thing I've pointed out and say it is a perfect game.
Bottom Line:  If you have a good pc and love metroidvania games, buy this immediately.  If you are at or just above the required specs for this game, wait until you have a better machine or don't bother.

ESCHATOS is basically the sequel to JUDGEMENT SILVERSWORD, which was a homebrew wonderswan color game that has also been released on steam (it's pretty fun too). All the systems from that game return, but with greater refinement. There's a really enjoyable time attack mode which starts off seemingly easy and gets increasingly frantic as you realize you don't really have as much time as you thought; there's multiple difficulties as well. The main gimmick is a shield which blocks shots but also turns them into a rotating damage-dealing swarm of purple things. Drop your shield and the purple gems grant you points, which increase over the course of the game -- it's a fun mechanic and offers a smart way to do risk-reward, since the shield can also be used to cheat your way through some difficult curtains if you haven't worn it down trying to net extra gems for your scoreboard. Take Civ V, strip away 80% of the content, slap a coat of Sci-Fi paint on it and ship it out the door.
Very disappointing.  Beyond Earth should have been sold as a Civ V mod for a fraction of the price.  This game has slightly more content and replayability than the Steampunk DLC released for Civ V.
There are only 8 civs to choose from, but that doesn't matter because they are effectively identical anyway.
There are only about 8-10 units in the game, and it's the same 8-10 units regardless of which civ you choose.
The landscape is crowded with features and resources that have very little purpose.  You can comfortably set your Workers on auto and ignore them.
All 5 Victory Paths are Science driven, making everything else largely irrelevant.  Even the Domination Victory depends heavily on the Science resource in order to unlock the automatic upgrades for the 2 or 3 units you will need to win.
Trade is crucial to success, but very tedious and not fun at all to manage.  Every turn, I would get 1 or 2 messages from Trade units asking me to confirm that I still want it to keep doing what I told it to do the last 20 times it asked.
Diplomacy is irrelevant.  All other Civs can be safely ignored unless you feel like conquering them.  Other leaders will frequently harass you with pointless offers or empty threats, though, and that gets annoying fast.
Exploration is largely pointless and unrewarding.  The whole world is one homogenous smear of resources.  Clear out your own little plot of land and don't bother going anywhere else.
Seriously, I want my money back on this one.

For those that may be unaware, Qute's ESCHATOS is the spiritual successor to Judgement Silversword and Cardinal Sins.  Those familiar with the predecessors will find many aspects of this game more than a little recognizable.  Sadly, gone are all the judges and sins.  The story line of ESCHATOS can be summed up in about two sentences: Aliens have invaded the earth and captured the moon!  It is your mission to save the Earth!
It's about the depth of story one might expect from a shoot 'em up.  One might say it's even preferable to have a bare bones story.  After all, if you're playing a shmup do you really want to see things like dialogue and cut scenes?  Having said all of this, I would have liked to see them build a little bit more on the judges that they introduced in the previous games.  It would have been more unique than an alien invasion.  While the judges themselves may be things of the past, it isn't entirely fair to say that they're gone.
Many of the enemies in ESCHATOS are recreations of the ones in Judgement Silversword.  Not only are they similar in appearance, some of them even have the same attack patterns.  When a mirror shield showed up I didn't recognize it, but as soon as it started firing I knew exactly what it was.  I was prepared to fight it too, as the ship in this game works almost exactly the same as it did in the earlier games.  It has a straight shot, a spread shot, and a shield.  The main differences are the shield being far more useful and the spread shot having significantly less reach.  It's also no longer possible to combine the straight and spread shots through rapid button tapping.
The game has three modes of play: original, advanced, and time attack.  Original is a very traditional mode that features screen clearing blue bombs that can be picked up without penalty.  Time attack is what it sounds like, you try to clear the game as fast as possible.  Advanced is a little more complicated than normal.  Your ship starts off very weak and can be strengthened via pickups.  The power ups will raise your attack power, lower your shield power, and increase your score multiplier.  There are two screen clearing bombs in this mode, but picking up either does the exact opposite of a power up.  A blue bomb will simply destroy everything on the screen, but a gold one will transform bullets into purple shards.  The shards can be picked up for points or transformed into temporary damaging orbitals by activating the shield.  It was a little tricky for me to figure it out without any instructions but it's a lot of fun once you get used to it.  Original and advanced have the following difficulty options: easy, normal, hard, hardest, and endless.  Whether you're completely new to the genre, or an arcade veteran, there will be something here for you.
There has been a major update in graphics since the days of the Wonderswan.  This is easily one of the most cinematic games I've ever played.  The stages flow into each other so effectively that it almost feels like watching a movie about a lone ship taking down an alien invasion.  Unlike many games there aren't really breaks between stages, the whole game is continuous.  It is handled very well, however there were a few perspective changes that I initially found to be very confusing.  After playing a few times I got the hang of it, but I can imagine some players finding it frustrating.  In addition to the  perspective changes, there is one bullet type I had trouble with at first.  I didn't find the semi-transparent green homing ribbons to be as visible as they probably should be considering their danger level.  Much like the perspective changes I was able to get used to them eventually, but I believe the developers handled these projectiles better in Judgement Silversword.  Aside from the visuals, it would be remiss of me not to mention the audio.  The soundtrack is so outstanding I've found myself listening to a few of the tracks on repeat.
When I first started playing ESCHATOS I wasn't so sure about it.  As cool as the cinematic game play was, the perspective shifts in several stages really had me questioning the style.  After putting some time into it, it has really grown on me a lot.  The scoring system is based around killing every enemy in a wave to increase your multiplier.  I found it to be straightforward, challenging, and a whole lot of fun.  It's a shame that this game doesn't seem to be very popular. It's a very solid shoot 'em up.  M-Kai and Qute have done a great job here. I'd certainly recommend it to fans of shooting games.

The aesthetic and OST have a great Dreamcasty nostalgic feel which is very fun. The gameplay is a perfect example of easy to learn, difficult to master which I love--unlike some crazy Cave game where you have to search for hours of poorly translated Japanese websites to decipher the BS, overly-complicated scoring/chaining system. (Looking at you, Espgaluda II. I'm not bitter though. Ok, maybe a little bit.) You just shoot every little thing zipping by on the screen to build a multiplier. Miss a little missle or die, lose the multiplier. Simple, fun, addictive.
No bombs in this one, but you have something arguably better: a shield that regnerates. It doesn't make you invincible but it can cut through like 90% of the crap this game throws at you. So if you suck at scoring (like me) and are focused on survival at first you can just whip out that trusty shield. Good stuff.
Like JSS this game doesn't both with overly long transitions or breaks between the actions--instead of 4-5 big levels there's 26ish stages that break up a bunch of mini sections and bosses. Like JSS, this gives the action an amazing flow and makes you feel like you're also pushing forward. There's also a generous amount of stocks so that the game usually feels fair apart from a couple weird camera angles that take some getting used to.
So yeah, buy it. You'll like it.

The most polished installment of the series by far. Giants has really grown up in the past few years and matured the game from obscure niche title, to commercial success complete with all the hype that go along with a new release.
So what's new compared to FS2013? If I had to describe it one word, REALISM. For starters the graphics and physics engine has been majorly overhauled and they've done a great job with. It runs like a dream, smooth as butter and isn't a huge hardware pig so it's well optimized. The screenshots really don't do it justice but there is a plethora of details added to the game, some very subtle and others not so subtle.
Graphics and lighting are just better. The new tractor physics are really improved. Underpowered machines now really struggle uphill when pulling heavy loads and in some cases will stall or the wheels will just spin. Crash physics aren't so great but I overlook this because the game isn't about crashing. Everything in the gameworld is more detailed:
1. Machines now get dirty and muddy over time and really grungy looking.
2. The machines can now be powerwashed and also get washed during a rainstorm.
3. Machines leave dust trails and tracks on the ground where you've driven.
4. Little bits of cottonwood and allergens floating around in the air.
5. All new and improved particle effects and animations from the chopped straw coming out the back of the harvesters.
6. New particle effects and animations when unloading/loading grain.
7. New realistic looking animations for churning soil when plowing or cultivating fields.
8. All new animations for crop harvesting. Instead of the crops just disappearing when driving the harvester like in FS2013, they're actually animated now and get pulled into the header and swept to the center to the pickup shoot just like IRL.
9. The drivers in the cab now turn the wheel when turning instead of having static arms/hands.
10. Mirrors in the equipment now work and you can see behind you.
11. Vehicle speed can now be fine tuned to your liking in 1mph/kph increments to better match harvester speeds.
12. An in game semi transparent map overlay of the gameworld can be pulled up now while you drive with most of the major locations labeled so you don't have to refer to an external map.
13. Sprayers and fertilizers can now be hired out. Woohoo!!!!
I won't list them all but there are many others. The biggest thing added in terms of mechanics is the addition of forestry and logging. You can now engage in the planting, cutting and chipping of trees and selling them to the lumber mill or wood burning plant for big profit along with a nice selection of wood cutting and processing equipment and implements. Is it fun? Yes but like real life the handling of logs with 6 axis or more machines has a bit of a learning curve and can be frustrating at first, but very satisfying once you get the hang of it.
Finally the interface has also been overhauled and is much cleaner, polished and more modern looking and generally better although I do miss the onscreen PDA which they've done away with.
The core gameplay remains essentially the same and that's a good thing because it works.

Good game overall, got it for £10 on the sale, definitely worth it. All combat retained from D2 which was nice, and there are some interesting new enemies on the last mission. However, the story was kind of a disappointment, and I think you should only really buy this game if you really like the dishonored series, as it just didn't really seem to flow all that well.
Completed the game in 9 hours on high chaos, so the length of the game is a meh, it could have been a bit longer as there are only 5 missions - 2 of which were set in karnaca, and one in the devine observatory, so there were really only 2 or 3 new areas. You only get 3 new abilities: Displacement, Semblance and Foresight, all at a default upgrade, with no runes. This means that bonecharms are much more vital in this game, as that's where you get your passive and ability upgrades such as agility (Which is on the first level, don't miss it).
Now, optimization. This game ran noticeably better than dishonored 2. With my mediocre rig with a 1060 that is being bottlenecked to 20% usage, I never really hit an unplayable framerate. Most of the time I was at 60fps, sometimes 40, and in karnaca about 30fps, however that area is much more CPU demanding. I had no problem with frame spikes ruining the immersion in combat like I did in dishonored 2.
I'd recommend waiting for a sale to buy this game to get the most out of your money as I personally probably wouldn't pay £20 for this, but I definitely recommend it to any dishonored fan, as it does feel like a new game.

This game is a very, very good game. I am currently at Chapter 9, and I must say I actually liked the game up until that point and I'm sure I will enjoy what's left. I got it on the Steam Summer Sale, for a very cheap price. I was compelled to try it since it was really, really cheap here on my country, and I had the money to spare, and it was a reboot of an old-school shooter, the original Shadow Warrior. I was curious, so I decided to buy it. I originally planned to buy the Deluxe Edition of the game on Steam, but I decided to try it first and then judge if I should. I waited a few hours, and then I booted it up. I had to tweak the settings to the lowest possible since about 5 minutes into the game an "Out of Memory" error popped up, but after that, I quickly enjoyed the game. The game immediately gained points with me just because you could use a katana, but the gunplay also gave it good points with me. The guns don't feel underpowered if used correctly, except the Uzi which is basically a peashooter. The revolver is good for headshots early on, the crossbow is useful for taking out powerful enemies quickly, and the shotgun is very powerful and can take out most enemies in a single hit. All the weapons can be upgraded, and the Katana is upgraded as you go through the story as I could tell. Using the katana gives you the added bonus of being able to use special sword attacks, one of them being required to advance with the plot. These attacks are very useful in various circumstances, and with an upgrade they can be used as a healing source. And let's not forget the Ki powers, that can give you some breathing room and set up some quick kills on the right hands. The story is interesting as of now, and the dialogue is very smart, and it reminds me of the old days where these were overly cheesy and that always gives me a good laugh.
TL;DR, this is a very good game. It blends the good parts of oldschool and modern shooters to make a truly enjoyable experience, and I really recommend it to everyone who likes first person shooter games or oldschool type games.

The multiple difficulty settings made the process a lot easier, though, and I was able to clear the game without needing to use a continue after several hours of play.
It needs to be mentioned that this game's soundtrack is frickin' incredible! I found out about the game through the song SILVER LINING and like other people have said, Yousuke Yasui is a fantastic composer.
If you love shooting for high scores, this game will keep you coming back a ton. The scoring is very skill based, and rewards you for learning the patterns and not letting any ships escape. As you get better, you'll almost always get a higher score than yourself, which is very satisfying.
All in all I recommend this game a ton, ESCHATOS definitely has me looking for more Shoot 'Em Ups to play, from Qute and otherwise!
