TLDR:
+freerunning system
+beautiful open world
+occasionally interesting characters
-nearly broken combat system
-mediocre setting
-extreme similarity to any ac game ever
This game is probably my second favorite AC game (obviously after AC 2) which might make you wonder why I would not recommend it. Well, unless you are a hardcore fan of the series or the pirate genre I really see no point why you should get this game instead of AC 2. My main problem is that upon entering this game you will either discover a new cool game idea - if you never played any AC - or you feel like you are doing exactly the same thing over and over that you already did in any other game of the series.
However, the graphics are beautiful and detailed while the game still delivers a solid 35-65 fps on my middle class gaming laptop. This is certainly a nice aspect, but in my opinion gameplay, characters and story are much more important in a game than how it looks.
Gameplay wise I love one part of AC and hate another. The freerunning is done really nicely and is by far the most exciting way of motion I have seen in an action role playing game for a long time. However, the combat system is really really boring. from the moment you enter the game you are basically unbeatable, because of the infinite blocking and countering mechanic. This system basically ensures that even if twenty enemies surround you there is no challenge in grinding yourself through all these opponents and not loosing any health. This takes away a lot of the fun, particularly since there is no incentive to play stealthy (no moral system or anything).
This brings me to another important point, story and characters. I did enjoy a few of the characters, which is largely thanks to a pretty well written situational dialogue and decent voice acting. However, the story is nothing really great and doesn't pull you in. This together with the pirate setting, which I personally think is not the greatest and used currently by way too many rpg developers makes the game a fun experience for an hour or two, but also bores you if you stay much longer. This is particularly true if you already played any AC game.
gist:
If you are thinking about trying out the AC universe for the first time, go with AC 2 over this game. If you know other AC titles and think that this one is very different - its not so consider leaving it on the shelf. If you are a graphics enthusiast with an aptitude for piracy and aren't interesting in a challenging comabt system, well this game is for you!

tl;dr:
PROS:
-interesting, immersive, and original setting
-engaging, tactical combat
-great character system and itemization
-unparalleled reactivity, choice, and consequence
CONS:
-requires a fair amount of experimenting to get a hang of the game
-skills are unbalanced
-game content seems somewhat incomplete
The Age of Decadence is a turn-based RPG focusing on tactical combat, urban and political intrigue, and choices with meaningful consequences. The setting is Roman-inspired low magic fantasy. The game is an aquired taste; it displaces many of the cliches of current RPG games, which will likely turn people off at first. You're not the Chosen One who can master every skill and cleave through hordes of enemies; you're just another guy trying to survive in a harsh world. You can't see everything the game has to offer in one shot, as a lot of the content is mutually exclusive to certain story choices. Theres no level grinding or respawning enemies; every combat encounter is placed on purpose and designed carefully. And they're difficult for the unprepared, but realistic; if a thief lures you into an ambush in an alley, the enemies aren't there to drop XP and loot- they're there to kill you.
The dialogue is rich and immersive, and the game builds an interesting world, even without AAA graphics. You use skills in dialogue through binary checks, though some have the possibility of partial success. The combat is deep and good tactics are crucial to winning even the earliest fights; if you run and start slashing, you will be dismembered. For the most part all enemies use the same derived statistics as you, so the playing field is pretty even. Theres no HP gain on level up, and the range of hit points is small, somewhere around 20-60; so every point matters. Simple decisions like poisoning your weapons or switching your outcome can be deterministic in winning a fight.
The level of reactivity in AoD is unparalleled. Theres more ways to finish quests than any game I can think of. If you play without spoilers, it will take you multiple playthroughs to see everything.
AoD was developed by an independent team over the course of 10 years. Unfortunately, this shows in the game. Its rough around the edges, especially in the later stages. The first act around the town of Teron is exquisitly crafted, its by far the best first town of any RPG. Theres so many options, secrets, and great dialogues. The second act of is strong as well, but theres not as many really inspired moments as in the first. After having so many options for resolving each quest in Teron, its jarring to run into quests where you have only the 'fight or pay' options. A lot of the content here starts to feel tacked on, just simple combats that add no real weight to the story. By the time you get to the city in the third act, the place feels empty and unfinished. I wish the developers had had enough time and resources to really bring this region to life.
A common complaint is that the binary skill checks and strict gifting of skill points requires extensive meta-knowledge and save-scumming; this is only partially true. If you play a focused character and stay true to form (e.g. a talker doesn't try to fight everyone), you will generally be fine. Playing a hybrid character does require a good working knowledge of most of the games structure, but I found this to be a very enjoyable challenge. Then not only did I have to contend with the quests themselves, but also the order I approached them. Its very rewarding to tweak your skills to just the right level to set up the perfect double cross.
The skills are diverse and interesting, but quite unbalanced. Lore and Crafting are far and away the best skills and practically required, whereas Etiquette is hardly ever checked, and most of the situation where you use Traps seem simply tacked on. The game keeps carefully track of your reputation with the world and each faction, but these stats are hardly ever checked, aside from Body Count. Again, I feel that these are more great idea that the developers simply didnt have the resources to flesh out, rather than oversights or poor design choices.
I've played through the game 4 or 5 times now, and its easily my game of the year, and definitely in my top 5 of all time. Its a contender with Fallout 2 and Planescape: Torment. The amazing thing is its this good while only being 80% done.

Before Purchasing this game, you should really take into account exactly what you are getting into. This is a military
meaning that this isn't another fast paced, guns blazing first person shooter where players rely solely on reflexes, aim, and a bit of skill to make it to the top of the scoreboard after a match. In fact, you may as well forget everything you know about first person shooters other than WASD is to move, because those ridiculous tactics you learned will be the very bane of your existence, also you should not play this game to win, this game is meant to be experienced, play it as though you were a real soldier fighting a real war, a single man cannot win a war and the same is true of this game.
Unlike most first person shooters you cannot simply jump into the campaign(do some boot camp first), the player's hand isn't held during the SP campaign telling the player exactly what they need to do. Instead, you are given a mission, a briefing of the mission, a briefing of your role in the mission, and the objectives that you must complete. The player must then decipher this information, create a plan of action before proceeding, follow on site orders, and fulfil their role, also the player must understand how to use their equipment before accepting a mission, because the campaign does not teach the player on site how to use them. There is a lot of thinking, tactics, planning, and strategy involved even in the SP campaign... just like real life. That being said, completing your objectives under these circumstances is a very satishfying experience that I can't seem to find in any other game.
Combat is slow paced, but it isn't boring, trust me. Every second in the field is intense, all it takes is one bullet to the head or vital organs, and you're done. Whenever I am ordered, or give the order to engage the enemy, my heart thumps out of my chest, and my palms sweat. One small mistake and its over, if you dont kill the enemy before they see you, chances are you will get butchered by heavy machine gun fire or sniped out of nowhere, and if you are really unlucky, you can get bombarded to hell by an airstrike, or become prey to attack helicopters. Even if you go an entire mission without firing your weapon once, your eyes are peeled scanning the field, skipping a heartbeat at the sight of a rock that looks even remotely like a person.
Did I mention that its really difficult to aim? no seriously, this game simulates bullet ballistics amongst many other things to keep it as realistic as possible, unless you are 100m or so away from your target, simply pointing your crosshairs at the target isn't enough, various things like gravity, wind, and the speed of the bullet will stop you from getting that bullseye, this isn't a bad thing of course, but you will have to spend a lot of time perfecting your aim.
Combat in vehicles (even tanks and jets) have the same feel, you can be destroyed in one shot with a well placed rocket, road mines, heat seeking missiles, and of course AA (and they are very common on the battlefield), so dont think for a second you are invincible, infact you may be even more vulnerable than your infantry comrades concealed in the bushes.
If you are here for DayZ, then you have come at a great time, the number of DayZ servers severely outnumber other servers that generally theme towards the original Arma 2 experience, if you are here for the original experience however, do not fear. These servers still exist, but you will have to look for them. Before you even consider looking for servers, get the DayZ launcher
Now I know what you are thinking, why the hell would I need the DayZ launcher if i dont want to play DayZ? The thing is, the DayZ launcher can actually find non-DayZ servers if you input the correct keywords, and as a bonus, it even organizes these servers according to your preference, such as ping or playercount, once you find a server you like, simply copy and paste the IP into Arma 2 OA and you are good to go.
Domination is a fun gamemode for players who just want to casually drop in and out of servers, communication via voice isn't mandatory, so you can type to your heart's content, and there is room for mistakes (just don't go full retard) Basically two teams (or one if its players vs AI) are set against each other, the main objective is to control as much territory as possible in the map, every time a team captures territory, they are rewarded with a new vehicle which they can use against the enemy. If one team controls the entire map, that team wins, and the game restarts. This gamemode is fun, but can get repetitive, and is very linear compared to most Arma missions, this is however a good place to start if you are new to the multiplayer scene, and it will teach you valuable skills like teamwork, synergy, co-ordination, tactical thinking, squad management, platoon management, and of course...patience.
[u ] Wasteland: [/u] Wasteland is a never ending death match between team Blufor, Team Opfor, and the independents (teamless, therefore can kill anyone they want), unlike DayZ, there is no zombies, and a mostly team based PVP playstyle, unlike DayZ where its one massive free-for-all. Players have to eat and drink in order to avoid starvation and dehydration whilst keeping an eye open for enemies, you earn cash by killing people which you can then use to purchase vehicles, guns, and of course living essentials. Just remember that it is impossible to win this gamemode, so really your ultimate goal is survival. I personally do not like this game mode for the same reason I do not like DayZ, it feels absurdly pointless knowing that whatever I do does not make a difference, at least in SP campaign and other game modes, my contribution made a difference towards a "greater cause" rather than just: "You live, you die."
Ironically, wasteland does not feel like a wasteland in anyway with the exception of Hunger and Thirst meters, at least DayZ added atmosphere (like wrecked cars, debris, etc)to the environment to make its setting believale.
Whether it is Takistan Life, or Island Life, or whatever life they make next, it all boils down to one core mechanic: Roleplaying as a cop, civillian, terrorist, or Opfor in one big city. These RP's simulate living, breathing cities that are inhabited by real players. If you like the sound of that, look up some videos on youtube first, because the community is not newbie friendly. I for one do enjoy this gamemode, but i bring friends, since soloing is boring.
THIS... is the holy grail of all Arma Multiplayer. Milsim Groups give you the purest form of Realistic simulation ever, granted you have the time and dedication of course, but it is well worth it.
If you want a realistic military experience, with highly community interactive gamemodes, or just want to play DayZ, buy this game, seriously its an unforgettable experience!

Very different from the previous Hitmans. Compared to Blood Money where the levels are huge sandboxes, the story is irrelevant and the accidents require Machiavellian plans to achieve, Absolution is a lot easier. Full disclosure: I am a big sci-fi geek and have been anticipating this game for some time. However, that is simultaneously a blessing and a curse: an overhyped game has a higher bar. The last time Firaxis published a game that obsessed me, (XCom remake) I hated it and wrote a scathing review (although they did fix everything that I hated in subsequent patches and DLCs). So I hope the two forces mitigate eachother and give you something mostly-objective.
---PROS---
Its Civ in space. Yes that seems horribly cliche, but the formula works and can be translated into other settings other than the bread-and-butter historical advancement sim.
They fixed a lot of the frustrations with original Civ and streamlined it.
The new world is fascinating, and they did a great job of making it kinda spooky and alien: The fungal map especially.
It has a degree of the Unit-Customization mechanic that Alpha Centauri had, without being so tedious. Rather than having lots of little units that get upgraded constantly with new techs, requiring players to go in and change their units every so-many turns, Beyond Earth takes a better approach: automatically upgrade, and allow users to pick perks. Those perks then compound over time as they stack. Very elegant.
No game-breaking bugs (yet), that I have seen.
Well-balanced, as far as I have seen.
Tons of fun.
---CONS---
The UI is really clunky in places. In some ways it feels a lot like Civ2, in that the number of units and buildings by endgame requires a lot of scrolling. If any developers are reading: I urge you to take inspiration from emerging web widget interfaces, particularly accordions. It would make the build list so much easier to navigate if the type of build (units, buildings, wonders) were slightly to the left, rather than dividers in the list. Then users could go "units", "marine". Rather than having to scroll and minimize. Also the tech-web, while innovative, is not as innovative as the developers would have you believe. This UI could also use quite a bit of improvement. In particular, the purple-blue-white-black color scheme does not really denote what's going on. I spent most of my game in the far-zoomed-out version of the web.
Developers let their colors show in the factions. Its obvious, both from the developer interviews and demo games, which affinities they like, and unfortunatley I think they allowed their own preferences to color the factions. Literally. Purity is red. That makes no sense unless game-makers thought of them as the bad guys. Purity should be blue, like water. Harmony should be green like nature. Supremacy is cool with yellow-gold. So the game developers don't like Purity, so what? Well.... the purity units are incredibly uninspired and boring compared to the other factions. They could have gone more "starship troopers" or "aliens" or heck: "avatar" (from the corporation's units). A large pool of inspiration exists of "humans versus new planet" in science fiction, and yet they went with this kinda blocky style instead.
I wrote in the pros that there are no game-breaking bugs. Yet there are a surprising number of bugs! I am a little shocked by the number bugs. Most notably rendering issues on the upgrade and diplomacy screens. Characters not showing up in the latter, not animating. In the former: units from previous upgrades being rendered over the unit that's supposed to appear, or being zoomed in too close to see anything.
The tech web could be bigger. Developers said that players wouldn't research the entire web, but I almost did during my first playthrough. This could be because I went heavy on science and on a huge map, and because I didn't really know what the hell I was doing. And as Purity as my first play, I didn't expect having to settle the 20 colonists after building the Promised Land gate. But it got to a point where I HAD to research non-purity techs because there was nothing else on the web, and my cities began to look like we weren't purity. Maybe after the last purity tech they should add an infinite tech that boosts some other resource like culture or energy.
Finally I have to comment a little bit about the creativity of the names. I know its a bit silly, this being a sci-fi game and all, but a lot of the names of  buildings and techs are just terms with some sci-fi sounding name stuck on the front. Xeno, or Nano, or Neo, or Gene. You've got your gene garden and your nano pasture (very small cows?). And some of the quotes that pop up for completed techs and wonders are totally asinine. I would have preferred if they had taken real quotes from history that were somehow applicable. Real wisdom from really wise people, rather than making their fictional people try to sound original and wise.
---CONCLUSION---
On balance: This game is great. Most of the cons are little annoyances that don't affect the overall game. But there is room for improvement. I'd give it 4.5 out of 5.0 stars.
One final thought that I was going to put in the "cons"... but I knew was not going to be in this game, so I can't exactly call it a "con", is this: players on their second play through understand the game. Its no longer such an alien world. We have prescient knowledge from previous play-throughs of the wildlife, resources, what techs we will develop, and how those techs might aid us. The only thing we don't know is the landscape. While this might seem kind-of obvious, I wonder if it wouldn't be better to throw some randomness in. Pick N native lifeforms from a set and randomize their stats. Randomize resources and what they do. While I realize this would make game balancing impossible, as long as the randomizer algorithm was designed right, factions might have underpowered units, but they would also have overpowered units. And they would have to rely on learning the strengths and weaknesses of their affinity every time that they play, as if it were the first time they played. Just an idea to make the alien world seem more alien.
I do hope developers read these things  :)  But probably not.
Anyway, thanks for reading!

The game is relatively fast-paced due to utilizing a simultaneous turns mechanic, with both players completing their actions at once.  This establishes a very engaging experience in which both players have to try and guess at what the opponent will do, and how to respond.  The game also allows for a great deal of strategy, utilizing both a "health" system akin to Magic or other TCGs, as well as a morale system (which effectively functions as a second health meter, except it drops from losing troops in battle), multiple combat zones, and an initiative system.  There is definitely plenty of depth to be had in this game.
The game is also very good about rewarding every portion of your progress.  There is a leveling system which gives you free cards when you level up, and you also get free cards from completing various achievements (termed "quests" in your profile window) such as beating the AI in training matches multiple times, completing the (very short) campaigns for each faction, and beating Academy challenges.  And the game even allows you to construct your own decks for facing off against players or AIs.
So why am I not recommending this game?  Well, I should be honest.  This is perhaps one of the first times I'm actually NOT recommending a game, it's simply not something I do often.  So I want to be perfectly clear: this game is fun, but there ultimately is one MAJOR flaw with its design structure.
No, before you say it, it's not that the game is Pay To Win.  On many occasions I actually beat players using mostly starter-level cards.  And some players have done quite a lot with their starter cards and worked hard to become top players.  But with that said, the community needs to be more honest with itself: newer, free players are definitely at an inherent disadvantage compared to players who have spent lots of time and/or money on the game.
I'll try to explain, since that sounds like it may contradict what I said before.  Again, I'm not bashing the game, and it does make some effort to give you lots of cards to play around with.  But it's not nearly enough.
In my experience, completing every single campaign mission and PvE fight possible only leveled me to just below Lvl 9 (there are 50 levels).  So it's relatively clear the game is trying to encourage you to face other players.  I had no problem with this, so I started playing some matches against other people.  But I quickly began to realize there was a problem: they had WAY better decks than I did, filled with cards that were in many ways significantly better than mine....and I had no way to prevent them from beating me into the dirt, no matter how well I understood the game or how well I played.
I can recall several matches in which I played my deck's strategy out perfectly, and even outplayed my opponent for the majority of the game, only to fall behind and eventually lose because they kept pulling out cards that I'd never seen before, cards I had no access to, and cards that I had no defense against.  And yes, I can tell the difference.  I played several folks who were just a lot better than me....but also a number of people who clearly were not, who ended up beating me anyways because their deck was full of cards I couldn't combat.
I recall one particularly egregious match where my opponent was being repeatedly outplayed card for card.  Every time he made a move, I was predicting and countering it.  I got him down to a mere 5 HP, while I still had 86, and I had multiple creatures in play with Flying (he had nothing that could block Flying).  So imagine my surprise when he started employing cards that I'd never seen before, turned the match around within a few turns, and ultimately won.  Not because he was "better", mind you, but because he was using cards that I had never seen and had absolutely no hard counter for amongst all of the starter and booster cards I'd received from PvE content to that point.
I made an honest effort at the Rift system, too, but ultimately it's got that same problem, but worse, because the players in that mode are clearly superior to the ones in normal queue matches.  The gap between a newbie and a veteran is simply too great to overcome, even if you get pretty good at the game relatively quickly as I did.
Now, let me return to a previous point: the PvE content only gets you to around Lvl 8 or 9, which doesn't yield you nearly as large of a selection as you'd think in terms of cards to build your decks with.  And to make matters worse, while the game does allow you to buy booster packs for free (using an in-game currency obtained during matches), the booster packs are prohibitively expensive.  15 cards costs over 5k points....and running all of the PvE content in the entire game only netted me about 5.5k or so, and losing a PvP match nets you less than 100 points per match.  So in order to gain enough points to buy a 15-card booster pack, you have to effectively run over 50 regular PvP matches.  Which is by no means reasonable.
I've seen former and current players who even admit to this being a major issue with the game, so I know I'm not imagining it.  One particular testimony came from someone who (at the time) was a Top 10 player.  He admitted that he got there by spending lots of real money to build a good deck, and after that, he was beating people right and left.
SUMMARY: No, the game isn't technically P2W.  You can earn cards for free if you have the patience.  But if you purchase cards with real money, you are saving yourself countless hours of grinding, and you ultimately WILL perform much better than you would have if you'd tried to play with just the freebie cards that the game gives you.  No amount of personal skill or TCG experience can overcome the significant gap in deck strength between a veteran and a new player.
You will either pay for better cards, or you will have to grit your teeth and lose a *lot* of matches in order to earn them for free.  I chose the third road: After several matches against opponents that I should have beaten, but instead lost to, I finally gave in to my frustration, closed the game, and uninstalled it.  The core game is a lot of fun, but it's mired in the "grind" of obtaining new cards and the game's significant balancing issues.  If the above stated issues are resolved at some future point, I might be persuaded to return at that time.  For now, it's a no-go for me.
EDIT (Nov 4): The game is effectively dead at this point.  The devs are still trying to update the game to the best of my knowledge, but the player base has declined dramatically since I first posted this review.  There are very few people still playing this game at this point, meaning your queues will be longer and you'll be seeing the same opponents even more often than I was back in January when I wrote this review.  At this point, you're better off investing your time and money into one of the card games that's still going strong, like Hearthstone, than spending it here.
It's a shame, too, as I had hoped the game would turn itself around and I might be able to reverse this review one day.  But it seems they never did, or at least, they never improved enough that they felt compelled to try and bring people back.  So I'm pretty much calling this review finished, and I likely won't update it any more beyond this point.

I have not played a better digital trading card game, and I have tried quite a few. Infinity Wars seeks to be truly unique by taking full advantage of the digital space, doing things a normal card game cannot easily do. We see basic things like animated cards and persistant health amounts, but we also see the major gameplay element of simultaneous turns, where both players plan out their turns, then once both players hit End, they resolve at the same time. Negatives:
People complain about earning packs and grinding... Let's get this straightened out. So you play a match against someone who has obviously paid for their cards, you lost, and no you are that angry little girl in the corner. Oh well, one match you lost, big deal!
How you can get free cards:
Campaign. You get a free introduction with a solid base of what you really need to make a deck. These are great trial decks to have some fun with the cards you already have.
Daily rewards- I logged in and received SOL.
Leveling up- Free 13-15 card packs?!?
Victory of the day
Master & Apprentice System- a pack with 3 free cards for every match you play together
Other negatives-
There are some minor bugs people complain about, even though they get squashed, but sometimes they can take a little time to be addressed.  Grinding takes too long
About the grind: What other game already gives you so many cards, ways to earn them and the fact now you can grind, which is optional to earn DECKS mind you, and packs you want. Research about the packs and decks before you buy them! Buy a deck, not a blister pack!
Now on to the positives:
The community is spectacular.  People are very helpful and will always point you in the right direction. Some people will provide you with free cards knowing they want you to enjoy a greater time.  There are often tournaments, and great communities you can join as well to "enhance" ;) your gaming experience.
The gameplay. Nothing, and not one TCG or game I have played has ever come close to this. From the commander zone combination along with an assault/defence, simultaneous turns/resolves. They offer two ways to win. By either health or morale. You have an option on how you want to defeat someone along with drawing them or 'double' explosions.
The developers/management: They are very close to the players that make the game. Teremus and Schumi are great people that always answer all questions, even the less logical ones. They hold conversations and not only answer questions, upon other duties expected by them. (hopefully?) xD
Music. The music is nice. +
The shop.  Decks, mats, card backings, it's all included in a shop for a reasonable price. For $20 you can walk away with a deck and 2-3 packs sometimes.  There is no place to buy singles, but you can trade for those easily.
Resource Pool- You have your resource pool. So want to complain about luck? Pay 3 resources to shuffle a card and draw 1. Pay 5 to draw a new card. 9 to gain a new maximum resource.
And there are cards that change the tide of battle. This goes in to the whole mentality of bluffing, when to play certain cards and when not to.
My community. {SSC}SoulSobriety Multi-Gaming Community is just SOULicious.  We bring players closer together, have a great time, create tournaments, and our very own website.
Now let's get real. We all know I wrote this interesting and lengthy review knowing that you, the reader, would read to the very bottom just so you could see my recruitment message. Outplayed!  In all seriousness, I would have babies with the game, it's staff, spend the $20 if need be, and call it a day.
Infinity Wars 2014 (psst it's 2015): Animated Trading Card Game deserves a 9/10.  This game provides a unique gaming experience, that will not only keep you coming back, but wanting to see more from the game. Thanks for the management who made this happen along with the developers. I can not wait to see what you will bring us in the future.
(I never write lengthy reviews like this unless I really appreciate a game >.>)

I have played this game twice now and I can safely say that I have absolutely no idea what happens in it or what it all means. I recommend it, but cannot point to any good reason why I should. It's strange, it's bizarre, and the entire experience is essentially "what kind of video game would I make if I were only allowed to code while blazed?" I'm relatively certain that the game is an exploration of the remains of a community on another world, but it definitely plays a lot better as an exercise in navigating someone's LSD-riddled subconscious. Because, as far as I can tell half of the time you stare at the screen going "What.", there is actually no right answer.
You progress by completing a number of puzzles and some of those can be tricky because there are times that it isn't immediately obvious that what you are looking at even is a puzzle, let alone what it expects you to do. You can ask the computer to give you up to three hints with various degrees of obviousness in order to solve the puzzles; however, in a number of rooms after spending ten minutes going "what in the world am I doing" or "this is impossible", you can press the hint buttons which will tell you "actually, this room does nothing at all and you're just wasting your time".
So, after a while, I don't know, you can just relax and slip into "ah, yes, another screwy thing in this dude's crumbling mind, of course it doesn't make sense, of course I have no idea what's going on". This game is a mental prison and you have to escape the prison. If you want 2-4 hours of going "wtf is this - wtf is that" then it's for you, but don't expect much.

I've been a longtime Dishonored fan, but I can't lie. Out of both main games, and all DLC, this one was the least enjoyable entry.
The story is compelling, and the new powers and levels are mostly great. I completely recommend buying this during a sale. The sheer height of the levels remind me a lot of the original Dishonored.
The downside is that out of all the missions, there are only 4 areas. One of them is a revisited level from Dishonored 2, and one of them you spend two whole missions in.
This is made a little better by the contracts, which are basically straight out of The Knife of Dunwall and Brigmore Witches.
But I have to take a lot of points away for the ending. I won't spoil it, but it is absolutely the most disappointing ending to a game I've ever seen.
Very little is explained, there's almost no exposition. I understand the value to leaving a little mystery, but this is just straight-up unsatisfying. You make your choice, which barely matters, and they basically say "congration, you done it".
All-in-all, I recommend buying the game to experience the worlds and new powers. But don't get your hopes up for the end.

The level design is mostly gated, but the levels are big and have quite an amount of detail.
It is also as bloody as the first Shadow Warrior from the 90s, but then again, what do you expect from a game where the protagonist has a katana and the setting is demon invasion?
When it is on sale it is an absolute steal.
Also, if you are an older gamer, you know, one who bought Doom (2016) because you liked the first one when it came out in the early 90s, you will definitively have fun. I did for sure.
Update:
For eyefinity / crossfire users: Use the DX11 folder with the launcher.exe to launch the program. Otherwise crossfire won't work and you will get 20-30fps instead of 150+ in eyefinity (in case of a Radeon R9 295).  Vsync will be a bit laggy, but disabling it will render the program working fine, and it looks better. Steam starts the usual exe.
Also, use the second difficulty, even if you are experienced with shooters. On the fourth difficulty, the first bossfight takes 25 minutes without dying. The second is ok and you should be fine.

You've probably heard a lot of comparison to other Metroidvania style games, primarily Ori and the Blind Forest. To be honest? Hollow Knight is pretty much the Ori for people who like darker toned games with the more grim style. This statement should be enough to explain what Hollow Knight is, should you have ever played Ori. I personally prefer Ori over this game since I like the brighter tone, high-detail artstyle, and the playstyle much more, but this dark theme for a game holds a special place in my heart and lets it fit up there with the greats.
For those who haven't played Ori, Hollow Knight is a very victorian-dark-age-styled game that - to what I've played so far and can tell so far - takes place in a world ruled by insects and other bugs. I'm unsure what the end goal really is because the game is simply so much of a challenge that I'm having trouble moving ahead, but even with that struggle the game persists to be something I want to go back to. The gameplay is pretty nice. The character you play moves in the manner of a hero who knows how to keep his cool, almost making him seem tanky in a sense. At the same time, you have to do all you can to avoid taking any damage because anything and everything has a cost. On top of that, the boss battles are
. Patience is key in this game. It's slow paced in movement, but fast paced in thought; an interesting mix that was beautifully compiled by the developers.
Overall, I say you should buy this game if you want a steep challenge, like dark and somber themes in games, and like to behave in a collected manner.

I've gotta be honest and say that it was gifted to me. (Thanks, buddy!)
Knowing Ubisoft, and whatever I knew about the entire series as I followed it through the year - never having played it, I wouldn't have bought it myself.
It is a very obvious casual console game. The controls are dredging awful with keyboard and mouse. You can tell there's too much delay and sluggishness, which would make sense if you're using joysticks on a gamepad.
Character ends up often falling to his (near-)death because he simply opts to go in an entirely different direction than what I feel he should go to.
All gameplay is tedious, repetitive, not original nor innovative and there is zero challenge. As far as difficulty goes, I didn't bother finding if it had any difficulty settings, but it reeks of 'artificial difficulty'. Meaning, changing the difficulty only changes superficial stuff like own/enemy health, damage (& resistance) and the likes. Perhaps even increase trivial things like the amount of currency X and Y that you need to collect for a specific upgrade.
Thus, not increasing actual difficulty. The challenge stays the same, it would just become more tedious.
Not that I can think of an adventure game that implemented proper difficulty settings. I'm not writing a review to competitively compare it to other games, that would be daft.
I feel the main story is, well, what you would expect from Ubisoft, or console games in general.
It's all straight forward, predictable, easy-going, simplistic muck. There are zero choices to make, for nothing has consequences.
Heck, even if you die at any point, you'll just magically re-appear at a very recent checkpoint. You won't lose anything either, except for time spent. I guess they covered that lazy♥♥♥♥♥♥up with the backstory to the series; in that you're always playing some sort of simulation.
The underlying main story of the series is really lacking. It's even more boring and tedious. There's a ton of stuff you can read for some background lore, I guess. I read some of it, but was appalled by the quality, so I stopped caring at some point.
This part of the game's story doesn't end in the game, but I guess that's because that's a story that's being spun out over multiple games in the series.
Adversarial multiplayer is a joke and the "co-op" stuff is agitating as hellhound dung to the eyes, don't touch it with a 10 foot barge pole.
If you happen to see this game for like, €5,- and you're feeling like having something to play that'll give you constant successes, with an easy-going storyline, then this piece of entertainment might suit you. As with a lot of games, treat it as an interactive novel with limited space to interact.
EDIT: It's pretty buggy, as well. I've got some screenshots (that should be public) that'll showcase how my ship usually spawns in like it rises from the seafloor, only to collide with any landmass that gets in the way.

I am a huge Civ fan starting back with the orignal on pc and snes version.
I consider Alpha Centarui to be the best of all the civs in the series for a variety of reasons.
This is closer to Civ 5 then Alpha Centarui but it does an exceptionally good job at being Civ 5 in space. It introduces several major changes and numerous tweaks to the formula that I do not think it is just a new skin on the game. Not all the ideas work but most of them do. The only major fault I have with the game is some serious backwards UI changes. Information is no longer at tip of a finger as it once was, and there also isn't ways to easily determine players strengths. The biggest offensive is icons are cryptic hyoglphs that don't make it obvious what you are creating without digging up more info via pop ups and such.
Ignoring some of the UI failings. This is a very fresh and fantastic 4X experience. The fantastic new features like quests with extremly meaningful rewards, unit progression, the fantastic technology web, and continued great 4X experience makes this game a great recommendation for me.
With future patching and Add-on's I hope to see this game go from great to must have as Civ 5 did with it's expansions.
What I really like:
------------------------------------------------
+ technology web - very functional wants you get the hang of it - very overwhelming at first.
+ quests - the quests themselves are bland and i skim most of the text, there rewards on the other hand server as dramtic changes to the game. they are for the most part very meaningful and you can almost blindly play the game and complete quests to get these rewards which is also nice
+ diffculty - so far nothing seems terrible outbalanced other then 1 oppents managing to make every single wonder...
+ graphics - not sure how much i would like a game like this in a crysis 3 engine...
+ diplomacy - works - like the idea of favours
+ trade - more important and useful thenever
+ aliens - neat and better take on barbarians
+ exploring - more meaningful rewards from exploring
+ starting bonuses - race development is fun and can allow for some meaninful tweaks
+ specializations - the game is broken into 3 major specializations which you progress through. how this naturally draws lines in the sand with AI is really fun to explore
+ combat - same basic premise but towards end game the units are quite unique per faction and have noticable diffrence once specialized.
+ multiplayer - fantastic and reliable. Had one link issue where it reloaded. This was something I saw in Civ 5 as well and base it on my weak wifi signal. Hybrid turns is fantastic and keeps games moving quickly.
What I don't like:
------------------------------------------------
- video/display bug: since purchase the game has crashed and says I don't have the latest video driver...when I do. I have to edit the config file so I can launch the game in windows mode then switch back to full screen. My friend said he had this issue as well and I have read on the forums it has been around for 1 month. That would make the game unplayable for someone not familar with computers. Not acceptable.
- UI - the UI is not clear enough at displaying important info. I.E. All the unit and building icons look far to familar and are not reflective of what you are building clearly. This is a serious problem when you have tanks called "vipers" and have no ♥♥♥♥in clue what that is until looking at the graphics. Sometime even the pop-up stats aren't enough to make it clear that it is a boat or a tank.
- open borders then declare war once city surronded tactic works again and AI uses it
- AI seems to cheat a bit - little frustrated seeing 1 AI player make every single wonder 300 turns in
- no demographics page (very frustrating) - diplomacy page is meager replacement
- no end game score / replay (unexceptable)
- misama (poison gas) graphics - sometimes unnoticable visually - which is unacceoptable since it is an important terrain feature
- civilization personalities (little dull)
- pre-order DLC - absolute garbage that generic planet layouts (island planets, etc) may be a seperate purchase some players - slippery slope
- explored strength and automation - my explores are both always weak and haven't gotten me in trouble with other AI players - I think they should be smart enough not to instagate fights via close expediations missions

A B- game from a AAA publisher. It's like a bad Civ 5 mod. There is no polish to this game. Building the wonders is unspiring. All the voice acting is done by one person regardless of who the quote comes from.
DO NOT BUY THIS GAME. YOU WILL BE SEVERELY DISAPPOINTED. I AM VERY SAD I SPENT ANY MONEY ON THIS.
INTERFACE
The interface is extremely lackluster, with very poor choices about how to navigate through menus. Even the menu design itself looks boring. All the icons are flat puesdo-gray scale images that would look better on a mobile app than in a AAA game. The trade route interface does not sort to maximize by science, energy, food, or production (as it did in Civ 5) and every 15 turns you have to renew each trade route, which becomes a huge time waste when you have 4 trade routes per city in the mid to late game. Trying to send people through the earth domination gate requires you to send military units one at a time for ~20 turns or so. This is a super frustrating experience.
This bad UI is pervasive throughout the game. If you highlight the technologies based on a certain type, you can't select anything else but the ones you've filtered by, so you have to go back and unclick it.
Moving a spy around requires multiple clicks through submenus when it should just be a single one.
The workers seem much, much stupider than the ones in Civ 5. I've seen them get stuck multiple times while multiples are automated near each other, and they will bankrupt you with the -6 maintence improvement if you don't watch them. They also don't proiritize maglevs at all, which are just railroads from Civ 5.
Satilletes
This is probably one of the most interesting, and equally dispapointing parts of the game. The satilletes come so late in the technology tree, and have such limited effects, that there are no interesting choices in boosting your production with them. You also can't stack them in any way.
Combat
The combat is actually less interesting than in Civ 5 which is pretty painful. I don't know how you take a step back here. There are less units, and you can only upgrade them by researching one of the three foundational systems, and then you upgrade all of them exactly the same way.
Research
The web tech tree is definitely a better setup than the linear one from Civ 5, but because of the three paradigms, it's much less expansive than it looks, you're virtually forced to pickup useless technologies because they happen to have a paradigm increase on them, which is super frustrating.
MISC
Wonders have no visible improvement on the city. Energy and health are just money and happiness. The three paradigms of Adaptation, Purity, and Improvement are super boring. There's nothing interesting about them compared to the society alignments of Alpha Centarui.

Hollow Knight is essentially one of my favorite games of all time. I do not think that any other game that is Metroidvania-style, or even simply with platforming exploration like this, will ever be able to break the love I have for Hollow Knight.
The game is definitely far from easy, but I enjoyed every single minute of it. The graphics, sound, and gameplay are all amazing.
But since many people have already gone on and on about the positives, I think that I will actually address some complaints from many negative reviews: (1) the difficulty; (2) bugs/glitches; and (3) the mechanics and gameplay.
(1) I understand that some people may get angry quickly if they are not doing well in the game, or not able to overcome the challenge. But at the same time, I will say that the game is
“too difficult.” In all honesty, a lot of the challenge simply owes to the definition of challenge in video games for many years: you must pay attention to what is happening, learn patterns, and react. That is usually only really difficult in places where you have a lot going on and need to be quick, but every single enemy and boss has some form of pattern that you can overcome.
(2) I played the game for over 60 hours, across 2 playthroughs. The first playthrough was for 100% completion and took most of the time. The second playthrough was a speed-run to just get to the last boss in a few hours. The last time I played was a few weeks ago, around August 12, after the original Hidden Dreams patch was released.
I never encountered a weird glitch in the game. I never lost my save file. I never had bosses disappear or get stuck anywhere. I never had anything teleport inappropriately. Nothing messed up for me in over 60 hours, and I got through 100% of the game!
With that said, it seems like a majority of the reviews complaining about glitches have been in the past few days. Maybe they released a patch that really did cause some issue, and if so, I hope that is fixed. But the original Hidden Dreams patch did not cause any issues for me, and I played for over a week after it came out.
(3) Someone complained about Fast Travel being unavailable for over half of the game because of the Tram. That is not true. The Last Stag is a creature that allows Fast Travel and has stations in just about every sub-dungeon, which you can easily identify because they have signs outside of the doorways.
Another complaint even said: “what really grinds my gears is that the most efficient way to fight in combat is to tank hits with no skill or style and mash the attack button like a madman, then heal it all back since 98.9% of all enemies/bosses in this game have some sort of downtime mechanic where they freely let you heal back all your health.” That is not true at all, either. You have to be quick and get out of the way with enemies, and a lot of the bosses or enemies later in the game make it almost impossible to heal. You just have to adapt to their actions and use the most effective abilities that you have (usually with a lot of dashing).
One complaint that I will agree with is some of the Charms you must use Notches for. To clarify, Charms give you extra abilities to help in exploration, movement, combat, and other things, which are different from permanent skills that you unlock as you play. Notches are simply slots required to equip Charms, though you can find or buy more Notches in the game. Some Charms definitely should have existed as normal gameplay elements. For instance, one Charm is required in order for you to see yourself on the game’s map as you explore, which I did not enjoy. Despite that, I used the Charm for most of the game and still got through fine.
___
Now, I spent most of my time addressing the above, but I think it is useful for new players, especially if they are worried about the difficulty or what some negative reviews say.
As said in the beginning, the game requires some work to get used to, but it is extremely fun, albeit difficult. The game’s art style makes every area so interesting to explore, and the music and sound effects fit great. You meet many characters throughout the game who are very interesting with their unique personalities, and they add to the lore of the game, which is figured out almost in a Dark Souls manner.
The combat starts off simple in your techniques, but you unlock a vast amount of new capabilities as you explore, defeat bosses, purchase or find Charms, and so on, so the gameplay is not boring by any manner at all. There are even little creatures that you can rescue throughout the game, and when you do, you can return to an early area to get extra Geo (the currency of the game) as well as upgrades for “free.”
Hollow Knight is quite amazing for an indie-developed game, and it beats out some AAA games that I have loved. I think many, many people should give it a try, especially since there is a large player base for other games like Dark Souls, meaning that Hollow Knight is truly not a niche market.

Civilization: Beyond Earth brings a lot of changes to the Civilization franchise. The most notable is the Tech Web which makes what science to research next a compelling choice rather than a simple rote pattern.
Rather than choosing a Civ, you choose a Sponsor which brings your first perk, there are three more perks you choose at the beginning of the game which greatly vary the conditions under which you start the game (extra civilian, starting wtih a Soldier Unit, Starting with all coastlines revealed, etc.). The variety of combinations here is already high but given more DLC/expansions to add more Sponsors and perks, it can only grow.
What this means is you won't always play every X Civ game the same way. Further, the conditions under which you find yourself at the beginning will have an impact on what Affinity seems most viable and that in turn will create other gameplay situations.
The game has dozens of tiny choices you make in sidequests and for building improvements and unit upgrades as well which all contribute to varying gameplay. Those who say it is too similar to Civ V are either myopic in their perception or simply not smart enough to see how these varying choices, conditions, and alterations to various Civ systems conspire together to create FAR more varied gameplay than in Civ V.
Further, the early game requires a lot more finesse in many situations creating tense situations that really feel like you're conquering (or adapting to) a hostile world that does not want you on it. Alien life (this game's verison of Barbarians) is diverse and often intimidating. Situations can crop up depending on the affinities of neighboring Civs. If you, for example, choose the Harmoney route and reuse to exterminate any Alien life while your neighboring Civs do the same, you may find an incredible buildup of xenos in your area after a hundred or so turns. This, in turn, will impact your ability to found new cities (a much harder prospect in BE due to the outpost mechanic), explore for salvage (this game's version of the artifact sites in Civ V: BNW), or to attack military targets.
There is a greater variety of technology overall compared to Civ V as well which lends to a sense of dynamic play from game to game.
The culture trees are also greatly improved in BE offering incentives to branch out into multiple trees rather than race to the finish on one or two.
If I were to sum up the primary difference between Beyond Earth and Civ V in one word it would be CHOICES. In Civ V, for each civilization there is a "right" way to play. Because of that there is no variety from game to game with the same civ. That is completely out the window in BE and again, will only get more exciting as more content gets added.
DO NOT LISTEN TO THE NAYSAYERS. Shortsighted people with narrow vision and slow brains will always look down on things that are too subtle or complex for them to discern.
This is a fantastic game and certainly my favorite already in the Civilization series.

UPDATED REVIEW
After browsing the latest round of reviews about "Beyond Earth," I must admit that this game does feel a bit "empty," at least in comparison to Civ V.  Perhaps because Civ V - and especially in its heavily expanded form - is such an excellent game (and arguably one of the best Civilization games ever released), "Beyond Earth" comes off as an empty and unpolished game.
Personally, I do not believe that Beyond Earth was a poorly released game.  I've not experienced any major technical issues while playing this game, and I've managed to spend quite a few hours enjoying this game.  What I HAVE experienced since I've started playing Beyond Earth more extensively is that it does feel more like an Civ V expansion rather than the dramatic departure (or Alpha Centauri throwback) that Firaxis Games was promoting.  And for 50 US dollars, I can understand why many Civ fans therefore feel disappointed, cheated, and even ripped off.  Perhaps alot of this negative feedback could've been averted if Firaxis had released a demo version of this game beforehand.  It would've given the Civ community a chance to try out this game and offer feedback to Firaxis, and, at the very least, it would've also allowed players like myself to try out this game before deciding whether or not to invest 50 dollars.
But I don't believe that Beyond Earth is broken beyond repair.  Sure, there are alot of things that should have been in this game that are currently in Civ V or in any of the earlier Civilization games (including Alpha Centauri), but much of the negative reaction by players to Beyond Earth seems to stem from a combination of: 1) Overinflated expectations due to marketing hype (and Beyond Earth is not the only videogame that suffers from this issue) and 2) Unfair comparisons between Beyond Earth and the fully expanded version of Civ V.
So in spite of all of the negative player reviews - and for those of you who have not yet tried out Beyond Earth - I would still recommend this game.  If you choose to wait for the (inevitable) expansions and sales discounts, that's understandable.  I agree with many other players that 50 dollars is a bit overpriced for a game that feels more like an expansion than a stand-alone game.  But there is potential here, and hopefully all of the negative feedback will force Firaxis to listen to the Civ community and make important changes to Beyond Earth, changes that will really help move this game beyond Civ V or Alpha Centuari.
--------------------------------------------------
ORIGINAL REVIEW
"Beyond Earth" may not be the groundbreaking game that everyone was expecting.  And it is not Sid Meier's Alpha Centauri, either.  But once you put these expectations aside, this is still an enjoyable sci-fi themed Civ game that will keep you busy playing for hours on end.
Of particular interest is Beyond Earth's  "technology web," which introduces a new element of strategy into the Civ formula.  Players no longer have to research techs one after another in a more-or-less linear fashion.  Instead, players can research based on how the game is developing.  Enemies knocking on your door?  Research military techs.  Need to boost your economy?  Pick up an economy tech.  The three affinities (supremacy, harmony, and purity) provide a broader base for planning, while the tech tree (or bubble) allows you to research in a more adaptive fashion.  You still need to plan your research a little bit, but the new tech tree and affinity system means that you have greater flexibility in your planning, rather than having to plan everything out from turn 0.
It is very difficult to adapt a best-selling game formula into a new thematic setting, and the "Civilization" series is no exception.  While Beyond Earth may not have quite the same feel as "Alpha Centauri" (which in many respects is still the stronger game), it is still a refreshing departure for the latest generation of Civs.  Hopefully, future expansions will help expand the scope and content of Beyond Earth in much the same way as Civ V.

Having played all the previous titles, I thought I knew what to expect. Fortunately, that went out the window with the first "woah" moment. And you'll find in Absolution plenty of them. The story is very well made and it feels like you're watching a good action movie. One of the most impressive features of Hitman Absolution is the voice acting. Every frame of any cutscene can be transformed into a beautiful art piece to hang on your walls. The cutscenes connect the gameplay seamlessly. Gameplay-wise, it's a good improvement from its predecessors as 47 feels more natural than ever. The cover system is really well made even though sometimes your head is way above the counter you're hiding behind. Intuition, as a gameplay mechanic, is great. It will convince even the most brutal player not to kill every NPC and it also serves as a "tutorial" for new players or for those who want to get their hands on the highest difficulties. If you finished any other Hitman game, be sure to try the tougher challenges too. The multiplayer part of it consists in creating and completing contracts made by your friends. Not only will it challenge your friends but creating a good contract will also challenge you to complete it first, to prove that it can be done. If playing on PC, I highly recommend using a controller when playing Absolution. Not that keyboard & mouse aren't great, but you'll get the most out of its cinematic experience. In conclusion, a great game, polished and not a full 10 because of a couple bugs. Final score: 9.5 - Must Buy!

A few years ago, when the game was released, it could not compete with other simulations. Yet, the developers have put in a lot of work to fix bugs and improve so many critical aspects. Today, I can say I am impressed with the result. The laserscanned Nordschleife is in my opinion the best version available, the force feedback has undergone massive improvements and beats every sim I have tried so far, including rFactor 2 and Assetto Corsa. While other racing games like Project Cars have prettier graphics, I personally really like the look and feel of Raceroom and it is absolutely sufficient for a simulation. Where it shines, is the sound. It is immersive and powerful. After years of updates, the physics are great as well. I can honestly say, the game has reached a point where the available content has the high quality, SimBin (now Sector 3 Studios) is known for.
Of course, as always there are a few negative things as well. At the time of this review, there is no implementation of weather conditions. If you get off the track, the effects of losing grip due to dirt on the tires aren't really perceivable, compared to Assetto Corsa for example. While there already is a lot you can change in the car setup, a few things other sims do offer aren't available yet. For example, different types of tires or tire pressure. You can select the time of day for the race, but as far as I know, it will be static. Would be cool to have a real daytime simulation and dynamic weather.
One big contra is the pricing and payment model. I perceive it as intransparent and unconfortable, as they use a virtual currency and the payment system has multiple steps, as it includes their webshop, Steam and its payment methods like PayPal. Not all the bundles they offer on their website are available directly through Steam. Prices are somewhat hefty, but still well below iRacing.
All in all, it is a racing sim with great quality tracks, cars, physics and force feedback. The multiplayer features are solid as well. It deserves more attention, and I recommend trying it, even if you've invested into other sims. The Nordschleife DLC alone is well worth the price and the best starting point. Happy racing!

The best puzzle games, imo, offer you some kind of simple principle which you are then obliged to apply in increasingly sophisticated ways to increasingly complex puzzles. You put 1+1 together, have a eureka! moment, and your brain is awash in dopamine. The Witness, Myst, Portal, and Fez are great examples of this.
Kairo does not offer this. It's a run-around-until-you-bump-into-something-that-happens-to-solve-the-puzzle type game, and for that reason, I found it incredibly frustrating and tedious. There's no consistent logical principle behind the puzzles, so you can't take what you learned from the last one and apply it to a new one.
Now, diverse puzzles with little consistent through-line wouldn't be that much of a problem, except there's no way to extract anything from the game's environment, either, as you would in say, Tomb Raider. The ''environmental exposition'' mentioned in the features seems rudimentary and not at all helpful. Because every room/level is the same flat, monochrome style, there's no suggestion that a certain block can be pushed, or anything like that. You have to wander around aimlessly in this bleak monochromatic world until you accidentally step or push something that happens to do something. And there's no compelling story elements from which you can derive why, and for what, you are doing this.
To my mind, that defeats the purpose of solving a puzzle. If you're just wandering around for an hour until you bump into the right thing, it's not really ''solving''. It's just stumbling around. There's no rewarding feeling in ''solving'' something by accident. This could have been compensated for with a more developed aesthetic, or a more interesting story, even just an overarching theme that ties everything together. But those elements aren't there, or they're rudimentary at best.

Oh it's so terrible....
If you select your units and accidentaly have one unit selected, that can not move (like build-up trebuchets or ballista-towers), most of your soldiers start dancing around..on the same spot where they were standing before you gave the order.
Another example? Ok!
If you have selected a pack of units, where archers stand at the front of the direction you are ordering them to go, a handful of your soldiers think that it is better to go the opposite way. Maybe they dont want to pass the archers because they smell bad or whatever, but you have to babysit your units for every move command you give.
The developer knows that the pathing has issues, therefore they nearly disabled the collision for units. When a huge army gets ordered to walk through a gate, the units funnel together into a thin line and expand after the gate has been passed. This looks ridiculous. In addition, siege weapons, that are visibly to broad to pass the gate, just ignore the collision and drive through it...just make that stupid gate bigger and this "issue" would have been solved.
If you can handle these (and some other) problems, you can enjoy this game, but for me its just a bit to much.

This game feels like an expansion or DLC more than a stand-alone. Wait until it goes on sale.
- It's very short - complete playthrough in 13 hours, and that was with a lot of time spent fooling around, exploring, and lurking (no pun intended).
- Powers can't be upgraded.
- You start the game with a complete loadout.
- Enemies (and locations!) are recycled from Dishonored 2. Part of what made that game fun was exploring new places and encountering new types of bad guys.
- Story and characters seem weak and underdeveloped. The main characters' connections to each other weren't fleshed out all that much in the previous installments, so there's no background to draw from, and their motivations feel hollow and forced. The end of the story will leave you wondering what the point of it all was.
Having said all of that, this is still a fun game in its way. The mechanics are familiar, and the ability to complete missions in many different ways is pretty cool. However, as a follow-on to Dishonored 2, which was fantastic, this was a tad disappointing.

They fixed the optimization issues. It runs WAY better than Dishonored 2. The only downside is that it still is drawcall/cpu bound for most high end systems. Prepare a 4790k/6700k/7700k or 8700k on 4,5ghz on all cores if you want to get past framedropcity in the city areas on anythign above 1440p if you don´t run a bloody gtx1080ti. I went from 135 fps (avg collected from indoors and small closed off sections, of whcih there are plents in this game. Endgame for example.) maxed out (See comments) on 1440p, down to 72 (avg), when I first arrived in front of the carnaca city gates, a heavily taxing scene in the game. Checked YouTube comparisons and I confirmed that it is a heavily cpu bound scene. Non the less, it never gets below 60fps no matter on what settings with a 1080ti, and as we all know, reducing graphics settings from ultra to high, barely changes visuals and I boosted my fps by a lot.
Especially environmental settings which cause a lot of level of detail and drawcalling, bumped my framerate up towards 88 or even 100 fps. Pretty sweet. Anti Aliasing is still garbage as with most Triple A games these days like Rainbow Six Siege, but you can always dream having Multisampling AA in a deferred rendered engine. Don´t expect Nvidia Profile Inspector to work either, this game is dx11 and Nvidia Profile Inspector only works with dx10/dx9 titles. The game is even so snarky as to block the nvidia driver settings for AA and even FXAA, so you can´t do any AA work on the game outside the graphics options present in the game settings. You have to run ENB/ReShade and inject SMAA. Otherwise you are locked by the devs, which obviously is absolute garbage as the game runs with barely effective FXAA (Vaseline mode), so you take TAA which is notorious for being the bluriest AA out there right now.
They included a sharpness filter and it works, but it also enhances the film grain too much. In the end when you move the camera around, the TAA motionblurs heavily, as it samples and filters through the picture. It´s only 100% sharp when you stand still. I´m royally   p  i  s  s  e  d   about such garbage. DOOM, Forza and Crysis 3 showed how AA has to be done. Proper SMAA. At least give people the option to downsample outside Nvidia´s DSR. Alert, even in 4K downsampled, it doesn´t get rid of all the stairs. They are still noticeable enough to annoy people with very sensitive feelings towards aliasing stairs. I managed to get rid of them in 6K but then I had to play in 30 fps locked which sucks in this game, especially on a 144hz panel, so I forced myself to like the TAA+Sharpness options I had been given by the devs. Input is raw and direct, triple buffering works excellent and vsync is decent with the option for half hz or full hz, if you want to lock the framerate and add the games engines feature of dynamic resolution scaling. The lower end users might like it, so it´s a nice thing to have.
Story.. mhmm it´s not even close to the epicness of Dishonored 2, but the story around Billie Lurk (main character) and Daud (Billies mentor) is truly fascinating and fills the lore gap very well, answering many questions about the characters I had before. They focused more on the actual reasons of their actions instead of unnecessary background stories and I found myself to be interested in the increasing mystery that surrounds the universe. It is compelling enough to follow the objectives. Combined with the decent, even if sometimes flawed level design, it makes for great stealth and story progression. I enjoyed every moment of sneaking past guards towards my goal, the exact thing you should feel in a dishonored game, accomplishment was a given due to that. I had some issues though.
It´s a Standalone DLC/Add-On, so don´t expect a full arsenal. There are 4 very balanced main powers and nothing else. Your crossbow/gun/thingie integrated in a device on your arm and your trusty blade, some grenades and new very fun sorts of mines. The devs gave us a fresh variety of things to toy with and they can be utilized in every scenario too! The balance thus is excellent and all mechanics grap into each other perfectly. The maps are free roamey/semi open and you can do contract missions, so to say, side missions next to your main objectives. You can skip them if you don´t like them. But many are fun and interesting with an own backstory, so I recommend giving them all a chance. They often string and flock together with the main mission areas and thus give you a sometimes easy and sometimes hardcore, extra sideobjective.
AI is decent and very aware of the sorroundings, remembering if doors were closed, sensitive to sounds even across several stories when it´s too loud, and they are great combatants too, if you like to play the game in an action style. The only flaw with them that I´ve found are that they are too regular in their patroulling and on reseting alarms, but that´s a given for balancing and difficulty, still, AI shouldn´t be on rails to me, it should be a task for arkane studios to add random patrol routes to the custom difficulty. Predictability in a stealth game is the key to making an enjoyable experience for most people, but some wish the element of clever, logical thinking, free roaming AI more. Tough job to code for sure though.
Even though the AI isn´t buggy anymore compared to earlier titles in the series, they still shoot each other in the back and all that stuff. Don´t expect an AI designer to become an AI demigod all of a sudden. Even the F.E.A.R. (shooter from the year 2005 known for its excellent AI to this date) AI had their limits..... at doorknobs.
The game until now is excellent in everything, story is decent, guns are fun, combat is excellent as always, game length is around 10 hrs, mine was even 17, it´s more of a Story Add-On and not a DLC if you take it for what it is, but two things which I loved and hated appeared. One at the beginning of the game, the other throughout the game. And those are:
1: Loved the !CUSTOM! difficulty!
2: Hated the Level Design in combination with the custom difficulty.
Let me explain further about this one huge flaw of the game. If you choose custom difficulty at the start of the game, you can choose from so much options, a stealth novice will make many mistakes and  f  u  c  k   up the AI. I didn´t gladly, but for one thing, how far the AI can see above their own cone of perception, I did. Usually AI barely sees danger above them, in custom difficulty I changed that to the max cone upwards. I thought it would be smart..... but man, you barely have any hiding spots above any NPC or enemy to begin with in the levels of this game, and if you do, they are too low and I´m easily 2/3 of all times easily visible. Without a shadow system like in Thief The Dark Project, it´s a horror in terms of difficulty balancing. I managed to sneak my  a  s  s  to the end of the game, but often times I simply didn´t have many options in terms of paths to go for if I wanted to do a ghost run. So I had the typical dishonored playstyle, hunting everybody in silence. I killed everybody from the shadows until no witnesses were left. Hitman Absolution style. It´s fun, but it somehow hurts the pride of a stealthplayer who tries his best to sneak past guards unnoticed. Also many times the power to copy the body and face of a person and go past guards hitman style for certain an amount of time was too op and most of the time there were barely any alternative routes to use, due to restricted level design. Ghosting is horrible in this game on the first run. Especially if you don´t know the level layout. It´s so much trial and error. Believe me, don´t ghost if you aren´t sure what you are doing, it leads to a lot of frustration, especially as the amount of guards running around in the later half of the game, is so moronically high. My concentration bar was hammering against the top. I had to take many breaks.
In conclusion, fun as heck game.

Pretty decent early-2000s fantasy RTS; nothing special but it'll scratch an itch for genre fans. The campaign was the usual generic 'thou must save thy kingdom' fare for the first two acts, then it surprised me with some writing and epistemology I honestly didn't expect from such an old game. Who would have thought "Warcraft meets LoTR" would actually try to humanize its orcs? I'm glad I stuck with it out of completionism at first, although the gameplay doesn't exactly stand out.
I also kind of liked the faction that was basically a ripoff of those goblin things from LoTR except they're also giants, and I thought the
easter egg was really funny for some reason, even if I don't actually play fighting games. That's probably a microcosm of this game: great writing and brilliant execution to carry an otherwise unremarkable work, something we'd see multiple times from the devs until they sadly went out of business in 2009.
Multiplayer's still ticking along on Evolve/Hamachi with a small base of dedicated and very skilled players. Wander in there and you'll probably get your butt handed to you, but on the plus side they're usually rather polite to new opponents, which was another surprise.

I've had this one on my wish list for a long time, and finally bought it today on sale despite having many games in my library that I haven't yet played. And I couldn't be happier.
There is a demo available on the main page, and I strongly suggest you try the demo first, as this game doesn't play quite like a traditional RPG. It is dialogue-heavy, but manages to be so without being full of silly melodrama. The plot and characters are great, there are genuine benefits for choosing interpersonal skills that go to waste in most RPGs, your stats matter, and there are real consequences for your actions -- you must choose your loyalties and stick with them, or suffer. In some ways it reminds me of an old DOS classic, Darklands, but without all the wandering all over the map, and a lot less combat.

Bearing in mind you should try the other games in the series first, especially the original and it's dlc. It's recommended as a game alone, not recommended above it's siblings in the series.

If you enjoyed Dishonored 2, warts and all, this is a good purchase.  The primary improvement is the more focused gameplay.  Gone are the customizations of skills - you have only three with no upgrade paths.  Bone charms are still in, but I found the effects pretty unobstrusive.  Some might find this lack of skill variety overly restrictive; I found it pretty liberating as I could just play the game and wasn't bothered by the tigher focus.
The story is absolutely nothing to write home about - same as Dishonored 2.  The world building, however, is fantastic.  If you stop and smell the roses this is a 12+ hour long game; decide to sprint through the levels and rush objectives and you'll find the length of the experience lacking.
Performance is significantly improved over Dishonored 2.  While the former always felt like there was some element of stuttering, even when above 60FPS, this title is smooth as butter.  Hope the engine improvements make their way back to the base title.
In closing, if you want more Dishonored this is a great purchase.  If you have gripes about the previous titles you'll find no material improvements here.
