In 1997, Shadow Warrior released for PC as a spiritual successor to Duke Nukem 3D, and starred a terribly racist Asian caricature named Lo Wang. This isn’t a premise that sounds like it would be able to endure nearly twenty years later, and yet developer Flying Wild Hog revived Shadow Warrior last year on the PC, which has now made its way to the Xbox One and PS4. Lo Wang’s return is a successful one, with all of the purposely-offensive humor and over-the-top gameplay you’d expect from it.
Amazingly, Shadow Warrior’s plot is not to be overlooked, as it is engaging and becomes more serious and grounded as the game goes on. This is tempered by the silly combat and hilarious dialogue throughout the game. The player takes on the role of Lo Wang, a gun-toting, sword-wielding, ninja mercenary working for the mysterious Orochi Zilla, a powerful Japanese businessman. What starts off as a routine mafia transaction quickly spirals out of control into a demon-filled murderfest wherein Lo Wang uses his last name to reference his♥♥♥♥♥♥on a regular basis. Accompanying Wang is the smart-mouthed demon Hoji, who serves as Lo Wang’s guide through the world of pseudo-Japanese culture and mysticism. The plot works perfectly with the insane gameplay and general silliness that Shadow Warrior provides.
The combat in Shadow Warrior can be described as fast, bloody, and insane. The player is given ninja stars, a samurai sword, and a lot of guns to blast through hordes of ninjas, police officers and demons in one of the messiest first-person hack-and-slash experiences I’ve ever played. The guns can be a little difficult to use, as the aiming system can be a little unwieldy and some guns feel underpowered, but the swordplay is a lot of fun and is intended to be Wang’s tool of destruction for the majority of the time.
Lo Wang also gains magical abilities to aid him, which include healing spells and telekinetic push abilities. My personal favorite is an ability that allows Wang to spin in a whirlwind attack that decapitates everyone around him. These abilities help to round out the combat and give players a multitude of ways to go about any given combat scenario, although I was mostly content just slashing enemies to bits.
Lo Wang has many upgrade opportunities at his disposal as well, which are cleverly broken into different categories that can be upgraded by different means. Karma, for example, will allow the player to purchase certain modifiers, while money allows the player to upgrade their equipment. The options for how the player can evolve and upgrade Wang are pretty vast, meaning that the each person can upgrade according to their play style. I like to run in swinging a sword, so I need to be able to take a lot of damage, so I upgraded healing spells, damage resistant perks, and maximum health modifiers. This upgrade system can be a little complicated, but is well-worth taking the time to learn, as it’ll make Lo Wang an even bigger badass according to each player’s personal style.
Shadow Warrior looks great on the Xbox One, for the most part. Slicing a demon into multiple pieces has never felt more rewarding, but some elements, like human characters are low-res and a bit fuzzy. The sound, however, is great. The music is fast-paced and has an Eastern flair to it, and the sound effects are top-notch. The voice acting is also surprisingly good, especially from Wang’s sidekick Hoji who helps out with a lot of the exposition and banter.
The combat is awesome, the dialogue is hilarious, and the excessive gore is a guilty pleasure that never gets old. Shadow Warrior is one of those games that reminds us that gaming, at its core, should be fun, and it delivers fun times in a big way.

Two things:
Firstly, this is an imitation Hitman on the most superficial level. About the only thing this has in common with Hitman games is that you have targets which you kill, and there are various ways to do it. This game offers nothing of the sort of level design, originality or, quite frankly, fun that the series is known for. It is a poor Hitman game.
Secondly, besides being a poor Hitman game, it's also a poor stealth game. Where they've adapted the game to be more like Splinter Cell: Conviction (by all accounts, a very mediocre stealth/action game) in terms of scenarios, they've brought forward all the Hitman jank that was so acceptable within the confines of the Hitman series. So as a non-Hitman game, it's pretty bad in that respect too.
Bundle this with a bunch of nonsense scenarios (grab the fuses, yay), pressing the Right Bumper to "win" by concealing yourself amongst enemies for significant amounts of time, and the story that is garbage and takes itself too seriously, and you have a seriously lacking product here.
In short, IO Interactive have not only sacrificed what made Hitman great to produce a game that is "more appealing", or some such nonsense, but they fudged the "more appealing" part too, since this game stinks.
Do not buy.

Oh boy... where to begin? Yes, this game is fun. Yes, I love the "blend in" kind of stealth as opposed to the "don't be seen" kind. Yes, I can enjoy the more linear levels, as opposed to the sandbox ones. Both have their advantages: the sandbox allows you to be more creative, but it can be very overwhelming, especially if you have to reset. Ah, there we go. Resetting. I have one problem with this game. Not the disguise recogtnition system - which is a very nice and realistic idea they unfortunately couldn't get around without the instinct system. Not the instinct itself: 47 covering his face with a cap might look stupid, but managing that resource bar is another layer of strategy, even if an exploitable one(it's easy to quickly tap into the instinct when you're about to get recognized and watch as your watcher's suspicion indicator resets); point shooting, on the other hand, seems unecessary - it's not the kind of game where I should be shooting a room full of people, which is a shame because 47's Silverballers look so cool they are begging to be used. - but it's there and it looks cool, if you want to use it; the highlighting key elements is useful in telling apart what's scenery and what's a potential deathtrap.
No, my problem is with the scoring system. It's what turns this game from a fun, if slightly limited - would say, not entirely without reason, the Blood Money enthusiasts -, sadistic workshop into an exercise of trial-and-error frustration in search of one of the optimal methods the developers designed into the level. No more of the free approach "I'll have that guard chase me into the garage, climb out by the roof and get into the door he was guarding" stuff. You get spotted, you mess up in a tiny way, and you have that negative score jeopardizing your whole run, regardless of how well or how brilliantly you manage to contain or even take profit from the situation. Instead, you reload your checkpoint and try to search for that one air duct the level designer put somewhere that will coincidentally end up somewhere the AI is programmed to trigger an event... say, lighting a cigarette near some convenient gas pump. It's less about creativity, more about finding the optimal solution, which, as far as I know, is not what this series was ever about. Maybe I want to use a silenced sniper to kill patrols, knocking their bodies off a bridge? Well, shame on me, 'cause my score will never reach my friend's, who preferred to go for the Silent Assassin bonus.Why should I be punished for using the many tools the game gave me to kill? Instead, it will slap my hand and make me shimmy from the edges around said bridge if I ever want to go for a good score. I don't even want to explore to find alternative methods(some of which are mind boggling, if funny. Rigging a power line so a guy gets shocked while♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Scattering a wrestler's guards by stealing his... teddy bear?), I just want to find the first solution that will get me through the level.
As for the story... yeah, it isn't great. It's cliché, it's predictable in 95% of its run. I do, however, enjoy how it provided an opportunity for 47 to be portrayed as a more humane, relatable character, even if sometimes he would make me bang my head on my desk. Showing your face in front of a crowd before snapping the neck of your target? I thought we were going for the subtle and unnoticed approach.
It's not a bad game, don't get me wrong. I had fun with it. Getting through the levels is fun, especially when I could manage to explore without setting off some score penalty. But there was a whole lot of frustration about trying to figure out and execute a puzzle in its most perfect details, not about exploring and coming up with a plan I would adapt on the fly. Again, not a bad game, just one that went the opposite way of my expectations.

Just won my first marathon game! I wanted to play the most alien thing I could so I played on a Fungal world, played for Transcendance, and set aliens to 'high'. I'll compare the game to Civ 5 rather than AC since I think thats more relevant to those claiming it to be DLC-like.
Pros:
-Game runs smoother than Civ5. Even in late game the game loaded turns faster which may be something to consider if that caused you major grievances on less than awesome machines.
-No happiness. Several things simply got a 'sci-fi' name from Civ5 counterparts, but happiness being replaced with the health system is a very good thing. Large empires in more difficult settings were kind of a silly thing to do in Civ5 so this really opens the game up more.
-Tech tree. Its more complicated than normal research in Civ5 and many of the sub-branches allow you to further your affinity that shape your civ. Its possible to go into mupltiple branches that dont link well early on, or do the opposite and go too far in one branch without getting basics from others that leave you crippled. I think there will be good metagame here.
-Starter perks. Unlike Civ5 where you start as some thugs beating rocks together, BE lets you pick your crew types, spaceship type, and supplies you bring with you that lends to a more custom start up appropriate to a sci-fi setting.
-Esp and Trade are the same and slightly improved from the Civ5 versions that came in DLC. The spys in BE have far more options here that can really hurt your enemies (I let out a thumper that called Alien Siege Wurms in an enemy city) and the amount of trade routes you have running rivals that of Venice without actually playing a 1 city civ.
-Aliens. I started my game with the sensors that locate alien nests, which populate over the largest xeno pools in the game (a resource needed for a heavy Harmony Affinity) so I knew right off if I wanted to re-start the game and where I would first go for my expansions. The alien hordes themselves feel more natural in civ. They basically behave like aggresive animals and I appreciated their AI far more than 'barbarians', even on their most aggresive setting.
-Satalite layer. I didnt get too far into satalites as some affinities might with orbital attacks but these really add new options. Some would populate un-modded areas with lux and strategic resources, another pumped down miasma (a toxic gas thats poisons enemies but heals and gives combat bonus' to Harmony civs), and this giant low orbit squid that pooped more miasma and gave combat bonus' to units down below. Its definately a good addition.
-Late game. The combat in late game gets really fun. All your units get upgraded for free based on your chosen affinity and by the end all your 'rovers' and 'missile rovers' are hovertanks flying across the ocean. The affinity-based units, and mega-units are a huge deal. 1 turn before my MInd Flower finished I had 2 Evolved Xeno Titans (think GDR *10) wreck my enemies earth gateway while shrugging off all the stuff they were throwing at them the whole time; it was a good ending!
Cons:
-NPC identities. The bonus' you get for each civ seem limited. In Civ5 you got more 'things' that defined you. You can definately shape your civ over time the way you want more in BE but by end-game you likely have your main affinity maxed and went on to others and begin to lose your uniqueness. The actual bonus' that are unique to your civ seem so marginal I kinda wonder why they even bothered putting them in. I'd have liked to see more special units/buildings or abilites for each civ that pushed them more in the dirrection of certain affinities.  One civ asked me to declare war on another by the name of their leader alone and without being able to open my diplomacy tab I was just left thinking 'who the heck is that?'. Its not like you had the same issue in Civ5 when someone asked you to kill Washington but... I'm sure I'll get used to it.
-City States, or outposts as they're called. The game dosnt just found cities; it starts them as an 'outpost' early on that developes into a city (which by itself I think is fine). My issue is these random outposts that pop up, never turn into full cities, and pretty much act like city states with even less options. Beyond a few good trade routes, they seem to be completelly irrelevant. NPC civs attack them without issue from the rest of the world, there is no friendship meter with these people. It seems a step in the wrong dirrection and lots of wasted potential.
-No global politics. I know this was added in a DLC, but.. considering how these people are supposed to be futuristic, and instantly connected the moment they pop into the world, I find it wierd that there would be no futuristic council when the story goes: they just left a world that HAD one. AI of NPC civs in BE is slightly better but the global politics and amount of favors we curried from city states made the Civ5 game feel more developed on a global scale.
-No terraforming. I know know, its not AC, and I was honestly too young to even remember much about that game. I do remember the terraforming though which allowing you to + and - land and ocean, and being able to build cities underwater. A 'terraformed' tile improvement is just a really good jungle and you can do some terraforming-type stuff with the new satalites but I was kinda hoping for a little more. Maybe its a limitation with the Civ5 engine, but I still have my fingers crossed some DLC with add this.
All in all I think this is a very good game. I'd give it a 8-8.5 depending on much you <3 sci-fi.  I think I'll have quite a few very good playthroughs with the different affinities but I'm not sure I'll get as much playtime from this as Civ5. If that turns you off maybe wait until its a little cheaper but even at full price I still think its worth it.

The trademark disguise mechanic has been drastically altered for the worse. Nick an engineer's uniform, & every single engineer in the country will be able to see through your disguise in mere seconds: it's like they all have an entire database in their heads of what each other looks like. Even if you're half way across a map, partially concealed by a dumpster & have your back to everyone whilst in the shadows, they can still see through your disguise! What the hell??? When you have a series that successfully utilise a unique mechanic that works throughout each game, then you change it so much that it becomes broken & frustrating that you end up just forgetting about it & shooting your way through levels, something has seriously gone wrong.
The absolute (see what I did there) worse offender of the disguise mechanic is that when you take the clothes of someone wearing a full face mask HE DOESN'T PUT THE FACE MASK ON!!! In all past games, Mr. 47 could hide his face, yet now all of a sudden he refuses to wear anything to conceal his face, like he suffers from an allergic reaction to face cloth. It's no wonder why everyone can spot you through your disguise, seeing as you're the only one wearing a hazmat suit without a gas mask on looking like a prick.

Best way to play past the flawed disguise mechanic is to sprint full speed everywhere, hugging walls, hiding behind objects & ninja rolling between cover. It's embarrassingly sad & hilarious that sprinting through the entire level hiding behind things & rolling all over the place like a hyperactive toddler grants less suspicion then walking around the place like a fully grown man would normally do. The NPCs even make remarks like “act like a grown man!” when you start trying to hide. Who would have thought that the game is self-aware.
But this is Hitman: Absolution I’m playing, not Splinter Cell or Metal Gear Solid Absolution, so why the ♥♥♥♥ am I rolling all over the place instead of blending in??? Speaking of which, you STILL can get detected when you’re wearing a disguise in a crowd of around 50 people.
New to the series is Instincts mode. Switch it on & time slows down, the background will turn monochrome whilst enemies, their walk path & important objects will glow. Instincts mode also allows you to blend in, such as scratching your head or tipping your hat low to obscure your face as you walk past people. But the problem is using this drains your instincts meter (mana?) so if it runs out, suddenly Mr. 47 loses the ability to simply lower his head again. Seriously???
There are a few select objects in the world that you can use to blend in: this not only recharges your instincts meter, people no longer suspects you of being an assassin. I think I'd be pretty suspicious of a guy constantly mopping a tiny area in front of his feet for a straight 5 minutes or a Policeman inspecting a doughnut like he's counting the individual atoms on it. Did I mention once this meter runs out, you suddenly lose the ability to tip your hat low or scratch your head? Maybe 47 has a stiff neck and the mana metre is actually his muscle fatigue.
Regardless, these features in the game are so strangely unhuman-like & illogical it's ♥♥♥♥in’ hilarious.
Other minor flaws of the game is not being able to choose gear during the campaign, linear missions, ability to hide multiple huge guns and objects in your coat, enemies not noticing you strangling someone to death right next to them, silencers attach instantly to guns,
Because it’s cool and it’s Square Enix, you have a scoring system that rates you on how well (or how♥♥♥♥♥♥ you are during each mission. Whilst it’s a nice idea to try to rack up the highest score as possible, it’s frustrating when bad game mechanics hamper this. As you can imagine, I’ve had to shoot my way through most levels, so most of my level score is in the minus thousands region. Anyone want to try to beat my lowest scores, huh??
Well, Hitman: Absolution isn’t that bad. It’s just far from good. As a Hitman game, it fails miserably. As a cover based shooter with minor stealth mechanics, it’s decent enough.
I brought this for my friend’s birthday sadly, and to this day I still don’t know if he forgives me. Heck, I don’t know if I’ve even forgiven myself.
How can I best summarise this game? It's like that kid at school who boasts about driving an expensive sports car, has the latest £2000 super computer & has 5 different girlfriends. Then one day to his horror, his over-affectionate mum comes to pick him up from school, tells everyone that he stays at home all day playing on his cheap Macintosh & he is scared of girls. Then he goes all embarrassed & tries to stop his mum, only to trip over & his pants fall down in the process, everyone laughs & ridicules him, then they all go away & never look at him the same way again & he is left disgraced & shamed. Hitman: Absolution is that kid.

It's around 2-3 hours long, depending on whether you get stuck on puzzles. The soundtrack repeats often, changing between tracks in most rooms. Approximately 30% of the game is spent walking across large expanses that do not stay interesting to look at for that entire time spent walking.

This is a review of Sparkle 2 Evo. I have written this after completing the game and all achievements.
Gameplay: 8/10
You explore three-dimensional levels by navigating along the X and Z axies and collecting colored orbs. Once you think you've got all the orbs you want on a layer, you can then go up or down layers. The colors of the orbs are very important because they influence your evolution. Although many of the evolutions seem to add only minor visual effects and slight stat bonuses, you can get special abilities and end up looking really cool.
Graphics: 9.5/10
No one is perfect, but the graphics here are spectacular. While not overwhelming, they definitely enhance the experience, from the awesome range of colors and enviroments in the game to the look of your... organism... thing... they really amazed me.
Performance: 8/10
Even on my low-power computer (two cores, $100 video card, 2GB RAM), this ran very smoothly even with everything turned all the way up.
Features: 5/10
This has no online multiplayer, as far as I could tell. You could play against a bot or create more organisms, but the lack of real multiplayer was a real bummer. The achievements were fulfilling, but not too hard to get, just the way I personally like it.
Ambience: 8.5/10
I got sucked in to the game immediately. The sounds were soothing and enveloping, and coupled nicely with the graphics. This is one of the few games I would not want to play my own music instead of their music. It was really nice.
Replayability: 4/10
Honestly, you could replay the game, maybe go down a different path, but the levels are the same, and coupled with the lack of multiplayer and very straightforward gameplay it would be a grind.
Summary: 7.2/10
Good game, it was a certainly a worthwjile $1 (I think I bought it while it was on sale) and probably a worthwhile use of $5. I had a very good time with it and I feel like it was less of a time-waster than other games, and more of an experience.

Hey.
Heres my thoughts of Infinity wars TCCG.
I played some (some will say a lot) of MTG , but last time i played is a few years ago. That way i know what to expect from a Card game like this. Was I dissapointet? NO. This game really bring some new and exiting aspects to the genre.
Many game mechanics is well known, and some even has familiar names (like haste etc..). The new mechanics are an awesome addition to the genres as well.
Gameplay:
The first thing you notice is the 3 Commanders sitting on the battlefield right from turn 1 , ready to use their abilities! Technically they're not actually on the battlefield, as the term battliefield is used for specific areas of the entire playing field. This is not a rule book though, so I wont go into further details here. The commanders will decide wich "mana colors" (MTG term), or "Faction" as we call them you can play. By determining the 3 commanders you choose weather you go for 3 different factions, or maybe just a single faction. "Purity" then determines how "powerfull" spell or characters you can have within that faction. The most powerfull will require 3 commanders of the same color.
One of the first thing that I noticed was the very fluid gameplay. You have something to play and do every single turn. The way resources are handled are so much better compared to MTG, at least in my opinnion. You start each game with 1 ressource, and you gain 1 each turn. By turn 10 both players should have 10 resources (resources are like mana). There are ways however to speed up the process of getting much mana faster though just like we know from other games. There are ALSO ways to Loose a step in the race for mana. Cards like asassinate will let you asassinate ANY character on the board. But the Price is that you Loose 1 ressource point. You will still reach 10, but it will now take 1 turn more than you're opponent, There are also ways to gain more than 10 total.
The way this Works results in a fluid gameplay. Everyone that plays MTG know that even the best deck can have a really bad Draw and either Draw no land, or just land land land. Both ways will destroy most decks in MTG. You will never run short of mana in IW, or get a bad Draw (at least mana wise). If you construct your deck wisely, you can rely on the deck to Work close to perfect everytime. In other words, you know that you have excatly 6 mana (at least) on turn 6 etc...
The playfield is divided into zones. This is a huge improvement!!! There is so much more "mind game" going on inside the game, since you can move most Cards from one zone to another, and even from the actual "battlefield" and back to a support zone. Even the most powerfull Cards from your opponent can be countered by simply anticipating what he will do, and move cards out of the battlefield when you expect him to. Awesome when it Works. On the other hand can you move your own stuff away from the battlefield to "bluff" that a mass destruction spell or similar are Brewing, and then ending up with a non defended "defense" zone at your opponent... Great new aspect to the Whole TCG genre :)

- You can play ALOT without paying a dime!

I've only played a few hours but so far it's fantastic.
My favorite change is the how the void power meter works. In previous Dishonored games, the void meter was a single bar that would empty and only recharge if you waited and didn't use powers for the next five or so seconds. This really prevented me from using powers in quick succession to perform nice combos, which I really wanted to do, so I would use a power, wait, then use a power again. In this game, the void power meter is split into three bars that will always recharge, no matter how quickly you use them. This is a fantasic change, it really speeds up the game and removes the anxiety around using void abilities. You also never have to worry getting the vials of addermire solutioons, which was always more of an annoyance than anything else.
The new contracts system in the game also introduces side missions and another way to make the in-game currency for spending at the black market. Having contracts gives the game a Skyrim/Oblivion esque feel, and makes the game feel more open and bigger than previous installations in the franchise. Plus the contracts are fun, and change it up a bit from the main story missions.
As for the story, it's pretty cool to see Daud again and so far the dialogue between him and Billie has been interesting.
In a world where singleplayer games are dying off, I'm really glad someone is still releasing great singleplayer games and stories. I'm really looking forward to playing more of this and highly recommend it.

Why should you buy Shadow Warrior?
Two words: level design.
I know that sounds like an odd reason, but for me it's the games greatest strength. Visit my profile page and go through my screenshots. The game is GORGEOUS.
So what about the rest of the game? Well from a long time and avid player of the FPS genera, it's a mixed bag. I played the game twice all the way through. Once on "normal" difficulty and then again on "insane". On normal I used the Katana the entire time. That was probably stupid, but the melee combat felt extremely satisfying. The Ki powers were also a blast to use. That wore off about 8 hours into the game. Little did I know there's 8 more hours to grind through. I got that feeling of: "Is this over yet?"
Well after some consideration I felt like I should give the game another try. My inner achievement hunter had something to do with it too! :-)
The second time I went with insane mode and used all the weapons. With the inclusion of the 1.5 optimization patch the game looked and ran better than ever. However, the weapons felt weak. Extremely weak. Even the bad♥♥♥♥♥looking quad barreled shotgun. Once I got my hands on the crossbow and the its chargeable shot upgrade, the game became cake. With fully upgraded healing powers and the one shot crossbow, yet again I got that feeling of boredom.
So why am I recommending this game after calling it boring? Because it's like a really pretty bowl of oatmeal. There really isn't anything "wrong" with the game. It just middle of the road with a great number of sights to see.
My main gripe with Shadow Warrior is it tries to please everyone at the same time. The attempt of fusing old school and new doesn't seem to work for me. The game contains the Bioshock "Look everywhere for cash" loot system. It also has RPG elements, unlockables, and a low assortment of opponent's to kill. My opinion is if you going to make a FPS, choose a school and stick with it.
Pro's +
+ Level Design + A huge range of environment's and aesthetics to enjoy! So many sights to behold!
+ Optimized + Looks great and runs really well!
+ Characters + The chemistry between Low Wang and his demon friend is quite entertaining.
+ Story + Easy to follow and keeps your interest.
+ Arsenal + Large variety of weapons and powers to make combat interesting - for a time...
+ Melee Combat + The Katana is really fun to play with!
+ Secrets + A must for any FPS.
+ EX Mode + Allows you to keep all your upgrades after you beat the game.
Con's -
- Enemies - Offers a limited amount of baddies to slay.
- Unbalanced Weapons - On the highest difficulty some of the weapons are pretty weak.
- Loot - If you want your weapons to have additional features, you better look EVERYWHERE for cash.
- Game Length - Game progression is entirely "gated". Everything is locked until you kill each wave of enemies.
Shadow Warrior goes on sale frequently at 75% off. Well worth it at that price. If your playing for the first time, play the game on either easy or normal. Don't do what I did, use all the weapon's in the game!

One of the indie stars of this year, and it sucks it took me this long to get around to reviewing the game. That's what happens when there's so many good games this year, but hey, more about Hollow Knight. Hollow Knights knows the genre like the back of its hand: and knew how to implement a basic combat system that's based on precision and timing perfectly. Enemies can be a challenge until you know how to approach them, and even then you've got to find a way to get in and out without getting hit.  The game does a great job of mixing up enemy patterns and boss challenges to keep combat fresh throughout the game, while not overly complicating it with overly complex mechanics or anything of the like. You have some choices and configurations with your charms: but this game comes down to avoiding enemies and striking at the right time: and I love it for that.
It's all complimented by a lovely presentation that has a LOT of depth when you start looking into its details in both the sound design and the visual presentation. The game does wonders with using only a few select colors at a time, giving a lot of details and life to the characters and giving them a realism that not many indie games can. Yes, realism when it comes to hybrid shadow bug creatures. Again, the devil is always in the details, and my god did Team Cherry nail the details in this game. Granted, I'm one of the only people who think that the music is medium level and not fantastic (it fits the game, it's just something I wouldn't listen outside of the game to), but pretty much everything that the game has to offer presentation wise is something that you're going to want to experience.
As for the story, it's where the game starts to misstep, at least in my eyes. It's very much a story for lore-hoarders out there, as the story is a bit piece meal and requires you to put it together to enjoy it. It's definitely a bit different, and I like what the story sets up and the mysterious world that it built: I just think it's going to be really hit or miss when it comes to the audience that likes/dislikes it.
So yeah, it's a must buy game on my scale, with it showing some of the best understanding of game mechanics and design in the genre that I've seen in a while. Well done Team Cherry, well done.

When Civ V came out, it seemed like a barebones, watered down game with weird little gimmicks that didn't really make it any BETTER, compared to the rich complexity of Civilization IV: Beyond the Sword. I was easily bored by it, though I had some fun, and moved back to BTS.
Now, Civ V is a game that I absolutely adore. G&K and BNW turned a fun diversion into a huge timesink. And here, I see the seeds of a same thing.
Civ IV was dull when it came out. Civ V was dull when it came out. Beyond Earth is... Well, similar. There's a skeleton of a larger game here, but only a skeleton.
Now, some people cynically say that they aren't releasing it in full, that the 'real game' isn't out yet. That I disagree with. I think what happened, both in IV and V, is that they listened to fan reaction. What did people nto like? What did they want more of? What were people saying was missing, and what can we do about it? And they addressed that. But they can't address it until the statements are actually made.
I'm going to start with a few things I didn't like in the game. The cons, if you will. The leader sleection is small, and feels somewhat generic. With only 8 leaders, I don't get the personality I feel in Civ V. When I see Montezuma, I immediately think "Oh, here's that♥♥♥♥♥♥" When Brasilia lands, I don't have as much of a reaction.
That would, honestly, be my biggest complaint. Lack of leader selection. Lack of leader selection is making many games feel like slight variants on the same game. The characters also seem to have less personality than they did in V, likely because they don't have the wealth of history to draw off, and the writers may not be as good.
The other thing that bothers me is the customization. As I progress along the affinity, my progression seems similar, like I'm making the same choices. Playing Harmony, Purity, or Supremacy hasn't made me feel like I've got a lot of options. Just the chance to make this choice or that choice, like I always do.
And yet, the decisions can feel meaningful. At least, playing Harmony, Purity, and Supremacy is a meaningful decision. What techs I research helps me build the future of humanity. I don't feel locked in one "History progressing as it progresses." I joke sometimes about certain people on the internet having an idea of science influenced by Civilization. An infinite progression. This isn't the case, here. I might have something that my friends don't even want to research, and never will need to. I've never once researched a tech just because I wanted to make sure I didn't fall behind in the future. Every tech had a goal in researching it. This is excellent.
The things I put on my ship are meaningful as well. They all combine together to make a starting civ. Perhaps that's why the devs didn't feel more civs were necessary. There are honestly, potentially, hundreds of ways to start.
I don't think they're cynically waiting for the real game. And I don't think it's fair to compare it to Civ V: Brave Nwe World. When CK2 was released, I didn't think the game was incomplete. Compared to it today, though, it was. But that was a fine release.
This is a fine game. Here's my recommendation.
Buy it if:
1) You like narrative. The game makes more of a story than Civ V does. You feel like you're building the future, your decisions matter.
2) You're a die-hard Civ gamer: There's nothing about this to stop you from playing it. If you gave Alpha Centauri a chance, give this a chance.
3) You find Civ kinda intimidating. The mechanics in this one are simpler, and the decisions you make are more obvious. You always know, immediately, what researching a tech will get you. There's only a few units, compared to the many that Civ will have.
4) You like Space, and enjoy Civ. If you're a sci-fi fan, and Civ is always kinda fun to you, then play this. You won't regret it, because this game is really, REALLY good sci-fi.
However, if you're unsure, and don't fit under the categories - Wait for a Steam sale. It may not be worth all 50 of your ollars, but at a $25 price, I'd be utterly unable to recommend missing it.

Kairo is the pinnacle of efficient and effective game design. Using nothing more than the most basic geometric graphics, it somehow manages to craft awe-inspiring vistas, mind-bending puzzles, and a complex open-ended backstory.
It ends up being less of a "game," and more of an immersive experience that stays with you long after you've shut off the computer. I would rank it in my top 5 titles of all time.
If you are a fan of exploration, or of Myst-like puzzlers, do yourself a favour and add this to your library.

Amazing game.  Pigeonholing it in a genre like platformer or metroidvania does this game some injustice, as it transcends these categories in my opinion.  Really, this game is a must-have, especially for what I consider its low price.  You're definitely getting value with this purchase.
The game has tight controls in a well-designed and planned environment.  I think the developers created an amzing atmosphere and tone in this haunted and haunting place.  The world is vast and holds many secrets, as well as being able to suit the slow and plodding explorer-types and the speed runner types. As you play through the game, you'll try to put together the story that is Hollow Knight, from the lore left behind and from the monologues that NPCs give.
Much of the game consists of platforming, exploration, and combat.  Mostly, you can navigate your environment with no real issues, but as the game progresses, the platforming becomes a bit more difficult, culminating in the ultimate platforming challenge for those who persist beyond the simple ending.  Honestly, I did not care much for that part, finding it a bit tedious, but it was the price of admission toward unlocking the game's deeper secrets. You'll know what I mean if you find the place!
Exploration was my favorite part, though you may initially be overwhelmed with how huge this world seems.  I know I felt near-frozen at one point, when I found I had created access to some 5 or 6 different zones, each one seemingly huge, each one full of new dangers and secrets.  Further investigation showed that choices were somewhat limited by the necessity for certain abilities, which get unlocked by combat or exploration. However, the world seemed less linear than other games like Hollow Knight, for I ended up progressing via a "non-standard path," in hindsight according to community thinking.
The combat is tough but fair.  Even the regular enemies can present a challenge to the beginner, who has no experience with their patterns.  However, you can defeat each enemy, as they all have some sort of "tell" to their patterns.  Some of the bosses can be extremely difficult, but here too each has his/her own pattern and you should eventually prevail with effort.  Note: the combat is not button-mashing.  There are slight cooldowns after most actions, so timing and precision are required.
The game is not without flaws.  Personally, the game seems vague with some of its mechanics.  Be warned at the onset that you can swing your sword in ANY direction, including down while in midair. This can allow you to pogo off enemies and the destructible environment elements, and will be required in some places. Also, the "save zones" in this game are not always conveniently-placed; you will need to backtrack after deaths many times, especially with bosses.  Few bosses have convenient save locations.
Which brings me to my last gripe: death.  Your death mechanic isn't well-explained, in my opinion; I believe it must be familiar to a mechanic in some other game I hadn't played, so it caught me by surprise.  I lost quite a bit of the game's currency learning how the mechanic works.  When a character dies, it starts back at the nearest save point, which seems easy enough.  The character's "mana" bar (called soul in this game) becomes cracked and caps at 2/3rds of the total capacity, and the character has zero money.  Near where the character died will be a "shade" of your character.  Killing it restores your soul gauge and money.  Dying before reclaiming the soul forfeits whatever money that shade held, as a new shade will be generated at this death spot.  Knowing this going in may save you frustration I experienced.
Further, the shade will not always be at the exact point you died.  The developers didn't necessarily want your shade trapped in areas (such as boss fight areas), forcing you into the fight again before reclaiming your soul gauge and money.   Always check your map for where exactly the shade has spawned before assuming you know its location!  Otherwise, you may end up in fights for which you are unprepared!
Otherwise, I do love this game and enjoyed playing it through.  The free update the developers gave us only sweetened the deal.  Rumors are that another may be forthcoming, allowing us to play the game as different characters.  Just more reason for you to purchase this game yourself!

To start this review off;
Hollow Knight has left me feeling like I lost more than I gained from it.
The sheer difficulty of some boss battles? Alright, fine, I expected a genuine 2D Dark Souls kinda deal, but the scarcity of safepoints and fast travel systems and the endless back and forth trekking from the safe point halfway across the area to the boss that killed you so you can get your money back from your corpse, and no way to save your progress before the boss room to then get killed again for the billionth time?
Not to mention doing this for pretty much every boss, as you're guaranteed to die a couple of times because you don't recognise the attack pattern yet.
The game is beautiful, don't get me wrong. The atmosphere, the post-apocalyptic premise of a glorious kingdom turned to a crumbling shadow of its former self, the music, the artstyle, the characters.
The bouts of light-hearted humour sprinkled in among the detritus of a fallen society etc. etc.
I love it.
... But not the difficulty or the lack of safepoints.
Another point I wanna bring up; Bugs.
Genuine game bugs. The "This-Should-Not-Happen" type;
Numerous occasions I've had to restart the game because some enemy slapped me back into the previous screen and through the boundaries of the level.
Same happened with an elevator once.
There's reports of the game sometimes outright erasing your saves (though this hasn't happened to me, so I have no way to coroborate this.)
Some miscellaneous thoughts (Things may not seem too coherent here);
I really like exploration, but at some points it becomes tedious backtrekking, again feeding into the problem of a lack of fast travel spots.
And the boss combat? I want to say that combat with regular enemies is an on-point thing, and it is imho.
But the boss battles are downright unfair at points, partially due to the constant need of running all over the place when you've died.
And there's another thing I dislike about the game, even if the intent was well meant.
The Charms system.
Basically, at the start you get three slots (or Notches, as the game calls them) for Charms, this you can expand when you find, earn or buy more.
However, a lot of those Charms take up more than one slot.
And some Charms you need for exploration; The compass, the Collection swarm (If you don't want to run around a single room picking up every little penny on the floor or, god forbid, beyond spikes)
There's upgrades to your blade and magic abilities, like increasing the range of your blade, which should be an upgrade that doesn't require a Charm, but rather going to the guy that is there to
In any case, with the ammount of Charms you need just to get through the areas of the game without getting all too lost with your maps, you might have a spot left for one or two of a few Charmss that can actually improve your abilities.
Again; A well-meant ingame system that is, sadly, poorly implemented as a weak patchwork over a bigger problem.
Final thoughts;
I really want to love this game, I do.
I love so much about it, and although I've listed only a few negative things compared to the many good parts of it, the negative things are hair-pulling, teeth-gritting, pulse-poundingly frustrating.
I've had moments where I spent a session playing this game just to beat one boss, quitting the game soon after because I felt physically exhausted and in pain just from all the stressful retries, desperately keeping my rage contained after each death and endless, ump-tillionth backtrek to the bossroom, only to have my♥♥♥♥♥♥handed to me with a side of cockroach garnish.
I want to love this game, but it's done so much to make it utterly unenjoyable for me.
If you're into Dark Souls-esque difficulty aplied to 2D platformers, Hollow Knight's for you.
If you want to pick it up for a decent challenge as a casual gamer that will leave you fulfilled at the end, buy something else.
In which case I'd suggest
Still hard, but at least I can bring myself to finishing the game without knocking ten years off my life due high blood pressure.
Overall, I wish I could recommend this game, but in all good faith and for your health, I can't, as much as it pains me.

On a more serious note, this game is extremely fun, and won't ever be surpassed by the sequel. Ever. (the reason for that is art style. Dark and moody beats Wind Waker 24/7 with me)
This game has a large amount of item customization, and even a bit of limited character customization(mostly colors). Along with editing items, at max upgrade level you could name them, which was severely enjoyable for me.
The enemy scale is also an interesting concept. You could have different shades of monsters for each difficulty, and the best part when you get to high levels is when you start wading through enemies. I have yet to find anything more satisfying than taking out 20 goblins at once with one swing.
Money can be a bit hard to come by, but grind and you'll make it through. Or you'll just install a mod that gives you infinite (not really) cash.
On the topic of mods, this game is almost built around the concept of them. You can find mods for different difficulties for existing stages, redone stages with new modes, and even user-built stages. There's also the community of mods for getting high-tier items instantly, and stages that instantly level you to 100.
On the topic of classes, you've got the 4 base classes unlocked at the start. There's actually 7 more to my knowledge, but those are sadly DLC. The DLC classes are just 4 genderswaps of the normal classes, and 3 unique ones.
Your 4 base classes consist of: The Mage, The Squire, The Monk, and The Huntress. Each of them have their specialty, although I won't go into detail about them.
So without further ado, my final rating is:
9/10

Steam sale -80%. How could I say "no"?
This game is like a Spore first evolutionary step. We are swimming around eating stuff and growing our bug-like thingy into the top predator of the seas. That's the whole story.
Gameplay is as basic as it gets. If one played some "feed the fish" games, he knows what to do. For other players, mostly who are not familiar with the "genre", it's basically a Snake+, where "+" stands for more content than parent game. You swim, eat, grow, rince and repeat.
Graphics are really well made. It's colorful and bright, eye candies are everywhere. Also our creature, no matter what evolutionary step we will take, is really well made and looks both astonishing and threathening.
Music is in pair with graphics. Relaxing tones mix rather well with blissful graphics, giving us something to ease our mind while endangering species with our gluttony. If this is a Lothus flower, it's pretty damn territorial.
About bad things, well, there are two. Firstly, steering is kind of buggy and can screw up sometimes. Especially, when we are not really good at it. Some times I was just wondering WTF is going on, because my species went ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ for no reason. The other time it needed so much time to "ignite the engine" I was bored dead.
The other problem with the game is the length. It took me 2 hours to PERFECT the damned thing. 1,5h to beat the "story" mode. BS? Well, it's economic class game, so what did you expect? It cost 5 euro normally, and there is constant -80% on it, so you can grab a bite for olny 1 euro. So I must say, that it really was money well spend.
Buy this game if you want really easy 100%, are new to the game whatsoever (or have anybody who is and want to play, just like Cursed Treasure), want to relax or just to grab a game because you really need to ease your wallet. Either way, buy it olny on sale, because 5 euros for less than 2h gameplay is a ripoff. Never the less, it was fun, and I will enjoy it even after some time.
Zawisza out.

They never said it was going to be easy. In fact, it's entirely the opposite. The Age of Decadence never pretends to be easy, never holds your hand except for the first message that says "This game is going to be difficult." This game doesn't let you play a jack of all trades; you're either very good at one or two things, or you're very dead. Hybrid characters are frowned upon; you have to play your cards right, trust no-one and say the right things to get out alive.
What this game has in difficulty it also has a counterpart in it's rewarding combat system, it's sprawling questlines and dialogue trees and incredibly gripping, mysterious backstories. The lore in this game is rivalled by only few games; it's ideas incredibly novel and unique.
Some people would claim that this game is too hard, too infuriating to play. I'd say they are looking at this game wrong.
This isn't an RPG like many others, where you're 'Killy Mcbeardyson', slayer of countless bandits, dragons and champion of the entire world. This is a game where you just picked up a sword, you barely know which way to hold it (if that) and everyone out there is trying to kill you. You're alone unless you choose a guild to side with, and even then you have to watch your back. Everyone, and I repeat, everyone, in this game seems to have an ulterior motive, a reason for doing what they are doing, and they all want to survive. No-one goes down easy in this game.
Even if you don't like combat, this game makes up for it in countless lines of well-written dialogue. None of it is filler dialogue, describing smaller characters or talking about the smell of a room or something redundant. Everything is concise, important and thrilling. Throughout many dialogues in the game I was kept on the edge of my seat, hoping beyond hope that my character's persuasion skill was high enough, that I'd taken the right dialogue tree to try and appeal to this character.
To summarise, this game has a unique, original and well thought out setting (Post-Apocalyptic Roman Empire... I'll let you discover the rest for yourself), a challenging yet rewarding turn based combat system, and interesting, relatable characters who you can never trust, not completely.

This game is a very worthy addition to the Hitman series. I have to admit, I wasn’t particularly a Hitman fan. Blame my best friend. One day he lent me Codename 47, Silent Assassin and Contracts all in order to play in retail boxes. Back then I was merciless to any frustration and played every single game on the hardest difficulty. These days I play games on Normal. And this is one of those games where I’d recommend playing it on Normal for the first time.
Hitman is all about achieving “Linear Gameplay Perfection”. And that’s a lot harder than you may think. You have to know your environment. You need to know the timing of the characters paths. You need to know the various ways you can eliminate a single target discreetly.
This brings me to say what you can do, but don’t want to do. You can go on a massacre run. I tried this out in a courtroom map for the fun of it. But eerily it was horrifyingly realistic. You can hear people begging for their lives and stuff. And all I could think about was, “My gawd, this is like some American high school shootout simulator.” Unlike the previous Hitman games where it felt like you were a badass against bad guys and nobody could mess with you. Hitman: Absolution penalizes you with a scoring system. In effect this game literally forces you to play the right way unlike its predecessors.
Ignoring the challenges, there is an XP system in place that unlocks skills as you progress. None of the older Hitman games did this. In fact I’m starting to feel like a lot of today’s game development companies are just chucking similar systems in for the heck of getting a player to play the game more. I’m not against this idea (because it hasn’t bothered me yet). But I also don’t endorse this idea. I’d rather have game developers focus on the real reasons why people return back to playing a game. Things like fun factor … etc. Not some progress bar that tells you how much you’ve done.
Hitman: Absolution is powered by the Glacier 2 game engine. This is a game engine that I would commend. It seems very sophisticated. A lot of the mechanics from the older Hitman games have been enhanced. Everything seems more precise and graphically illustrated, as opposed to just having a hunch.
Hitman games have a certain aesthetic that evokes a particular mood that is truly unique. Whilst Hitman: Contracts has my favorite introduction movie, Hitman: Absolution has by far one of the most classy, simplistic and quick switching main menu interfaces you will ever witness.
I want to talk about the crowd which literally looks like hundreds of people on a single map. When I first spotted this in “Hitman: Blood Money” back in 2007, I was like, “This is just ♥♥♥♥♥♥ic. How the ♥♥♥♥ did they do this?” Forward to 2013, the technology is still unbelievable. You can still bump into each individual or kill them one by one if that is your thing. Whilst this was the same for “Kane & Lynch 2: Dog Days”, they made an improvement for Hitman: Absolution. Now you can hide in the crowd, with certain parts of the crowd being “thicker” to conceal your location. In other words all those people aren’t just a visual aesthetic anymore.
I still like “Hitman: Blood Money” the best, but Hitman: Absolution is a definite for any fans or someone who hasn’t played any and is looking to get started. It takes about 20 hours to complete it properly on Normal and by that I mean always aiming to be a Silent Assassin. I think the game is an 11GB download but takes up 24GB of Hard Drive space. I’ll definitely be playing this again but on the hardest difficulty now that I know what the maps are like.

Shadow Warrior really suprised me with just how great of a game it really is.
It's an FPS with a sword fighting mechanic that has been polished up with several abilities that really make it shine. Every big hit you land, and every enemy you shred with your katana feels so satisfying.
Along with the sword fighting, you have several ranged weapons as well. Most of the guns have a very visceral and satisfying punch to them, and they have their uses and come in handy when you're frantically trying to take out a hoard of enemies, or just that one tough enemy. Landing a head shot on the tougher enemies with the charged shot of the crossbow felt so damn good.
To accent all of fast paced combat is, my favorite addition to the game, a great dash/dodge system. The dash you have is quick to get where you are and works in every sitiuation, from avoiding combat to running head first into it. It just feels great to use and is the cherry on top of how satisfying the rest of the action is in the game.
All in all you have a very solid FPS with a great sword fighting aspect to it and a top notch dash mechanic.
I can't recommend this game enough if you're a fan of frantic, bloody first person action.
The only qualm I really have with the game is that the writing is pretty lame at times. And, while I love dumb stories with dumb writing, some of the writing is a little too dumb for me, but all of that is pretty easily overlooked when you diving head first into a hoard of demons.

В игре используется новый движок — Glacier 2. Он поддерживает все самые современные технологии, включая тесселяцию и сложную физику, новую изящную анимацию и высочайшую проработку лиц персонажей. В игре прекрасная, детализированная, стильная картинка. Искусственный интеллект, создает уникальную модель поведения для каждого отдельного персонажа, что делает действие более насыщенным и разнообразным. В игре есть и драки с бомжами, и боевые монашки, и салочки с вертолетом, и прятки в конопле, и побег из горящего отеля. В игре введена система особого рентгеновского зрения. Главный герой может смотреть сквозь стены, подсвечивая важные предметы, отслеживая самих охранников и даже маршруты их передвижения.
В игре  есть сетевой режим «Контракты». Это любительские миссии. Игроки выбирают локации из одиночной кампании, назначают жертв – любого человека на карте, выставляют сложность, ставят дополнительные условия, затем сами проходят это задание и публикуют его. Выполнение контрактов дает деньги, которые тратятся на открытие новых костюмов, оружия и апгрейдов, чтобы создавать еще более трудные контракты. Моя оценка 10/10.

First and Foremost, this is a review of the single player as I'm just not much of a multiplayer person. This review also assumes you enjoy the civilization format of gameplay (because if you don't, why are you even looking here?).
Overall, this is a good game and if you enjoyed Civ 5, you'll be right at home here. Music, Graphics, Controls are all spot on and presented with the same polish you'd expect from a Firaxis top down strategy game and while the menus can be a little less than intuitive at first, there is  the standard tutorial/advisor to hold your hand if you ask it to. Singing its praises is not the point of this review though, the point of it is to take issue with the one glaring negative.
This is not the spiritual successor to Alpha Centauri. If you buy it hoping it will be, you're in for a let down. Alpha Centauri had two major things going for it that no Firaxis game has managed to replicate since and Beyond Earth hasn't either.
The first thing lacking from Beyond Earth is faction leader personality. Each faction has their pre set agendas, but beyond slightly varying the phrasing, they may as well have a copy paste conversation with your faction comprised of two word declarations and one word responses. DECLARE WAR : Yes/No SIGN TREATY: Yes/No. ACCEPT TRADE: Yes/No.
No game since Alpha Centauri has been as verbose or had as much backstory behind each character. Gone are the days of two paragraphs of response text to you insultingly offering to buy a base for 2 credits. Nowhere does the game name your advisors, assign them to a unit and then name your next city after them if they die in battle. You might see this as stream lined gameplay, I see it as not immersive.
The second missing element is the customization. In Alpha Centauri, you had a workshop and infinite combinations to play with. Granted, most were redundant or silly. But if you wanted a recon speeder with heavy armor and an inferior reactor, you could do it. If you wanted to create a prohibitively expensive airship with maintenance and development costs that were more than your entire energy savings, you could do that too. And yeah, it may have been wasteful, but it sure was fun to take that overdeveloped waste of resources and defeat an entire faction with it alone. Sometimes it was a good strategy to develop a unit solely to convert or combat alien life.
That whole system is gone, replaced with the much more traditional Civ base unit with earned upgrades and faction achievement upgrades. Again, an argument could be made for stream lining the gameplay, but it sure made me feel like I was in charge to design an underarmored (but cheaper) unit just for its police presence capabilites and give it some inferior armor because I liked the color and wasn't in any real danger anyhow.
At any rate, great game if you enjoy Civilization 5, but I'm still waiting for a strategy game to suck me in like Alpha Centauri did.

The lore, the quotes, the ideas in this game are just, amazing. The quotes upon winning a victory are more than worth the effort required to win. And when starting a new game, it really does feel like launching an expedition into the unknown.
The AI is still too chatty, and trade routes are still a pain to manage, and the prosperity tree is really overpowered, but I predict some of these things will be fixed in future patches. The tedious unit upgrade system of Civ V has been removed, and replaced with affinity-based upgrades that are instant and global. The linear tech tree has been replaced with an open tech web that I have yet to explore even halfway after winning two games against the AI. Exploration early game is dramatically improved. There is ample opportunity to use skill and clever decision-making to maximize the number of excavations you can uncover. Exploration continues late into the game as well. The aliens provide a nice enemy to fight in the early game, and quests to kill stations further improve the interactivity of the first hundred turns.
This game is more about improvisation than Civ 5, which was more about planning. There are far fewer wonders and the AI doesn't spam them early game like the Civ 5 AI did. The games are a bit shorter too, where as a game would last 400 turns in Civ V, in this game they last about 300. Overall, I feel this is a great experience and it will only improve over time.

Please do give this game a try. It's free in beta. And who knows? Maybe you'll end up buying it!

I'm always on the outlook for a metroidvania but I was hesitant to download Hollow Knight just because I wasn't too keen on the art-style. Insects and moody darkness? Nah.
Well, that was my mistake. Frankly Hollow Knight is one of the best Metroidania ever made, if not the best. It’s easily better than “Ori” in my opinion. The overall charm and thoughtfulness of the style and artwork grew quickly on me. The world is so well put together and VAST. This game is HUGE. I’ve been ploughing through big unique caverns only to find non-vital trinkets in the end and realizing the whole area is optional.
The gameplay is smooth like a dream. It can be hard, really hard but mostly it just comes down to upgrade and return or learn the enemy’s patterns. This is not a big problem for a seasoned gamer and since the controls are spot on it is rewarding and fun to invest and engage in the game. “Git gud” -sure but odds are that you will curse less than playing any “souls” game.
In conclusion, to my surprise this is the best game I’ve played in ages. GotY in my book (this far). Only gripe I’ve got is that I’m getting closer to the end of the game and it saddens me. Hollow Knight has burrowed itself into my chest and laid its eggs in my heart. May it continue to spawn happiness for some time more.

For me, this was the most anticipated game of the year for me as I am a huge fan of the Civilization series. So I immediately pre-ordered the game and waited in awe of what I would expect from this game. Will this game improve on Civilization V, or will it just be a reskin of it?
So I opened the game and instantly the intro appears before me. The intro creates a suspense as it is the greatest intro I've seen since Uncharted 2: Among Thieves came out. They have kept the menu very simple, ranging from "Other" to "Single-player" as the new planet you are about to enter is spining on its axis in the background.
This year, they have made the seeding interface for the game really simple to navigate. You have four options to pick which include Sponsor (Your leader), Colonists (Your benefits from Science to Culture), Spacecraft (Extra bonus), Cargo (What you want to begin with eg. worker or pioneering technology ) and lastly, the planet you want to choose.
So on my playthrough, I played with the Pan-Asian Cooperative who are really in the form of China, Japan, Korea and Vietnam. To begin with, you are given a explorer (Scout) and a colonist (Settler). When you settle, you can then build your empire from there on. Now what I really liked about Civilization Beyond Earth is the layout and interface they have changed. It is easier to browse with this layout than Civilization V which I had a problem with. The interface may take a while to get used to, but in the end, it is phenomenal how they have layed it out. Also the bright colours for the indicators really stand out and is pleasing to the eye as in Civilization V I felt that the colours were really bland and simple. So this year they have improved on the whole look of the game.
Now for the visuals of the game. They have made some changes in this game than the predecessor. They made changes to the Tech Web, now its not linear as they have made it into a web meaning that you can branch out instead of just following one path. This makes the game unpredictable as certain technology can be vital to victory while some may not prove as compelling.
This leads to the Affinity path which is probably the biggest change in this game. Affinity is path you choose when you arrive on your planet. If you choose certain technology, you have acquired one of the Affinities. The first one is Harmony, this is a path which makes you learn about the aliens and how you can use their technology to your advantage, also its a choice that make you decide if you want to evolve into their way of life. On the other hand, Purity is the exact opposite of Harmony. Its the path that makes you not embrace this new ailen enviroment and instead try and emulate Earth on to this planet. The only way you can do this is by brute force. Lastly, Supremacy is in my opinion, the best of both worlds as they don't want to emulate Earth on this planet, nor do they want to embrace the ailen world. The three Affinities have their own perks which can be used to your advantage but if you want to aim for a certain victory, than you are bounded to pick that Affinity that it is related to.
This leads to the victory conditions you decide to choose. First is Domination, which is to capture all the capitals of the leaders. Second is Emancipation which is available to the Supremacy affinity, the goal of Emancipation is to build a portal back to Earth and send through military troops to emancipate the old humans from the weakness of human flesh. Mechanically, players must build a portal and send through some number of military units until victory is achieved. Then it is Promised Land which is for the Purity affinity, victory requires players to build a portal back to Earth and bring through a number of colonists who must be protected from rival factions. As this occurs late in the game, finding a place to settle new colonists is part of the challenge. Then its Transcendence, which is the victory condition of the Harmony affinity. It calls back to the SMAC ultimate victory condition whereby the players becomes one with the global consciousness of the planet itself. The goal is to build a machine that interfaces with the planet and to defend that machine until victory is achieved. And finally, Contact, which is a signal that is received and has to be decoded, then a device needs to be built to contact the Aliens who sent the signal.
Now for the gameplay, which is the main focus of this review. The gameplay is the same as its predecessor, the only implemented minor changes which aren't really that defining. For example, the new Orbital Layer which can shadow the area surrounding your capital or city, and can be used to attack the enemy, which is a cool feature, and provide extra bonuses to the area you have locked on. It also can be used on another Civ's city if its near you, so that you can spy on them early on the game but it causes a diplomatic arguement with that Civ. The aliens are very annoying when you start the game. They all win in numbers unlike the barabarians who at the start of the game, began with this one or two units to trouble you. But in this game, there are 6 or 7 aliens around the same place, trying to kill you when you just have one offensive unit. This isn't nuisance anymore when your offensive units are upgraded. Although, be careful when your next to a siege worm which can initiate a devastating attack and can eliminate your unit within one turn. However, I managed to defeat one early on as it was near my capital. It took about 7 hits and 3 units attack to just kill it. But, your patience is rewarded with an acheivement which is totally worth the effort...
The difficulty is actually hard on normal considering that none of us know yet on how to use the Tech Web properly. I nearly lost my first game until I researched Nanorobotics to achieve the Transcendence victory. I just about snatched the win, thanks to the Harmony Affinity. If it wasn't for that, I would of been decimated to shreds.
Overall, this game is better than Civilization V by a long shot. The Affinity system and Tech Web saves the game from being just a bit better than Civilization V. But what makes this game not perfect or masterpiece that it should receive, is that the game felt more of a reskin than a completely new game, Its just Civilization V in Space with new features. But don't get me wrong, this game is amazing but lacks the finishing touches it needs. So this game will be deemed as 8.9/10.

I haven't played it much, but I like it. EDIT: And I just wrote a real review.
EDIT 5/27/2017: I guess it's been a while and some people did not like the overused joke, so I have decided to write an actual review.
I came across this game when a friend gifted it to me. I had always seen videos on YouTube such as Frankie or DevilDog, you know all of them I'm sure. Anyways, I'm very happy to have been given the opportunity to experience as much gameplay as I did with that gift. From playing on unmodded servers, such as Takistan Life, Wasteland, Warfare, etc., all the way to very modded servers like Island Life. This is probably the biggest waste of time in my life, but also the one that I'm glad I spent so much of my life playing on and making friends.
Overall the game mechanics are good for a game from 2008. (at least that is my belief .-.) You have all the good old movement keys and shooting keys and some extra things for moving around and stuff. Just about what you can expect from a military sim trying to appeal to normal people. Honestly, for all I heard about the game's controls, it was really nothing hard to learn besides the special keys for life servers and such.
Physics are something that is half good and half bad. Take a wrong step and youre flying down a hill, but I cannot really blame it; it's what made the game extra fun!
I know that writing this review is pretty useless because many of the servers I once loved and spent so much time on are now gone, but I'll talk about those experiences anyways. Some of my favorite moments on this game were spent making friends by just meeting them and experiencing situations in a way that you do not see as much on Arma 3. (or maybe that's just me too .-.) Getting into shootouts, RPing a little traffic stop into something much more, assassinating a VIP and robbing the bank truck and trying to get away in a lada taxi from SWAT. All of these things are what made it one of my favorite games of all time.
Moving away from my personal feelings, (and missing all the fun servers :C) the game was quite revolutionary for me. I had grown up playing Call of Duty and Battlefield and I never knew what real tactics or an open world military experience felt like. Arma 2 really showed me how rewarding it is to take the long path, to actually take your time around solving a situation. I learned that it's not so great to run into a situation because you would be dead from running and the person you were after is perfectly fine. I learned that small assets like a grenade launcher really can be more important than a full on tank. I am sure to many of you that these little things are so obvious, but I did not know that for a long time. I have been in so many tactical situations that even when they did not end well, they were fun.
I've obviously run into a few glitches that made the game less desirable, but in the end it was just part of the game. By the time I was familiar with it, we would just say: "That's Arma" because that's what it was. A lot of people dislike this game for their reasons and that is just how feel about it. Keeping in mind of that, I love this game for all its flaws and faults, and all its fun and fulfillment.

is a damn good game. There's a lot of things to praise, and not a lot of things to complain about. Hollow Knight drips atmosphere and flavor, but doesn't sacrifice solid gameplay at all. Character designs are distinctive in their stark, minimalist design that works. Sound and music are very good as well.
isn't a particularly innovative member of the genre, and instead rests on a bedrock of comfortably proven mechanics from earlier examples of the genre. Throughout the game you'll find the usual- double jumps, dashes, charge-attacks, etc. None of it will feel particularly new, but everything feels
. Unfortunately there were a few bugs during my playthrough, including a really obnoxious one where my character whigged out and slid on its own sideways into a spike-pit during a boss fight over and over again until I died and reset the game.
often gets compared to Dark Souls, and I think that's fair but not entirely accurate. Like its metroidvania origins it takes what worked with what people liked about the lore in souls game, and made it its own. The story is interesting enough to keep you playing and exploring, though it can get frustrating that the map requires you to find an NPC in each area to unlock. Bosses can be hard but fair, attacking in pre-determined patterns, though i found the hardest part of the game was the numerous platforming challenges more often than not. A ton of free DLC bosses and multiple endings encourage additional exploration, which is nice.
For under 20$ I can't help but recommend Hollow Knight.

As someone who loves video games, I love this game. As someone who loves Dark Souls, I love this game even more. Hollow Knight couldn't seem more different from the souls series on the surface, but it manages to capture the essence of the series in an incredibly original way. I wouldn't consider Hollow Knight a "souls-like" because the character uses a sword and the game is hard, but because of the atmosphere of the world, the partially hands-off storytelling, and the ability to choose your own path. I initially thought that the game was fairly linear when I found many paths that were barred off until I discovered something, but several hours into the game, it felt overwhelming how many paths I could choose from and how many things there are to do. The art style is insanely beautiful, the music is incredible, and the gameplay is tight. I honestly can't believe that the devs aren't charging more for this game. Oh, and did I mention, free DLCs.
You don't need to wait for this game to go on sale. Buy it now, you won't be disappointed.

Kairo: A unique four-spice blend of vague pretentiousness and pretentious vagueness.
I didn't exactly have high expectations for Kairo going in, as walking simulator/puzzle games aren't really my cup of tea. No such luck, unfortunately, as the game's minimalist style meant that the majority of the game was a series of isolated floating platforms and empty rooms punctuated by puzzles and tedious drag-face-along-every-wall style collectable hunts.
The Garden segment in particular was a complete pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ as they randomly decided 2/3rds of the way in to completely change how the portals between rooms worked, and I spent a good half an hour wandering around the level hub trying to find the way forward because absolutely no indication was given that the decorative arches scattered around the level were teleporters, given that they weren't every time they had shown up in the set design prior.
I will say this, though: the secret ending ALMOST made up for it all. Almost.

Very simple tower defence. No story, decent graphics. Something best suited for mobile/tablet portable devices and best suited for many short bursts of gameplay (something to pass time while on the train/toilet, etc.).
You have to switch between regular tower placement mode and first person turret mode to do some damage yourself. There are some enemies that your towers won't be able to hit that you have to take care of in first person mode.
Later on there are elemental enemies that you'll want to use the correct elemental towers for.
Gold is pretty easy to come by and there are so many levels that I think you could get very close to unlocking all upgrades by clearing the 45-stage campaign on easy without grinding.
Other random thoughts:
Worth a look if you're need to pass time and want a generic tower defense (though the simple first person mode gives a twist) with plenty of levels to play through. I don't think it's worth it at full price ($9.99) but maybe at mobile prices (~$1-3).

If you are going to get this then do so at the absolute lowest price. It's amateur hour for the most part. Does that offend anyone? I guess people are too involved in the creator's personal life or something. I have no idea. I'm not rating personal drama here. I'm rating the game. And there isn't much here beyond a bare bones approach to the puzzle genre. I still recommend it for super cheap, but just barely compared to the rest of the puzzle genre.
Some of the puzzles are fun, some of the music has a nice ambient tone, and I guess the graphics are okay. But there isn't much here. This is archaic modeling, basic sound loops, and not much else to be quite honest. I mean, I can see why people appreciate indies, I'm just not sure why this game is worth my time. I come back to it and do a bit of a puzzle I guess because the game is in my library. But I'm not sure I will ever complete this game, and I don't really care.
I find the the extras to be tepid, and some of the puzzles are illogical or just downright irritating. This is not Myst, Obduction, Antichamber, or Talos, so don't even start to compare it to those masterpieces. It has nothing on them. This game is like a game some programmer set up in 1999 as a project to test out a graphic engine. It's okay.
But I really cannot 100% recommend stuff like this when there is so much more out there. It's one of those games, because it has a decent tone to it, that I will give a 5.5/10. The reviews are so overwhelmingly positive that Kairo needs a couple more negative interpretations because it doesn't really do anything special to earn those positive reviews. So yes play it and try the game out. But I am giving a thumbs down because this is clearly just a shell of a real, immersive experience.
