I bought this game because I has a coupon and I must say I rather enjoyed it.
Sparkle 2 Evo does heavily favor flOw in mechanics and general design. However, Sparkle 2 does address a few of the issues I had with flOw such as the time it took to eat a group of creatures and the lack of a major change in the appearance of the player creature.
There is one thing I will specifically praise:
-Visuals. The colorful, almost alien world of Sparkle 2 is definitely one of the highlights, creature design is overall just as impressive.The Sparkle's appearance also actively changes based on whichever color of food you focus on in that evolution segment. Even focusing on one color has dramatic changes as the Sparkle starts out as a small larva and eventually develops wings, legs, and assorted appendages.
However, the game is not without its flaws, and they aren't in short supply:
-Above all else, the game is relatively short (easily beaten with 100% in 2-3 hours) so don't expect a particularly engaging tale
-The collision detection is somewhat off and sometimes the passable and impassable barriers were difficult to distinguish.
-The beginning decision, carnivore, herbivore, or omnivore is little more than a "Choose your color" decision and overall has little effect on gameplay as your Sparkle can eat all colors regardless of their current forme.
Overall, Sparkle 2 Evo is a short but enjoyable title that I recommend if you can get it on sale.

The Age of Decande is a top down RPG with isometric battle mechanics, much to the likes of games like the old Fallouts. It excels at what most of the RPGs nowdays try (without success) to portray: a big, live and dynamic world and a actual sense of freedom. I say "actual sense" because in this game you can be almost anything you want to and still be able to go through the main quests and much more. You can be a gigantic brute dumb as a bag of bricks, an agile swordmaster, a sweet-talking merchant sociopath, a silent thief or assasin and even a loremaster seeking knowledge of the past and new experiences. There is depth to all of these choices in narrative and gameplay. To make a good analogy, If Skyrim an ankle-deep ocean this game is a "Mariana's Trench-deep" lake.
Of course, this game has problems. One of them, which is the graphics, are not objectively a problem. Hell, as someone who plays Dwarf Fortress this game's graphics makes me shed a tear of joy. The main problem to me seems the lack of polish, which is understandable considering the gigantic amount of content and the small but ever-persistent to help team of developers. It's also their first RPG, so I'll give Vince and his guys a break. I'm looking forward to throw my money at their future works.

Considering how differently the game plays based on what type of character you choose, I should preface this review by saying that I played as a loremaster on my playthrough (though I plan on replaying the game and trying other roles).
Age of Decadence offers most one of the most unique and interesting settings I've encountered in an RPG. It's a post-apocalyptic world in a Roman & Arabian inspired setting. However, as you explore more of the world and discover some of its long lost secrets, you'll also find elements of fantasy and sci-fi as well. It makes for a strange & interesting mixture but the game manages to pull it off without making the world feel random and incoherent.
In terms of gameplay, if you play the game as non-combat based character, it plays less like a typical CRPG and a lot more like an adventure game with stat-based dialog checks and a heavy emphasis on choices & consequences and non-linear progression.
One of the great things about the game is that there's practically no filler content. There are no tedious slogs through boring dungeons or endless waves of repetitive combat encounters. The game also has a fast travel system that lets you instantly teleport between locations, something I'm not a huge fan of in most RPGs but here it actually works in the game's favor. This results in the game being on the shorter side for this type of game (it will take you about 15 hours on your first playthrough but I can easily see someone finishing the game in around 5 hours on repeat playthroughs). However, considering the game just begs to be replayed multiple times, this is something you'll appreciate.
The biggest issue with AoD is that it doesn't make the greatest first impression. The starting area is visually the least interesting area in the game and a lot of the stuff you do in the starting area is relatively mundane compared to what's in store later in the game. Also, the 3D graphics and top-down viewpoint don't work well together, resulting in you constantly having to rotate the camera. But if you can get past these things, you'll find an incredibly compelling world to explore where you'll go to any length to learn more about its secrets (like sacrificing a whole bunch of slaves!)
Highly recommended for fans of turn-based CRPGs with a heavy emphasis on replayibility & choices and consequences. Actually, due to the variety of playstyles available, even if you're not a fan of turn-based combat, I'd still recommend trying to play it more like an adventure game with a non-combat character just to experience the setting and story (I completed the game without once getting into combat).

As a longtime fan of the Dishonored series, I was greatly looking forward to Death of the Outsider. I was left wanting in terms of the powers, and I can't say I enjoyed the bonecharm-centric gameplay nearly as much as the old rune system. However, this may be in part due to the limited number of powers to begin with. Though many prefer DotO's mana system to the old potion system, I must say that it added to a more fast paced game that I didn't enjoy as much, in combonation with the game's lack of Clean Hands and Ghost achievments.
However, Dishonored's level design continues to impress. The Bank level is particularly fun, and although there is no incentive to play non-lethaly this time around, there are still plenty of options for such a run.
All in all, this is assuredly my least favorite Dishonored title thus far, but at the end of the day, it is still Dishonored. If you enjoyed the first two games, you will enjoy Death of the Outsider as well.

Despite having played 23 hours I still feel I'm in the early stages of the game, and may change my mind as I understand it better, but for the moment I have to recomend this game.
I played this after feeling burned by Hearthstone so comparison is inevitable. It isn't as polished, I've run into bugs with where text is, the campaign broke and asked me to choose decks instead of using the set one for some missions, some card text is misleading (I've seen one card whose 'in play' actions trigger in the command zone and another that doesn't), but none of it is deal breaking. The animated art is of varying quality and some is rather amauterish. Sounds are good, though not up to the high standard of Hearthstone, there seems to be no voice acting outside of the tutorials.
That seemed fairly negative, but now for the good. The simultanous turns work well, preventing constant pauses to ask whether anyone wants to react without leaving one side completely still. The different zones work well into that and add some interesting chance for outplay. The F2P aspect seems pretty good, giving cards or letting them be bought more easily than Hearthstone though as reward cards are untradable and trading bought (whether with earned ingame or paid for currency) cards adds some hassle, especially for low value cards.
EDIT: After some more time with it, and a bit of money on it I still recomend it despite some of my fears coming true. I feel like I cannot put together a good deck for ranked, but am hopeful that with a bit more time cards I get from daily, weekly, xp and IP earning will fix this. Some cards are bit useless or autoinclude, and looking into the history high level play has been dominated by single decks but there is variety lower than that and it appears to be improving a little. Rift runs, the versions of arenas, don't give very good rewards for decent runs, my first was a 3-3 for which I got back 800 of my 1000 IP enterance fee and an uncommon card- which seems OK except I didn't seem to earn IP at the end of matches so in reality lost at least 600 compared to playing normal games for just one uncommon. You can buy your deck at the end, but without massive wins the cost is very high. Doesn't seem worth it IMO.

I received a review copy of this game and was very excited to play it because I adore turn-based role-playing games (RPG), especially ones that take place in a post-apocalyptic setting (ex: Metro, Fallout, and S.T.A.L.K.E.R. franchises). I was thoroughly satisfied with my gameplay experience.
If you like post-apocalyptic settings, turn-based combat, exploring open worlds, dialogue trees, immersive role-playing, and gritty storylines, then you will really enjoy this game. The game takes place in a world where magic and science are relics of the past, and the current populace has resorted to medieval-age weaponry and equipment.
The aesthetics are very good – the amount of detail in the character models and environment is high. Equipping different weapons and armor will change the appearance of your characters – a rather simple feature I love seeing in any game. The sound effects and music are good and add to the hardcore, post-apocalyptic atmosphere. The story is great and each character starts of a bit differently (a la Dragon Age: Origins). I really like how each person you can play as offers a different perspective of the overarching story. For example, if you roll (create) a mercenary, you will be tasked with protecting a merchant – who later gets assassinated. If you roll an assassin, you will be the person doing the dark deed. Decisions are far-reaching in Age of Decadence (AoD), and new missions can open/close as a result of your actions. One of the game’s critical strengths is brutal realism – if you try battling in a 1 versus anything-more-than-1 match, you will most likely die. The game is unforgiving in its realism.
Controls are easy to learn and typical of turn-based strategy games. The tutorials are very helpful and each element of the game (there are many) are explained in detail. The learning curve is minimal to moderate depending on your experience with turn-based strategy game – the most challenging part of AoD is accepting that you will never be a godlike character, and trying to fight an army by yourself will result in your demise.
Gameplay begins with you creating a character, and the role (merchant, assassin, thief) determines your main mission and reputation with the numerous factions in the world. Next, you will be introduced to a set of tutorial missions that will quickly get you accustomed to many relevant mechanics that you will be using to progress. The game emphasizes that you do not always have to resort to violence, and a bit of guile and willpower can help you complete events without bloodshed; many of the side opportunities that result in combat are extremely difficult.
During combat, everything is turn-based, with higher initiative characters moving first – this is why trying to take on a gang by yourself can be near suicide. You can try to move/attack during your turn, and the artificial intelligence (AI) is proficient enough to use advancedtactics against you – like closing the distance if you are a ranged fighter, flanking/surrounding you, and trapping you in place with nets. Fortunately, combat is not the main lure of AoD, as plenty of dialogue events have more depth if you have the associated skills (like being able to bluff your way – with disguise and persuasion – into an enemy camp).
Overall, the gameplay and story are interesting enough to keep you entertained, especially if you are a lover of branching storylines and turn-based strategy in a post-apocalyptic setting. The game is worth trying for both veterans and new people to the genre.
Highly recommend!

Fieldrunners is a grid-based tower defense game where your job is simply to throw in enough defenses to make sure as few (or non) of the enemy units make it across the field. To do this, you are given a variety of towers, from slow to gun, from zapper to artillery, from missile to anti-air. Enemy units comes in various types as well, from weak swarm to heavy crawl to fast charge to air to heavy airships.
As this was originally a mobile game, the graphics are a bit on the simple side, but this doesn't affect the playability. Additional modes with more weapons (flame and other towers), plus other modes adds to replayability if you are not bored to the repetitiveness. As each kill gives you money to buy, but building at the wrong time or wrong lace can be disastrous, this is as much resource management as it is tactics.
While it's not a bad game, it's not necessarily a good game either. There are certainly more colorful, better graphics, more variations, better story, and so on other tower defense games out there. This one is nicely polished, but it's snack... it's not meant to be deep. and for $5.00, it's not expected to be.

"Beware of Wang."
The original 1997 version of this game could be summed up as having the gameplay style of Doom with a character who is like a japanese Duke Nukem. This remake is still that, but with a much better graphics engine and UI overhaul.
You play as Lo Wang (AKA "Mr. Two Million Dollars"), a hitman who is sent to buy an ancient sword, the Nobitsura Kage, from a collector. You're orders are to obtain the sword through an offer of two million dollars or by killing everyone inside the mansion and to steal it. Neither of those options go well when you are captured by the collector with the help of his demon jester friend "Hoji." That doesn't go very well either (at least for them) when demons show up, kill everyone, and a female golem steals the sword and runs off with it. Now, it's time for heads to roll!
This is a fast paced, action FPS where you utilize your skills with the katana, as well as with an array of guns, while empowered with the magic of Ki (pronounced Chee), a mystical power of balance between mind and body and gives you awesome powers to kick some demon butt! You can heal, blast foes with a wave of energy to knock them down, and empower your katana with Ki energy to perform special attacks.
The game is a very well made remake of the original release and pays homage to its retro heritage through easter eggs and secret areas strewn throughout the game's 17 chapters. I'll leave it to you to go find them. I bought this game of sale for $25, and I haven't regretted my purchase. While I may not have purchased it for the full $40, I would say that for fans of these types of games, it's worth a buy.

Death of the Outsider also runs buttery smooth, on my GTX 970 I was getting constant 60+ frames running at high/ultra settings so this game is not the unoptimised mess that was Dishonoured 2. There was one specific area in a bar where I saw frame dips but overall my experience was optimum.
If you liked the previous games, you will probably like this one as well. If you haven't played the previous games, this is a good starter to the series however many of the nuances in the world and story will not hit as hard without the history from the past games. Overall I hope we get more games of this style in this universe because the possibilities are now endless...

Placed in combination with the lovely handrawn artwork + the swirling typography, the game is always atmospheric, with a strong sense of place and wonderment in each level. The levels are enormous, each containing their own secrets, with something new to find each time - one isn't wandering through enemy after enemy with nothing of interest, but that challenge is combined with a new gameplay aspect, a new piece of lore, a new NPC travelling amongst the depths. The writers have created a very unique world with a fantastic design and I'm honestly spellbound.
Combined the challenge of playing this game - with so few lives and protections, and with enemies with far greater health and powers, this game requires you to analyse your oponents and improve your technique in order to win - this game is a fantastic little gem. I've had a great time playing it.

Short Version: This game is good but with some things missing.
I really don't know what I went into this game expecting. I had watched the videos, so I know it played similar to Civ V. But I also knew it would be nothing like Alpha Centauri (which it seems like a lot of people expected for some reason). The Tech Web is a common complaint, but one I feel will lessen as people get used to it. It helps if you have played games with similar Research setups like Endless Space. I didn't have a problem with it myself.
The only real thing that aggrevates me about Beyond Earth is the lack of flare. I don't mean good graphics, it has that. I mean cut scenes and story. The Intro Video is good, but I had already seen it before release. I was expecting some sort of story for the various leaders... nope. Nothing. As many have already reviewed, it makes you not care about the leaders and as such, it loses a lot of the appeal Civ has. My BIGGEST complaint is lack of end game cut scene. There is a lot of build up to the end (I choose Mind Flower) and all I got was a text box saying I had won. REALLY!? That's it? There is more effort put into the minor animations of the scenery than there is in a 20+ turn build up to victory. I love the scenery, don't get me wrong, but when all I get is a note that says "Job well done" its disappointing.
Hopefully future patches, or more likely, expansions will put in some awesome 20 second cutscenes for the various victories, but until then, the game is still fun to play.
UPDATE 2015.01.22 - I haven't played Beyond Earth in awhile so I decided to give it a shot instead of Civ or Endless Legend. I was bored. I still think the game is solid, but I choose a completely random setup to try something new... and it wasn't new. It was the exact same game I had played before. Don't kill aliens, get on everyone's good side, aliens attack me anyway - Gain a ton of money from trade routes (the new "Previous Route" feature was a nice touch), research WAY above everyone else, explore everything, don't care if I win because the ending is boring.
I will still recommend this game, but as has been stated A LOT, don't expect much flare. The units are cool as they upgrade but even they get boring to look at.

While the game takes place in the future, it is essentially a step backwards in some gameplay mechanics. Right off the bat, I'll say if you're a fan of the series, I suggest getting the game. Things are different, and unlike a lot of other reviews made by others I will point out that this isn't like a Civ 5 mod. Like the direction most games seem to go in nowadays, the learning curve has gone down a bit, and the difficulty of higher settings isn't as harsh as before. If you're looking for religions, you will be waiting for a while, as you can only choose 3 specific affinities. On to the good, bad and interesting, starting with the interesting.
INTERESTING:
- The tech web is the most drastic change to the civ series. Instead of going down a path, where everyone eventually gets the same stuff, you get what is the tech web. Everyone starts in the center and has what the devs call "branches" which form the base of the tech web. Each one has it's starting component (IE: Computing, Genetic Design, Alien Sciences). With each branch, it has "leaves", each branch has two or more leaves which are subcategories in the branch limbs (computing>autonomous systems> transcendental math). In each of these branches also holds the affinities of Supremacy, Purity and Harmony. You don't NEED to research each tech in a leaf in order to move on to the next branch.
- Starting placement is in interesting feature. Instead of starting with a settler, you are placed randomly on the map and you choose within a radius of hexes where you want planetfall to happen with your starting city. So you can't go around looking for a great spot to put your picnic basket down and have a nice lunch. Before all that, you do have a chance to choose what sort of goods you bring with you, a tech from the old world, and give your starting area a bit more uniqueness in order to even it out.
- Miasma. Miasma is something essential to those who go under the harmony affinity. It does cause -10 hp to units that stand on the tile, yet they are able to be cleared or harvested with specific units or tech upgrades in the tech web.
- Orbital satellites are an interesting unit. Within the tech web, players can research orbital satellites that either benefit you or make your opponents have a bad time. Ranging from ones that make crops flourish, to removing spies from territory to raining down a good ol' energy storm of death, they are pretty neat.
- Victories. There are 5 different victories: Transcendence - You become one with the indigeonous life on the planet and encounter the brain of the planet). Emancipation - You become borg. Establish a link with Earth and free them from their own individual thought and become part of some collective robotic hive mind. That or you assume direct control. Contact - Through research and exploration you discover a more advanced life that once existed on your new home, and through your advancements in tech, you are able to establish contact with this advanced race of individuals through "the signal". You meet up, have sandwiches and give each other high fives and talk about how you utterly destroyed the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of those Siege Worms, then realize that the aliens left because siege worms are ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s. Domination - You pretty much watched too much Pinky and the Brain as a child and then took over the world. Finally, there is the promised land victory - You and the rest of humanity skip hand in hand through a field of alien flowers (and miasma) into the sunset, and eventually get eaten by siege worms because you didn't research the proper tech to prevent them from eating your men, women, and children, you fool.
GOOD:
- More than just barbarians, the life forms on each planet are a host of bugs and sea creatures. Theres ranged aliens, melee aliens, and the unholy demonic terraspawn that is the Siege Worm. Each land based alien often comes from a hive just like barbarians did. More often than not, the aliens (unless its the siege worm) will not attack you unless provoked.
- Quests! Ah the quest system, it adds a spice to the game. Throughout your playthrough you will encounter failed outposts, fallen rocks, crypts, or scripted quests which offer rewards. Some of these rewards present you with a choice that can alter your civilization with increased resources, a free tech, culture (basically its like a pick your own ancient ruin adventure from previous games).
- The palette of the game is pretty good. Colors are vibrant, and units look neat. You may play on the same map but through the randomization feature, it might look different in color and variety. I'm not talking about a similar feature in previous games that would determine the age of the planet and if it were mountainous or arid, but the look of the planet changes.

BAD:
- With the dying planet that is Earth, people formed factions to go forward into the stars. The amount of leaders you can choose has gone down quite a bit (I'm not including DLC from previous games).
- Amount of specialized units has been changed, while the skins of your units change, it isn't really much of a change considering as your units level up you can only choose between raising their attack by 10% or heal them for 50hp. Its really when you go through the tech web and raise your Supremacy, Purity or Harmony where the changes occur, and they apply to every unit of that type instead of being able to pick and choose each level. Each affinity doesn't really make a huge leap of a difference, only that each affinity gets their own specialized units the further you progress in said affinity, using a specialized resource mainly suited for that path you choose. You can actually do like a cross hybrid of some affinity units, the skin stays that of your main affinity but your upgrade is different than staying true to the course.
-  The end. Maybe this is just my idea of it, but the REAL bad part is that the game gives you absolutely no inclination that a civilization other than yourself is about to achieve victory like previous games. For example, in a previous game of mine, I was in first place thinking I was close to winning (okay I was 12 turns away from it) and another civilization, dwarfed by my superiority as the borg, wins. I get the pop up window of "one...more...turn...".   So really, thats just the bad part. The victories are generally the same from other ones in the series except they each have a story and the name is changed.
- The amount of building and wonders within cities is dumbed down. I spent most of my time pumping out 25% of this or that resource because I had nothing to build. There is a large lack of wonders (which I'm sure will be changed in later dlc) and buildings, and the functionality of these buildings really all do the same. This building increases health of your people, while this building increases production etc. and there are advanced buildings that just do the exact same as the others but have different names, but with a few added mechanics.
- Outposts are the city-states of the future. You can't do anything with them but trade or attack. They don't pump out their own units or require protection, nor do they project their own territory hexes. They are just trading hubs.
- AI personalities in Beyond Earth are dumbed down too. If you pick an affinity not like their own choice, they will more than likely dislike you. This does not mean they will go to war with you, but they will complain to your about your choice every so often. Also, the AI will constantly ask you to help them fight another civilization. I'm not sure if this was on purpose to create an illusion of agression on the new frontier, everything being a land grab, or in the fact the random AI personality in the advanced options is not there.
There you have it, I will update this as time goes, since I know I've missed a few things here and there.

Pros:

✓ Phenomenal world-building. The "infected beetle" theme is pretty novel and most of the areas aren't ones you've seen in other games. The plot isn't spelled out so you have to pick up clues from the environment.
✓ Mood is on-point, especially in Deepnest and the crypt. (Arachnophobes, watch out!)
✓ Impossible depth. Every time I thought I'd gotten to the end, several new areas revealed themselves. 20-30 hours of not even 100% gameplay is not an exaggeration.
✓ The beginning of the game is pretty linear, but at a certain point the world branches out exponentially. A real feast for explorers. Reminds me of La-Mulana in that respect.
✓ A massive variety of enemies. Seemingly every screen has some new creature to interact with.
✓ Soooo many boss battles. Some strange horror is lurking around every corner.
✓ Some novel gameplay ideas, e.g. the Dream Nail that (incidentally) lets you read the thoughts of any creature.
✓ Neat sub-challenges: dream boss battles, ghost fights, the arena, caterpillar collecting, and more.
✓ Excellent orchestral soundtrack, if a bit unusual for the genre. Reminded me of Philip Glass at times.
✓ The game really does feel close to perfect, combat and lore wise, in the last quarter. Sticks in your head!
Cons:
✗ Ugh... the controls. Maybe this is a Mac-exclusive problem, but my d-pad would misfire CONSTANTLY. There are many, many situations in this game where you need to slash directionally or trigger a very specific spell to avoid damage, and it felt like half the time the wrong thing would happen and kill me.
✗ The combat in general is pretty slow, at least until you get some of the sword charms. Combined with the languorous, floaty movement, the game just doesn't feel very kinetic.
✗ The freeze-frame effect when you get hit is infuriating. It's like the game is emphasizing how much you suck. Just flash red and jump back like every other game, PLEASE.
✗ The map system is not very well designed. Having to find the map-maker in every zone is bad enough, but then having each area show up as a solid block instead of just the parts you've visited makes it hard to remember later what you've missed. The compass as a charm is also very frustrating, since it's way too easy to get lost without it but charm slots are too valuable to waste. (I ended up disappointedly leaving it on for most of the game.)
✗ Speaking of which: the charms are interesting, but it feels like most of them are pretty useless, and the ones that aren't are relatively minor stat boosts. How about some sword powerups, e.g. poison or electric slash?
✗ Blocky, maze-like environments. The scenery is very nice but navigation mostly involves jumping around similar-looking blocks and punching through walls to previous areas.
✗ I know it's a staple of the genre, but I'm not a fan of the Shade mechanic. I don't want to have to worry about spending or stashing my Geo before every major battle. At the very least, there should be a quicker way to get back to town or to access the bank. As it is, it's nothing but extra frustration.
Overall: one of the better metroidvanias I've played to be sure, but not without some incredible frustrations. 8.5/10.

This game made me really understand what a love/hate relation truly feels.
I've played dozen of games under my years and childhood and few of the games I've tried have had this much impact as this one! You get to mix pure happiness, enjoyment, awe and excitement with frustration, anger and sheer hat all at once!
It's a game where wherever you go you find something new to explore and marvel while at the same time you need to tread carefully or else you might be squished, pierced, hit or just fall to your death.
It's a game with so much passion for the lore, controls, beautifulness and overall smoothness. A game that moves you with the music, the background, the story and the whole world that you explore and sometimes seems endless.
I've played over 60+ hours while writing this and although you can finish this game in ~20-30 hours there's so much more hidden secrets, achievments, nooks and places to discover that you automatically wants to play this game again, over and over. (With the second run as a steel attempt where if you die the savefile delete itself you can understand the pure sadness and anger I felt when I died +9 hours into the game..)
Some of the bosses and places took me hours to complete and although I'm not usually a angry person I can't remember the last time I felt so frustrated or disapointed when I couln't hit the right buttons properly or overcome the obstacles the game provided.  The gameplay that I've learned for the last hours just wouln't help me overcome the challenges and my control took a few bumps along the ride ;)
Story - Fantastic with so much mystery, characters, dialogue and extra content to find if you are willing to. A linear story but with different paths for you to find out the next clue to unlock new areas.
Gameplay - Controls which responds to your every move instantly and makes the game feels incredible smooth and simple to learn but hard to master.
Music - Every region has it own theme and you really feel the atmospheric tones the game sets. Sad, glad, stressful, harmonical or terrifying tones  makes you remember all the moments you fought in the game.
I try to justify games and not praise them unless their almost perfect and in my opinion THIS is one of the few games that really deserves a high score on every category - and to belive that this game was created by only 3 (!) people just amazes me even more!
For me this game is a solid 9/10 and I will not give it a full score because after finishing the game every other metrovania game (or any other storydriven game for that matter) just feels bleak and empty now :P

I bought this game because I has a coupon and I must say I rather enjoyed it.
Sparkle 2 Evo does heavily favor flOw in mechanics and general design. However, Sparkle 2 does address a few of the issues I had with flOw such as the time it took to eat a group of creatures and the lack of a major change in the appearance of the player creature.
There is one thing I will specifically praise:
-Visuals. The colorful, almost alien world of Sparkle 2 is definitely one of the highlights, creature design is overall just as impressive.The Sparkle's appearance also actively changes based on whichever color of food you focus on in that evolution segment. Even focusing on one color has dramatic changes as the Sparkle starts out as a small larva and eventually develops wings, legs, and assorted appendages.
However, the game is not without its flaws, and they aren't in short supply:
-Above all else, the game is relatively short (easily beaten with 100% in 2-3 hours) so don't expect a particularly engaging tale
-The collision detection is somewhat off and sometimes the passable and impassable barriers were difficult to distinguish.
-The beginning decision, carnivore, herbivore, or omnivore is little more than a "Choose your color" decision and overall has little effect on gameplay as your Sparkle can eat all colors regardless of their current forme.
Overall, Sparkle 2 Evo is a short but enjoyable title that I recommend if you can get it on sale.

I have to say, this game is genius. It manages to utilise the digital medium to a large extent to do what physical card games cannot, such as simultaneous turns. Game balance is pretty good as well.
The game is not pay-to-win, given the large amount of ways one can earn the in-game currency, and the amount of free card drops they give. Additionally, the quality of a card does not scale with rarity; you could win as easily with a deck made without Epics and Legendaries, as a deck filled with them.
Instead of a crafting system, it has a trading system, which in some ways is better than the former. The majority of the community is quite friendly, so feel free to ask if anyone has any spare cards willing to donate.
The 2 main issues are the tendency for bugs to pop up now and then, although the devs are working harder in preventing the game from becoming unplayable, and the relatively small player base, because unfortunately Hearthstone came out at around the same time, and Lightmare didnt do much marketing. Players are steadily increasing though.

Raceroom Racing Experience was my first racing sim.
I noticed R3E when steam presented me an ad for the DTM 1992 pack, featuring the Mercedes 190E. Since my first car was a Mercedes 190E and I've been watching the DTM since 1992 I had to get the game and DTM 1992 pack.
My first steps in the game were kinda rough. I only had an xbox controller and other than that no clue about racing.
I went to the Sector3 forums and got immediate help. Not just the usual Buy a wheel kind of advice. Also advice on how to play with a controller.
Ever since my first experiences with R3E I got Assetto Corsa, Project Cars, iRacing and a wheel.
People generally seem to complain about the payment system. I don't really understand what the problem is. For Assetto Corsa or Project Cars you have to pay about $50 on steam when it's not on sale and then you still have to buy DLC if you want to.
R3E is free to play unlike the other sims. Ok, the free version only comes with a handful of cars and no real life tracks, but you can buy every single track and car individually or in packs. In iRacing you also have to buy cars and tracks individually but on top of that you have to subscribe to use their service.
R3E's multiplayer mode has been suffering in the past, however, it's constantly being improved. My personal experience wasn't very good in the beginning. I had high ping and was constantly ghosting. That issue has been fixed and in the last few online races I haven't had any issues at all.
Raceroom or Sector3 is constantly working on new content, improving the physics, and working on fixing multiplayer issues.
It might not be as shiney as Project Cars is, might not have a multiplayer base like iRacing has, but it has a sound which makes the cars sound like cars, has good physics, force feedback, official licenses for DTM, WTCC, ADAC GT Masters and a growing user and fan base.

Imagine Ace of Spades, except actually improved upon and not turned into a Call of Duty-like game. It features a variety of weapons and interesting mechanics. I think one of the big sellers of the game is its custom weapon and playerskin makers, as well as map making system. The combat is fairly good, though it has room for improvement. I found that matches tend to be rather... Quiet. It felt somewhat isolated when playing with other players. Hopefully the community grows to circumvent this issue.
The loadout system is very interesting. There's a weight (In KG) system that dictates how fast you move. If it's 6 KG, you move pretty fast. If you weigh 10 KG, you'll be slower.
There's weapons like a rifle, a sniper rifle, an assault rifle, an SMG, a shotgun, and a heavy machine gun. They all tend to synergize well with a certain side-arm. Yes, there's more than just your pistol. You're given the choice between choosing a regular pistol, uzi, and a small shotgun with two shells loaded in. Ontop of that, you can also pick your grenade type. It can be a frag grenade, a C4 that can be detonated on command, a claymore that detonates when a player touches its laser, or a freakin' RPG... With only one rocket.
You can also use a block placing tool and a shovel to manipulate the terrain.
A few issues I have encountered is that the game does NOT autosave your custom skins, maps, characters, etc. This means if you accidentally quit, it's gone. Yes, it happened to me when I was least expecting it. Another issue that I feel like only I get annoyed by is making weapon skins. Whenever you make a weapon skin, there's certain blocks that cannot be broken. This is so that you don't make an SMG look like a shotgun. I tend to get a little annoyed with it, but I can understand why it's there. I would like if there was some system that lets you delete those blocks, but on the offset that only you can see the skin. The only other issue is that the community is small. Hopefully by the end of the two week free-to-play event, the community would had grown by then.
Other than that, it's pretty good. Get it if you liked the original Ace of Spades. Cheers for monthly updates!

For those who just wants some keywords, this game encompasses spirit and quality similar to the titles Nox, Arcanum and Fallout1-2. It presents a postapocalyptic world in the past, low magic married with technology and many different main story arcs of different spirit: fighting, deceiving, assassinting, thieving, learning.
I would say that this game leans more towards a RPS, that is a role playing simulation.  It asks you to act rationally, rather than epically. If for instance you choose the path of a warrior, in the start of the game you are simply a mediocore character that knows how to handle a weapon so so. This means that if you are getting into a fight with a thug that you see in the street, you better have some strategy or some plan on how to beat that guy. Otherwise if you just charge on and start slashing at him/her, chances are you will probably die. For this reason the game offers you a wealth of strategies very specific to each class of weapon that you choose. Weapons are no longer about damages and resistances but is about strategies. While directly slashing at a legionnaire with a dagger feels like chipping a wall, if you use the correct strategy and if you are skillful enough then you simply open him up like a can of tuna fish. And also for this reason the game does not randomly throw enemies on your feet. Every enemy you meet have some reason why they are there. They are not like a random encounter, it is you who is more like a random encounter for them. So yes, the game asks you to behave as you would in a real life situation but in a fantastic setting. If you were really a fighter skilled in using a dagger, you must use every bit of your skill in order to survive against an opponent who is a seasoned fighter, otherwise you will die. You must fight like you mean it, not you click it. And combat is of course by no means the only option. This game deserves the title role playing simulation because you can literally finish the game with 0 combat with only speaking your way around, by deceveing or persuading people, by impersonating people, by intimidating people, by forging documents. There are more than atleast 4 different story lines which you can follow, be it a fighting path, an assasinating path, a persuading path, a burglary path or learning the secrets of universe path. In this aspect this game is quite akin to Nox with the exception that it has more than 2 possible different paths that you can choose to finish the game.
It is an ambitious project, quite unique. It is first of its kind in a very long time. With a larger dev team, this game could have been easily the best game of the last decade. But due to time limitations, I think the devs could not give the desired amount of attention to each quest line. The only thing that feels unsatisfactory is the length of the game, it definitely leaves you desiring for more and it definitely could have been much longer had the devs had the right resources. But this game shows that what people would deem as impossible, is indeed possible. And should be pursued.  It is quite a refreshment from the late trend of making games that is guaranteed to never challange the mental capacity of the player. I hope the devs of this game expand their team even more with like minded individuals and makes game on an even grander scale so that my children don't have to suffer games made for morons. Thanks.

While the game takes place in the future, it is essentially a step backwards in some gameplay mechanics. Right off the bat, I'll say if you're a fan of the series, I suggest getting the game. Things are different, and unlike a lot of other reviews made by others I will point out that this isn't like a Civ 5 mod. Like the direction most games seem to go in nowadays, the learning curve has gone down a bit, and the difficulty of higher settings isn't as harsh as before. If you're looking for religions, you will be waiting for a while, as you can only choose 3 specific affinities. On to the good, bad and interesting, starting with the interesting.
INTERESTING:
- The tech web is the most drastic change to the civ series. Instead of going down a path, where everyone eventually gets the same stuff, you get what is the tech web. Everyone starts in the center and has what the devs call "branches" which form the base of the tech web. Each one has it's starting component (IE: Computing, Genetic Design, Alien Sciences). With each branch, it has "leaves", each branch has two or more leaves which are subcategories in the branch limbs (computing>autonomous systems> transcendental math). In each of these branches also holds the affinities of Supremacy, Purity and Harmony. You don't NEED to research each tech in a leaf in order to move on to the next branch.
- Starting placement is in interesting feature. Instead of starting with a settler, you are placed randomly on the map and you choose within a radius of hexes where you want planetfall to happen with your starting city. So you can't go around looking for a great spot to put your picnic basket down and have a nice lunch. Before all that, you do have a chance to choose what sort of goods you bring with you, a tech from the old world, and give your starting area a bit more uniqueness in order to even it out.
- Miasma. Miasma is something essential to those who go under the harmony affinity. It does cause -10 hp to units that stand on the tile, yet they are able to be cleared or harvested with specific units or tech upgrades in the tech web.
- Orbital satellites are an interesting unit. Within the tech web, players can research orbital satellites that either benefit you or make your opponents have a bad time. Ranging from ones that make crops flourish, to removing spies from territory to raining down a good ol' energy storm of death, they are pretty neat.
- Victories. There are 5 different victories: Transcendence - You become one with the indigeonous life on the planet and encounter the brain of the planet). Emancipation - You become borg. Establish a link with Earth and free them from their own individual thought and become part of some collective robotic hive mind. That or you assume direct control. Contact - Through research and exploration you discover a more advanced life that once existed on your new home, and through your advancements in tech, you are able to establish contact with this advanced race of individuals through "the signal". You meet up, have sandwiches and give each other high fives and talk about how you utterly destroyed the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of those Siege Worms, then realize that the aliens left because siege worms are ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s. Domination - You pretty much watched too much Pinky and the Brain as a child and then took over the world. Finally, there is the promised land victory - You and the rest of humanity skip hand in hand through a field of alien flowers (and miasma) into the sunset, and eventually get eaten by siege worms because you didn't research the proper tech to prevent them from eating your men, women, and children, you fool.
GOOD:
- More than just barbarians, the life forms on each planet are a host of bugs and sea creatures. Theres ranged aliens, melee aliens, and the unholy demonic terraspawn that is the Siege Worm. Each land based alien often comes from a hive just like barbarians did. More often than not, the aliens (unless its the siege worm) will not attack you unless provoked.
- Quests! Ah the quest system, it adds a spice to the game. Throughout your playthrough you will encounter failed outposts, fallen rocks, crypts, or scripted quests which offer rewards. Some of these rewards present you with a choice that can alter your civilization with increased resources, a free tech, culture (basically its like a pick your own ancient ruin adventure from previous games).
- The palette of the game is pretty good. Colors are vibrant, and units look neat. You may play on the same map but through the randomization feature, it might look different in color and variety. I'm not talking about a similar feature in previous games that would determine the age of the planet and if it were mountainous or arid, but the look of the planet changes.

BAD:
- With the dying planet that is Earth, people formed factions to go forward into the stars. The amount of leaders you can choose has gone down quite a bit (I'm not including DLC from previous games).
- Amount of specialized units has been changed, while the skins of your units change, it isn't really much of a change considering as your units level up you can only choose between raising their attack by 10% or heal them for 50hp. Its really when you go through the tech web and raise your Supremacy, Purity or Harmony where the changes occur, and they apply to every unit of that type instead of being able to pick and choose each level. Each affinity doesn't really make a huge leap of a difference, only that each affinity gets their own specialized units the further you progress in said affinity, using a specialized resource mainly suited for that path you choose. You can actually do like a cross hybrid of some affinity units, the skin stays that of your main affinity but your upgrade is different than staying true to the course.
-  The end. Maybe this is just my idea of it, but the REAL bad part is that the game gives you absolutely no inclination that a civilization other than yourself is about to achieve victory like previous games. For example, in a previous game of mine, I was in first place thinking I was close to winning (okay I was 12 turns away from it) and another civilization, dwarfed by my superiority as the borg, wins. I get the pop up window of "one...more...turn...".   So really, thats just the bad part. The victories are generally the same from other ones in the series except they each have a story and the name is changed.
- The amount of building and wonders within cities is dumbed down. I spent most of my time pumping out 25% of this or that resource because I had nothing to build. There is a large lack of wonders (which I'm sure will be changed in later dlc) and buildings, and the functionality of these buildings really all do the same. This building increases health of your people, while this building increases production etc. and there are advanced buildings that just do the exact same as the others but have different names, but with a few added mechanics.
- Outposts are the city-states of the future. You can't do anything with them but trade or attack. They don't pump out their own units or require protection, nor do they project their own territory hexes. They are just trading hubs.
- AI personalities in Beyond Earth are dumbed down too. If you pick an affinity not like their own choice, they will more than likely dislike you. This does not mean they will go to war with you, but they will complain to your about your choice every so often. Also, the AI will constantly ask you to help them fight another civilization. I'm not sure if this was on purpose to create an illusion of agression on the new frontier, everything being a land grab, or in the fact the random AI personality in the advanced options is not there.
There you have it, I will update this as time goes, since I know I've missed a few things here and there.

This is about as simple as a puzzle game gets. There are no instructions or notes to read - only those you make yourself.
However, I figured out everything except for the secret ending without any outside help. First, note that it is practically impossible to get truly stuck. Yes, you may be unable to solve a puzzle, but you cannot break anything so that it is unsolvable, and you cannot get trapped anywhere. I encountered no glitches at all, which is definitely a plus.
There is an in-game hints system, which I do recommend using. Be prepared for some backtracking (the game makes this easier later on), and to write down everything. Some things look like puzzles but aren't. Some puzzles can be solved through a simple trial-and-error approach, others require finding the clue or simple logic.
I say "simple", though there are a couple of rather fiendish puzzles in here. Investigate everything. Try everything. Like I said, this game is impossible to break.
There is no save button, the game simply saves when you quit - which made me a little nervous but always worked as intended. There is no way to return to an earlier save, but there is also no reason to want to; unless you want to solve the puzzles again, in which case you should start a new game.
If you like puzzles, don't want your hand held, and find the screenshots intruging, you will likely enjoy Kairo.

This is a pretty tough one to judge. Let me first say that I usually tend to like abstract games, as well as had a few good "walking simulators". However, I don't find Kairo to be one of them.
On the question of whether games can be art, Kairo certainly makes a solid case for a 'yes'. Within the individual levels, there is certainly a sort of surrealistic atmosphere that remains intact despite the used engine (I think unrealED 2.0) itself being pretty outdated at this time.
However, my gripe is mostly that this theme isn't consistent between levels. There is no natural progression or any overarching sentiment that ties the levels together. Each and every one could have been the first, somewhere in the middle or the last one.
And while the atmosphere is okay (even good), the puzzle aspects feel tacked on and added "because it's expected". They are rudimentary dabblings that IMHO doesn't add much. I had no fun in solving them (or attempting to), and frankly found myself bored more than intrigued.
So...end result: perhaps get this if you just want to watch some interesting minimalistic design. But to be honest, that's exactly what the trailers already provide. :\

One of the indie stars of this year, and it sucks it took me this long to get around to reviewing the game. That's what happens when there's so many good games this year, but hey, more about Hollow Knight. Hollow Knights knows the genre like the back of its hand: and knew how to implement a basic combat system that's based on precision and timing perfectly. Enemies can be a challenge until you know how to approach them, and even then you've got to find a way to get in and out without getting hit.  The game does a great job of mixing up enemy patterns and boss challenges to keep combat fresh throughout the game, while not overly complicating it with overly complex mechanics or anything of the like. You have some choices and configurations with your charms: but this game comes down to avoiding enemies and striking at the right time: and I love it for that.
It's all complimented by a lovely presentation that has a LOT of depth when you start looking into its details in both the sound design and the visual presentation. The game does wonders with using only a few select colors at a time, giving a lot of details and life to the characters and giving them a realism that not many indie games can. Yes, realism when it comes to hybrid shadow bug creatures. Again, the devil is always in the details, and my god did Team Cherry nail the details in this game. Granted, I'm one of the only people who think that the music is medium level and not fantastic (it fits the game, it's just something I wouldn't listen outside of the game to), but pretty much everything that the game has to offer presentation wise is something that you're going to want to experience.
As for the story, it's where the game starts to misstep, at least in my eyes. It's very much a story for lore-hoarders out there, as the story is a bit piece meal and requires you to put it together to enjoy it. It's definitely a bit different, and I like what the story sets up and the mysterious world that it built: I just think it's going to be really hit or miss when it comes to the audience that likes/dislikes it.
So yeah, it's a must buy game on my scale, with it showing some of the best understanding of game mechanics and design in the genre that I've seen in a while. Well done Team Cherry, well done.

Amazing game.  Pigeonholing it in a genre like platformer or metroidvania does this game some injustice, as it transcends these categories in my opinion.  Really, this game is a must-have, especially for what I consider its low price.  You're definitely getting value with this purchase.
The game has tight controls in a well-designed and planned environment.  I think the developers created an amzing atmosphere and tone in this haunted and haunting place.  The world is vast and holds many secrets, as well as being able to suit the slow and plodding explorer-types and the speed runner types. As you play through the game, you'll try to put together the story that is Hollow Knight, from the lore left behind and from the monologues that NPCs give.
Much of the game consists of platforming, exploration, and combat.  Mostly, you can navigate your environment with no real issues, but as the game progresses, the platforming becomes a bit more difficult, culminating in the ultimate platforming challenge for those who persist beyond the simple ending.  Honestly, I did not care much for that part, finding it a bit tedious, but it was the price of admission toward unlocking the game's deeper secrets. You'll know what I mean if you find the place!
Exploration was my favorite part, though you may initially be overwhelmed with how huge this world seems.  I know I felt near-frozen at one point, when I found I had created access to some 5 or 6 different zones, each one seemingly huge, each one full of new dangers and secrets.  Further investigation showed that choices were somewhat limited by the necessity for certain abilities, which get unlocked by combat or exploration. However, the world seemed less linear than other games like Hollow Knight, for I ended up progressing via a "non-standard path," in hindsight according to community thinking.
The combat is tough but fair.  Even the regular enemies can present a challenge to the beginner, who has no experience with their patterns.  However, you can defeat each enemy, as they all have some sort of "tell" to their patterns.  Some of the bosses can be extremely difficult, but here too each has his/her own pattern and you should eventually prevail with effort.  Note: the combat is not button-mashing.  There are slight cooldowns after most actions, so timing and precision are required.
The game is not without flaws.  Personally, the game seems vague with some of its mechanics.  Be warned at the onset that you can swing your sword in ANY direction, including down while in midair. This can allow you to pogo off enemies and the destructible environment elements, and will be required in some places. Also, the "save zones" in this game are not always conveniently-placed; you will need to backtrack after deaths many times, especially with bosses.  Few bosses have convenient save locations.
Which brings me to my last gripe: death.  Your death mechanic isn't well-explained, in my opinion; I believe it must be familiar to a mechanic in some other game I hadn't played, so it caught me by surprise.  I lost quite a bit of the game's currency learning how the mechanic works.  When a character dies, it starts back at the nearest save point, which seems easy enough.  The character's "mana" bar (called soul in this game) becomes cracked and caps at 2/3rds of the total capacity, and the character has zero money.  Near where the character died will be a "shade" of your character.  Killing it restores your soul gauge and money.  Dying before reclaiming the soul forfeits whatever money that shade held, as a new shade will be generated at this death spot.  Knowing this going in may save you frustration I experienced.
Further, the shade will not always be at the exact point you died.  The developers didn't necessarily want your shade trapped in areas (such as boss fight areas), forcing you into the fight again before reclaiming your soul gauge and money.   Always check your map for where exactly the shade has spawned before assuming you know its location!  Otherwise, you may end up in fights for which you are unprepared!
Otherwise, I do love this game and enjoyed playing it through.  The free update the developers gave us only sweetened the deal.  Rumors are that another may be forthcoming, allowing us to play the game as different characters.  Just more reason for you to purchase this game yourself!

A VERY fun game. It's like Counter-Strike and Minecraft had a baby (or rather, it's like Ace of Spades when it was still good). You can make your own skin literally block by block (and the skins in this game are VERY detailed because of it), you can even edit the turret and zombie skins (yes, there are zombies in the game!) You can even customize your weapons so they look whatever you want them to look like (though there are some minor restrictions in that field, it's still cool). To top it off, it even has a MAP EDITOR, so you can make whatever kind of map you want, build your own prefabs (structures that you can later use as assets for other maps or share), and pick what modes and weapons you want on the map! You could have snipers only, make it run for Team Deathmatch or CTF, etc.
All in all, this game will never leave you bored of creativity, and it's a really solid game (aside from some minor bugs, but again, MINOR bugs). I fully recommend this game to anyone who wants a nice Minecraft-style shooter with good weapons balance, and a wide variety of creative tools at your disposal. (And if you are wanting to scratch that itch that Ace of Spades used to give you before Jagex screwed it up, this is the game you should get).

To start this review off;
Hollow Knight has left me feeling like I lost more than I gained from it.
The sheer difficulty of some boss battles? Alright, fine, I expected a genuine 2D Dark Souls kinda deal, but the scarcity of safepoints and fast travel systems and the endless back and forth trekking from the safe point halfway across the area to the boss that killed you so you can get your money back from your corpse, and no way to save your progress before the boss room to then get killed again for the billionth time?
Not to mention doing this for pretty much every boss, as you're guaranteed to die a couple of times because you don't recognise the attack pattern yet.
The game is beautiful, don't get me wrong. The atmosphere, the post-apocalyptic premise of a glorious kingdom turned to a crumbling shadow of its former self, the music, the artstyle, the characters.
The bouts of light-hearted humour sprinkled in among the detritus of a fallen society etc. etc.
I love it.
... But not the difficulty or the lack of safepoints.
Another point I wanna bring up; Bugs.
Genuine game bugs. The "This-Should-Not-Happen" type;
Numerous occasions I've had to restart the game because some enemy slapped me back into the previous screen and through the boundaries of the level.
Same happened with an elevator once.
There's reports of the game sometimes outright erasing your saves (though this hasn't happened to me, so I have no way to coroborate this.)
Some miscellaneous thoughts (Things may not seem too coherent here);
I really like exploration, but at some points it becomes tedious backtrekking, again feeding into the problem of a lack of fast travel spots.
And the boss combat? I want to say that combat with regular enemies is an on-point thing, and it is imho.
But the boss battles are downright unfair at points, partially due to the constant need of running all over the place when you've died.
And there's another thing I dislike about the game, even if the intent was well meant.
The Charms system.
Basically, at the start you get three slots (or Notches, as the game calls them) for Charms, this you can expand when you find, earn or buy more.
However, a lot of those Charms take up more than one slot.
And some Charms you need for exploration; The compass, the Collection swarm (If you don't want to run around a single room picking up every little penny on the floor or, god forbid, beyond spikes)
There's upgrades to your blade and magic abilities, like increasing the range of your blade, which should be an upgrade that doesn't require a Charm, but rather going to the guy that is there to
In any case, with the ammount of Charms you need just to get through the areas of the game without getting all too lost with your maps, you might have a spot left for one or two of a few Charmss that can actually improve your abilities.
Again; A well-meant ingame system that is, sadly, poorly implemented as a weak patchwork over a bigger problem.
Final thoughts;
I really want to love this game, I do.
I love so much about it, and although I've listed only a few negative things compared to the many good parts of it, the negative things are hair-pulling, teeth-gritting, pulse-poundingly frustrating.
I've had moments where I spent a session playing this game just to beat one boss, quitting the game soon after because I felt physically exhausted and in pain just from all the stressful retries, desperately keeping my rage contained after each death and endless, ump-tillionth backtrek to the bossroom, only to have my♥♥♥♥♥♥handed to me with a side of cockroach garnish.
I want to love this game, but it's done so much to make it utterly unenjoyable for me.
If you're into Dark Souls-esque difficulty aplied to 2D platformers, Hollow Knight's for you.
If you want to pick it up for a decent challenge as a casual gamer that will leave you fulfilled at the end, buy something else.
In which case I'd suggest
Still hard, but at least I can bring myself to finishing the game without knocking ten years off my life due high blood pressure.
Overall, I wish I could recommend this game, but in all good faith and for your health, I can't, as much as it pains me.

At this time, I just cant give this game a thumbs up.  Between the account creation issues everyone is experiencing, and the actual gameplay itself..  it's just not worth it.
First, the gameplay itself..  it's ok, but it's SERIOUSLY flawed.  The game has no built in "counter" system.  This is rather hard to explain, but the BEST way I can describe it is by telling people to imagine the old Super Nintendo Mario Kart vs a Friend.. the first one to get smacked by a power up... lost.  It's the same here.  The first player to plop out a stupid amount of 10/10+ creatures in rapid succession ... wins.  Period.  There's nothing  you can do about it.  Decks are 1 dimensional this way as well, as there is no point trying to get creative.. just create dozens of mega creatures (Which ANYONE can do... even with the worst possible deck.) and swarm the opponent.  Honestly, it's hard to describe properly unless you experience it for yourself.
Now, in OTHER cardgames, the Matchmaking system will provide a check and balance to this..  not here.  First, you wait an average of 10+ minutes for a single game.. and then it  pairs you (just starting out..) against a guy who's spend $4-500 in cards.  You get smashed in 4 turns.. (about 3-5 minutes.) back into the que for another 10+ minutes.  Repeat.  In fact, in the 8 hours I have played.. I have not played a single other "newbie" player.  Just people with a bunch of gold medals, custom avatars, custom cardbacks, custom battlefields and decks full of Rare powerful cards.  It's INCREDIBLY frustrating, and basically forces you to flush MASSIVE amounts of money to compete.  (Which yes, of course, is a staple to any cardgame.. but here they practically wave a banner at you screaming "BUY CARDS OR YOU'LL NEVER ENJOY THE GAME HAHAHAHAHA!)  The matchmaker woes continued for me as I played the SAME player 4 GAMES in a row.  ..  well.. it TRIED to anyways.. after he completely stomped me in 4 turns the first go round, I didnt waste my time on subsequent attempts, just immediately quit out.
This game, while cute for a VERY short time.. just isnt worth a long term investment.

Age of Decadence is a turn-based RPG set in a post-apocalyptic wasteland that is based on a technologically advanced Roman Empire that suffered a cataclysmic event due to the influence of extra-planar beings.  It's also one of the best games I've played in close to 30 years of gaming.
This game reacts to your choices in a way very few games do.  If you help one noble house, you risk alienating another.  And this has consequences that affect the ending you get, the quests you receive and your path through the game.  All of this adds to replayability and to see the whole game you will have to playthrough multiple times.  Each playthrough should take about 10-20 hours depending on how thorough you are.
This is also a game that gives you multiple options to get through a quest.  One of the early quests in the game gives you the task of investigating an archeological dig that is being conducted by a rival house.  You are given multiple options with how to resolve this quest:
Note that while all of these options are available (and I might have missed a stealth option), not all of these options are available to every character.  The game demands that you specialize and while specialization will open some solutions and quests, it will close others.  For example, the character who specializes in negotiation and diplomatic skills to convince the raiders to attack the dig, will not have the combat skills to fight their way through the guards.  That means that the combat heavy quests, like becoming a gladiator, will be closed to that character.
The combat in this game is fairly challenging.  You will only control one character in the game, although you may have NPC allies, and most of the time you are badly outnumbered.  Combat is turn-based and you action points that you spend for actions like movement and attacking.  Different attacks have different action point costs and you target specific locations for various effects, e.g. you can attack an opponent’s legs to make them easier to hit.  The penalties you impose on your enemies with these attack stack and you also have special attacks with consumable items like nets, flasks of Greek-fire and grenades.  The enemies also have these abilities and they use them fairly effectively.
This means that combat can have a snowball effect, e.g. you might be fighting an opponent who you can defeat quite easily, then they land a lucky leg hit against you, which lets them land another and soon you are defenseless and being torn apart.  While you can use this snowball effect to your advantage, because you are outnumbered it tends to be to your disadvantage more often than not.  This is really a game where one bad roll can lose you the battle, while I like this, I can understand how it would be frustrating to many players.
While the game is well written and offers many paths through the game, there is a sense of diminishing quality as the game progresses.  The second town for example feels very empty compared to the first town, and the game feels a little rushed towards the end.  There are also two stories going on simultaneously, there is a civil war and the exploration of the ruins.  The stories are linked, but the skills you need to explore the ruins might not be the skills your character needs to support their faction in the civil war.  Such a character will end up missing half the game on their playthrough.
The game is also not without some bugs.  While I have not encountered any game-breaking bugs, I have encountered updates to quests that cannot be completed, or characters forgetting some of the things that I have done.  However these bugs are few and far between.
Synopsis: if you liked Fallout 1 and 2, Wasteland 2, or just a good story driven RPG, give this game a try.  However, this is not a game where you can do everything in one playthrough, so be prepared to playthrough it a couple of times if you want the whole story.

I don't normally write reviews, but this game has made me so heated...so...annoyed...and so enraged I just can't help myself.  I bought into the hype and bought the game.  Put plenty of hours into it, and can finally put into words why it drives me insane.
At first I was very impressed with this game, but now the shine has fallen off and I hate it. I hate it a lot, because it has potential but the devs are so smug and proud of the garbage they've created that it will never ever be fixed.
Let me describe a typical scenario in the game to you. You find a library (from another quest) and go there on your first playthrough (at about the 10 hour mark). In the library is a generator, and your current character doesn't have the stats to fix it. "Alright, I'll just make a guy with those stats on the next play through and find out what this is all about," you think. So you make that guy. You play through mostly the same♥♥♥♥♥♥again, for 10 hours with your new guy, and get to the library. You pass the skill check, and find out the generator lets you open a secret door.
So you go through the door and find...nothing. Jack♥♥♥♥♥♥ See there WOULD be something here, but your perception is too low. Perception is decided at character creation, and you can NEVER RAISE IT THROUGH GAMEPLAY. OH, and the only way to know what level you need it at is to read a guide or check online, because the game doesn't tell you...so the surprise is ruined anyways. So now you can either remake AGAIN to try to see this crap, or do what I did and right click -> uninstall.
The game is FULL of multi-level hard gated skill challenges like this, and sometimes it's totally arbitrary. Combat is very RNG and swingy, which makes save scumming a necessity. Basically it's everything that was terrible about old school RPGs coupled with game devs reveling in the "difficulty" of their game. News flash, that's not difficulty. Trial and error requiring hours of investment between each trial isn't difficulty, and it's sure as♥♥♥♥♥♥not fun.
I wish I could have figured this out before spending the time on the game I did so I could refund it. Don't fall for the Steam reviews and the hype. Game is♥♥♥♥♥♥ but it shows at least some twinkling of potential...which is why I'm so upset over it. It should have everything I like, but because of the way it's designed it's hot garbage.

Kairo is as simple as it gets. It is an artsy, abstract and super minimalist walking simulator. I recommend using a guide though. Due to the minimalistic approch of the game, some puzzle are very cryptic.

I've just finished the game after 67 hours (Yeah I took long, I wanted to finish every level perfect, without getting spotted and so on, it's a tradition of mine to finish every Hitman that way). So, Hitman Absolution is a wonderful game, if you like stealth, assassinations and disguises (which I personally love). If you've played Blood Money, which is the last before this one, I can tell you some key differences between the two, both being played on the highest difficulty (altought I didn't make my purist run yet, I've tried it, played on Expert). The good additions to the series are :
-Throwable and usable objects, like bricks, books, you don't throw coins and the best thing is that you can actually throw sharp objects on the enemies' head.
-Contracts mode, where you can make your own contracts, share them with friends and have fun in a variety of ways!
-New moves, now 47 is a "human" being instead being a statue with a gun, you can fight in close quarters combat with different situational weapons or just your bare fists, you can fake surrender when they point a gun at you and then turn the situation around disarming the person stupid enough to get close to you and lastly, you get a "special ability" where you target your enemies in slow mo and then take them out all at once.
The Bad :
-Many scripted events, some patrols start only if you get near an area, some dialogues start when you get in the area, stay clear from a place and the guard supposed to talk with the guy and then move to patrol will never move.
-The maps are somewhat smaller, divided into "levels", which was never really Hitman style, usually they gave you these huge levels, like a sandbox, and tell you "here's your target, now go find an opening to complete the mission in a breathing world, not one who exists only because you are there".
The Questionable :
-Disguises are remade, I personally find them more realistic now, but harder to use them, from afar, people of your same disguise group will start noticing you but nothing serious if you don't stick around too long, but if you're close, you may get spotted being the fact that they recognize their buddies, and since you're "new" they might ask you for I.D.s(oh-oh). Example, Policemen will recognize you if you get too close disguised as a policeman, BUT you have this instinct bar that can let you fool them for some little time, enough to stay clear. The thing about Instinct, especially on higher difficulties, it's that it's kinda precious, so you wanna save it when you really need it. Overall I find it a good system, you're no longer a god when wearing a disguise, of course, a body guard will not recognize a police man, so you're clear with other groups, and different disguises have different "accessible" areas (a policeman shouldn't be let's say in the back stage of a club).
All in all I had really good fun with the campaign and contracts and while there are some cons, mainly the scripted part, where you feel the world revolves around you, I'm not one of those haters telling you to back off from this game. Some steps were made forward, some steps were made backwards, I hope this was a good lesson for everyone and let's hope the next Hitman is even better.

The Colossal Games website doesn't even link to Commando Jack on Steam. (Only iOS and Windows Phone) This tells me they know it doesn't belong here. It's a mobile game that was ported to PC. The only thing added was some basic, not-so-good, keyboard controls.
I can't say very much good about the game for PC. It's low resolution and has a bad aspect ratio for modern PC monitors. There are in-game achievements, but they are not linked to Steam in any way. It has "free coins" in the usual mobile methods of getting other stuff you don't want. It does have free coins that you can hack from the aliens' bank accounts (why would invading aliens have bank accounts on Earth you can hack?), but only one free per day, and a hack you can pay for with in-game coins, but you're more likely to lose coins on that deal.
Some mobile games make the transition to PC just fine and are either as good, or sometimes even better. This is not one of those games. I won't mention titles, but there are even other tower defense games that started on mobile, then got ported to PC, that are far better than this one. Same basic gameplay (without first-person) with better controls, much better graphics, and even the same price.
It does have some decent mechanics as a tower defense game, and the graphics would probably look pretty good on a tablet or smaller screen. The first person view is a nice twist, but other than that, it's basically just a generic tower defense game.
Other than how this game is monetized on mobile, I would suggest you get it there if you really want to try it out, but I can't recommend it on PC, but to be honest, I don't think I could give the mobile version a sincere recommendation either.

-Early game avoids hitting next turn until you get a worker/warrior/explorer like previous civ games, allowing you to pick starting bonus/tech/unit you receive from the start
Cons:
-Aliens are basically stronger barbarians that are basically meaningless in the late game
