I don't normally write reviews, but this game was so amazing I just felt compelled to. This game is a fantastic "metroidvania" style game, that just compelled me to keep playing, exploring, and I couldn't put it down.
Pros
+ The atmosphere is truly fantastic. The small details in each area make the world feel truly alive. The story is minimal, so most of your story is delivered through character's recollection, and the atmosphere. It's done beautifully.
+ The soundtrack compliments each and every zone perfectly. It is a fantastic score, one that you'll never get tired of.
+ The hand drawn graphics are superb. Each area design, monster design, all wonderfully creative and unique, and very enjoyable to look at.
+ The gameplay and design are wonderfully creative. You'll find new items which will invite you to explore old areas in new ways, and the abilities are all intertwined well, with many of their gameplay possibilities explored, pushing you to your limits of what you feel you can do with the abilities.
Cons: While there are only a couple cons, I do feel that they are worth mentioning. However, I don't feel like they detract from how much I loved and enjoyed this game.
- There is a decent amount of backtracking. Fast travel points alleviate this some, but a decent chunk of the game is plotting a quick course back to an area you've played before. However, it will most likely to get something new with a new ability.
- There are a couple strong difficulty spikes, which can be frustrating. One in particular feels a bit out of place with the tone of the rest of the game. Some bosses also seem a fair bit harder than others, so the difficulty can sometimes seem lopsided. Luckily, a lot of these areas are optional it seems.
Overall, this game was an absolutely fantastic experience, one that I wanted to constantly keep playing, and one that part of me hoped wouldn't end. I enjoyed almost every second of it, and I could safely recommend it to anyone even remotely interested in the game at all.

Hollow Knight is a quite easy recommendation, but contrary to what others may say, it is not a flawless experience in my opinion.
Team Cherry's first major game squeezes the positive impressions and respect out of people playing it. You simply cannot ignore the effort and artistry put into the project with enormous scope of many of its aspects. Hollow Knight is probably one of the most sizeable metroidvanias on the market. The world of Hollownest is cohesive and smartly designed with countless different, massively interconnected areas filled to the brim with sidepaths, new enemies and bosses, both mandatory and optional. Developers made a bold move reducing the amount of handholding in the game to bare minimum, maximizing the non-linearity that accentuates the authentic feel of adventure and wonder in this insect populated world.
This game is MASSIVE and to finish all of it for the 100% completion, one needs to dedicate TRIPLE the amount of time required for other popular games on the indie market from the same genre. The ratio of content to the default price point on the store page so off the charts that it makes games like Owlboy faint on the mere thought of it. If that would not be enough for you, Hollow Knight tops everything up with the exceptional artstyle and assets that are so high quality and quantity that they could bankrupt a small animation studio. Taking all of this into the account, you simply cannot refuse to pay respects to the amount of work put here on display. I may have some gripes with the game, but I cannot deny that great work was done here and it absolutely deserves recognition.
you may ask. The problem with Hollow Knight is that it is based on very simple gameplay mechanics that eventually clash with all of those positives I mentioned in the previous paragraph. The gigantic world, tons of side quests and optional attractions end up as a double-edged sword when they are put in the game with basic melee combat and predictable, easily countable upgrades.
To visualize this: your character can use a short range sword, small selection of spells to deal with the enemies and a charm system that can change some gameplay aspects quite a bit. On top of that are crucial to progress ability upgrades that are members of the standard Metroidvania Quad-fecta™ of dash, stomp, wall and double jumps. Unfortunately, It's not enough the carry the game for the extended amounts of time that are required even for simply finishing the game.
Since the upgrades are in humble numbers, they end up being very well hidden in the world. Giving the amount of freedom the game gives, you can end up reaching a roadblock after a roadblock, constantly backtracking in different areas, trying to find yet another undiscovered path that hopefully will mean getting that long desired bit of progress. On itself, the backtracking isn't bad in Hollow Knight, just like aforementioned combat and mechanics. They are absolutely serviceable on their own right, but they aren't unique to make whole experience constantly fresh and exciting.
For more miscellaneous points and observations I would like to make: despite art and animations blowing my mind, the music part of the presentation slightly disappointed me. The compositions are good, but they get repetitive very fast and, surprisingly, they are much better suited to the to out-of-the-game hearing than in game action. I found it very interesting, but it's a study for someone more experienced with creating music and sound design.
As for more positive minor observations: I very much liked the map system in the game. It's very obtuse at first, requiring you to find the special NPC and buying map of the area from him first and then you can only update it with you own findings on save points. Seems crazy, but in addition to freedom of choosing you next destination, this makes new areas a quite a interesting exploration-based challenge that I appreciate and would like to see more in similar games. I would also like to give the shout outs to the extensive and diverse enemy pool inhabiting the underground and friendly NPC designs that are very likeable and well written. All of them add their important brick to creation of distinctive and unique world of bugs to explore.
Concluding my thoughts, I ultimately enjoyed my adventure to the depths of the Hallownest. While I wouldn't put Hollow Knight extremely high on my list of awesome indie sensations, I cannot say that it isn't an experience worth trying out, especially for such a excellent price. If you are not a veteran of the genre and you are not extremely familiar with the conventions, you can grab it right away. Alternatively, if all other metroidvanias you played hold you by hand, telling were to go and what to explore (like Ori and the Blind Forest for example), you can give Hollow Knight a shot as a something more demanding and difficult. Those who beaten countless games in this genre, may still try this out, but be vary that it may not be as amazing as newcomers may tell you.

EDIT: 30APR2015
I am honestly too lazy to write reviews, but this game actually deserves some attention and a larger population.
To begin, I am not a fan of minecraft or any blocky looking games. However, the graphics do not affect the gaming experience whatsoever. Blockstorm feels like a proper FPS game, and the map destruction, and ability to build structures/barriers using blocks provided to all players, result in often unique gameplay every time.
The guns, although a small number, have their own feel and characteristics. Unlike other FPS', Blockstorm is successful at delivering a different combat experience with each weapon. The sniping mechanics were a little difficult to master, but the skill necessary to one-shot kill your enemies is cleverly nerfed with the scope sway.
The maps and game modes seem very appropriate for the price tag, and the map/character editor give you an even bigger bang for your buck.
The player mobility is affected by gear type and weight. This feature encourages the player to think about the weapons and gadgets to carry to be effective in the current combat situation, or to match their playing style.
Blockstorm does have its issues. One of those is the spawn system; the enemy team can overpower your team and spawn kill quite easily. There is a few seconds of invincibility right after spawning, but a skilled spawn killer can ruin your game regardless of this feature.
Overall the game is worth every penny, and a must have indie FPS.
NEW INFO
After giving it some thought I forgot to mention another major issue the game has, and I feel obligated to share this information to avoid encouraging people to make a purchase without this knowledge.
The game, at its current state, does not have a large player population. It can be difficult to get a full server, but most of the time when I have played I actually found one or two servers running with enough players. I do not believe this is an issue with the game itself, but with the lack of popularity. As previously mentioned, the game deserves a larger population.

So, what is Infinity Wars, and why should you try it over any other TCG? First off, let's get this out of the way: the game is pretty complex and your enjoyment of it may vary depending on your TCG experience.
Either way, the basic game mechanics should be familiar: players have a health meter, draw a card each turn, cards have a resource cost, you get 1 resource per turn. (I will not be using the game's own terms because there's no point in doing that if you have never played it).
There are creature cards, spell cards, artifacts and field/location cards, which all work in a similar way to MtG's equivalents.
Cards have attack and defense values, and they do not gain their defense back at the end of the turn. Now, here's the part that sets Infinity Wars apart from others: the zones and simulaneous turns.
Let's start with the zones. You have a Support Zone, a Defense and Assault Zone and a Command Zone.
The Support Zone is where a creature will go if you play it from your hand. Call it summoning sickness if you want, it's what prevents you from playing it on the battlefield right away. You can keep a creature there for as long as you wish, and you can also retire your active creatures there at the start of your turn.
The Assault and Defense zones are where creatures attempt to attack the enemy's health or defend their player respectively. When attacking, you have to go through your enemy's defending creature pool if you are to deal damage to them. If the enemy has 5 creatures and you have 4, no matter their stats, you will not manage to attack his health (assuming all creatures don't have some form of text that changes that).
However, the opposite is not true. If you have one 1/20 creature defending and the enemy attacks with 20 1/1's, everything will die at the end of the turn.
So how does battle work? The answer is pretty simple: it is done automatically. Once you place your creatures on one Zone, they will all attempt to attack or defend starting from the leftmost creature. You can change the order or the Zone during your turn at will, but not after the automated battle has started.
Before I continue, I have to mention that one player gets Initiative each turn alternatively. You will see what that means very soon.
And that's where the simultaneous turns come in. While you were planning your trades to be statistically in your favor, the enemy has been doing the same. When you both click "end planning", spell effects will be triggered first (and, if both players used a spell, the one with the Initiative has his trigger first), and then, if any creatures are left alive, the battle begins.
If you are a little confused by this, don't worry, the battle phase is very easy to figure out once you actually play the game. As a side note, you can get amazing trades if you position any creature that gets buffed correctly. If you have a 4/4 that heals itself for 2 every time it kills something, it can kill an infinite number of 2/2's.
Remember the Support Zone? If you think that an enemy is going to use a spell that kills one or more of your creatures, you can retreat your vunlerable creatures back into it for the turn, and the enemy is going to completely waste his spell.
This creates a lot of "mindgames" during matches, and you feel incredibly satisfied when you manage to outsmart your opponent in such a way.
The Command Zone contains any 3 cards in your deck that are chosen prior to the game's start. They are revealed to both players to make the mechanic more fair. Their cost is the same, but you can put them directly into the Assault or Defense zones without making the transition to the Support Zone. If you do not do that, they stay in the Command Zone. So how can you use that to your advantage? Apart from playing powerful cards quickly, you can let them build up stats if they have a passive ability (+x/+x for every creature that dies, for example) or activate their abilities safely (pay x: deal x damage to a creature, for example).
Finally, there are two more small mechanics that make the gameplay more varied: cards have a Morale cost, which is a secondary resource. When a creature with 2 morale dies, you lose that morale. If you have 0 Morale, you lose the game, exactly like your health. This is useful if you are running a defensive deck that doesn't have much damage, and makes tanking and stalling strategies more viable. The last mechanic is the Trading Post, where you can use your leftover resources to shuffle a card (or your hand, on turn 1), draw a card or increase your max resources by 1. This means that you have always something to do with your resources even with a bad hand, and it also means that some cards can cost more than 9 resources (which is the normal maximum) and have absolutely gamebreaking effects.
Now that we're done with the game's rules, let's talk a little bit about the game itself. It has a client of its own (like LoL, for example) where you can play, buy packs, edit decks, see your achievements and tweak the settings all in one. The client is a little slow, and I have often encountered some bugs if I click things too quickly before they load properly. There are also some minor connectivity problems, but most of the time you are not going to lose any of your progress. My biggest gripe with the UI is the deck builder, it seems really clunky and counter-intuitive to me. Also, more customization options for text size would be welcome.
You can play a wide variety of game modes, ranging from an impressively large campaign with voice acting and a storyline (something a lot of TCG's shy away from) to a ranked mode and a rift run (which is something like random draft, or Arena in Hearthstone). There are some free decks to choose from each week, and some of them can stand on their own against custom decks, which means a newer player can have a shot even if he hasn't accumulated many cards on his own. You can buy packs with in-game money or real money, and the pricing model seems fairly standard. There is also card trading, which is a major plus for me.
There are multiple factions in the game, and their gameplay mechanics and art style are really varied and interesting. All cards also have Purity, which means that you need to have at least x of a certain type of Commander to be able to play them. For example, the most extreme rush cards would require 3 Flame Dawn Commanders. Some of the game's 9 factions include:
War40k-inspired demons that have chaotic and destructive discard and exile effects.
Cold and calculating machines that buff themselves or deal long-range damage.
Anime-style tech angels that fly over your defenses and ascend to higher forms.
Mechanical zombies that eat creatures so you can play them yourself next turn.
The card art is really cool and fitting for each faction's ideals, and so are the animations. Some of them even go as far as telling a small story in a few frames, which really shows the work put into each individual card. Speaking of which, there are a LOT of cards in the game, I am stil discovering new ones every day.
The battlefield in which you play in is 3D rendered, and can even change if you play a Field card.
The music and sound effects are not exactly brilliant, but you will probably not notice them anyway, as anything too distracting would've been detrimental to the game.
As a final thought to close this colossal review, if you are somehow still undecided, I have to say that this game deserves to be tried at least for its attempt to introduce new mechanics to a fairly tired genre. It has MtG's complex mechanics, strategic battles and card trading while also boasting nice visuals and a free-to-play model.
I'm glad I found it, and, even though it's not perfect, I think it deserves way more recognition.

The good additions to the series are :
-Throwable and usable objects, like bricks, books, you don't throw coins and the best thing is that you can actually throw sharp objects on the enemies' head.
-Contracts mode, where you can make your own contracts, share them with friends and have fun in a variety of ways!
-New moves, now 47 is a "human" being instead being a statue with a gun, you can fight in close quarters combat with different situational weapons or just your bare fists, you can fake surrender when they point a gun at you and then turn the situation around disarming the person stupid enough to get close to you and lastly, you get a "special ability" where you target your enemies in slow mo and then take them out all at once.
The Bad :
-Many scripted events, some patrols start only if you get near an area, some dialogues start when you get in the area, stay clear from a place and the guard supposed to talk with the guy and then move to patrol will never move.
-The maps are somewhat smaller, divided into "levels", which was never really Hitman style, usually they gave you these huge levels, like a sandbox, and tell you "here's your target, now go find an opening to complete the mission in a breathing world, not one who exists only because you are there".
The Questionable :
-Disguises are remade, I personally find them more realistic now, but harder to use them, from afar, people of your same disguise group will start noticing you but nothing serious if you don't stick around too long, but if you're close, you may get spotted being the fact that they recognize their buddies, and since you're "new" they might ask you for I.D.s(oh-oh). Example, Policemen will recognize you if you get too close disguised as a policeman, BUT you have this instinct bar that can let you fool them for some little time, enough to stay clear. The thing about Instinct, especially on higher difficulties, it's that it's kinda precious, so you wanna save it when you really need it. Overall I find it a good system, you're no longer a god when wearing a disguise, of course, a body guard will not recognize a police man, so you're clear with other groups, and different disguises have different "accessible" areas (a policeman shouldn't be let's say in the back stage of a club).
All in all I had really good fun with the campaign and contracts and while there are some cons, mainly the scripted part, where you feel the world revolves around you, I'm not one of those haters telling you to back off from this game. Some steps were made forward, some steps were made backwards, I hope this was a good lesson for everyone and let's hope the next Hitman is even better.

I want to recommend and like Age of Decadence... I really do.
But this game has issues. I do not just mean that it has bugs, though it has those.
Its issues are... How best to describe it? Alright... If you like Indie games (and if you don't, you definitely won't like AoD any way, so why even bother looking at reviews for it?) you know that every indie game has some rough edges where you're slightly disappointed at how a little more effort could have made it good, but that you're willing to tolerate because the rest of the game is good and the developer doesn't have a huge budget to work out every kink.
AoD is a game comprised of nothing but those rough edges and that can get really grating. Especially if you've followed the development of this game from the start and know that the reason for this isn't so much lack of budget (though there was never much of a budget) or lack of talent (Vince and co.  are certainly talented) or even bad engine design (Dead State uses the same engine and uses it much better), but simply the fact that with every one of these issues the developers went 'it's good enough for now, we'll smooth it out later' only to never go back and do that because they were busy with the next part.
That doesn't make it a bad game... Just a very rough gem that never ended up getting the polish it needed (and won't in the future). If you're the kind of person who doesn't get a constant sense of 'this could have been better with just a bit more work' or if you're able to enjoy games despite it, AoD is worth getting. If, like me, you're even more bothered by it than the average person, though, avoid this game and the frustration it brings.
At the request of several commenters, here are some examples:
The writing is often far more verbose than needed, while at other times lacking relevant details.
Dialogue options come with heavy consequences without actually having any indication what those consequences are going to be. ("Come into my shop." "Sure" *start inescapable combat that's not winnable for a non-combat built character*)
Equipment isn't balanced. (fully half the armour in the early game doesn't offer enough protection to balance out its penalties and with the exception of throwing weapons, only one or two weapon types per weapon group are worth using)
Location maps frequently only bare a token resemblance to the actual location and navigating locations at the hand of the map is a daunting prospect.
Various conversation bugs (or else design flaws) such as the conversation with the group of refugees at the gate not allowing you to talk to gate guards again.
Various animation glitches, such as an npc moving and attack whilst still in the 'getting choked by a bola' animation.
Mouse develops a mind of its own when not in fullscreen on a 16:10 monitor.
But don't take my word for it: Play the demo. It's a good representation of the game as a whole and all its flaws are not just there because it's a demo. Ask yourself if you enjoyed it enough to be willing to go through 20 hours of that. If you are, buy AoD, if you're not, don't.

Kairo is a slightly flawed gem of a first-person walking and exploration game. It requires a bit of investment to stay interested in the beginning, but if you're into discovery and piecing together parts of a mystery, it eventually rewards that patience.
In the beginning, you appear in Kairo with no explanation of who you are, where you are, what its or your purpose is, and no apparent indication of what you should do next, other than possibly head towards the one visible structure in the distance. Hints as to possible answers to all of those questions gradually unfold as you proceed through the three main levels of the game. Ultimately, the game never concretely answers any of those questions, but gives you enough (especially if you're determined to hunt down and unlock all of its sometimes-obscure riddles) to put together
guess,
interpretation of what you've just been through. For some this may be frustrating, not to know the absolute official canon truth of the matter, but I see it as one of the game's strengths in creating a real sense of mystery. This is not your typical berk-without-a-past-uncovers-his-past story—however much you discover, you remain without a past.
The game suffers from some minor flaws in execution—the occasional video clipping problem in tight spaces, oddly getting stuck on stairs and needing to jump to continue, footstep sounds that are weirdly unsynchronized to your movement—that reflect a slight lack of polish. For me, these minor issues pale in comparison to what the game achieves artistically. It manages to create, through the grand scale of its environments, the use of colour, and its moody, atmospheric soundtrack, a feeling of being very small and alone in an intimidating, unknown world which is somehow broken and needs fixing. The puzzles involved in the fixing range from trivial to frustratingly obscure, but for the impatient there are guides and walkthroughs, and for the determined, there's a great sense of accomplishment in untangling the secret.

I received this game for free, in advance of it's release. This does not influence my opinion of the game.
I wanted to wait to write this review, and give the developer a fair shot at their Early Access game. I'm writing the review now because I think I've seen enough to be impressed. Is the game impressive as I write this, not necessarily (well, I can't make games myself!), but I am impressed at the amount that has changed since I got a key.
I first played the game on March 20th. It was absolutely atrocious. The only thing to do was walk around the forest as a rabbit. There was nothing to eat, nothing to do, no threat of death, and no sound. I saw no point in uploading what I recorded when I played it at this time.
On March 29th I checked back in to see what was going on and give it another shot before it released into Early Access. I'm glad I did! It was clear that there were some marked improvements - I could smell things, I could eat things, and there was sound.
On April 8th, just over a week since I last played, and 4 days after the game released into Early Access, I popped in again. I'm blown away at the updates that have come from this one-person dev team in 9 days. There are more sounds, the AI is aggressive, there's a way for me to unlock the other animals now, I can do a lot of the things the controls suggest I can do, etc.

Is it perfect, no, but do I think it will improve more, absolutely. I will continue to document the development journey as I play the game. I am not affiliated with the developer.
The number one item I am hoping to be implemented soon is normalized sound volumes (the mating sounds etc are VERY loud right now, especially compared to the ambient forest, even when 'out of range' of the mating), and in-game volume controls. There are other things I could mention but they're probably in the works already and are likely minor. This is also probably on the list, but is my one big-ticket wishlist item right now.
EDIT: It's September 2017 now and the game hasn't been updated since ~May 2017.

I've been following Age of Decadence since around 2008 and have been greatly looking forward to playing it. When it comes to video games, I seem to completely share the same opinions and tastes as the lead designer; I'm a bit of a fanboy of his so that only increased my hype.
I've enjoyed playing it, but I do have numerous issues with the game. I completed this game soon after release and was planning to only submit this after having played it several more times and editing in additional thoughts, but I haven't had the time to do that so I'm just going to post this review as is, though I will probably end up adding additional thoughts whenever I get around to playing it more (and I expect my opinion of certain aspects such as the story to improve after spending more time with non-combat characters). The following review might contain minor spoilers.
Story, Writing & Quests
I found the writing and story pretty good but if I'm honest I expected better. Some parts, especially Ganezzar, feel very rushed to me. The ending is unbelievably abrupt and anti-climactic. The choices and consequences weren't as frequent or as important as I expected from Vault 'Choices and Consequences' Dweller; it seems like the biggest choices are right before you see a story slide, which I think should be secondary to in-game effects. If I side with a faction, I want this choice to affect me; perhaps if I betrayed them, they send assassins after me or something in the next town over? Things like that. But the consequences were rarely there from what I could tell.  Half the reputation systems aren't ever checked so are literally pointless and the other half are checked infrequently.
There wasn't as much to do in cities as I would've expected; if combat was as easy as it is in, say, Fallout 1/2, I think the game would go by WAY too quickly. Certainly could've done with more quests and I hope that they add some more in the next 3 months of development.
Combat & Skill system
Many people claim that the combat is too difficult. It's not uncommon for people to struggle to get past the first fight and it's recommended that you restart with different builds until you find the right one. This wasn't necessary for me, and I found every fight apart from two quite manageable. Occasionally there would be a fight that I couldn't do right away, but going away for a bit and doing a few quests to get some skill points and then returning solved that. The only two fights I had severe trouble with were the Aurelian Outpost, which I'm pretty sure wasn't possible with the character build I had at the time, and an end game fight that I'm not sure is even possible for anyone to win.
So overall I thought the difficulty was good. Not too difficult, not too easy. You have to reload regularly but it doesn't get to absurd levels. Even if you do have to reload a bunch of times, it never bothered me much because you're very quickly back into the action. I tend to only get frustrated in games where there's needless tedium, such as in Dark Souls where you have to constantly, needlessly, run back to the challenging part through a bunch of weak enemies, which to me seems as though they might as well give you a maths problem to do before you can get through the fog door. It doesn't add anything.
That said, I was disappointed with the tactical elements. I was playing an assassin with a dagger (speaking of daggers, I got a steel dagger in Teron (I believe) and not ONCE did I ever find an opportunity to upgrade it throughout the rest of the game. Unique and high quality metal shields, hammers and swords coming out my ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, but not a single good dagger. Why?) and high dodge with some critical strike added to the mix. I very rarely found any reason to use anything other than Arterial Strike. As far as I can tell, the only reason to use anything else is if 1) you don't have enough AP (I had 12 AP, so for me that only occurred when I had moved the same turn), 2) the opponent is lightly armoured (so, like, <10% of enemies?) or 3) the opponent was really hard to hit. There wasn't a reason to use other aimed attacks from what I could tell, I tried them out but I'd rather do 10-15 damage than cripple their AP very slightly for a few turns. I thought Aimed: Torso might be useful so 100% of my dagger's damage wouldn't be absorbed like it is with every attack apart from Arterial Strike, but no; that too was much worse than Arterial Strike.
Numerous skills, such as Traps, seem to be really underutilised.
Personally, I think that you get too few civil skill points. Combat skill points are fine, no need to increase those, but as an assassin I would've liked to have been able to have felt like a more competent one who could do more than just fight. I feel like the design limited my character too much and I would've liked to have been decent at Streetwise, Lockpick, Sneak and Impersonate, all skills I'd associate with an assassin. Presumably the reasoning for not giving more is to encourage replaying with other builds, so this is somewhat understandable.
Technical Issues
Graphically the game isn't a champ, but that's no surprise from a small indie team with a low budget. Some areas managed to look quite nice and had a good artistic vision, such as the monastery.
I had dozens of crashes throughout my playthrough, some of which happened JUST as I beat a fight I had been reloading on for awhile, which was rather frustrating. At times the game would randomly decide to crash before I could get to the menu screen over and over, so I had to close Steam and start is as admin before it would work. The next day, that fix didn't work so I had to directly launch AoD.exe as admin.
At one stage, in Ganezzar, the game stopped recognising my saves and started listing them as 'beta saves' and a lot of them got corrupted all of a sudden. That could've been the end of my playthrough right there, but luckily I save like a mad man and had a suitable backup from 20-30 minutes ago that didn't get corrupted.
A few times when starting fights or going into buildings, enemies would be invisible and I had to reload to fix it.
At one stage, I failed a Dexterity check despite having 10 Dexterity.
There were some other really minor niggles like a few typos here and there; surprisingly the very first line spoken to you when you start as an assassin had a typo!
I know how difficult it is to test these things and make the game run well on all systems, so I don't consider these issues much of a big deal.
Conclusion
Overall this review has sounded quite negative, but that's a problem I have where I don't know how to review anything other than by pointing out its flaws and going from there. I enjoyed AoD, I think it's easily the best RPG in years and MUCH better than recent games like Pillars of Eternity. Any fan of classic isometric turn-based CRPGs needs to play this game. I'm really glad that Iron Tower Studio is going to continue making games and I will definitely be buying any of their future games including the upcoming  AoD dungeon crawler.

Hitman: Absolution is definitely a next step in the stealth gaming paradigm. It plays a lot like a mix of Assassin's Creed (focus on blending in and variety of weapons/takedowns) and Batman: Arkham City (movement, controls, use of the environment), but stays true to the classics of the Hitman series: being able to take down targets in multiple ways, disguises, and Agent 47's dedication to higher values in spite of being a cold-blooded murderer.
There are two basic ways to complete the game while trying to complete challenges as well: you can play through the same scene a half-dozen times or more, or you can spend twice as long a playtime scoping out the situation and being sneaky. I have to agree with the other written reviews. The game play feels like a Civilization V reskin.
I originally reocmmended the game, however after some binge playing over the weekend I had to change my mind. I can not recommend the game as a "gotta have/gotta play game." Maybe with a few patches, mods, or expansions it could be a lot better.
The Good
--------------
The satellites are a new thing and give good bonuses for income and defense. Except for attacking cities they become nearly useless because you can not deploy a satellite near an enemy city because they will shoot it down.
The new trade system is nice because it trades basic income instead of commodities. However the trade system requires far too much micromanagement because you have to resend the trade unit every 10 turns. Multiply 1-4 convoys per city by five or six cities and the game quickly becomes a load of unfun and unnecessary clicking.
The espionage system is streamlined and quite nice and balanced. Most games it is far too complicated, resource intensive, or a pain to bother with.
The Bad
---------------
Diplomacy with other leaders is HORRID. There is so much wrong wiht the diplomacy it is not even funny.
- The introduction of favors makes the diplomacy system annoying because all the AI wants to do is trade favors. Favors have little to no value and the AI has endless supply of them.
- When negoiating peace the AI actually used all their strategic resources to negoiate the peace deal which crippled the AI.
- The AI will constantly complain about doing ANYTHING outside your territory and act as if you performed these actions just outside their territory. I founded a new city on the other end of the map from an AI and received a complaint about settling close to their borders.
- AI will not cancel current actions. If you tell the AI "dont settle near me" it will still do it anyways because that order was already made.
- You lack ability to "complain" to the AI for doing things near your borders (yet they can complain to you.)
Then there is a compilation of other stupid annoying things.
- One being you can not build a new army unit if there is an army unit in your city.
- Neutral stations and bases are a joke. The AI will kill them if they get the chance.
- The forced unit upgrades suck. If you want a certain unit form a certain tree then you have to plan carefully what to level and what not to level.
- The limit to a unit only advancing to level three, four with a wonder. Then the difference betwene the levels is barely noticable.
- AI on harder levels is not smarter, it just gets more bonuses.
The Missing
-----------------
Civilization has been around a logn time and has had many features in the past that are not present here.
- Terraforming does not exist. What ever terrain you got you are stuck with. This one one of the best features of Alpha Centuari, the ability to change terrain and evne raise/lower terrain.
- Ocean content is missing. You get to build on the three different resources and that is it. No sea cities, no building in shallow water.
- No Great People. I never cared too much for them, but they did become a used aspect of the game.
If you were hoping that after more than fifteen years you found a sequel/replacement for Alpha Centauri then you are going to be disappointed. You would think after fifteen years they could have done a much better game.

I have a soft spot for tower defense games that stretches all the way back to the glory days of Onslaught 2. Commando Jack is a welcome edition to the genre, putting you (Jack) in the position of ridding some base of some aliens somewhere. You control a large turret from first person perspective, and can swap camera views in order to build your turrets. The game sports a small tutorial at the beginning, but learning becomes very organic (and a lot easier if you're familiar with tower defense games).
Each variation of alien comes with it's own soft spot (a weakness for you to hit with the turret) and there are SEVERAL different variations of small turrets to soften them up before they reach you. Turrets are purchased with in-game currency that is both readily available, and easy to earn. A single successful round will net you about 50,000, with the new turrets typically costing around half of that.
A feature strongly promoted by the game is building a maze of turrets for the aliens to go through. It's a bit remniscient of "Pipe Dream" in that you have a starting point, and want to funnel the aliens through it in a complex path that allows for maximum damage output.
Highly recommend for any fans of tower defense games, as this is a really well thought out title in the genre.

Civ is supposed to be a game about interesting choices. In BE, there are lots of choices, but few are interesting. While BE does have some good new ideas (affinities, tech web, quests, orbital layer), those ideas are implemented in a way that is overall bland and mediocre, and the game just feels flat. 4-5 hours into my first game, I just didn't want to go one more turn.
Example: Affinities. As a tree-hugger, I immediately aimed at the Harmony affinity. Unfortunately, there really wasn't much that was harmonious about it. I tried to avoid the aliens, but they (understandably) objected to my expansion, and regularly attacked my units. Even after I'd achieved level 6 Harmony, they still attacked my units on a regular basis. Sure, I'd picked the quest option that allowed my citizens to adopt alien pets, and I'd constructed all sorts of alien-related buildings in my cities, but all that did was change the numbers (culture mostly). There was no real change in the gameplay. Could I tame alien units, as in Civ 4's Fall from Heaven? No. Could I build special improvements on alien nests? No. Could I get access to a unique luxury resource that I could then trade with other civs? No. Could I live in piece with the native aliens? No. Harmony was a sham.
Example: Tech web. It feels kinda nonsensical. I think that's partly a result of the futuristic setting, where I just don't have a good feeling for what techs mean. In Civ IV/V, I was always excited to learn Gunpowder, or Mining, or whatnot. Techs felt like useful transformative goals. In BE, if I was getting behind on a certain resource, I just clicked the filter button to highlight the techs of interest (e.g. techs that gave culture boosts), and then aimed at the nearest tech of the appropriate type. I imagine this would get better with time. I'd learn what the techs did, and they'd start to have meaning. However, I don't think I'd ever get over the basic problem of banality. Techs allow bigger/better units/buildings/improvements/etc, but they don't really affect the gameplay. There's no sense of growth or expansiveness. For me, the gameplay at hour 5 was just the same as it was at hour 1, and that shouldn't be.
6/10: As a 4x junkie, I'll probably come back to BE from time to time, to scratch the 4x itch, but BE is a poor excuse for a Civ game. Civ is the flagship series of the 4x genre, and BE doesn't deserve the name of Civ.

If I had to sum up my experience with this game in one line, it would have to be this:
"Good, but not as good as it could have been".
Don't get me wrong. The game is fun to play and will likely eat up a lot of my free time. I can certainly recommend it to any fan of the 4X genre.
But throughout it all there's a lingering sense of wasted opportunities.
The orbital layer could have been so much more than a way to add temporary buffs or stationary weapons. The variety of units is tiny compared to any "main" Civ game and even though the existing units look pretty cool and the upgrade paths make for interesting strategic choices, they somehow lack personality.
The AI leaders don't seem to have any personality. A large part of the fun in Civ V was dealing with things like good old blood-crazed Monty and his amazing ham acting. By contrast, the mission sponsors in this game seem...anemic.
And there's only 8 of them, and the differences between them are minimal compared to Civ tradition (or, for that matter, Alpha Centauri).
On top of that, the interface is clunky as hell. I've seen somebody refer to it as Firaxis' Windows 8, and I think it's an apt comparison. They tried some new stuff and it just doesn't work as well as it did.
The affinity mechanic is interesting and adds something new to the standard Civ formula, but it's just a straight progression of bonuses and upgrades with no variety or choices beyond looking for yellow, blue or red in the tech web. What really
work amazingly well is the quests system, particularly in the ability to fine-tune your civ through permanent changes to the way buildings work. That was a stroke of genius and would probably make a nice addition to the next mainline Civ game as well. The larger storyline quests are fun as well, although I've noticed a few annoying bugs with them on my first playthrough.
And while the various victory conditions are interesting (and the victory progress tracker is fairly useful for figuring out which of your competitors you need to stomp on first), the flavor text for it isn't as engaging as it was in Alpha Centauri, and the short static images you get as a "reward" for winning a game are basically a throwback to the "Congrats, you won, back to the main menu" days. There would have been room for a lot more coolness there. Hell, Alpha Centauri's cutscenes were low-res renders that really didn't age well but they've still got more
than what this game offers.
And speaking of style, the narrator's voice in the tech/wonder quotes is a definite step back from AC as well. She's not bad, but she's just one relatively generic voice compared to the different VAs and personalities that game had for its voiceovers.
Again, missed potential. Its absence doesn't make this a bad game, far from it, but it still kinda hurts to see
.
Overall, I still recommend the game, but my recommendation is tinged with a slight hint of regret...

Let's get one thing straight, this is NOT Civilization 5, and this is NOT Alpha Centauri 2. Are they similar in some ways, yes there are some similarities, but directly comparing both is just an exercise in futility. If you are expecting something revolutionary, you might be disappointed. If you are expecting Alpha Centauri 2, you may be disappointed. If you are expecting to lose hours for just one more turn? I recommend this game.
From the get go, the game feels similar, but different at the same time. This familiarity helps while learning the game, but it can also hurt you if you get too comfortable. At the same time, new features like the miasma that is dangerous to your units can force you to change your strategy.
Depending on where you start, you may very well not get to play how you want right away. For some, this might be a drawback, but for me that is part of what a strategy game should be. Your choice of affinity may dictate what resources you need and if none are close by, you may miss out on some unique units. You can still be competitive without that specific resource, so the game never forces you to totally abandon the hope.
The units may feel immediately familiar, but as you upgrade and get farther down the affinity trees, they become better at each tier and "evolve" to match your affinity. At each upgrade, you are presented with 2 choices for their bonus, so that you can edge your units to match your playstyle or preference. A potential downside is that there are less choices overall, yet no unit ever felt "useless".
The AI so far has shown it is smarter in some regards, just how much remains to be seen. I typically fight a lot of wars, so I was pleasantly surprised to see on a few occassions I was not steamrolling the AI. They react to you and one another based on your affinity, so over time your best ally might hate you, or your worst enemy might at least become a decent neighbor.
Most importantly, after finishing my first playthrough, I never felt disappointed about why the developers did x or y. I did have a bunch of "that's awesome" moments however, and was ready to immediately start another game. That is why I recommend Civilization Beyond Earth. It was fun, and I want to play it more.

Aliens, solar collectors, and xenomass mining--not common terms when brought up in a conversation about Civilization games, but Sid Meier's Civilization: Beyond Earth takes this franchise above and, well, "beyond".  In the sixth installment of the Civilization series, experienced veterans will feel right at home, despite the numerous changes in gameplay.
First and foremost, you start by picking one of eight sponsors--or "races"--led by a fancypants CEO, or president, etc, each of whom have their own passive bonuses.  For example: If you choose American Reclamation Corporation (ARC), you will get an increase to spy efficiency, and added intrigue to enemy cities.  If you choose the Pan-Asian Cooperative (PAC), you will receive a bonus for your workers and wonder production.
Next, you choose your colonists, which specialize in something different.  Scientists, not surprisingly, add +2 science to every city, while refugees add +2 food to every city.  Upon choosing that, you go into choosing the spacecraft, and its specialty.  For example, "Lifeform Sensor" perk allows you to view all alien nests on the entire map, while "Retrograde Thrusters" gives you a wider area for choosing where to land your first city.  Just a heads up, these are all just simply passive upgrades, you do NOT have an option to customize or even get an indepth view of your spaceship.
And finally, you choose your spaceship's cargo, which defines what you start with at the beginning of the game.  Hydroponics, for example, allows you to begin your first city with two population, instead of one.  Machinery allows you to begin the game with a worker.
Now that your "team" has been assembled, you choose from many maps, all very similar to former Civlization games, just worded in a different manner--all ranging from single to multiple landmasses, islands, larger oceans, etc.  When first playing the game, even a veteran Civilization player can be quickly overwhelmed by the TONS of resources on the map;  however, most of these are simply basic resources.  The strategic resources will be seen at the top of your map, and they are useful in many ways...from creating specialized buildings, to certain units, to even upgrading them.  The most important resources, however, like ALL Civilization games, will determine your fate.  And those are Energy (equivalent to gold, or money), Culture, Research, and Health (equivalent to "Happiness" in former games).
Virtues are a large part of your game, and mostly how you will customize each game you play to your playstyle.  Virtues are gained through culture, and choosing virtues in the Might, Prosperity, Research, and Industry trees, will help your cities in various ways.  There is a new "synergy bonus" system, that will give you added bonuses depending on how you choose your virtues, giving people lots of customization, whether they want to throw all points into one tree, or disperse them in multiple trees.
Ideologies help you further customize your civilization, and allow you three different unique ways to win the game, depending on which you choose (and you can choose multiples).  One is Harmony, which devotes study and research of alien lifeforms on the planet, and works towards living with them and using them to your advantage.  Another is Purity, which shows that humans are the true power, and all else will fall.  Mankind is the best, and that is the ideals behind that.  The final is Supremacy, which is somewhat of a balance...using genetic coding of alien lifeforms and using cyborgs and robots to do the dirty work.  Each of these adds its own way of winning the game by building a wonder once certain objectives are met.  Other than that, there are a couple other win factors:  Domination, which is to control every player's capital.  And Contact, which forces you to try to decode a signal to transmit back to Earth.
Research is a vital part of your game, no matter how you wish to win the game.  You start in the middle of a VERY LARGE circle of main technologies, and "leaf" technologies that stem below those.  Many will add "affinity" to the ideology listed under the technology, which adds experience to said ideology, giving you upgrades.  For example, by researching Swarm Robotics, you gain Harmony affinity, among other things...that would be enough for Level 1 Harmony, which makes neutral aliens considerably less aggressive towards your units.  By researching, you can find ways to add many different resources, bonuses, tile improvements, ideological units and buildings, to your arsenal, as well as build wonders and work towards your ultimate endgame victory.
Combat is identical to the combat used in Civilization 5, where you have melee and ranged units, and there are no stacking of units.  Combat is crystal clear, and the tooltips adapt to tiles you're on, or research, or virtues, etc.   Units receive promotions, adding simply damage, or consuming the promotion for an instant heal.  Each player is able to upgrade, and even CHANGE their military units by investing in the affinity levels of the ideologies.  A Ranger can become a Striker, which can become a Shredder, for example, and you can add movement over difficult terrain, or perhaps bonus damage to fortified units.
Civilization: Beyond Earth is a fantastic game, and perhaps one of the best of the franchise I have played.  The game is somewhat of a steep learning curve for people not familiar to the series, but the ingame "Civlopedia", your advisors, and all of the tooltips make things incredibly easier to learn.  There are not many things I dislike about the game, except for the fact that there are ONLY eight races, but I suppose that is Sid Meier's way of saying "I want more expansions!".
I strongly recommend this game, unless you can't handle another one of these "JUST ONE MORE TURN!" games in your life.  I rate it a 9.2 out of 10.

Hollow Knight is a sort of metroidvania game where you explore Hollownest and meet it's denizens, all to stop this plague that has broken out.
It's pretty fun. The basic mechanics are simply move and swing, with more complicated mechanics being unlocked that are simply stuff such as "Dash", "Doublejump" and "Magic attacks". This makes the platforming an interesting mix where you unlock simple mechanics and your ability to get around relies on your skill with these simple mechanics. The combat stays pretty consistent through the game, aside from "Charms", which augment how your perform. It adds a nice sense of versatility that you can change as you feel you need.
The music is also god damn amazing, sets a mood. Sadly it isn't as catchy as some other video game OSTs, but it's a nice OST nonetheless.
The story... it's a great and emotional story but you aren't exactly the center of it. The story is more about the world, and you're only a part of it. As you progress you see this world change while you continue on what you're doing. It gives an interesting sense of progression because of this.
Exploration also has a unique idea here. Most areas have numerous ways to get to them depending on what ways you went about unlocking stuff, which I felt was a cool idea for a metroidvania game.
Also for anybody who likes a good challenge in there games, this is definitely a solid call.
That said there are some downsides. On major one being how random the difficulty can be. One moment you can have no  problems with it and the next you'll basically hit a brick wall. It leads to some pacing issues to say the least.
Another issue I found was how arbitrary some progression to get the "true" ending can be. Some parts are obvious but some you need to do some unintuitive interactiosn to get to it, and it definitely cause some confusion because of this.
A lot of side challenges also seem very arbitrary and only there for the sake of tacking on extra challenge. I don't mind stuff like that but it can lead to some challenging aspects of the games to feel very unsatisfying (I'm looking at you, Collesium of Fools, final challenge). Don't get me wrong, if it was obvious that it was just a "Braggin Rights" challenge, I'd be okay with it, however some of these challenges seem like they will give a genuine reward, which leads to a huge let down.
Also, the main collectables don't often have a huge impact on the game, something that metroidvanias are usually very good for. To get a single HP increase, you need 4 "Mask Shards", however there's only a total of 16 in the game. I think you can see why this can become somewhat of a let down.
Great game, but some non-direct progress can definitely feel a bit underwhelming. Strongly recommend to people who like a good metroidvania, but I'll also warn about that this isn't the type of metroidvania where you get "God Mode" as you progress.

I can't believe I had to find this thing out from the Steam reccomendations page. This game should be talked about far more widely. If you enjoy magic or any similar card games, please try this out, it needs far more love. It is free to play, but not pay to win, as a glance at the store can tell you. Finished the entire campaign, which teaches you rather well how to play each faction and various deck strategies they use. The AI opponents are rather dumb once you play against them enough, but PVP is very fun, and not the least bit stressfull. Even if you lose, you still get way more experience and cash than the AI would give you, and its very quick and easy to play the 3 games you need to get the second free card a day. With weekly quests to give you more free cards, and the 2 daily ones having a chance of being anything from a common to an epic (got 2 already this way), it never feels like you're stagnating. You can always build new decks and try new strategies, it doesn't hurt you to lose (in unranked anyway), and if you don't feel like that, there are always the rotating decks to try out, with varying difficulties of use. So to reiterate, if you like card games, play it!

I'm in your base, killen your dudes! This is a very simple and shallow tower defense game with a cartoon look and characters that look straight out of Team Fortress 2. For those that don't know, it has no affiliation with TF2. The game is basically a wide open empty map. You start with a certain amount of cash to buy your towers. You can place these towers anywhere, well almost anywhere. The enemies don't attack, they just run from their starting gate or gates all the way to your base. The game says your base, by base, I assume they mean your gate, because you don't see a base. These are basically open courtyards. If enough enemies get into your base, you'll lose the game. The limit is 20. Each game has at least 100 waves of enemies, so in 30 minutes you can get through 60 or so waves. Its very easy, it just takes a long time to make it through, but luckily when you quit it saves the game.
You're tasked with arranging these towers, making walls of towers, and making a winding path for enemies to follow. Basically make a maze of towers. Can you plug a gap and make an unsolvable puzzle? Nope. The enemies will plod through from left to right. If something blocks their way, they'll path around it, but not intelligently. They'll chose a path that can end up having more of your towers. There is a wide variety of enemies, standard soldiers that look like TF2's soldier character, a heavier character, that looks like TF2's heavy, they'll eventually get jeeps, motorcycles, tanks, helicopters and giant robots. What do they all do? Just walk. Again they don't attack you. The helicopters and planes will at least fly over your towers in a straight line headed for your gates. Your job is to destroy them before they enter your gate. Since every map is just an open courtyard, you can just make the same maze over and over again.
Now that we've covered the enemies, let's talk about the towers, there are a few types of towers based on what mode you're on. Classic mode has only 4 towers on every map. Extended adn endless mode have 6 towers. Gun towers with short range, goo towers, that have a longer range, but will shoot goo to temporarily slow enemies down. Next up there are long range missiles, which are great to have. For the fourth tower in classic mode, there is some sort of electro tower. You don't unlock any new ones. In extended and endless modes, there are flame towers and minimum / maximum ranged giant bomb spitters that are pretty expensive. You can upgrade each and every tower by right clicking it and selecting to upgrade it for a price. Do you want to know which towers do the most damage? The stats are in the help menu item, but they should be hover items that just appear when you go to select which tower you'd like to place. The tower guns turn, but the electro towers don't turn and you'll pay extra for it. You can hit the space bar to pause the game to plop down towers, but there are only two speeds, normal and fast.
The big issue that I have with this game is that its dull. There are far better and deeper tower defense games out there. This game throws 100 waves of enemies at you. It shows you a list of what enemies are coming next and where.... which is good, if I didn't have to click on it to open it up each time I wanted to see the list. Other wave based tower defense games simply have a list of what's next, like how Tetris would show you what block is next. Then the fact that each level / map is 100 waves. That's just far far too many. The game gets dull and boring long before you're done with 100 waves. If you beat 50 waves, then you unlock new maps. But really, the maps are all the same, entrances and an exit. The only difference is how it looks. If you get past 100 waves then it unlocks new modes for the map. The modes are painfully the same, just longer! After 90 waves I didn't even have to touch the keyboard anymore. I just watched the game play itself. There are also three difficulties for each mode if you dare.
When you die or beat a map, it lets you enter a high score with leader boards for your friends and all of Steam. The sad part is the score system is flawed. When you defeat an enemy, you get X amount of points, so if you have a perfect game where you kill everything.... you'll get the same score. It should have been time based. Kill an enemy quickly, get more points. Another problem that I have with the game is the fact to move the map around to see everything, you need to click and drag, but for the most part maps are the size of one screen, so you don't even really need to move the map, except for when a helicopter gets past you.
A lot of people on the forum complain about mouse lag, but really I don't notice it that much, other than in the menu, but its a game breaker for some. Another headache of this game is when you lose, you need to exit out of the level, then play it again, select the level and wait for it to load. A restart button after losing would have been appreciated.
Maybe this is a great mobile game, but for PC and Steam, there are better tower defense games out there. This one is just forcefully long, boring and offers no depth or variety, but at least there are nearly 100 achievements. You can tell how dull the game is when you look at the achievements, there are 85+ easy achievements that only 15% of people have unlocked. Go buy Field Runners 2.
Had its amusing moments, but no longevity. Mind was not blown away by any of it. It's definitely an overhyped experience.

Let me start by saying that Age of Decadence isn't a bad game, at least not as far as I could tell.  It's clearly a game where the developers have put effort into in terms of decisions and consquences.  It's also a game that is exactly as it is advertised: really hard and unforgiving.
That said, I just couldn't get into it Age of Decadence.  I really wanted to enjoy this game, but I guess it's just not the game for me (and, thus, I have a hard time recommending it to others).  While interacting with other characters was fun and I was interested in seeing the impact I could have on the world, the world itself was not particularly interesting or fun.  There is a moment where you feel like the game might encourage and reward exploration, but places outside of the main cities are small and serve little purpose other than their original quests.  It becomes really hard to care about what's going on or your role in it.
The combat system does not make this any easier.  It's a simple (not in a bad way) system, and the game doesn't lie when it says its very difficult.  It is, but not in a good way.  I don't mind difficult games, and I typically feel like greater difficulty enhances the gameplay experience, but the difficulty here feels artificial and forced.  Losing isn't learning experience that helps you figure out a puzzle, it's just frustrating.  And, consquently, winning isn't particularly rewarding either.
Finally, there's not much to say about the story.  It's not bad, but it's not particularly interesting either.
Again, the game isn't bad, but can I honestly recommend it to others?  No, I can't.  I wanted a refund but I was 3 hours over the limit, so I guess this review will have to do.  Thanks Steam!

As a puzzle-lover, I was really looking forward to this game since so many reviews compare it to other games I rather enjoyed, such as Anti-Chamber. However, I only got an hour into this game and was completely bored by it.
The graphics look like they were made in the mid-90s; things like the original Unreal had higher poly counts than this does, and more graphical cohesion. Just about everything is done with blocks and the textures, in-as-much as they are even used, seem to be just tossed on to objects as almost an after-thought. Even "water" is just a bunch of disconnected rectangles. Rooms have seemingly random color selections, with almost everything being very monotone (a violet room, a red room, a grey room, etc.) There is no way to know if the fog means you'll fall, or you can walk on it (like the intro area). In fact, there's no way to know if a block is meant to be walked on or not except to try and see if you go through it or not.
Gameplay is very simplistic. You can move, move faster (run) and jump and that is all of the controls. They have the option to do this all with the mouse, but since the game doesn't bind the mouse cursor, this doesn't work well with my 3 monitor set up since I jump out of the game the next time I click to start walking after turning around.
Like everything else, the puzzles are very minimalistic. The ones I could find were very easy to solve. However, several of them you cannot even tell if they are puzzles or not... or even what you should be doing.
For example, in one (red) room in the second area, there are a bunch of pedestals that make sounds. If you look up, you see stars above them that have lines drawn on them from the last 4 pedestals... and no indication of what you should do. It has a triangle in the middle that is aligned and shaped without matching the stars, so there is no indication which of the many triangle shapes you should be making, or if that is even the correct thing to do. I spent probably 20 minutes making various triangles in that room, to no avail.
In another area, there were what looked like a lot of pods that had screens on them. Most of the screens had static, but one showed a low-res version of what you were seeing, and a couple others showed something else. The significance of this place was totally lost on me.
Also hidden in the game are tiny symbol things you can collect for... no known reason at all. They seem to largely be hidden in various rooms, so trying to collect those turns into the "look very closely at every wall from every angle" sort of thing... it was getting tedious.
The "world" is also very minimal. It is just a bunch of separate "rooms" with portals connecting them. There is no real plot to be found, no idea why any of this exists, who you are supposed to be, or what the point is to "solving" the puzzles. It felt pointless, and not really rewarding for solving anything.

This is not a spiritual successor to Alpha Centauri. This is a thematic re-versioning of Civilization 5, with the same core mechanics, a change of vocabulary here and there, fantastical rather than scientific or philosophical explanations of new technology and research items, less voice over work, less dramatic score, no narrative progression or character progression, no sense of exploring a new planet and building a new civilization etc.
One of the dumbest mistake in the game has to be the setting. You leave earth and resettle in a new solar system in a new planet with EXACTLY the same civilization you left earth in. For example, the factions you are rebuilding in this new planet could be from australia, asia, europe or others (the names has been altered somewhat) segregated by geography on earth rather than idealogy, thus effectively making the backstory something like "earth is decimated and its people has to leave the planet to inhibit a new planet all together even though we are are flying off in different rockets just so we can continue our discord and differences in a the exact same alien planet even though theres clearly many different choice of inhabitable destination..." Why not fly off in ONE rocket, to inhibit a new planet as a HUMAN RACE, while exploring and carving out our SURVIVOR in a new planet with alien intelligent lifeform? Why fly to a new planet just to continue what we are doing on earth? Its like if North Korea says "oh hey, the americans chose THAT planet to settle in. Lets spend billions of dollars, fly light years to that same planet at the risk of our entire nation and continue our nuclear threat on them just to♥♥♥♥♥♥them off for eternity!"
Well, with a flawed logic like that to start off with, I just couldnt get myself to believe that I was humanity's last hope in a new planet, the game falls quite flat in most ways since you are essentially just playing civilization on a new map, with new wordings and the occasional alien lifeforms to battle with. Sure, its still fun as a game but compared to Alpha Centauri, its science fiction story is too stale and common with little new ideas and compared to CIV 5 Brave New World, its just not as robust.
If you look beyond the new sheen and wordings, its really just a gimmicky rehash of CIV 5. If your a REALLY SERIOUS science buff (and not just science FICTION buff), then its really dissapointing because the subject matter intrinsically hold alot of potential for the stephen hawkings kind of cerebral approach. As a narrative its not Asimov, its more like some high school level science fiction story.
I say this with a weary heart, as I grey up playing Civ 1 - 5 and almost all of sid meiers games for the last 25 years and loved every moment of those earlier games....

It is difficult to describe Commando Jack. I suppose the closest game I can equate it with would be Plants Verses Zombies, only with a Military fighting an Alien Invasion twist, multiple boards to play on, and an array of purchasable weaponry, designed to combat various threats. You earn coins by completing levels, which you are graded on similar to the 3 star level grading system on many Facebook games. You can spend those coins upgrading your weapons, to combat various alien threats. Each board has a different layout, and the layout changes and becomes more complicated depending on the difficulty setting you are playing at. The game allows for Easy play, which is fairly straight-forward and is recommended for the casual player, Medium, Hard, and Extreme, for only the most serious of gamers. You are tasked with stopping Alien threats, which come in the form of a portal, after which you must defeat waves of aliens, by placing weapons in strategic places to destroy the aliens as they advance from the portal. This game really took me by surprise and was a lot of fun to play. It is a very inexpensive game, fun, and easy to learn, so I would give it a thumbs up if it sounds like the sort of game you would enjoy. I don't think you will be disappointed.

I unfortunately got this game just days before it went on sale, but at full price it still felt like an amazing deal.  Imagine LSD: Dream Emulator but texturally subdued and transformed into a relatively linear puzzle game, with just a dash of the Assassin's Creed 2 glyph sequences for flavor.
The graphics and designs of the game are unimpressive, but not uninentionally so.  The minimalism of both the visuals and the music create a complexly desolate atmosphere, and, like LSD, the emptiness of the world never comes off as a result of laziness but of tasteful restraint.  It's easy to fill a puzzle game with distracting elements that intrude on the experience as a whole, but it's refreshing to see one that makes an enjoyable experience using only movement controls and basic graphics.
In the vein of games like Fract OSC, Antichamber, The Devil's Tuning Fork, and Against the Wall, this is a game that does not hold the player's hand at any point and does not even provide any form of communication or instruction to the player until the ending, allowing for total uninterrupted exploration, and the game is intuitive enough to keep going at a steady pace regardless.  This makes sense in an internal way, as well, as the game is set in a long abandoned universe in which the player is a complete stranger.
The ending is a bit cheesy and the sequences that reveal the world's story are unoriginal at best.  I was also unimpressed by the various photographs and videos that attempted to connect Kairo to Earth, which appear incessantly throughout the game just incase the message wasn't received the first few times.  In a puzzle game that involves some amount of thought in order to progress, this felt patronizing and undermined the feeling that the game developer trusts the player to make the connections themselves.  The alien and deserted tone of the game was also diminished by this forced message, which left me wishing that the game had remained mysterious and totally detached from the real world like it initially appeared.  It seems as if the game was created first, but in the later stages of development the developer decided to tack a deeper story onto the game, conflicting with the original vision for the project.
Bland connotations aside, I didn't expect to spend nine hours in this game, and it says something about Kairo that I can spend a day backtracking through every area multiple times in order to unlock the achievements and the secret ending and still have fond memories of the experience (even if the secret ending was a massive disappointment).
Ultimately, I would recommend this game if you want something that has a poweful and moving atmosphere, but if you're just looking for a puzzle game then look elsewhere, as the puzzles here aren't as memorable as the overarching experience.

1) по сути, если вы играли в 4 часть, то ничего нового здесь найдете, кроме совершенств и паутины технологий.
2) на момент написания, игра обладает некоторыми серьезными багами (некоторые не могут построить бюро разведки для шпионажа или не прибавляется здоровье от соответствующих зданий), которые портят немного впечатления, т.к. без шпионажа не так уже весело играть, да и вы являетесь легкой добычей денег, колб, технологий и прочего, но надеюсь это быстро пофиксят.
3) довольно тугоумный и пассивный ИИ: играл на высокой сложности (Джемини) и при захвате столицы шпионом, у ИИ было ноль эмоций. Также при атаке на нейтральные аванпосты не имеется никаких защитных мер (тупо не атакуют с города, если только не нападете юнитом ближнего боя).
4) в большей части бесполезные чудеса света, у которых есть более дешевый аналог и то часто у аналога выше показатели.
5) отсутствие религии
6) нельзя бомбануть лонга, спи***в чудо у него из под носа
Из плюсов можно отметить следующее:
1) различные рандомные события (типа летит астероид и нужно решать, что с ним делать; падение спутника; появление храма после бури и т.д.) очень сильно вносят разнообразие в игру и собственно могут устроить небольшое приключение.
2) налиие квестов, которые позволяют также тонко настраивать свою колонию, при этом больше всего доставляют квесты, связанные с рандомными событиями (смотри пункт 1).
3) очень тонкая и гибкая настройка колоний, войск и так далее, которая в корне может поменять стратегию в той или иной игре (правда у юнитов разный только 1 скилл из 2 доступных, насколько я понял). Довольно-таки продуманные совершенства, обладающие своими достоинствами и недостатками.
4) продвинутый шпионаж, позволяющий совершать те или иные действия с городами, получая от этого большую выгоду и что собственно ведет к тому, что нужно уже больше контролировать положение в городе, дабы не стать жертвой воровства денег, науки и т.д.
5) паутина технологий от части напоминает дерево технологий из предыдущих частей, но при этом вы в большинстве случаев будете развиваться по разному, т.к. кому-то нужно одно, другому второе и т.д. и при этом вам необязательно качать, например, ненужное мореплавание, чтобы изучить астрономию для постройки обсерватории.
6) в некоторых ситуациях довольно жесткие инопланетяне, которые могут вас взъерепенить в начале и до середины игры (пока не начнут появляться очки совершенств) и которые могут тупо вас не выпустить из первой колонии, гуляя в окрестностях города.

"Well done on achieving this great feat. You persevered and you triumphed. We hope you enjoyed yourself in the world of Hollow Knight."
I did, I really did. This game does just about everything right.
From a presentation standpoint, the game is pretty much perfect; the animations are beautiful, the environments are gorgeous and varied so the game never feels repetitive, the music is atmospheric and lonely when it needs to be and intense and blood-pumping when it needs to be.
The story is interesting, though it's not something that's at the forefront. A lot of environmental storytelling, a lot of lore that you'll find if you seek it out, but it's never in your face and most of it is quite good, it's just not obvious about it. But that's fine, because the focus is clearly meant to be on the gameplay. Speaking of which...
The gameplay hits pretty much all the right notes. Learning enemy movements and how they're meant to work alongside your own is the key to getting good at this game; the movement feels nice and the combat is simple, but the enemies are complex enough to keep you on your toes (especially the bosses). The charm system is great, too, allowing for a wide variety of experimentation and seeing what works best for you.
That being said, the majority of the game I wouldn't say is difficult. There are a few curves here and there, but there really aren't any massive off-putting spikes in difficulty except for one, which I'll get to in a moment. Aside from that, the game hit just the right balance for me most of the time; never too easy to be boring, and almost never too hard to be off-putting.
There's one area I need to talk about, though, and that's
For all of my gripes with that, though, this game was still overwhelmingly a blast for me, and a real reminder of what a great metroidvania feels like. I got through 95% of the game and spent around 38 hours in it according to the in-game timer. And for just $15, that is an absolute steal.
9/10, absolutely worth playing.
