Summary: Orcs Must Die with experience and loot.
Multiplayer: up to 8
Completion: 20 hrs
Cards: No
Cloud: No (but has online-mode saves)
Dungeon Defenders plays out much like Orcs Must Die, where you attack waves of enemies emerging from several entrances by using towers, traps, minions, or just plain weapons. The game supports up to quite a few players, though four players is a safe bet for most maps.
There's a lot to like about the game. It has a fairly good progression, as level-ups and items felt like large improvements in the early game. As you head towards the endgame though, item upgrades become much less frequent, and you may struggle on a number of later hardcore maps. Notably... there's a distinct lack of a proper tutorial. It does not teach you things like what your health bar and mana bar is. It does not teach you how to equip things. It does not teach you about sets. It does not teach you about upgrading items.
Interestingly, the game allows you to switch heroes on the fly between rounds. Thus you can benefit from defenses another character you have, and then switch back to the one you want to level. It's an interesting idea, as it greatly simplifies the need for grinding, but at the same time, the early charm is entirely lost because you are packing high-powered defenses on a low level character and can just afk to victory with minimal strategy. Shrug. It's hard to say if the benefits outweigh the downsides.
Each map allots you and your party a shared Defense Unit (DU) pool with which to summon  your defenses. I kind of wish there was a slight change to DU. I'd like it so that every character had a minimum DU devoted to themselves, and the rest would be a shared DU. That way all players would have at least some use for tower stats.
Tower placement can get a but clumsy, since you can only summon within a short radius of your position. If the tower is too close to certain things, then you can't place it. All too often I find myself needing to cancel, reposition, and try to summon again, which can be problematic in combat when mobs may be attacking you. Unlike OMD there is no means to shape your enemy paths, but you can place structures that enemies will attack.
The game likes to throw loot at you. A lot of it. You'll be seeing items left and right, polluting the entire field, and you won't know what to grab. Fortunately the game includes a rudimentary system that puts an indicator on items it thinks may be an upgrade for you, however more often than not the indicator is completely wrong. All the items you loot go to your item bank, which unfortunately is very poorly managed. You can create your own folders, but doing so shrinks your items visible per page. I would have really liked a way to sort and reorder items myself. At this point I would settle for nothing but a columns of text instead of the gigantic 12 icons at a time.
This game offers one very nice feature most other games in this genre do not - the ability to change camera angles. By zooming in and out with the mouse wheel you can go seamlessly into first person, over-the-shoulder, and overhead views. I can't tell how much I wanted a feature like this in other games! There's even a 4th sort of view if you play as the Summoner, who can enter an RTS-like mode, which is even better. One handy touch is that if you die, especially in hardcore, you are allowed to free-roam the map while dead. It's nice to see the outside environment and to scout for other party members while in this mode.
Dungeon Defenders offers five difficulties per map. You can probably ignore the first few, as those are almost always too easy. However, the game could probably use another difficulty between insane and nightmare. There is a sudden spike when you hit nightmare as you fight enemies with considerably more health, and the ability to air drop from anywhere. I had a lot of fun playing through the maps with some friends when the maps would just barely kick our butt, typically beating us on the last wave. Eventually we got our act together and can blow through almost everything, but the process of discovery was great. With the exception of one map, the game seems to run pretty well in multiplayer with minimal lag, so thumbs up for that!
I am impressed at the variety of play modes the game offers. It goes well beyond the standard tower defense, including modes such as PvP, run a gauntlet, escort the crystal, and more. I much enjoyed the journey to reach high levels. It's a shame I can't really experience that again. It's a great multiplayer experience, I'll grant it that. I give Dungeon Defenders a 8.5/10, mainly knocking points for the Item Bank that is incredibly tedious to sift through. If you like tower defense + shooters, this game will serve you well.

This game's very highly rated, and it's definitely good. However it does have one critial flaw; No difficulty slider. Simply put, Some of the game's bosses are too difficult to be fun. To progress further in my play-through I'll need to endure hours of frustration enducing repetition facing off against either Soul Master or the Mantis Queens. I've already lost to each at least 10 times. I'm sure If I were determined enough I could defeat them. But it's just not worth the irritation borne of the ineffectual attempts it'll take to continue. Not even Bloodborne annoyed me this much. Perhaps my gamepad controls are too loose. I'm using a Logitech F310 with an extension cord. There's a slight delay from button-press to on-screen reaction. It's almost undetectable but it's there. Enough that I can't always dodge an incoming attack in time or land a hit reliably enough. Or perhaps I'm just a mite too sloshed to play this game well. Every time I loose, I have to trek all the way back to said boss to retreive my regret. It'd probably be bearable if it weren't for the fact that the save benches are at least 10 minutes away. By the time I get back to the boss I'm already irked by the delay and the fact that I never manage to get there at optimal health. Visually the game looks good. The map layout is intriguing. But the boss difficulty ruins it. I think part of the problem might be that they've tweaked the timing for consoles; where everyone has the same exact hardware. But on PC that's never the case. Every PC game needs a difficulty slider to help compensate for variations in hardware, and in my case player inebriation. This game lacks that. For these reason I can't recommend it. It's definitely a good game. But if you're like me and you just want to kick-back and enjoy a mildly challenging adventure while pleasantly intoxicated, this isn't the game for you.

Fieldrunners was a great iOS tower defense game (although probably the difficulty could use tweaking on some of the later maps), but it's hard to recommend the Steam version for the following reasons:
1. The price was always ridiculed on iOS, especially when the devs refused to ever bring it down, even during holiday sales, despite the fact the extra maps were actually at one point DLC that had to be purchased.  Even including the DLC levels, $10 seems a bit off for a bare-bones PC version that doesn't function properly (more on that later) and has been a mega-success for going on 4 years or so now.   This barely rose to the $10 level on iOS, and it's not remotely a $10 on PC in this condition.
2. The Steam version has a horrendous bug/glitch that the developers have yet to fix where mouse input becomes severely lagged after the second time you play it.  In other words, the first time you play it's fine, but after that the game is unplayable with virtually any form of mouse.  Touchpads on laptops tend to work, but some bizarre problem with the port causes serious issues with mice.  As of my writing this, this is not fixed.  The glitch does not seem to effect everyone, but it effects enough people that it's unfortunate it is not mentioned in the game description.
Fieldrunners is a great, basic tower defense game, but this port is really shoddy and the shoulder shrugging response on fixing the bugs frankly makes me regret ever supporting these devs back before they made their fortunes on the Fieldrunners IP.

Excellent game. Very rich, deep, immersive world. Despite the graphical limitations (not a complaint, btw, I love them the way they are), the world feels very alive and encompassing. The excellent writing, both narrative and dialogue, fuel this feature and set this game apart from so many on the market today. The learning curve is fairly steep and most of the negative reviews I have read stem from that fact. This isn't a Bethesda sandbox. Your character cannot and will never be able to 'do everything' at once. Initially, you will only do a very few things very well. As you learn the game and the story, you'll be able to expand a bit on subsequent playthroughs and be more multi-faceted.
There is an incredible story here, with dozens of smaller, elegantly-interconnected side stories woven throughout. Perhaps the most satsifying aspect of the experience is discovering different angles to each story depending on which faction you ally with.  It is really fascinating to worry your mind at a plot 'hole' when playing an Imperial soldier only to have it fully explained much later on during  your 40 Thieves playthrough.  Very smoothly put together narrative running behind the scenes here.
If there's one complaint, I suppose it would be the 'linear' nature of the game. Personally, I don't mind it, as I understand its necessity in order to tell a cohesive, meaningful story. But some people probably will mind it, so I mention it here. There are MANY different paths through the game and it will require several playthroughs to see them all. But once you've chosen your 'path' for a particular playthrough, that path generally runs on the rails until it completes.  Which isn't to say that you can't change paths partway through, if you're good enough to survive betraying your masters. ;) Each path also has significant choices you can make which will dramatically affect the life of your character and, in rare cases, the fate of the faction you serve or the world as a whole.  So while there is some linearity in order to maintain the story, you do have a reasonable measure of liberty within that structure.
A truly great game here. A masterwork, in my estimation. I've had more fun with this title than I have with most in the past few seasons.  I hope that those of you who follow my recommendation and take a chance on it find the experience as rich and rewarding as I have.

- Beautiful visuals and sound design, just like Dishonored 2
- Excellent music, just like Dishonored 2
- Regenerating mana, not like Dishonored 2 but a very welcome change
- Great powers - Displace is awesome, Foresight is awesome, Semblance is situational but cool
- One mission in particular (
) is absolutely exceptional
- Michael Madsen's voice acting
CONS:
- It's too short. I know this was never sold as a full Dishonored 2 sequel, but just five missions is still underwhelming
- Lack of originality. Missions 2 and 3 take place in the same areas of the city, mission 4 takes place in a location from Dishonored 2. The levels are changed somewhat between iterations, but it's still disappointing, especially considering the underwhelming length of the game as a whole
- Lack of powers. While the powers we did get are cool, we only have three compared to six in the other Dishonored games. Also, there's no runes to upgrade the powers with. The only magical enhancement comes from bonecharms, which seriously decreases power diversity and replayability.
- No chaos system. Seriously, one of the core unique traits of the Dishonored games that gave so much depth and replayability, and they axed it for no apparent reason.
- The story is APPALLING. Seriously, it's miles worse than Dishonored 2's, and Dishonored 2's wasn't even very good. The whole plot is just finding out how to kill the Outsider, and then killing the Outsider. No subplots, no nuances, no nothing. There aren't even any supporting characters. In previous Dishonored games, we had people like Havelock, Piero, Sokolov, Emily, Meagan -  whereas here Billie (the player) and Daud are the only two.
- Where were all the assassination targets? In the five missions, there is literally only one target -  the Outsider. The first mission is spent rescuing Daud, the second third and fourth are spent gathering information and relics, and only the fifth mission is actually spent going after a target. Sure, there are optional people to kill - "key figures" - but it's not really any compensation for the lack of targets. Dishonored and Dishonored 2 both had six targets each - how come DoTO, a game slightly over half the length of those two, only has one?
-
OVERALL: I wish Steam had a "meh" button rather than just yes and no. If you like Dishonored or stealth-action games like me, you'll probably either like or tolerate it, so I'm going to give it a yes. However, the numerous and fundamental flaws will stop a lot of people getting enthusiastic about it, including myself. This is a game that many will like, and equally many will dislike, but almost no-one will love.

Commando Jack is an android port of the same game now on steam.
There is barely any story at all. Basically, aliens have invaded earth and it's up to Commando Jack to stop them.
Gameplay is a mix of tower defence and first person shooting. Each level starts you off on one side of the map with a turret, trying to defend against the alien invasion. You have limited time at the start to build towers and set traps for defences before the waves begin. Besides building defences you can also switch to your main turret and shoot the aliens via first-person. Enemy waves get more numerous and stronger as the level progresses. The aliens will move towards you main turret and try to destroy it, which results in a gameover should it happen. After each level, you will earn up to 3 stars depending on whether the enemy was able to attack your main turret or not. You also earn credits, which are used to buy/upgrade turrets at the store before each level. There are variety of aliens including snipers, tanks standards and elemental which all have certain strengths and weaknesses. A variety of turrets are also available including machine gun, rockets, mines, lasers and sand bags. One of the problems I found was that when you upgrade turrets' you don't know how the turret was improved as you don't get to see any statistics.
Graphics aren't great. The android history, shows off on the low detailed models for guns, environment, turrets (everything really).
Sound effects are quite poor. Weapons sounds are basic. Background music is forgettable. There is not voice acting in the game.
Unless this game is highly discounted, I recommend that you stay clear of this game. It's not that this game is terrible, its just that there are dozens of games which do a better job at representing the 'tower defence genre' and cheaper too.

CIV 5 dumbed down even further. This is what happens when the lead developers favorite civ game is the casual-friendly Civ: Revolutions. I'm not kidding. That's the lead developers favorite and inspiration for this game...and it shows.
All the design choices come from Civ: Revolutions, limited amount of cities, limited amount of units (1 of each basic type), minimal player feedback, minimal complex decision making, minimal everything.  I fully expect them to port this game to the Ipad within 6 months since you can tell it was designed with that idea in mind.
In addition to being an even more simplistic version of civ than civ 5, which was already pushing its luck with longtime fans. This game also feels unfinished. If you spy on a faction and get caught, nothing happens. They don't confront you or tell you to stop. I stole energy, research, and techs from the same faction over the same game. Got caught repeatedly and they never said a word. Did your city just build something, good luck knowing what it was since the game doesn't tell you. Because why bother tracking how a city is progressing since a casual might have to pay attention over just mashing buttons? Build a wonder? Get a pop-up even MORE minimalist than Civ 5's art box pop-ups. All of your futuristic buildings, no explanations of what they do or any story telling elements like in Alpha Centauri, because casuals can't be bothered to read flavor text I guess. The aliens are very passive, as is the AI overall. Got declared war on once in my first game and am steamrolling it on my first playthrough on hard difficulty.
The bottom line is they've managed to dumb civ down to the point were it feels like i'm playing an ipad casual-oriented "Strategy" game on my PC, and that sucks, especially coming from firaxis.
Avoid this turd. Get endless legend for a similar experience with more imagination. Time to go play CK2 again...

Commando Jack really baffles me. It only takes some cursory browsing to see all the bizarre raving from (what I can only imagine to be) sorely out of context quotes and even nominations for awards. Yet after only a very brief period of play in which I made it through the tutorial and first couple levels, it was overwhelmingly clear that this game was just another bland mobile port.
At first glance Commando Jack would strike you as a typical mobile shovelware quality tower defense; however, upon digging into the game a little deeper you will discover that it is in fact.. exactly what it appears to be. The store page has GameTrailers hailing it as “...unlike anything we’ve ever played before.” It pulls into question the actual amount of time anyone at GT has ever really been in the gaming community. “Tower defense with a first-person twist!” proclaims another hideously flagrant screenshot. On and on these quotes go, yet the game is bad. Even if I had gotten this on my android phone or tablet I would have been revolted by the graphics, infuriated by the responsiveness of controlling the turret and utterly bored at the experience of playing yet another tower defense game.
I’m so very glad I spent nothing on this game, that is all it’s worth. Even then I didn’t get my moneys worth.

Essentially a different skin for Civ 5 without expansions, lacking polish and personality. Do not buy.
Due to the way the faction generation and affinity system works, all factions and leaders end up being completely generic, other than the ethnicity of their leaders, which is a lot less interesting than developed characters characterized by their ideologies. Tech-tree falls completely flat as generic baseline sci-fi, lacking the interesting speculation into the development of future technology that was present in Alpha Centauri, and and the combination of the two above factors makes all the tech-quotes completely uninteresting. There aren't even cutscenes for Wonders or Victory conditions. The one saving grace is the quest system, but even that could have been handled better and less predictably (Like the quest system in the Fall from Heaven mod series for Civilization 4).
In the end it just feels like a board-game. If that's what you're after, fair enough, but if you an actually good sci-fi game, go on GOG and get Sid Meier's Alpha Centauri. Or get the Planetfall mod for Civ 4.

The hints lead you astray.  Once you learn it, it makes a lot of sense.  The competitive mode is not very difficult, but it's more fun than running around alone if you ask me.  The boss battles are kind of drawn out, but make for a spectacle.

Well, I tend to write very short reviews, but I'm going to make this one as all-encompassing as I can becase if there was ever a game I felt needed more publicity,  it would be this one.
As I write this review I have around 750ish hours logged in this game, with no signs of stopping. It's addictive, wether you count that as good or bad. And as someone who played Yu-gi-oh and MTG for about 6 years, I can say that this is the best TCG I've ever played. So this is my perspective as a diehard fan and avid player.
Pros:
- It's free to play. Not much more to say there.
- The Card art is phenomenal. Each one is fully animated (as seen in the trailor) and the artists do a fantastic job taking          their time on each one to make them perfect.
- The playstyle is unique and innovative. Simultaneous turns is perhaps my favorite part about this game, and what seperates from every other TCG I've played. It allows for players to use a prediction skill and creates the most skill-based plays and combos you can imagine.
- The community is fantastic. Players are helpful towards one another and the devs who hang around in the global chat do a wonderful job making sure new players are fitting in and having a good time.
- There is a quest system where you can unlock achievements for winning games, or even just playing a lot. These quests have reward cards and other vanity items to make yourself look way more pro when you play. Which, at least to me,  is really awesome.
- There is extensive lore behind the game and the factions within (as seen in the trailor, there ar several factions that you can think of as  "types" of cards in yu-gi-oh or "colors" in magic). The lore is well written and the community writes fanfiction for it all the time on the game's forums.
- There is a great set of campaigns for each faction that allows you to get a starter deck for that faction to play with and adapt.
- Lightmare has recently implemented a system of weekly free decks that players can use without having to actually own the cards. This is great for new players who want to develop strategy and see new ideas, or even for older players to just have some fun.
- There are already several fantastic sets of cards available for purchase at the store with in-game currency or irl money, as well as starter decks preorders when applicable. New sets are released regularly and are heavily hyped with previews and sample cards given as rewards proceeding the release.
Cons:
- Not a whole lot of players yet, or at least not as many as this game deserves. This can lead to taking a few minutes to find a game sometimes,  especially when you reach higher rankings, though I have never taken more than 3 minutes to find a game myself.
Now for some other info that will only matter for a couple weeks. From november 21st to december 12th the preorders are available for the new set, Order.  On the weekend of the 28th-1st, there will be a double IP/XP weekend. So, if you were thinking about joining this game, now is probably the best time to do it.
Lastly, Teremus, the community manager for this game (also known as the beloved/dreaded Terror Moose) streams this game very every saturday.  In particular, during this double IP/XP weekend he will be streaming with another dev and some of the top players of the game to review some unseen cards from the new set, Order. On regular saturdays, he just messes around with the community and plays for fun, and he's always willing to help people out. If you don't know how you feel about this game yet, I encourage you to check his stream out on saturdays.
That's just about it for me. I fully and wholeheartedly recommend this game to anyone who likes TCGs. 10/10. Enthusiatic thumb-up.  5 star quality. However you wanna say it, it's amazing.

I have to be honest, I was a bit unsure of Infinity Wars at first. This is due to the fact I had been playing a lot of Hearthstone and wanted something different. I had tried other TCGs and CCGs but I could never really get into them. I then came across this game and the fact there was simultaneous turns and deck commanders which peaked my interest. And if I'm honest, I'm happy I downloaded this as it is very good.
I like the simultaneous turns as it adds a little more strategy to the game itself. As you have to try and guess what cards your opponent might play each turn. The turns themselves are timed so you won't feel like you are waiting an age for the next turn to be played.
The battlefield itself is a nice touch as you have 4 zones: Defense, Assualt, Support & Commander (More on that in a little bit). Defense and Assault do what they say, Defense is where you put cards to protect your hit points, Assault is where you put cards to attack your opponent. Support is where most of your cards will be placed when they are played unless they have an ability that lets them be played straight away. As in most cases, you are planning for your next turn and where you want the cards you just played in the Support zone to go. All the zones can be seen by each player so this lets you plan ahead or try and guess where you opponent will play their cards.
The deck commanders is also an interesting idea and for this game, it does work. You can choose to have 3 commanders all from the one faction or a commander from 3 different factions. Keep in mind that this can change how much of a choice you have when creating your own deck. As if you choose to only have 3 commanders from one faction, then you can only choose cards from that faction. Adding a different faction commander lets you use that faction. And they can also be played like normal cards. So if you don't think you have anything in your hand that is suitable, you can play one of them instead. And try and change the outcome a little or a lot.
The commanders themselves are placed in the Command Zone of the battlefield where they lie in wait for you to use them. They can go straight to the Assault of Defense Zone so long as you have enough mana to play them. And they are in full view always so your opponent knows that they are there. During each turn you have to decide where to move your cards, should you keep it in your assault zone and try and take out some more of your enemies health? Or do you think you need to boslter your defenses a little?
You have two sets of hit points as well: Health & Morale. Health is your typical bread and butter health of any TCGs and CCGs. Morale is something a little different. Nearly all cards have "Morale", which means when it gets destroyed, you will lose how much morale that card had. If you run out of Morale, then you also lose regardless how much health you had remaining so that is something else you need to keep an eye on whilst dueling.
This all probably sounds confusing but there is a an option in game to help you practice and learn the rules of the game and even a campaign in which you earns cards for each faction as you progress through it. And you get a free card every day you log into the game. It is only once a day it happens so don't expect it every single time you log in. There are also quests that once completed, give you cards to add to your ever growing collection. New cards are also released nearly every week and new sets of cards are released every few months. And you can also trade cards with friends. And the developers have said that: "THERE WILL NEVER BE EXCLUSIVE CARDS THAT ONLY A SELECT FEW CAN EARN." As pratically everything in the game can be bought with Infinity Points (IP) which are automatically gained from playing matches and cost no money. In fact most things in the store (aside from cosmetic touches) can be bought with IP. So you never need to buy anything with real money... ever.
Next we come to the animation which I just love. Each card is fully animated and all look amazing. I coud happily spend a lot of time in this game just looking at the cards and most of the time I do. Also included is the option to play weekly free decks given to you so if you are finding it hard to create a deck that helps you win matches, try one of the free decks and see if that works for you.
But before you go headfirst into your 1st PvP match, I suggest you play the campaign 1st, this will give you an idea what to expect from all the factions in the game and what cards you might find. After that, all I can say is get out there and fight!

If you're looking for a game review you've come to the wrong place. But if youre looking for a fantastic ravioli recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients
- To Make the Dough
375 grams (3 cups) plain flour
1/2 teaspoon salt
2 eggs
1/4 cup (50 ml / 3½ tablespoons) olive oil
1/2 cup (120 ml / 8 tablespoons) water
Extra flour for dusting
- To Make Cheese Filling
15 ounces (425 grams) container Ricotta cheese
5 ounces (142 g/about 1/2 cup plus 2 tablespoons) "3 Cheese Italian Blend" (Parmesan, Romano & Asiago)
Note: grate these cheeses yourself and create your own custom blend.
1/2 cup cheddar cheese
2 eggs, lightly beaten
1/2 teaspoon salt
1/2 teaspoon pepper
- Extras
Your favorite sauce for the ravioli (i.e. marinara/ marijuana)
Parmesan cheese
Basil
Fried vegetables
Shrimp
Fish slices
Chicken pieces
Make the Ravioli filling.
- In a small mixing bowl, add the ricotta and mash with a fork.
- Add in the 3-cheese blend, Cheddar cheese, eggs, salt, and pepper.
- Mix all ingredients thoroughly until you have a smooth, paste-like consistency.
- Cover the bowl with plastic wrap and place it in the refrigerator for about 30 minutes.
Make the Ravioli dough.
- Crack eggs into a large mixing bowl and beat them with a fork. Add water, oil, and salt. Mix.
- Add 1 cup flour to the bowl. Use a fork to mix the flour with the eggs, water, oil, and salt. Repeat with the rest of the flour. Mix until a smooth dough is formed.
- Clear and clean off a large work surface and dust it with flour. This is where you are going to roll out your dough.
- Take the dough out of the mixing bowl, shape it into a ball, and place it on your work surface. Knead for at least 10 minutes or until it becomes elastic.
- Dust a rolling pin with flour to prevent the dough from sticking. Roll out the dough until it is about 1/8 inch (1/3 cm) thick, or about the thickness of 2 stacked quarters.
- With a cookie cutter or upside-down water glass, cut out circles in the dough (will make about 15-20 dough circles).
- Ball up the unused dough and either roll it out and make a couple more raviolis, or wrap it and put in the freezer for another time. Dough can keep for weeks when frozen. Just make sure to wrap well so that it doesn’t suffer from freezer burn or absorb freezer odor.
Fill the Ravioli shells.
- Take the ravioli filling out of the refrigerator and place a tablespoon of it in middle of a dough.
- Fill a small bowl with water, dip your fingers in, and moisten around the outer edge of the dough circle.
- Fold the dough in half over the filling, making a half-moon shape. Be sure all the filling stays inside. Pinch the edges together and then seal the edges of the ravioli with a fork. Make sure to press firmly and go all the way around. This will add a “homemade” touch as well.
- Repeat this process for all your dough circles.
- Dust the finished ravioli with flour to keep them from sticking together.
Form the Shells and Fill Using a Ravioli maker.
- Roll the dough into two sheets
- Place one sheet on the ravioli maker, and form the filling cups.
- Fill with the ravioli mixture.
- Lay the second sheet of dough on top, and roll it out. This will seal in the filling.
- Remove and separate the finished raviolis.
Cook the Ravioli.
- Fill a large pot with water and bring to a boil.
- Place the ravioli in boiling water for 5-6 minutes, or until they float. You can also test for doneness by nibbling on the edges to test.
- If you don't want to make all the ravioli at one time, you can freeze the rest
- Take ravioli out of boiling water with large slotted spoon and place on warmed plates
Serve it up.
Top with your favorite sauce, grate some fresh cheese over it, and enjoy!

I don't know... something just seems a little off about the balancing of the game and its linear narrative. Let's take a look:
The game isn't actually hard (much to every other reviewers chagrin). Instead, you have to be crafty and calculating. The game forces you into a Game of Thrones-esque universe. It would be sort of fun if you were given multiple ways to handle situations. I like to play RPGs as myself - what decisions would I make in a given situation? But before you have any options, the game forces your character into murderous plots filled with espionage and crooked politics. Once you accept that you'll make Cersei Lannister look like a saint, the game becomes a bit more fun. However, the linear gameplay is somewhat of a bore.
"But Nothing!" another fan says, "how is this game linear with 7 different factions to join/help!" It's linear because you DON'T have 7 different factions to join. You pick one at the beginning of the game, and then you're stuck on-rails to do their bidding. If you fail, there are a small handful of quests that you can do, but they're seemingly inconsequential, or they benefit only one faction. In other words, the game dictates what you do and how you do it, limiting choice.
Choice is further limited by the situations and encounters you have. Since the story is linear and you have only one faction to truly be apart of, your "choices" come down to how you kill someone or advance yourself/your organization. Do you bring some extra muscle and do it yourself? Or do you cleverly convince a group of assassins to do it for you? Either way, that one person is going to die with little to no consequence as to how he dies.
Finally, there is the problem of balancing. This is indirectly related to choice because you have to know exactly what skills to invest in at the beginning of the game based upon the faction you chose. Otherwise you'll find yourself at a critical juncture without the necessary skills to progress. Do you die at this point? Can you reload to reinvest your skills at an earlier save? No. The game just sort of awkwardly stops. It would  be nice if you could try something else. Think of it as a "boss fight", only instead of swords, you fight with words and perhaps a clever diplomatic approach will win the day. But no, you're either given one choice, or both choices involve skill sets that maybe you didn't develop all the way. You'd literally have to restart the ENTIRE GAME just to have another chance at it. That's not fun. It's frustrating. This isn't Dark Souls or some other Rouge-Like, where half the fun in the game is in the mere combat/progression, while the other half might be in a narrative arch. This is a game that is almost purely a narrative, with little to no variation in the story based on your choices (except the all-important choice of which House/Guild you work for at the beginning) - it is nothing but an unnecessary chore to have to replay different segments of the game AGAIN just because the developer made a problem insurmountable.
That's not "hard". It's just obnoxious.
So, I can't recommend this game. I definitely would love more games to put less emphasis on combat and more emphasis on diplomacy, but I don't want choice and consequence sacrificed as a result. This is nothing more than a novel as far as I'm concerned. Is the story good? Yes. Does the player have any agency in it? No.

Age of Decadence is a good game, and which development I followed for a long time. It was pretty exciting to see the result of years' worth of labor come to fruition and experience for the first time the craft and dedication put into the title.
To preface, I believe I gave this game a good shot, explored the systems as much as allowed despite early struggles, and in some cases reached the limits of its game design. The released demo helps to get a fair grasp of what is to be expected, primarily the level of difficulty in its turn based combat. And the demo extends to other game mechanics as well and serves as a pretty good alternative to a proper manual, which is limited to in-game help section. If anything, if you are interested in this game and its underlying roleplaying gameplay, you'll do well to try this demo before reading anymore of what I want to vent.
Now, having said all that, I must confess unfortunately, my first go at the game was less than ideal. I started out as a hybrid character who does not specialize in any specific task, but realizing my error, later tried at every turn to focus on a defined set of skills. The game experience changes markedly depending on what character you create, to the point that the most important choice in this game becomes the character creation.
Some of the skills are definitely more useful than others, the most overlooked of which is Etiquette that I made a mistake of investing a couple points in, deluding myself a well adjusted swordsman or some such. Many skills aside from Alchemy and Crafting find their use in dialog checks, especially Streetwise and Persuasion. It is rather unfortunate that Stealing or Lockpicking are relegated to dialog choices rendering many of the NPCs and buildings in the game to merely decorative stand-ins.
I found that due to the emphasis on choices and consequences, a large swath of content is gated behind certain checks based on these skills. For a character who against common sense aspired to be a jack of all trades, this created a funneling effect where I didn't have any choice being carried along the base plotline just to continue the motion of seeing to its conclusion before finding myself in a yet another similar situation of a pigeonholed exit. Rather ironic that the character with a broad skill set has no place to apply his trade, however meager they be. The passage of time remains as much of a mystery as the relics of the bygones world strewn about this post-apocalyptic world, burying some quests under the sands of time leaving no trace while others remain unperturbed.
It all snowballed to a point the game simply and literally refused to budge, a hard crash within the game world with no exit to desktop, only an obscured 'exit' sign awaiting those who had failed the experiment to boot you unceremoniously to an ignoble end. Exit and New Game would have been a more fitting and compassionate choice.
Did I have any more fight in myself after this draining exercise to subvert the game system to deliver my game avatar to an end commensurate with the effort to create him, identify with him, and navigate him? Not really. What I had really wanted was the game experience tailor made that gave way to whatever whim my character may take fancy in, the menagerie of choices borne out of randomness. Age of Decadence wouldn't give an inch to such nonsense and will hold no prisoner of my miserable dreams and hopes, of working with my deeply flawed character, holding his hand as we skip toward the Gates of Hell. It boiled down to 'decadence' in exclusivity that ran contradictory to my usual playing habits.
It is understandable that there is only so much the developer of six or so people can do to take account of all options and actions that a player may take, and the game doesn't suffer any fools. A fool that was me bumbling through the wonderfully created world of fascinating lore and history. Overall I enjoyed it while it lasted, but there was no catharsis in this suffering, only the New Game offering a glimmer of new hope, and richer experience to be borne out of more wiser and determined roleplaying.
Recommended, for the richness of the world, the choices a player has, and the world that compute and react to those choices. Just be sure to specialize, use common sense, and stay within the pages of this Choose Your Own Adventure. Do yourselves a favor and try the demo.

Warning: Can cause motion sickness.  Can not even imagine playing this with Oculus Rift, considering how motion sick I got playing on a console in ten to fifteen minutes segments.
Interesting concept.  Abandoned? quantum distorted world of unknown purpose and design.  As the player traverses through this alien world? they complete tasks to restart machinations in three locations: the "lighthouse/power" room, the "engine" room, and the "control" room.  Why? and for what purpose? is left for the player to decide but the end shows the revilitalization of the planet Earth.  Many questions are left open, most starting with W, as in What happened? Why? When? Where is kairo? What is kairo? But the most intriguing question I find is Who is the player really?  An unknown entity? A survivor? An explorer? A tasked performer of intergalaxic goodwill?
Gameplay: Walking simulator with point and click elements, no inventory, just "touch" to perform certain tasks.  A puzzle game that focuses on solving how to restart the massive machinations of world building proportions.
There are extra "finds" to be looked for in each area: 6 runes and 1 "vision" puzzle to find and solve.  Once all of these are found in every location a "secret" ending is revealed.
A very unique game with a very unique perspective, and more questions then answers.

This game has ruined the Civilization series.
Whoa! Big words. Maybe that was a slight exaggeration, but what is absolutely for certain is that this game is terrible, ESPECIALLY in comparison to Civilization V, and it really brings me no pleasure in saying that. I loved Civ IV, and I loved Civ V even more, having played it for a stupid amount of hours, usually in massive 8+ hour marathons. I loved the varied gameplay, the many routes to victory, the feeling of epicness that came with every session, and the sheer novelty of playing as Gandhi and sending giant death robots to kill Napoleon who’s still stuck in the Renaissance.
If you’re being charitable, Beyond Earth could be called a reskinned expansion of Civ V, except that’s actually rather inaccurate as expansion packs are supposed to add content to a game. Beyond Earth strips out all content so that there’s the key components of a Civ game (hexagonal map, turn based city building gameplay, technology tree, several routes to victory, etc.), throws in a few sci-fi related gameplay mechanics that ultimately end up changing very little, and calls it a complete new game in the series.
First, let’s look at the content that they ruined in this game, of which there are two egregious, unforgivable reductions: civilisation choice and victory conditions. Civ V had a whopping 43 civilisations to choose from, each with their own unique personality, in terms of both gameplay and diplomacy. There was a really cool feeling interacting with all those historical leaders, all with their unique backdrops and animations, and, of course, they all felt different to play against. Alexander could send a wave of city states to overwhelm you, while Napoleon would subvert your own culture so that your own population would revolt against you. Meanwhile, Civilization: Beyond Earth has eight ‘sponsors’, each of which with a completely boring leader. I never felt like each civilisation was interacting with me in their own unique way, and diplomacy went from ‘OH♥♥♥♥♥♥GENGHIS KHAN WANTS MY URANIUM’ to ‘Give me energy. I’ll do owe you a favour.’ Behold favo(u)rs the biggest joke in international trade. Not once did any of the leaders I attempted to make a deal with accept the 15 favours they owed me as an even vaguely valuable commodity. Oh, and the leader screens have lost the backgrounds, and the leaders are all just standing up and doing the same two or three animations and lines of dialogue every time. Great.
Now, victory conditions. It’s very simple to explain how they messed this up. Remember in previous Civ games where each route to victory was completely distinct? Cultural victories you had to carefully plan which wonders you built, and arrange works of art within them and swap them with other civilisations. Diplomacy victories you had to gain the support of all of the city states by doing them favours and aiding them with potential disadvantages. Science victories you had to rush towards amassing technology before everyone else, and plan accordingly. You get the picture. You couldn’t really switch from one to the other mid-game, instead you had to shape and play the game according to the way you wanted to play it, and each route brought a completely new experience with the game. On the other hand, Beyond Earth’s victory conditions simply a small series of tasks that feel completely interchangeable, like a quest in an MMO. Find two things. Research a technology. Build a thing. Wait 30 turns. You win. You’re not getting a hugely different experience from one experience that you wouldn’t get from another, especially because the affinity system is a joke. Sure, if you choose harmony you can tame the local aliens and with superiority you can make big robots, but these are in the end just standard military units.
But what is the affinity system? It’s an attempt to bring ♥♥♥♥♥♥ RPG elements to the Civilization franchise. There’s harmony (yay for aliens!), purity (aliens are gross!) and superiority (I bet there’re really cool aliens somewhere!). It replaces ideology (kind of), semi-locks you in to victory conditions, and presents a couple of perks that are too weird to be a technology or cultural virtue. You level up through affinities by researching arbitrary technologies. Doing so gives you unit upgrades, the aforementioned perks (e.g. aliens [read: barbarians] calm down faster, etc.), and after an arbitrary level is reached, you can enact the final stages of your victory condition. Here’s the thing though: these affinities are so vague. In Civ V, it made sense that a nation that chose liberty would be hostile to a nation that chose control, as we have a real life reference of capitalism vs. communism. Here, other civs will act hostile because you picked superiority over purity. Such vague terminology and ideology makes the decisions seem so arbitrary (there’s that word again). What’s more, the unit upgrades you get from levelling up affinity do not vary between affinities - they’re visual/name changes that branch off. What’s EVEN more, the traditional variety of units is gone, and now the game is limited primarily to upgrading the same small selection of units.
I think one of the big problems of the game is ultimately its futuristic setting. I think a lot of Civ's charm derived from its grounding in reality; it made it really fun to have Stonehenge, the Pyramids and the Eiffel Tower under control in Kyoto in the year 1600 or something. The made-up wonders and of course the move 'beyond Earth' have made this game hard to relate to and hard to care about.
There’s a lot more that warrants complaint, but I can’t be bothered anymore. Don’t buy this game, especially if you liked previous Civilization games. If you’ve never played Civ before, get Civ V Gold Edition instead. This game is a horrible, lazy cashgrab that saw the big sales of the previous game and thought it could milk a bit more from the inevitable upcoming overpriced DLC/expansions.
Do note, however, that these are my first impressions from one and a half games. If my opinion changes, I'll update this review.
If you wanted some positives, Grant Kirkhope did some of the music and he’s a cool dude.

This was what I thought after the first 3 hours. If you can get past the initial frusteration, it gets good:
This is a great looking game with ok controls, let down by an absurdly miguided save/player punishment system. The game so far goes like this: Each time you get to an interesting boss fights, you are killed in 30-45 seconds (but at least it's fun and exciting). To get back to that interesting boss fight, you have to go th exact same 3 to 4 areas between the save point and the bosses, and they are always filled with unintersting, frusterating, repetive combat against low level enemies. You will spend the bulk of the game re-playing these same frusteratingly dull sections, again and again, to get back to the good parts, so that this time you can last 5 seconds longer. Then you die, then you play the boring parts again for 5 minutes to get back.  What makes this worse is that not only is the combat against non-bosses is dull and ceaselessly repetitve, it still requires fairly accurate timing, so you still have to pay attention. This is the worst way to make a game difficult. This is not a challenge, it's a slog. Life is too short for games with a wheat/chaff ratio this severe, and this one is especially frusterating because the chaff is literally completely unnecesary. With a new save system this would be probably be a great game.

Shadow Warrior is a very good shooter with a bit of buts.
I honestly recommend playing this game to every fan of FPS games. It's fun, it's wild, it's well made. It has great humor and some dirty jokes and innuendo thrown in. We have 9 weapons, some with consierable different alternative fire mode. Overall mood of the game is mysterious and full of chineee (?) demons, ancient magic, some weird artifacts and a bit of Yakuza or other Asian mafia group. If you like games that follow the spirit of Duke Nukem 3D, classic Shadow Warrior or Serious Sam First and Second Encounter then go for it! You should not be disappointed.
That was at least the short version. A bit longer and more detailed text will follow. This game has some weak spots. Lets do standard Pros & Cons.
Pros:
- explosive gameplay - yup, really a lot of things in this game explode
- great and juicy graphics
- early level design as well as well as demon world design - small town looks as it should - claustrophobic; cementary looks creepy and mysterious with all of those candles; demon world reminds somewhat worlds from Zeno Clash games. Also winter levels look good.
- good looking chinese demons
- badass protagonist, nice sidekick - maybe not as fun as Mad Max's Chumbucket but Hoji is still memorable
- lots of guns and alternative fire modes - katana & shurikens, revolver, smg, crossbow, shotgun, flamer, missile launcher, demon heart and demon head
- three separate ways to upgrade hero - you buy weapon upgrades for money, spells for ki crystals and skills (that gives some bonuses like +10 to Health Points) for Karma points that you get for killing demons and finding chalice secrets
- sword fighting and spellcasting works very well
- when killing demons in special way you get more points like in arcade games - when you kill a demon with a rocket you get a DETONATOR bonus, when you behead him you get HEADSHOT or BEHEADED depending on weapons used
- humor is really fun, fast and sometimes references good old classic games
- speaking of good old classic games - this game has a lot of GREAT and FUN secrets. You can see Godzilla in the background on some levels, you can find pixel rooms just as in the Shadow Warrior 3D so on, so forth. Oh, just to give you a taste of ingenious humor - one of the main bad guys is called Zilla and he wants to become a god. Just add those words. Ring any bell?
Cons:
- although the first 5-6 hours into the game are brilliant, the rest are just somewhat dull. Somewhere during play I just felt that I am slashing or shooting the same enemies over and over and over (yada yada) again. Later levels are long. Not just long but loooooooong. Winter levels can take as long as 1 hour to finish each.
- whole game takes about 12 hours to beat. Although this seems fine for a shooter, it's about 2-3 hours too long. Most of the original ideas become familiar after playing for about 6 hours and there is not much more original content later.
- boss fights are prolonged. I am not bickering about this one. Just compare Serious Sam bosses to this game bosses. Big Aludran reptile was challenging and the whole fight was rewarding. In Shadow Warrior after beating those big armors I felt tired. Especially second windged armor was tedious and took too long to beat.
- no point in playing this game for the second time - when we have seen those levels the only thing that remain is slashing demons over and over again. If you like maxing out your characters then that's fine but that may take some time in this game.
- after getting the final weapon and buying some upgrades we can see that some of weapons are not really useful. I think that the best gun for wiping weaker demons is shotgun. SMG is a bit weak, although useful when fighting bosses. Revolver is fine for flying demons as it kills them with one shot. Katana is fine. Crossbow is the weapon that you will use for most of the time as it is somewhat powerful and I recommend buying exploding bolts upgrade as fast as possible. Missile launcher is powerful but slow. Flamer is well, slow and not really that powerful imo.
Alternative fire modes are fun but not really useful except revolver, shotgun and crossbow ones.
- fights are fine when there are small packs of demons but battles tend to drag on when there are more enemies. You need to hack and slash through every one in order to progress to some ares. That's just tiring. As tiring as grinding in mmo. This is why I recommend boosting your shotgun with upgrades because shotgun in this game is one shot = one kill when it comes to weaker enemies.
Phew, that was long. Don't hesitate after reading my Cons. These are my free thoughts on this game.
Overall this a great game. Go and play it:)

We can change it to e.g. Serious Sam 3 sledgehammer or Saint's Row♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ It does not change weapon 1 characteristics, only visuals. Yeah, that means you can slash with a hammer. Well, I finally finished this one.  Shadow Warrior is f**king great. <walks off stage>
---
Okay, fine... Shadow Warrior is the reboot of Duke Nukem 3D's companion game, Shadow Warrior, a Build Engine FPS from the Doom-clone era of shooters.  This game was overlooked back in its time with Quake literally rendering 2.5D engines outdated and only Duke Nukem survived to become a fan favorite, but as Gearbox bought the rights to Duke Nukem and sold it out for Borderlands 2 funds, it seems that the tides have turned with Shadow Warrior coming out on top.
Lo Wang is as stereotypical as it gets.  While it may be quite toned down in comparison to the BuildEngine classic, Wang is a parody of Eastern films and action flicks alike, with a sword and ego to match.  As an origins story and precursor to the original, this game also introduces a mix of Chinese and Japanese mythos, and with it a companion character that grants you magic powers.  This undead character also happens to be a snark, and the dialogue between the two characters is priceless.
The combat features 7 guns with upgrades, 2 consumable weapons, 1 badass katana with three combos and two swing types, and 4 magic powers, as well as a shuriken or quick-stab key.  As many of the guns have alternate fires and the sword or magic powers can be used in your left hand with any gun, there's plenty of room for diversity.  The enemies themselves range from wallrunning to tankish, exactly as you should see, and the combat keeps fresh for the duration of the game.  Every aspect of the game is incredibly well thought out and the game never feels artificially difficult.
As a retro shooter, there are also countless secrets and easter eggs throughout the levels, including fortune cookies that generally read out to something incredibly immature or stereotypical in proper 3DRealms fashion.  These give you progression points for your magic powers, extra perks, or even just money to upgrade weapons.  By the end of the game, you'll most likely have a good 70% of the weapon upgrades and will be missing around nine power/perks, assuming you aren't a completionist whp needs to find every single secret before being satisfied.  It plays very similarly to Hard Reset, minus the strange machine interfaces.
As for the story, it's very well-written, though a bit hard to follow, especially with the sub-plot of Hoji's relatives and the Whisperers' memories.  It's definitely worth listening into, but you're not looking into Dark Souls levels of deep lore.  The story is also very well-acted and full of dark but silly over-the-top action.  FWH nailed the 3DRealms style of this game in every way.  It'll take you about 13-15 hours to complete on average; a replay may be closer to 11-12, but a worst-case scenario with loads of screwups will probably be around 14-17 should you get horribly lost.  It doesn't happen often, but occasionally the placement of the door seals combined with some areas' mazelike design can get annoying.
Overall, there are certainly flaws you can nitpick out of the game, but what's important is that it's a fantastic game that definitely is worth a look.  It's like a retro shooter the way you wish you remembered them, and doesn't disappoint in the slightest.  There isn't too much for replay value-- singleplayer with survival and new-game+-- but the main campaign is great enough to justify the price of admission alone.  Devolver is a great publisher and often has excellent sales on this game, but I wouldn't wait that long, especially with Shadow Warrior 2 coming soon.

tl;dr
It's a great game with a lot of really interesting features that differentiate it from Civ 5. Your civs are differentiated less on which civ they are and more on which choices they make throughout the game. The only downside is due to it being decoupled from earth history you lack context between the civs and in the tech web, this is made up for by your civ being *your* civ rather than a historical civ for the former and from experience from multiple games in the latter.
Now if you want to read about specific features and what makes them interesting, keep reading:
Beyond earth is a really good game with a lot of interesting ways to customise your civ. The civs are pretty similar at the offset, just different bonuses and personalities. However as the game progresses they specialise to be very different.
The affinity system is like ideologies except less restricted. You can advance in all three at different rates by gaining points for that affinity by taking related techs. Each affinity gives different bonuses as you level them up and you gain access to specialising units once you hit certain levels. Some units have special specialisations for when you have sufficient levels in two affinities. The different affinity units and buildings rely on certain resources so if you are without any of one type you may have to go an alternate affinity. For example I had no Firaxe so I was unable to go Supremacy, however I had a lot of Xenomass so Harmony was a very good option.
The tech web is very different to the tech tree in Civ 5. You are not required to take techs in a specific order (although clearly they are bad choices). Your choices change what type of civ you become because a lot of techs are aligned with specific affinities. Downside with the web is that all the tech is futuristic so you have much less context about what is actually important to get.
There are 5 victory conditions. 2 generic and 1 for each of the affinities. You could unlock all five if you got enough techs to level the affinities up. Some involve constructing a large unit that hangs out in the world and then defending it for <x> turns.
Difficulty level 2 is very easy and I fought no wars the entire game. Definitely go higher up if you have literally any experience with Civ games.
The culture trees have been simplified and lengthened into four trees that just give flat stat boosts. Very much like the old World of Warcraft talent trees. That is not a good thing.
Aliens replace barbarians and are actually interesting to fight because they have their own unique units. Despite having no wars I still needed to build an army and fighting the aliens satisfied by blood lust. Although it♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off the harmony civs.
Diplomacy is pretty good. The addition of favours means that granting someones request can be useful as you can pull the favours out at a future date to get them to do things for you. Be that accepting an unbalanced trade or to stop spying on you.
The quests are a great addition as they provide a tangible goal in the world to gain benefits. For example, launch two satellites to map a region of the world, or make choices that shape the future of an outpost (city state equivalent).
Ancient ruins and archeology sites have been merged into crashed satellites and derilict stations. These appear throughout the game and provide varying benefits. Building scouts is useful throughout the game to find and retrieve these.
Health replaces happiness and it's less important when you're negative. But I spent a large amount of time trying to keep my people healthy because being majorly positive can provide some very nice bonuses.
Trade routes are far more numerous. I had 3 per city at the end of the game.
Each type of military unit has been reduced to just on, so you get one soldier and one archer, it's like this in Civ 5 except the upgrades come from leveling your affinities rather than unlocking techs. As you advance through the affinities you upgrade your units to match visually and mechanically with the affinity you are and then within that more specific bonuses. For example I upgraded by units into Harmony units one by one and they became more alien and green. And then I was able to choose to make them more adapted to fighting in toxic environments or more generally strong.
Covert operations have been much improved over Civ 5. They are back to the Civ 4 style where you can perform specific actions in cities. For example, siphoning money or science. The more interesting ones involve hiring defectors to gain military units or performing a Coup to take control of an enemy city. Stealing techs remains, but as a specific job you give you a spy.
I've only given a brief overview of each feature, I would recommend picking up the game and playing it to experience them all in full.

TL;DR More like free to demo. For your *average* person, I probably don't recommend this game. If you love racing games, follow real world motorsports, want a simulation style handling, and you have some money - the handling and driving experience is quite fun.
OVERVIEW
basically DTM, the game...
The FIFA/Madden of FIA SRO racing franchises.
You can compete with actual real-life DTM drivers on the leaderboards.
Mostly centered around the larger real-world commercial FIA motorsport series like Blancpain GT, WTCC and DTM.
PROS
If you know you want more of a simulator feel, this game is decent. I like the handling of the simulator and it feels quite realistic, and it's fun, challenging and rewarding to drive at the most realistic difficulty setting. It will really enforce smooth driving, proper technique, correct line, etc.
* Diverse handling between different cars
* Suspension tuning
* Realistic simulator style grip physics
* Good sound
* Reasonable track selection, nordschleif, monza, SPA, laguna seca
* Test drive any car from the store before buying
CONS
(minor issue: missing some important tracks I'd like to see such as Silverstone, Long Beach, Catalunya, Pikes Peak)
#1 Limited free content
#2 Car selection
1) Like most so called F2P games, it's not as free to play as you'd probably hoped. Free car and track selection is very limited. If you are willing to spend $30-$50 USD you can get a reasonable selection of cars and tracks. All content, however, could be very expensive to purchase, easily hundreds of dollars.
If you are hoping for a free game... well, I don't know of many other free sim titles, so this may be your only option, but realistically this game is probably something you'll need to spend money on if you want to have fun.
If $70 is not a difficult decision to make, or if you literally just want one or two specific cars and tracks, then pricing will likely not be an issue for you.
Most car packs say claim to include like 20 cars only actually include 3 or 4 cars, what they mean is that they have 22 skins total for the 3 cars.
As far as a campaign and paid content, the most promising feature is the "experience" series where you get to replay the actual 2015 DTM season, however, this feature only exists for the DTM series and doesn't appear to exist for other racing series like Blancpain or WTCC etc.
2) Race cars only. All cars are regulation style, i.e. they conform to some FIA spec like F1 or GT3 for competition racing - so not like the kinds of cars you could by from your neighborhood sports car salesman.
Furthermore, cars all seem to be tied to some specific year and championship, like 2015 DTM. There's a fair amount of variety, but overall it feels a bit one sided and limiting. Again, if you like this, then maybe this isn't a con, but for your average person, and for myself - I find this at least a small drawback - other payware titles have a more versatile experience that includes both consumer road cars and regulation racing cars.

Not recommended, yet. This is an expansion pack, wait for it to drop to $30 or less.
The primary emotion I felt while playing was disappointment.
To be sure there are some great new additions this game adds. The tech web is an improvement on Civ 5's tech tree, although it is not nearly as restrictive as it was promised to be. On my very first playthrough at minus 1 from max difficulty I researched every single branch tech and only had a few leaf techs left over. Affinities are another fun new system, but again there are no hard choices to be made, you can hit level 7 across all affinities pretty easily and then choose a final affinity to max out if you want the unique units. The Virtue trees are good analogues for cultural advancements + religion from Civ V but nothing new.
Unfortunately, while I like those two changes even they have notes of disappointment in their implementation. This trend carries with all the other new systems they added. Quest decisions? Very cool, but they are universal and practically unchanging from game to game beyond extremely minor differences. Unit upgrades? The affinity differences are cute, but they aren't game changers.
And then there is a ton of functionality that is just disappointing or flat out bewildering. The UI is in many ways worse then Civ V, no resource view, hidden menus that have vital information, trade route management is as bad as Civ V but with 3x the trade routes. Large portions of the late game are devoted to clicking (Previous Route) ad nauseum. The Wonders are incredibly disappointing, no movies, no character, and bonuses like +5 Science, that's it, that's the joke. Endings are abrupt single image pages with You Won! or You Lost! No replay, no graphs, you don't even see your score unless you find the Hall of Fame entry in the main menu. The orbital layer is a cute addition, but again just isn't implemented fully or well enough to make it an enjoyable experience.
The art is a mixed bag, they certainly created a lot of it but the maps and units are fairly bland. The UI is mediocre to poor on most screens. It's great seeing a Xeno Titan, but where are the wonder videos? The AI opponent human characters are wooden puppets like personality.
I think what this game is missing most is soul, this game lacks thats hard to define animating spark that could have made it a classic x-pac despite its flaws. I'm sure a lot of people worked super hard on this game but the end result is a well-marketed overhyped expansion pack. Firaxis has moved off the list of companies that I would purchase games from on launch day.
Don't buy it until it is substantially reduced in price or the inevitable ultimate edition releases.

This review is for the early access Blockstorm. Sit down and listen to me carry on and allow me bore you to death. :)
Brief Summary
Don't get me wrong, there are many games out there that allow you to build your own maps out of blocks and then allow you and some friends, or some random people to completely lay waste on your map. Although most of them are unfortunately terrible, sometimes due to pay to win with the free to plays, or some just are out there in Early Access floating around trying to grab your money with a game that is only 20% complete. No, this game is not like this. I can easily say that I had fun with this game with the many shenanigans that have happened to both me and my mates. Despite the lack of servers, as the only official servers that aren't empty are demo servers meaning the player will need to host their premium servers to play their maps with other premium members.
Now I'm going to go back for a moment, and trust me I won't take long. This game is fairly limited content wise, there are very little prefabs, however I have noticed that more and more prefab packs are being released in the workshop, which is very good. The weapons are lacking in numbers and the gameplay mechanics can be refined. Again however this game has only been out for a short while, and in my time from when I bought it, I have noticed quite a few interesting changes and additions such as turret editors, new developer made maps (which I really don't care much for as the buzzing workshop community has made.) I really do see much potential for this little, but as this is only gameplay wise, as again the weapons are lacking, some of the animations can be cleaned up and multiple other implementations would be nice.
I actually urge you to buy this then to play the demo as that means the community grows and the developers get more money to kickstart this game from where it is now to a full complete game in no time.
Pros
- It's fun editing and creating maps... then completely annihilating them with friends.
- The workshop community is always at it creating new refreshing and unique maps.
- This game is fairly good for what it's potential may become.
- It's got some pretty fun maps, despite them being on the demo servers.
- Endless creativity, building tunnels, to making massive defense towers it's almost endless with the map maker.
Cons
- It does need a bit more content, however it is still in very early access.
- Unfortunately this game is overrun with demo users... again I urge you to buy this to support the developers.
- It is fairly basic, some new mechanics would go a long way.

A diamond in the rough, Age of Decadence is what any hardcore RPG should aspire to be. There is no good vs evil or black and white. Everything is grey.
It's a wholly immersive world with its true value being in its replayability; there are so many ways to do quests, so many quests to miss with several factions to align with or betray. You can avoid combat altogether if you're an exceptionally smooth talker. That's how I played my first character, and that was the most immersive and enjoyable experience.
It's merciless. It doesn't hold your hand. There's even an achievement for dying 100 times and that's actually one of the easier ones to get. It's not like every other RPG where your character happens to be the chosen one, although ironically, you can convince a religious preacher that you actually are the chosen one which opens up a whole new branch of options (but only if you have the right stats for it).
It's definitely one of the best if not the best RPG I have ever played and the fact that I have 50 hours logged and *still* haven't uncovered nearly all of the content or even played as half of the backgrounds (thief, assassin, grifter, drifter), speaks for itself.
If this even slightly piques your interest, check out the store page and try the demo.

Shadow Warrior is a very good shooter with a bit of buts.
I honestly recommend playing this game to every fan of FPS games. It's fun, it's wild, it's well made. It has great humor and some dirty jokes and innuendo thrown in. We have 9 weapons, some with consierable different alternative fire mode. Overall mood of the game is mysterious and full of chineee (?) demons, ancient magic, some weird artifacts and a bit of Yakuza or other Asian mafia group. If you like games that follow the spirit of Duke Nukem 3D, classic Shadow Warrior or Serious Sam First and Second Encounter then go for it! You should not be disappointed.
That was at least the short version. A bit longer and more detailed text will follow. This game has some weak spots. Lets do standard Pros & Cons.
Pros:
- explosive gameplay - yup, really a lot of things in this game explode
- great and juicy graphics
- early level design as well as well as demon world design - small town looks as it should - claustrophobic; cementary looks creepy and mysterious with all of those candles; demon world reminds somewhat worlds from Zeno Clash games. Also winter levels look good.
- good looking chinese demons
- badass protagonist, nice sidekick - maybe not as fun as Mad Max's Chumbucket but Hoji is still memorable
- lots of guns and alternative fire modes - katana & shurikens, revolver, smg, crossbow, shotgun, flamer, missile launcher, demon heart and demon head
- three separate ways to upgrade hero - you buy weapon upgrades for money, spells for ki crystals and skills (that gives some bonuses like +10 to Health Points) for Karma points that you get for killing demons and finding chalice secrets
- sword fighting and spellcasting works very well
- when killing demons in special way you get more points like in arcade games - when you kill a demon with a rocket you get a DETONATOR bonus, when you behead him you get HEADSHOT or BEHEADED depending on weapons used
- humor is really fun, fast and sometimes references good old classic games
- speaking of good old classic games - this game has a lot of GREAT and FUN secrets. You can see Godzilla in the background on some levels, you can find pixel rooms just as in the Shadow Warrior 3D so on, so forth. Oh, just to give you a taste of ingenious humor - one of the main bad guys is called Zilla and he wants to become a god. Just add those words. Ring any bell?
Cons:
- although the first 5-6 hours into the game are brilliant, the rest are just somewhat dull. Somewhere during play I just felt that I am slashing or shooting the same enemies over and over and over (yada yada) again. Later levels are long. Not just long but loooooooong. Winter levels can take as long as 1 hour to finish each.
- whole game takes about 12 hours to beat. Although this seems fine for a shooter, it's about 2-3 hours too long. Most of the original ideas become familiar after playing for about 6 hours and there is not much more original content later.
- boss fights are prolonged. I am not bickering about this one. Just compare Serious Sam bosses to this game bosses. Big Aludran reptile was challenging and the whole fight was rewarding. In Shadow Warrior after beating those big armors I felt tired. Especially second windged armor was tedious and took too long to beat.
- no point in playing this game for the second time - when we have seen those levels the only thing that remain is slashing demons over and over again. If you like maxing out your characters then that's fine but that may take some time in this game.
- after getting the final weapon and buying some upgrades we can see that some of weapons are not really useful. I think that the best gun for wiping weaker demons is shotgun. SMG is a bit weak, although useful when fighting bosses. Revolver is fine for flying demons as it kills them with one shot. Katana is fine. Crossbow is the weapon that you will use for most of the time as it is somewhat powerful and I recommend buying exploding bolts upgrade as fast as possible. Missile launcher is powerful but slow. Flamer is well, slow and not really that powerful imo.
