Warning! This review contains lots of comparison between Civilization: Beyond Earth and Civilization 5!
TL;DR
1. Changes from linear tech-tree to "tech web", allowing higher degree of freedom
2. Customizations of units
3. Better spy system
4. Orbital units provide more options for economy / military
5. THERE IS NO GANDHI!
1. Lack of personalities for faction leaders
2. Removal of background when talking to leaders
3. No cultural music related to the faction
4. No scenarios to play with, only normal game can be setup
5. Bad minimap design
6. Doesn't feel like developing a civilization over the course of time
7. Different terrains looks same to me.
1. Not worth the $49.99 USD, wait for sales until it is priced about $30
2. Consider Civ5: Complete Edition if the background setting isn't a factor to you
As a player that owns all the expansions + DLCs of Civ5 and has more than 200 hours of gameplay, I must say that Civilization: Beyond Earth is a step back from Civ5.
First, stations (city-states in Civ:BE) are simply just trading stations. You simply establish a trade route with the station to gain its advantage. They aren't considered as a small faction and doesn't have any armies. You no longer need to deal with them to earn a diplomatic advantage over other factions.
Second, almost all of the victory conditions except domination are about advancing in the tech-web and earning affinities to unlock the victory structures. They are actually the same thing albeit their names. In Civ5 however, different victories requires different strategies and aspects of gameplay to achieve. Take cultural victory and diplomatic victory as an example, you dig up different artifacts or create arts / writings / songs to earn tourism points for the cultural victory. You also need to consider rushing certain wonders / buildings to get the theming bonus. But for the diplomatic victory, you will have to do many quests for the citiy-states to earn their trust and bring them under control, or simply trade with other civilizations to make them vote for you. All of these are gone in Civ:BE.
Third, different terrains in the Civ:BE look almost the same to me. It is probably related to the colour tone of the game that makes the contrast between different terrains type not so obvious. Or simply that I don't enough game time to spot the difference between them. I should also point out the bad design of the minimap. There are only 4 types of things on you minimap: 1.) Land (owned / not own), 2.) Unexplored region, 3.) Sea and 4.) Resources. To study the terrain better, you must pan you camera to that area. There are actually a lot of impassable terrains that are not marked on the minimap.
Other than that, dealing with AI factions hasn't improved at all. They share the same dialogue and chat options as in Civ5. Even worse, the background when you are talking to the faction leader is removed. The only thing you got is the leader standing and talking to you, with the map you last viewed as the background. No, you don't have Ceasar sitting in the throne room anymore, nor will you have Washington talking to you in his office. Interactions with AI factions aren't dynamic already, removal of backgrounds just make it even worse. Speaking of that, although you can tell the origin of the factions in Civ:BE, you somehow don't think they are related except the name. It is probably about the futuristic settings and lack of cultural BGM.
There are a few improvements that worth mentioning. The spy system has revamped that allows you to perform different actions in other cities. You can steal energy (gold), science point or cause havoc with a giant worm. With different level of affinities, you can customize your units through choices of traits. This is what makes you army "unique" to others as the basic units are always the same. You can also launch orbital units to assist you through different buffs. For example, a solar collector can provide +1 energy for the grids it covers, while others can improve combat strength. One cannot simply ignore the usefulness of these orbital units.
To sum up, I only recommend Civilization: Beyond Earth to players who prefer Sci-fi 4X games. It doesn't worth the $50 USD, probably just $30, so just wait for a sale. If the theme setting is not a factor of consideration, go and pickup Civilization 5: Complete Edition instead. The game system of Civ 5 may not be the best as compared to older Civ series, but it is more versatile, enjoyable and replayable than Civilization: Beyond Earth.

This is Fallout in a Post-Apocalyptic world IN ROME!!!!11! (Or is it???)
TL;DR, I recommend you buy it.
The game is a throwback to the 90s Fallout, before it made the leap to FPS. Meaning it's a classless system with stats and skillpoints in an isometric playing field, with factions and enemies looking for more power with you thrown into all this, at a pivotal moment in history. I'm gonna break down the review to COMBAT, SKILLS and STORY.
COMBAT: Rich tactical options with tough difficulty. The tactical options are almost as diverse as the ones found in the Temple of Elemental Evil. Should I fire my crossbow bolt now, or do I bait them so I can unleash a timely whirlwind? Should I heal myself now or save it for another encounter later? The choices, and consequences, are yours.
SKILLS: Skills matter. You can't be an overpowered master of all here, you have to choose a path and stick with it. While there are numerous encounters in the game, these do not give enough skill points for you to be a god of everything. I learned this the hard way, early on I played a jack of trades guy, who got into some quests, but got locked out during certain points due to lack of skills. Pick a profession and skills and focus on that as you make your way in this post-apocalyptic Rome. As an aside, alchemy did save my life more often than not, so I would recommend that.
STORY: You have to pay attention to the walls of text. This is a throwback to the 80s and 90s RPGs, where there's not much voice acting, but a lot of exposition and character development done through the text. There's a complex plot involving "gods" and "demons" in the game, so you'll have to pay attention to all of it. DISCLOSURE: I have not finished the game myself, but I have encountered a "DEMON" and I'll leave it at that. There's something big going on, and I intend to get to the bottom of it.
Bottomline: If you want to see more RPGs from Iron Tower, you have to buy this game. I have enjoyed every hour I put into it. But, if you're still not convinced, play the demo for yourself to see if this game's up your alley.

Good ideas: Affinities, siege worms, quests, unit upgrade system, terraforming options, espionage system (for the most part).
Not so good ideas: Underwhelming faction differences, trade system, virtues, aliens, diplomacy, orbital layer, lack of any kind of narrative, no recap on winning, pacing issues, AI, resource implementation, general lack of information.
I'm a big fan of Civ games, and I'm sure I'll be a big fan of this one too once a couple of patches and expansions come out to address what feels like a game that didn't get a whole lot of polish before being kicked out the door.
As a huge fan of Alpha Centauri I had high hopes that this game would bring that same attention to detail and sense of wonder and exploration. Oops. Don't look for little vignettes to flesh out the world or leaders you are interacting with. Factions are pretty vanilla and don't play that differently.
There is no diplomatic victory or cultural victory. Diplomacy in general seems to be a whole lot of the AI asking for resources for "favors". I haven't figured out what a favor is and why I should trade a material good for one, but maybe I just need to play with it some more. There are no resources affecting health, so if you don't have the tech to build health improving buildings to keep up with your expansion there is no other alternative way to address a negative health number.
Virtues do grant some pretty nice bonuses, but are lacking any sort of context as far as your affinity goes.
Customizing your starting bonuses at the beginning of the game is nice, but a lot of the options are filler and I ended up picking randomly.
The orbital layer maybe useful if there is a specific area you need to boost, but with satillites falling out of the sky every couple of turns I decided to focus of permanent buildings and units instead of diverting resources there.
By the midgame, trade starts to get absolutley ridiculous. Depending on improvements, each city can have 2 or more trade routes and the distance limits to other cities/settlements seem pretty non-existent leading to trade route choice overkill. They really need to either cut down the number of possible routes or have a button to just pick the most profitible one.
The most purplexing part so far are the aliens that have take the place of barbarians. They are randomly hostile toward units. In the begining of the game they will leave you alone for multiple turns and then kill your explorer who you can't effectively guard because they are technically a military unit. This was never an issue in Civ 5 because you would just need to move any unit into a ruin to get the benefit and then run before a barb could catch you. Needing to send out an indefensible unit to camp out for multiple turns is a little baffling.
There is no demographics screen in game as far as I can tell, and on the screens showing info on the economy, military, etc... the information just seemed to be either lacking or complete overload. However, since the AI never attacked me or showed any hint of aggression other than strongly worded language, I didn't end up needing to get into the gritty details.
Get to the end of the game and besides an underwhelming picture and a brief voiceover, there is no recap of the game. No graphs, no maps, no rankings. Just spent hours of your time transcending the bounds of human existence? Well, either keep choosing your trade routes for another 5 hours or go back to the main menu. Yay!
Don't get me wrong, theres nothing here that's beyond redemption and maybe if I spend another 40-50 hours with it I'll come to appreciate what the developers were trying to do here, but do yourself a favor and wait on this one until it gets a price cut or an expansion.

So I think a lot was missed during my first initial review and so I decided to go through a second time with this not so harsh.  I really enjoyed the time spending on a map which by the way all of the maps are very "decent" but looking at the map list, shows a ton of them.. I would have stuck with a few maps and worked on them a bit more as far as adding more obsticles or choke points instead of just open planes all over the place.   "But Blooded Cyborg, all you do is camp!"  While that may be true but it gives the level more diversity to explore other areas of a map with more dynamics.  Though sometimes emptyness can be a good thing as far as how a match starts to pan out.
Secondly ther isn't any options for game modes making it very boring to keep playing the same match style over and over again.  A lot of the good developers usually tend to focus on pure mechanics of a game. (How does one even begin to capture flag, or even a simple TDM?)  There are very good examples from early 2000 that I am not going to mention.  So think about game mechanics at this point forward then worry about driving your graphic development further afterwards.  Also add in reasonable achivements or goals, this also adds more replay value to your game.
Overall the texture colors are very vivid and the texture resolutions are pretty standard in terms of no more than exceeding 512x512 resolution base, and the textures are using the mostly used effect known as POM.  Which is a combination of heighmap and bump textures. Fairly used in a lot of commercial AAA titles such as Crysis 3 and etc.
For the fact that only 1 developer has been working on this, *Clap* there is not going to be a certified list of compatible GPU's or CPU's that will be able to run it.. Not even in your Honda.. No.
Me using a GTX970 with an i5 4440 and 8 GB of So-Dimm memory is enough to run this instantly like   melting a block of ice-cream in the oven. So the game isn't really demanding in terms of graphics.  I would bet a 2nd gen i3 should have no problem running this all by itself.
So I know this is a long review but I think we all get the point that right now this does have a long way to go and the more time is spent working on this the better it will get.

Bought this game on sale for a dollar, and its certainly worth it to have in your library. Its great to leave up on the big screen at a house party or something. Both kids and adults would pick up the controller and play for a while. Its not a game with a backstory or objectives you need to learn; there is no learning curve other than the five control buttons you need.
This game is like the game Flow on playstation3, or any other kind of idle-time adventure game. There is no real 'end' or 'death' in the game; you begin by selecting one of a few single-cell creatures to play as, then spend however much time you have to kill kind of just floating around, eating stuff and exploring a visually appealing environment. As you eat, you grow, and can eat larger and larger prey. If you get damaged by other craetures, you shrink. Depending on what you eat, and in what order you eat it, life grants you different evoloutionary advantages as you progress.
The game ends when you get bored and put the controller down, or pick another creature to play as. If you are looking for a game with some kind of structure, missions, real objectives, an ending, a story, or that is an educational experience ... this isnt for you.

I'm all for porting and localizing japanese games for PC – bring them all to me. Unfortunately the quality of the PC games from a Japan seldom reach the polished level or get the finishing touch that is accustomed here. There are games that are extremely buggy and unoptimized and then there are those that surprise and work quite well enough.
Unfortunately Magical Battle Festa belongs to the former category. Crashing of the game is really blast from the past and gives very strong window 98/ME vibe. I'm not exaggerating much if I'd state that game crashes every twenty or thirty minutes. Which is a shame, because it is such fun game. This is more of an advice of caution than a steep warning to stay clear from the game. Let's say that the game crashes every 25 minutes or more if you are lucky. That would still mean perhaps 6 or 7 matches before the need to restart the game. Game is quite small (about 500 mt), so it could be installed to a ssd drive for easing initial loading time.
The game has 12 playable characters and each of them has a characteristic playstyle ranging from speedy character to heavy hitters and from long ranged ones to special attack empahisizers. The arenas are somewhat big and there is even a little room for hiding and sneaky fighting styles. Still the arenas are somewhat repetitive, mostly flat surfaces and the platforms of the arenas add quite little to the gameplay. This might perhaps act differently when playing against four human opponents, especially on the same sofa.
The game supports local and network multiplayer. And is something which could have much potential gather four person around the same tv-screen – a feature that pc games seldom have. The network lobby on the contrary was quite a ghost town, so there isn't much hope for beating strangers. Creating and playing on public server seemed to work well, so there is much unused potential. I played one and a half hour online and there didn't seem to be any other problems (atleast with two human players) except the general crashing which happened three times.
The game contains story mode which takes about four hours to beat and was quite amusing. Playing the story mode is also needed for unlocking some characters. Plot was same kind of garbage that every fighting game has but the overal excperience was highly positive compared to some more well known fighting games. Some story arcs could have been longer, for three battles isn't nowhere near enough to master a character.
For those familiar with recent anime, it comes as a nice extra that the voice cast of the game consist of stupendously well known japanese voice actors and puts into a shame vast majority of better known japanese games. Lines are few but there are surely many who'll appreciate.
All in all I liked the game much, but I'm strongly against the trend of publishing half finished games as final products. In those cases I believe it wouldn't be fair to recommend the game for anyone, even if it is great fun.

For anyone, who is into simracing, with r3e you probably get one of the best, if not THE best racing simulator on the market. I can compare to Assetto Corsa, rFactor 2 (Demo), Stock Car Extreme, Project Cars, Grid Autosport, NFS Shift and NFS Shift 2.
Different to f.ex. Assetto Corsa, in r3e you can only drive real racing cars, no stock versions of them. There are not only features like tyre rubbing or fuel consumption, enthusiasts have many options to mechanically set up the car the way they want.
Physics and force feedback feel great on the G920. It doesn't take long to get a feeling for the car you drive. Never the less it can be preety hard to get controll back after oversteering with some cars. Also you can set up the ffb settings by yourself, if the default ones doesen't suit you.
In singleplayer the AI difficulty can be set up in small steps, just like in Asseto Corsa. There also is an adaptive mode.
As far as my experiences go with multiplayer, I have a pretty good impression of the community. Didn't met a "NFS crash kiddy" yet (EDIT: you actually meet some, especially in races with free content). There are not only extremely quick hardcore racers on the way, r3e is also played by some real life racers, even from DTM.
Graphics are state of the art and performance is very good. Only things I miss, are "bad" weather effects like rain and wet tracks for more slippery action sometimes.
R3e may be called "freetoplay". I would describe it more like a bigger demo version of a game, which allows to configure its content the way the customer wants it. So f.ex. if you don't want to drive formula cars, you don't need to buy them. There is the option to do as many test drives as you like of every car, which is very fair in my opinion. You also can drive in hotlap competitions with cars and tracks you don't own.
You can purchase every car or track seperately or buy packs (what can be cheaper). I recommend to buy VRP on the r3e store website. As far as I know, this should be the cheapest way to buy content.
One thing that is pretty annoying, is the fact, that if you bought a car in the f.ex. GT Masters 2014 Version, you still need to buy the same car again (at least cheaper) in the GT3 or GT Masters 2015 Version.
To sum it up: if you really want to play the game with as much content as similiar games offer, r3e is a bit expensive but the price is still OK if you buy packs or take offerings on sale.
If you are looking for a racing simulation game and you have a ffb wheel, at least test the game in freetoplay-mode.
If you are an "arcade racer" and don't want to put much effort into playing and paying, this probably isn't the game for you. Never the less you still have the option to give it a try for free :)

An abysmal excuse for a Hitman game. Gone is the assassination sim that we enjoyed in previous iterations of the series. Now we have a stealth game in the vein of something like Splinter Cell: Conviction.
The disguise system is completely ridiculous; if you are disguised as a police officer, other officers in the level will see through your disguise and detect you, even if you are walking around like a normal person! But, if you walk while spinning around, so that they can't look at your face for too long, they won't detect you!
Further, on all but the hardest difficulty level, 47 has access to an active wallhack (think of Batman's detective vision from the Arkham games) that lets him see enemies through walls. This is intended to replace the map screen from previous games, but all it really does is pander to the casual audience that has never existed for these games.
Bottom line: this doesn't have the Hitman DNA - it's a stealth game that focusses more on telling a poor story over providing interesting emergent assassination scenarios.
Not recommended.

First thing you need to remember is that it is in Early Access. That means the game lacks a lot of basic features and the games may not be balanced due to the poorly made ranked system (which is to be fixed).
I'd highly recommend this game if you ever liked arena kind of games. If you never heard of those, it's a great alternative if you are sick of your favorite MOBA. The game is based purely on combat, which means that you won't have to spend a lot of time farming and trying to control the map. Instead, you will focus on such things as players' ablities and zoning.
As I previously said, the game may lack the features that many popular games have and you might be having difficulties  keeping the same interest over the time. The daily quests are boring, the ranked progression is broken, some battlerites do not fit at all.
But what's so good about the game? The gameplay itself. There are 2 options: 2v2 and 3v3. 2v2 is considered a more interesting gamemode due to the possible amount of comebacks, while 3v3 is more skill-based one - there are many more abilities to consider.
Is it worth the price? If you've read up to this point and are still not sure about it, the answer is yes, definitely. But if you're not into this type of games, it's up to you to decide whether you'll be able to quickly understand the mechanics or not.

4/10 TL;DR 50,000 men in RTS multi-player only with no one to play with online.
Legion means MANY.  Identical units against each other in a massive fight of 10,000s.
Barracks create troops very fast (5? per second).  Moreover, with some Jade mined, you can spawn necromancers anywhere your troops are.  Necros spawn new troops out of corpses in the ground, which means that you can continuously create more troops at the front line without worring about the long march to get them there from the barracks.  Massively large map.  Necros seemed overpowered to me but so are the barracks.
Also with Jade, you can spawn clay soldier from nothing but the ground and explode a tiny nuke anywhere on the board which kills soldiers only.  Resource points have an infinite supply until destroyed by enemy.  All abilities (Mines, Barracks, Necros) cost more and more each time they are launched.
You have one leader which is like the King in chess.  Unfortunately, his position is highlighted on the map; if killed, you lose.  Since equal fighters create a stalemate without fresh troops behind them, the basic tactic like any RTS is to strike the enemy resource points and barrack spawn points.
The game has Easy, Medium, Hard, and 4Square map for training grounds with set computer opponents with no AI.  So, for a SOLO play session, the last 3 can be a small challenge.  Hard is quite difficult, but no AI is opposing once you figure out a proper strategy.
8/10  Great little game of massive RTS proportions that you cannot play without a friend opponent
3/10  Upper Left corner: Options for pause, quit, sound, effects.  No key mapping out of WASD or Arrow keys. No video changes
1/10  No one online in a multiplayer only

I just keep coming back to Evochron.  There's something about the FEEL of it that I just love.  That lone-wolf-space-captain, free-as-a-bird, do-what-you-want, big-wide-galaxy type vibe.  I find it a great way to just relax.. in space.  It feels big and free and immersive.  It's a hoot to jump into that cockpit, and just do 'whatever' in space for a while.  The 'flying' is great: point-to-point jumpdrive, planetary landing, station docking, all seamless and all FUN.
I do, after a while, tend to find myself wishing there was more to do in the way of mission variety, just to intersperse with other activities like mining and exploring.  Maybe this is partly because I play single player, and tend not to emphasize combat all that much.  But really I think this is in many ways a space-euro-trucker, and the feel and experience of the journey(s) are what's important.  You set your own goals, you make your own fun.  The spacey sandbox is all set up for you, and all the 'bits' are fun to play with.  Strap yourself in and set out and see where you land up.
Steam tells me I have about 60 hours logged in Mercenary and another 70 logged in Legacy.  Those may not be huge numbers for some, but for me they are pretty big.  There's only a few games I've played about as much or more (X3; X Rebirth; Skyrim; Morrowind; Elite Dangerous; Starsector; STALKER).  But maybe even more telling is that Evochron just keeps pulling me back, to this day!
Bottom line is I give this game two very enthusiastic thumbs up: it's everything Mercenary was, and more, and better.  This game won't be for everyone, but no game is.  I love Evochron and it has a permanent place in my rotation, and in my top 10 or top 5 all time lists.  If you're a sucker for space sims, space rpgs, space flight, space trading, space exploring, space whatever - I'd suggest it's at least worth a try!

This game looks amazing and has great and inventive mechanics.
I'd recommend it if I could actually play it, but currently the game is as broken as I've ever seen a game be, it's a flip of a coin on whether I'll be able to interact with menus, load into a game with my deck and hand, or even be able to get into the play menu. The game is unplayable without restarting ever few matches, and even when playing it's really clunky. Building a deck is a major pain that takes forever since you have to add cards some cards in an obtuse way to get them into the deck, and if you're unlucky your deck just won't save, or card sprites will stick to the window, or you won't be able to add/remove cards from your deck.
The unranked play is an absolute joke. I played two games, went up against people that either grinded for hundreds of hours to buy the cards they had, or dropped few hundred dollars to make incredibly strong decks. I, on the other hand, had only the cards the game had given me for completing 19 campaign missions, and a deck that was legal and possibly decent if it didn't go up against decks that were stacked with Uniques, epics, and rares. The ranked play is locked behind level 10, which is a bit ridiculous and generally just turns me off of the game entirely.
The campaigns are okay, but generally they just give you a deck and put you up against an AI, tell you very little, then assume that you can use whatever trick or gimmick of your deck to beat your opponnent's deck. It's unintuitive and generally a slog, though some missions are fun, most are very boring or luck based.
The game could be amazing, it really could be; but at the moment it's a broken mess that I will not be revisiting anytime soon. This game is not fit for release, do not pay money into it until you've played at least a few hours and experienced the many bugs and glitches the game has to offer.

- The constantly regenerating mana instead of having to chug a limited supply of elixirs during a situation all the time is a refreshing change and to me is something that all the Dishonored games should've had to begin with.
- So are the contracts: Which basically exist as tricky but devoid-of-needless-exposition side-missions that offer coin only upon completion of the main mission, thus adding an element of uncertainty wether you get to spend that coin or not in the next level, which urged me to be more tactical about my purchasing. "You know that black-eyed whimpy-voiced demi-god that may or may not♥♥♥♥♥♥you off? Yeah you get to kill him."

Personally I do not believe it is made clear enough. So I will state it here:
Therefore I do not recommend this untill there is a drastic price drop.

There's many disappointing things about this game. It's been in development for a long time, and most of those development hours clearly went into raw amounts of content (this is being generous, there really isn't much content) and lots of mediocre writing rather than improving the general experience. I wouldn't be surprised if a fair bit also went into begging for positive reviews and downvotes on any negative reviews - there is no way this game warrants an 88% positive rating otherwise.
Pros:
-Semi-interesting setting, acceptable writing, lots of reading if you feel like it - but there are much, much better works you could be reading instead.
-You get to play an isometric RPG as a single character rather than a party, which is uncommon.
Cons:
-Advertised as "hardcore," but really, the game is extremely simple at its core. Tedium is NOT difficulty. Dying a lot doesn't make the game "hard," either. Yes, you'll die a lot in Age of Decadence, but it's not like, say, Dark Souls, where you can outplay your death. You just reload and click the other option in AOD; nothing about this game requires much thought and it certainly doesn't test your skill, ever, at any point. Allow me to elaborate:
For a non combat character, you essentially just click choices in a dialogue. For you, that's the game - it's like a tedious visual novel. You also have to keep old saves and save your skillpoints, because you need to level up the correct skills to pass dialogue checks, otherwise you can't progress. You will get lots of game overs as a non-combat character just because you invested your points into the wrong skill, whereas a combat character always has the (realistic) option to muscle their way through any situation the game might present. It's a bit disingenious that the creators say that combat is the hardest way to win the game; you'll probably reload LESS as a properly built combat character than you would a non-combat character.
-Combat is extremely simple, and is mostly RNG based. You mostly spend your Action Points in the most damaging way possible, then move as far as you can to force your opponents to spend additional AP travelling to you on their turn, so they get less attacks. You'll beat the game just fine taking the violent option in basically every situation, as long as you keep your equipment and attributes updated appropriately, and you won't break a sweat doing it. It's heavily random, though, so you might have to reload some fights until your attacks actually connect. But all in all, both combat AND dialogue in this game are really, really simple.
-All combat is set pieces. There's no random encounters, roaming enemies, or anything like that. Every battle is a pre-made set piece that comes behind a loading screen.
-NO EXPLORATION. You get to places by clicking on the map. That's it. There's no roaming the plains and discovering things yourself, nothing like that. How shallow. In the few situations where you might find something interesting, instead of exploring itself, you're usually going to be clicking through a couple of dialogue screens that explain what your surroundings are like, etc.. Hey, how about you SHOW IT TO US instead?? Too much effort?
-Each location hub is heavily lacking in content. You should finish Teron in about 30-45 minutes once you know your way around, Maaadoran is the same. You'll run around thinking "surely, there's something more to do here?" mousing over every NPC you see hoping they are interactable, only to find that no, there isn't. Those npcs are just scenery.
-Every second bit of dialogue will be full of swearing. Not that this offends me, but really, writer: there are other, less obnoxious ways to emphasize that your setting is "gritty." The overuse of profanity is just hamfisted and lazy.
-Game looks like crap. I'm no graphics nut, and I'm well aware of what the devs are going for, but that's just an excuse. Visuals are an afterthought in this game, and it's not good enough that the package as a whole can make me ignore that. Compare the look and feel of AOD to other new isometric games like Project Eternity. There's no comparison.
If you're an oldschool RPG fan, I advise you to stay away unless you've played every other oldschool RPG and you're just desperate for another. This game isn't for you, I'm not sure who it's for, really. The only ways to really enjoy are:
1-Treat it like a choose your own adventure game where you have to reload your last save every 2 minutes, and save every 30 seconds, or
2-Just make a completely OP combat character and put up with the extremely random, simple, tedious and boring combat so that you can experience the story.
But the story, even on its own, isn't anything special - so why would you suffer through a bad game just to read it?
This game should have been a mostly ignored e-book on Amazon. The only reason it's getting any attention at all is because it shoved itself into a genre it doesn't deserve to be a part of. I hesitate to call it a game, let alone a "hardcore old-school RPG."

I just love the Dishonored franchise, but this chapter is a disappointment.
Don't get me wrong. It's funny, and Billie's powers are awesome, thought they are only three (plus one you get later, but it's somewhat lame).
But here come the negative things: there is not only a lack of powers, but a lack of levels and level depth, too. There are only five levels: in one of them you can't use powers and it's very linear and short, two of them share a big part of the same setting, one recycles one of Dishonored 2's locations (Thought a little modified) and one is probably the worst level in the Dishonored franchise: linear and with a terrible desing, it's like it was rushed. But the worst part is that for four levels yout goal is not kill/eliminate non-lethally someone, but you just have to find something. Yes, you have optional killing with the contracts, but the concept of Dishonored is to have a target to eliminate, lethally or not. Then, levels that are not linear have very few different ways to complete them. And, finally, the story is not that intriguing: the characters seems to have forgotten the development they had in previous games/DLCs, and theire motives are quite.... absurd.
I repeat: don't get me wrong, it's funny, but for the last terrible level. In particoluar, the third level is awesome. But overall, for now, it's the worst Dishonored installment. However, the second and third levels are really good, so my suggestion is to buy it on sale: but beware of the last level, it's really, really, awful.

There are no likeable characters in this game. There are no honest NPCs in this game. SIde quests involve either being robbed, stabbed, or misled, and the main quest involve either murdering people because you were told to or manipulating others to murder each other because you can. Role playing as a decent human being will get you killed very fast. Why would anyone play a game that involve this much reading when you just don't care what happens to any of the in game characters? Blah Blah Blah, House X will benefit if you do this, House Y will benefit if you do that.... So what? They are just as bad as each other, and whatever the ending is, it is definitely a bad ending because none of the factions are ran by decent people.
This is a old school RPG, so if you want to complete the game you have to either save and reload frequently or read online guides. Compared to other RPGs like Pillars of Eternity and Mass Effect, which can be played blindly with very little reloading and no help from the internet, I feel Age of Decadence is simply inferior because the death and reloading is immersion breaking. It was a business driven game mechanic for the 1 coin for 3 lives arcade machines of the 1980s, but today it just looks out of place. I like permanent death no reload games like jagged alliance 2 1.13, x-com long war, and this war of mine. In those games death matter because you have to keep going and the person you spent hours interacting with is now lost forever. Whereas in this game death doesn't matter because you just reload. This is just bad game design.
There are other little annoyances, such as font size is too small on high resolution monitors, you are forced to start combat encounters in melee in tiny rooms even if you try to play as an archer, map areas need to be unlocked and you can't free roam, camera angle changes after every text interaction, too many stats are displayed on screen in combat when only chance to hit and damage range actually matter.
If you have the morality of a typical GTA protagonist and you enjoy tweaking complicated excel spreadsheets, and you don't mind dying and reloading all of the time. Then sure, pick up this game. For everyone else, there is simply a lot more games which are a lot better in storyline, gameplay and game design.

A great many people critisize this game for being a simplification of Civ V. They are not wrong.
However, they don't give up the foundation of what makes a civ game a civ game. City management is the same, warfare is the same. But research is better, more varied. Instead of flowing what is basically a straight line you have increased control over how you progress technologically. Espionage is miles ahead (I'd even say, out of this world). What they lost from Civ V, is not nearly as important as what is gained.
It is understandable that to increase customization the base unit selection needs to be reduced, along with the number of nations to choose from. But as soon as you start playing the game, what variety is lost to having only 8 nations and about as many units is overwhelmed by how much you can customize them.
At launch this game is the equal of Civ V with all of it's expansions. And it will only get better. If you have any doubts, hit "Follow" and wait for the first sale. But if you're looking for more Civ, more grand strategy, pick this up.

The Dishonored franchise continues to impress in the field of level design, smooth gameplay, entertaining and useful gadgets and powers, as well as new types of enemies and side missions. If you enjoyed the gameplay in the other Dishonored games, or alternatively enjoy any level-based Action-adventure game (Thief for example), this game sure won't disappoint you.
What surprised me most about the missions / levels in this game was the re-using of the same new area twice, as well as one from Dishonored 2. Whilst this initially seemed like a greedy move to squeeze as much out of everything as possible, I found that, after exploring them for a longer time, they had large differences from previous iterations, and provided a weirdly entertaining experience, knowing where to go, but finding a way blocked, or changed in some way. The additions of different goals and different enemies spiced them up even though they were in the large scale the "same" map.
New powers and gadgets give a new layer on top of these levels, and I continue to have fun with everything they add in the different iterations. Billie Lurk's powers are reminiscent of others, but have their own twist, working equally as well while also making it different and fun.
The Contract system is not exactly the Granny Rags storyline from the first game and its DLCs, but are fun enough and add some extra incentive to explore.
By god, the music in this game and its predecessors. Daniel Licht, the composer of most of the Soundtrack, sadly passed away mere weeks ago, leaving us with this game and its music as his final goodbye. Boy, does that make this already terrific soundtrack even more powerful, raw, and emotional. I sometimes simply sat and waited in a corner to hear the full song playing in an area, afraid I would miss it if I walked off. The songs, as well as the general ambience, add so much to the game, and create an enhanced experience that you definitely should not miss out on. HAVE THE MUSIC ON!
I guess this might be the area where many would disagree with me. As a huge fan of the Dishonored series (My favourite games), I expected a good ending to what had been built in the first two games, and I'm completely satisfied with what was given to me in this game. I've seen people criticize the depth of the characters, and how the Outsider is portrayed, but I find none of these things accurate. Whilst the plot in a nutshell is simplistic, and might seem a bit unmotivated, looking between the cracks and reading the lore of these games shows to me that all the actions and personalities in shown in this game are very true to color, and very well done.
The following is my spoiler-heavy personal interpretation of the Story, and why I find it so satisfying.

Personally, I like the game. Though I do find it a bit too easy. Only a couple of battles so far have taken any real skill. But the story, while kind of cliched, so far is at least kind of fun. I feel like it would be a great multiplayer game as it stands. Since a human player would boost the difficulty considerably.
Besides the easy difficulty, the other issue is that you can get trapped in combos pretty easily. And there's no way to break out of a combo once you get caught in it. The game does at least have a decent recover. But it would be nice if you could counter, dodge, block, or cancel an opponents move while in a combo. The last three would already be possible if the recovery time was shorter.
But, like I said, I like it nonetheless. It's got a lot of great ideas (they just aren't implemented perfectly). And it's got a lot of heart. So it's definitely got some things going for it. I just wish that some things (a lot of things really) were tweaked. It could be an amazing arena fighter if things were just fixed up a bit. Honestly, if they fixed these things, I'd easily put it near the Gamecube Custom Robo. Not quite on par, simply since it still would have too little customization. But it definitely has a lot of potential. And I hope they make another one with everything polished up a bit more.
Basically, if you like arena fighters, or if you like magical girl anime, I'd say you'd probably like it. But if neither of those are your thing, it's probably not quite to where it needs to be for it to be worth your time. Also, if you do play it, try using lower settings than you think is good. It's a bit of a resource hog, and even though it has PS2 level graphics, it takes a bit to run at max settings. Probably due to the average object count and the effects used for attacks, I'd guess, coupled with some inefficient code (probably).

I've reviewed this game before but I judged it unfairly since I went off of previous versions that just flat out didn't work. So let me tell you about THIS version that I played not five minutes ago...
Are there bugs?
-Many (one I can point out is the fact that I tried a "hill climb" race, and no matter what I ALWAYS got a "false start")
Is it optimized?
-Not at all (when driving in a straight line I got about 60 FPS, but try to turn one degree to the left and the turning animations nearly freeze the game until my computer figured out how to handle it)
Are there "in-game transactions"?
-Well, that's a fun question... You CAN buy stuff whenever you want with real world money, but it's not a requirement. You can solely base your game around "grinding" for cash in single player like Gran Turismo or Need For Speed, which brings us to our next point.
Is this like Gran Tursimo or Need For Speed?
-This is another hard question to answer since, even though all of them are enclosed racing games by now, this is almost completely different... The physics are wacky (your car can spin out at random), the camera is just awful (you use V and N to look from left to right in your car, and it's not even smooth, no, it instantly looks to a predefined position), and half the time where you shouldn't get a "false start", you do anyway... Whereas with those games, they have, decent physics, the camera moves WITH the car, and false starts are a bit rare...
In conclusion, I honestly hated the game. Go ahead and try it, I mean it is free, but be warned, if you like realistic racing games, this might not be the best choice...

There is no AI that tries to out build you or gather more resources or anything of that nature, so the only real strategical matches you'll play in this game will be in multiplayer. Nonetheless, if you have someone to play with, then you'll have a good time.
Also, after launch the devs added a "Map Editor" feature that allows you to design your own scenarios and maps (much like the scenario editor in Rise of Nations). This is a great addition; however, you cannot use the custom maps in multiplayer matches. Thus, the feature is somewhat worthless considering the lack of a single player AI.
Honestly, this game feels like it should have been an early access release considering the sheer lack of features. And like many early access releases, the developers stopped pumping out patches and additions in September.
Overall, I wouldn’t buy this game unless it is heavily discounted or the changelogs reveal some more recent updates.

I will first start off with saying that this is the first review I have ever written on a game on Steam. This should also bring confidence to potential buyers of this game.
PROS:
I have found this game to be outstanding. First off, the game is literally like 150 mb (as of Sept. 9, 2014); I was blown away by this. The game is VERY well optimized and runs extremely smoothly.
There is an option to select which weapons you would prefer as your primary, secondary, and grenade/bazooka slot. The primary weapons range from a standard semi auto rifle, AK47, sniper, belt-fed machine gun, and shotgun. The secondary weapons range from pistol, shotgun, uzi. Finally, the grenade slot ranges from a standard grenade, RPG, and one more thing (can't remember at the moment).
One of the things that make this game so unique is the fact that each weapon has a specific weight. With increase in weight, the slower you run (and significantly I might add). This helps mitigate the overuse of some weapons. For example, If you were to equip the belt-fed machine gun, Shotgun, and rpg, your character would run so slow that it would make you an easy target. So balancing your weight is a must.
Another fantastic feature is that the environment is completely destructible. I have seen building in a map completely collapse when the lower blocks are destroyed. I am serious.. it isn't like minecraft where blocks will still be floating. If you blow-out the lower structure blocks in a building, the building actually collapses.. that is so cool!
CONS:
Everything has a good and a bad. The cons I found for this game was the limited number of weapon choices (however, dev's are likely going to be adding more). There is currently only Deathmatch, Team Deathmatch, and Assult (atk and def); it would be nice if there were more game options. Final con, not at many people playing as I have hoped for.
Conclusion:
I am one to cringe at early access games, however, this one has definitely change that. I found this game to be exceptional for what it is worth and have had a great time. Also, developers are ALWAYS talking with players on the community channel so check it out!

I kind of hope for some sort of "Blood Money HD", but instead got a game filled with level segments, which is honestly quite disappointing when you're used to the Hitman games taking place in huge levels.
Don't get me wrong, I'm not saying that the whole game is filled with corridor-like levels, but the lack of big open evironments is rather noticeable and it seems like a real step backwards compared to the previous games.
Other than that, the game has quite a lot of illogical things going on, such as finding Agent 47 with his original suit right after a cutscene (super annoying), even though he was wearing a disguise, or have pockets big enough to store an assault rifle and a sniper rifle (previous games made you drop any two handed weapons you had equiped).
But the ONE thing that gives a killing blow to this game is... The stupid "Instinct" rubbish ability, which was one of the thing the devs talked about a lot, and maybe a bit too much.
Now here's what this does: It allows you to see through walls and conceal yourself while wearing a disguise. The whole game revolves around this stupid (dis)ability), and when I say revolves... It's like the whole game was designed for this feature alone.
Why is this feature stupid? For one, it's basically some sort of wallhack, sure you can NOT use it, but, and this is the 2nd reason why it's stupid, as I mentioned above, the WHOLE game... Is tailored for this feature.
Say you knock-out a cook, or a janitor, or any innocent law abiding citizen, and then steal his clothes,  well guess what: ALL his lil' buddies will see through your disguise. If you want to avoid being detected, you can use up your instinct to... try to hide your face. INSTINCT... HIDE YOUR FACE... The simple fact that they see through your disguise so easily is stupid enough.
"Hardcooooooooooooreee" as I am, I like playing first playthroughs in the hardest difficulty a game might offer. The highest difficulty in this game is Purist: Extremely limited HUD, NPCs reacting much faster, reduced player HP, all that good stuff that makes a game fun, not to forget, perhaps the most important thing, less "instinct".
Well guess what? Thanks to the whole "Instinct being a big deal" deal, the game is ruined. Yes, RUINED.
All in all, this could have really been a true Hitman game successor, but unfortunately end up being a completely forgettable experience that pales in comparison to what 47's previous adventures were like before.
Come for the Legendary Agent 47, don't stay at all, leave as fast as possible in fact.

After wasting crap load of time and money on MTG, I decided to return to TCG once Digital TCG started rising again (i.e. Hearthstone).  Hearthstone didn't do it for me because it was one of the most casual♥♥♥♥♥♥I've ever tried in my life.  So I looked for a better alternative.  Then I found Infinity Wars.  I'll cover IW in two main aspects: F2P and Gameplay/Strategy potentials.
I think the game is pretty fair.  Firstly, yes you can actually TRADE cards in this game.  You can buy Lightmare Points to buy booster packs but you can also earn IW Points to buy booster packs.  You earn IW points from playing games online, including private games with your friends.  How many games does it take to buy a booster pack?  I think it is around 30-40 games (Just a rough estimate, haven't done the math myself), assuming 50% win rate.  But there's more.
When you start the game, you will have to play some campaigns.  They will teach you about each factions and you will earn starter deck of each faction when you complete first 3 or 4 missions of each factions.  Also, any games you play, you get experience points for your account and you will get a free booster pack every time you level up.  Every level requires more experience than the last but in the beginning you will level up often and you will be showered with booster packs.  But there's more.
There is a thing called daily rewards and weekly quests.  Every week, you will be given 3 quests.  It can be just gaining certain amount of experience or playing some amount of PvP.  You get one random card for each quest you complete.  You will get 1 random card for logging in daily and you will get another random card for playing 3 PvP games.  So assuming you are diligent, you get 2 cards per day, another 2*7+3 = 17 cards per week.  And these are truly RANDOM cards.  I've gotten couple of legendaries just from logging in every day.   It's pretty rare but it's really nice when you get them.
I also need to note that free cards you get from daily, weekly or levels are SOULBOUND, meaning you can't trade them.  Only the cards you get with Lightmare or IW points are tradeable.  I think it's fair considering how many cards they pump into you and you don't want to screw the trade economy.
So in summary,
1. 2 cards every day (untradeable)
2. 3 cards every week (untradeable)
3. 1 booster pack (15 cards) every level (untradeable)
4. In-game points you earn to buy booster packs (tradeable)
IW is definitely unique.  I'll cover them in sections.
1. Simultaneous turns
Most card games are turn-based but this game has SIMULTANEOUS turns, meaning you and your opponent plan at the same time and things happen all at once.  This means you have to plan according and predict your opponent's moves instead of waiting for them to make a move and react.  If you played MTG, then you know about saving that kill spell in case your opponent buffs a creature into a raging hulk or saving that counter-spell in case he casts some devastating spell.  Not in this game.  You have to predict them coming.  On the other way around, you can dodge certain spells by moving your characters in and out of the battlefield.  This adds an element of mind-game.  Instead of casting spells and hope that your opponent doesn't have an answer for it, you can move around it, dodging, baiting and calling shots.  It really depends on the deck but some games can be very intense.  You don't just play your strategy and hope your opponent doesn't have an answer to it.  If you know they could potentially counter you, you can find a way around by baiting.  This is only possible in Digital TCG so it's taking full advantage of the digitalized TCG!  This fact alone is worth checking this game out.
2. Deck building
Alright, magic has 5 colored factions but IW has 8?  (There's 2 more factions for Star Trek series but I won't cover that here)  And you can only have up to 3 factions for each deck?  What's up with that?  Well, IW is different in a sense that your deck will be based on 3 cards and they are called Commanders.  Every deck has 3 commanders and their faction alliance determines how you build the deck and each faction has their unique strategy and combining them.  You can build a pure faction deck and play to its fullest strength or you can make a deck of hybrid factions, playing with jack-of-all-trade playstyle.  You aren't just limited to 3 factions because there is a card that allows you to play any factions.  ANY character card can be a commander.  The 3 commanders are placed in the commander zone at every game and you can play them whenever you want, provided that you have enough resources.  Most of the time, you can play the character's ability from the commander zone so you can even build a deck around that entire aspect.
If you played MTG, you know well about resource management.  In IW, you gain 1 resource every turn so you rarely have to worry about being mana-screwed.  The commanders are like lands in a sense that they determine the color of your deck.  There are characters and spells to boost your resource to get ahead early so there are some resource management in the game.  Your deck should be consistent with your intended gameplay every time since you won't get mana-skrewed very well, provided that you balanced the resource curve.  Consistency is the key because I really hated getting mana screwed in MTG.  Honestly I think that is one of the major design flaws of MTG.  MTG is more flexible with deck building in a sense that you can have any color and any cards in your deck provided that you have the lands to support it.  But ultimately you have to buy those 20 dollar rare lands to even make your dreams possible.  I miss the potentials in MTG but not that much.  Coming from MTG which has beautifully balanced 5 color scheme (each color allies with 2 while opposing one), I felt kinda iffy about the whole factions thing, especially since the devs seem to intend to add or subtract them in the future (super not sure about this but there were 7 factions in the beginning but now there's 8. 10 if you include the non-canon ones) but I learned to love the lore and each faction is quite fun to try.
In summary:
1. Simulatneous turns for mind-games
2. Commanders and 8 unique factions for intersting deck building strategies
3. Basic resource management so you won't get mana screwed most of the time

As with any card game, there's ins and outs to know for mastery of a game, and with simultaneous turns and a rather fun deck building system, this game may heavily appeal to some players.
However, as of right now, I wouldn't recommend this game. The game itself isn't bad by any means, it simply hasn't grown enough, and feels as if it still needs to establish itself. Different paths for different factions are available, but at the same time it's readily apparent that some vastly outclass others, and not enough options as of yet exist to balance that out in a truly feasible way. Many times the recommended counters can alter the structure of a planned build too far to have remained true to the original intent, limiting the truly 'good' builds.
On the other side, being able to mix and match factions can be rather fun, and I've enjoyed being creative, as well as playing against other creative builds, even if it's clear that one is stronger using aforementioned faction paths. Utilizing commander abilities also added a rather nice edge to the game, swinging games from victory to loss (unless playing against verore since they can just kill them outright, which sadly happens frequently). It adds a stable foundation to your builds, and enhances synergy. Along the same line, being able to swap your resources for drawing cards, swapping cards, and increasing resource cap can also help players stay in the lead or bounce back, even when seemingly out of any other options, as when given a bad hand.
So overall, I'll be looking to come back to this game in the future, but not right now.

This is a really solid game for some things, but lacks infrastructure to be satisfying for others.
I didn't spend 40 hours dogfighting.  That's the first point I make, because this game mostly attracts flight-sim nerds, and the whole basis of my review is that the game DOES have enough content outside of that to be worth a look.  From what I understand, combat is tough, mostly because the flight physics are well-developed.  It's unlikely you will make just one pass through the tutorials, as there are MANY things to keep track of.  Outside of combat, you'll likely just need basic controls for your ship getting around, but the depth is here if you want it.
The economy isn't anything particularly special, but some things should be pointed out.  Like every space sim/sandbox, you have many commodities to trade, and unfortunately like every sim/sandbox, there is an illusion of choice.  Sure, you COULD "vulture" trade goods off of exploded ships, or buy anything that's on a good sale, but the reality is diamonds and platinum will be your biggest moneymakers without actually crafting something yourself.  However, unlike every space sim I've ever played, the game doesn't give you sh*tty money for this activity.  Even putting aside the deployable mining bot, you can make a few million in the right quadrant just with either of those commodities in one sitting.  That would take MUCH longer in other sims.
Ships are modular, and you can swap out different components whenever you like.  Every ship has an assembly rating, and once you max it out, you'll need to decrease some things to increase others.  Do you choose more room for crew, more cargo space, more weapons, etc?  Cargo bays hold only one item type each, with a total of ten possible bays.  There are blueprints to find to craft weapons and tools, and upgrades you can purchase.
Civilian ships are a separate class from military ones, the latter requiring special currency from missions.  My complaint here is that all military ships are restricted to one cargo bay, and you cannot change it.  Now, you can muddle through the game just fine without a military frame, which I did because there's no such thing as configuring the space however you want it.  Since much of the game is about exploration, acquisition of treasures, weapons, resources, etc, the game basically forces you to have two ships if you want the full experience.
A special note about travel: space is big, naturally.  You are not technically restricted by speed, only fuel, but it brings me to a minor complaint about the map.  While the autopilot is decent enough for some things, if you click one PIXEL over from the target on a map and hyperjump to it, you're still going to be at least 20,000 km away, and that's if you're lucky.  A better zoom feature would fix this.  Don't expect to get anywhere quickly without at least a few minutes of coasting in.
You can pick the Alliance, the Federation, or Neutral if you just want an uninterrupted flight sim.  You can contribute to the spread of your chosen side throughout the galaxy by doing missions and building permanent structures such as cities on planets, starbases, and the like.  None of these structures are owned by you, they simply contribute to your faction's presence within the system, while providing convenient locations for you to refuel, trade, etc.  This is kind of a bummer for me, personally, and represents a part of that lacking infrastructure I mentioned.  You wanna be a trade baron?  Too bad.
Planets have one station on them, or nothing besides resources.  You can fly uninterrupted in and out of the atmosphere, though inner atmospheric flight controls are wonky.  If you've deployed a sensor within the sector, you'll find planets littered with goodies.  It might be anything from materials, to weapons, to wildlife (sort of).  This treasure hunting is something I very much enjoyed, along with getting tips from AI pilots about hidden caches.
The unofficial quadrants of the universe are procedurally generated.  That's pretty damned amazing if you ask me, but this expansive element comes with a price.  The universe is essentially homogenized.  For example, asteroids have three ores:  diamonds, platinum, and metal.  The third is the sole resource for building anything, the previous two are commodities.  You will visit many quadrants, and see many asteroids of different colors, but they will only contain varying ratios of these three elements.  Sure, there are technically thousands of planets, nebulae, and other little anomalies, but no matter where you go, it is likely going to be something you've seen before.
Then again... Perhaps I played the game backwards.  Maybe all of these other things were meant to be side activities to a dogfighting sim.  Someday I may come back to the game and make a combat pilot.  But, even with the slim pickings of the other systems, the game is a good romp if you catch it on sale.

So, where do I start...
Speaking from a technical standpoint, this game is pretty impressive. Even though the graphics aren't the most impressive ones, the seamless transition between planets and space is wonderful. Flight controls are pretty deep and are pretty easy to learn, but very hard to master. Music and sound effects are pretty decent too, so that's something. Ship building is rather unusual I'd say, because it has many layers, from basic "buy new modules" to more advanced (and more interesting) "calibrate your hull", where you can get rid of some things in favor of the other (like sacrifice rocket slots for more cargo bay).
Now, to the main problem I have with this game (which I wish I realized sooner and refunded the game, but even the 1.5 hour demo wasn't enough for me to understand it)...
If you start as an independent pilot, you're basically cloaked for an eternity. Let me explain.
Imagine living on near the border of a county that wages war with that bordered country. Bullets and bombs flying everywhere, soldiers running left and right, but you... You didn't side with either faction. So one day, you go all "yeah, I'll probably go out, see what's up, maybe drop by a grocery shop to buy meself some milk". And guess what? That's exactly what you do with no one batting an eye, asking what would a civilian do on a GOD DAMN BATTLEFIELD.
If you start as an independent pilot, there's no danger. Pirates don't exist, and two major factions simply don't give a slightest damn about who you are and what you are doing. So here's your gameplay options:
-Mine asteroids, which means: fly up to an asteroid, press a combination of keys, go make yourself tea or something, hang out with friends, get drunk and call your ex, the game won't care and you'll end up with a full cargobay of precious minerals, safe and sound
-Trade, which means: buy a random ware (I mean it, there are no production chains or station types a-la X3/Unending Galaxy , which defeats the purpose of knowing where you can buy specific things), spend half an hour staring at your star chart looking for a place to sell it, finally realize this is all pointless and go back to mining
-Combat (read: piracy). I don't know why you would ever do that because you can't capture ships that you could sell for a good price, and the resources NPC ships drop can be acquired by mining which is far safer
There is one thing that makes all of those irrelevant, however, which is
-Doing contracts. Those are HILLARIOUSLY overpriced in your favor, and something like "refuel a spaceship" mission, which is a "jump to location, wait until you're in range, press one button" type of mission pays you 50k on average. This takes you a little more that two minutes. For comparison, you'd have to spend about ten minutes to mine three cargobays of ore from asteroids (those would sell for about 60k). There are some pretty interesting missions, or you'd think so, until you start breaking them down and they all happen to be on a "kill X mobs missions" level of bad MMORPGs.
You can also contact other "pilots" and sell them stuff/ask them for information. They will either rip you off completely or give you coordinates for a box of resources that you could mine anyway. Oh, and did I mention that you can't recover cargo without a mining beam (which can be installed, but it's installed into an equipment slot, and in the beginning, you could install much better things in there as a combat pilot)? Yeah, I didn't. Live with that, my dear rookie pirates, just another reason to not go full combat in this game.
Oh, and I forgot about the story. Probably because it's completely irrelevant and the game doesn't make you care and it doesn't affect you anyway.
So here I am, sitting in front of my screen 7 (read: about 10, because they allow you to carry save files over from the demo) hours later with a fully equipped mining ship asking myself "what's next?".
The answer is pretty simple: nothing. Grind for the next hull/engine/wings/battery/modules/whatever. This game had the potential to be an ultimate space game, but gameplay-wise, it's empty and unfortunately, there's no incentive to play it.

Temporary thumb up, 20H+ in it, the game is a lot of fun. No review yet but some comments.
It's not really XCOM nor Night’s Watch in the Game of Thrones. Borderline it's that but from very far and not from the mood. But roughly since 3rd week of campaign, I definitly get a feeling reminding XCOM, because there's a significant dificulty, Normal difficulty feels a bit like Veteran in XCOM, and you feel the pressure rising and the urge to improve your roster fast enough to follow the pressure/difficulty increase from campaign progression.
A few comments to describe it in short.
It's an indie Roguelite with party turn based combats on a grid, random missions that are series of text events, roster management, equipment management, party building, light base improvement along the campaign, and light base management.
No AAA here, the game uses modern realistic 3D which cost a lot. But it's no modern AAA 3D level/quality, it's indie. There's a lot of storyteller voices but it's not fully pro. It's ok and it's a plus, but it feels a bit forced and requires some time to get used to it. There's also a good amount of features, multiple classes, each classes has multiples skills and many skills have multiple levels, each class has a lot of equipment, there's many different missions, many different enemies, and more. But it's not the wide quantity of features that have "AAA" indie.
Still it's a lot of fun because manage the roster and party building is very interesting, the combats are quite good with a good depth and diversity. There's also a clear effort to provide  a constant evolution and diversity of combats along the campaign. Manage your base is simple but fun, and there's a good sense of progression along the campaign.
I noticed only one negative point in matter of diversity, the game would benefit of more misc events. After 2 weeks, so probably about 14 missions, I have already seen some misc events multiple times. But behind the same events it's not the same combats as there's a scaling to campaign progression. So it's not just the same enemies with more Hp/damages, but it's also new enemies or enemies with new skills/abilities.
But overall, beside on this specific point, it's quite diversified, with a fair depth on various aspects, the whole is very coherent, it seems well tuned, and it's a lot of fun. Overall the real fun starts at end of 2nd week, before the difficulty is a bit lowered and the game doesn't show yet its real face.

I've been playing Civilization games for a very long time, I've clocked in over 1000 hours between the past 3 games and I have to say that BE brings this feeling back. However, within its current state of development, it feels as if I'm playing a beta. During my first game, after all of the over civ's arrived to the planet, only 1 talked to me and took interest into what I did. 2 other players I communicated with in game, but the other 2 I never even spoke to, and they never spoke to me. When we look back at Civ 5 for example, communication between other nations was rich and made the game intruiging and felt like your race to victory mattered. On top of this, the AI is extremely passive. I ended up warmongering a nearby nation and I still remained friendly relations with all of the other civs, even the ones that were friends with the nation I destroyed. Mind you, I was playing on Apollo and still I got no feedback or even a sign of concern.
One problem I have in particular is how easy I pushed my way to victory. When conquering other civs, I found myself only needing to make an army with 4 or 5 melee units to destroy an entire nations army and their cities. I captured a city with 31 strength in 1 turn with a boat, and 2 melee units. Capturing cities is one thing that needs to be fixed because at the moment, domination victories are laughable.
Although this game brings an interesting twist to the series, I find that it is confusing and plain boring at times. Halfway through my first adventure I felt like retiring and going back to cheerful, exotic Civ 5. The city screen layout is loaded with too much information and makes navigating through the different options very confusing. Although the tech tree is one of the finest aspects of the game, I found it very difficult to make my way around it and find out which techs do what. But this is what people expect in a new civ game, correct? It does feel refreshing to learn a brand new civ game, but the layout of the menus and options are so clunky that it makes me not want to put any effort into it.
Saying this, the developers did an excellent job at bringing back the civilization feel without changing too much. The soundtrack is heart-warming and really draws you into the mysterious maps and the graphics (although run from the same previous engine) look great within these random generated planets.
This new installment is a very clever twist on the series, and I think the developers wanted to get their feet wet and experiement with the different options that can be brought into the series. In future games, things in BE will be present and things will change, and that's how developers learn from present games in a series. BE is in general an okay game in the series with much potential in the future. Now I understand that others look more positivley towards this game and I don't blame them, it's very refreshing and beautiful. However, with the current AI and the confusing layouts, it is a game that will indeed change in time. I would not recommend buying it at this time for these reasons, but for die hard civilization fans that want to be refreshed, go ahead.

I've seen a high amount of negative reviews for this game, and as a longtime dishonored player I feel like I need to make some comments.
First of all, if you haven't gone through at least 8 playthroughs and invested at least 100 hours... you aren't playing Dishonored.  One playthrough where you rush through on easy mode, slashing away at every enemy that comes into your wake, and finish in a ten hour spree isn't enough to review this game.  Each level is IMMENSE.  I thought some of the Dishonored 2 maps were huge, but this blew my mind.  Every corner there was a new challenge or enemy to face off against with 4 or more different possible scenarios to defeat it.  The VoidEngine is looking better than ever, and it makes Dishonored 2 feel like a beta for some larger project.  The shadowing, effecting, retexturizing is BEAUTIFUL in this game, and it's the little things in the game that make or break it.
However I would like to go over some of the pros and cons of this game.
Pros:
>The VoidEngine is nearly perfect, and I didn't have a single glitch on my mid-tier rig running at medium settings.
>Awesome lore in the game that matches perfectly with all the lore found throughout the entire Dishonored series
>Displace was VERY difficult to get used to after using Blink, but once I got the hang of it,  it blew my mind on some of the cool stuff you could do.  I set a marker, ran literally across the map to get around to a window where I could see the marker, then teleported inside a locked room.  And none of that describes the awesome combat ability that it bestows upon you
>Just an awesome all-around experience for this series, and I genuinely hope to see more from Arkane.
Cons:
>No rune system - Instead of using runes, the game has hundreds of bonecharms strewn about Cyria, and a few dozen of them are the powers from the original Dishonored.  I didn't like this because the game felt cluttered and I wasn't able to use some of the bonecharms due to having such a low limit.  I personally recommend doing a system where runes are collectible and instead of using the mark, the runes upgrade your Void Arm's potential (i.e., Strong Arms, Instant Blink, Possesion, Stop Time) and give more of an opportunity to create better fatalities.
>Displace has it's cons as well.  It was difficult to teleport onto ledges and it would try to drop you 30 feet in the air.  Although the bonecharm made it possible to instantly Displace, it was difficult to place exactly where you wanted to go.  I was a huge fan of Blink in Dishonored 2 with it's stop time ability and it made exploring much more fun.  I found it difficult to go some places with Billie's Displace, and it proved that exploring Cyria would be much more difficult that expected.
I HIGHLY recommend this and every Dishonored game.  Easily my favorite game series of all time, and I cannot wait to see more from Arkane.  A+ job to an A+ story.
