Case 1: You never liked the previous Civ games and thought it needed a space vibe to get you into it (but somehow never played Alpha Centauri).
Then you'll probably love this game and think a load of us are being nitpicky.
Case 2: You've played Alpha Centauri and/or any previous Civ title and liked it.

Go back and dust off your Alpha Centauri or Civ ; wait for the obviously missing DLC (or at least modders to pick up the developer's slack) and eventual steam sale.
The only reason I don't try for a refund is because I don't want the hassle right now, and want to save my refund rant for something that is 'broken' and not just ... 'lacking'? (I wanna say bad, but that's harsh)
The biggest problem I have is lack of flavor and clarity. All the 'quests', 'excavations', etc... add nothing. It just looks like 'ok you built/discovered object#21 ...now pick option a or b in dialog box #21...now rinse repeat'. There is no real power in storytelling in this game that I felt the developers were pushing so strongly. It's less a tool, and more of a forcefeeder; It forces choices into your personal story that you might not like and it takes you out of the game and into a wall of text.
I noticed a big issue was also the AI...or lack thereof really.. Compared to Civ 5 (which is saying something), they just sit there. Granted I was playing Mercury; but never in a Civ game have I been able to sit down first time ever playing, and absolutely dominate the AI start to finish (and this new game with all its new mechanics, I'd hope I couldn't just pick it up and let it beat itself...I sort of want to learn it before I'm good at it.. At least that's how I feel about Civ games). It felt boring and unfortunately I was glad to ignore them most of the game, because talking to them is even sadder. Absolutlely no innovations in AI. They are also completely devoid of any individuality: personality, background, or 'fleshing out'.
Then there's the question a lot of people brought up during it's development and it was heavily echoed during my playthrough:
"Why did they do ___ ?" Because they didn't want it to look like Civ 5 as much as possible.
It's a reskin. Maybe not something that could've been easily done in a mod, but B.E. is not a standalone game. It's Civ 5 the space paint DLC. That's what you're paying for.
Which is why I say people who just want a space game are going to love this.
Which is also why I say people who played previous Civ games are going to be annoyed they could've just sat in front of a Civ 5 game making laser noises and modded some textures in and got the same experience
(and not had to drop all the cash for it).
I know there are people who prefer Civ 1 & 2, to Civ 3, 4 & 5; I don't think I know them peronally, but I do have friends who preferred 3 & 4 and therefore did not want to buy the later versions.
Although I can see why they chose so, I always felt that the later versions always brought something to the table that made it stand out enough that I could buy it and enjoy it as a seperate game, and then go back to previous Civ titles to enjoy them again....but B.E.? I have nothing to bring back to those Civ 3 & 4 (and now 5) friends to make them see that B.E. is a cool new game.
It's just mediocre. Something that could've been pushed out as a pricey DLC, instead of a full blown standalone game.
(heck, if they had just slapped 'Civ 5: Beyond Earth' on the box title I bet half of the complaints would disappear LOL).
I also thought the level of micromanaging needed when building/moving/trading at some points was absurd but this is getting long enough as is and it's ranty enough
basically good game for newcomers to the series who only want space and not history; absolute ire to those of us fans whom dropped standalone money for what feels like DLC
also the aliens are just barbarians...except sometimes they don't swing their axe (I mean tentacle) at you.
Missing some nice features from the first game, but its quite fun. Not worth 35€ tho, wait for it to go on sale

For those of you who don't know, Civ 5 was famous for being simple, easy, slow, boring, poorly optimized, and almost completely broken.  It took two expansions and more patches than can readily be counted to fix it, and it's still only really worth it for the immersion it grants you in the history of our world.  For the first year it was out almost the entire multiplayer community snubbed it completely in favor of its predecessor, Civ 4.
This is mechanically and spiritually the same game.  The story, the flavor text, the setting, and the appearance of the game are all new(ish).  However, almost everything else in the game is a gussied up version of Civ 5.  Same culture, same resources, same resource management, same global resources, same complete failure to understand the game's mechanics in a balanced and sane manner.
The game is still poorly optimised and will try to crash your computer on every load even if you meet the recommended system requirements.  Load times are long and waits at the end of turn can be excruciating.  Oh, and the AI is flat out dumber than a bag of rocks.  First time I played I set the AI to cheat slightly and still easily doubled the next highest score in the first hundred turns.  Two of them declared war on me at the same time and not only did I defeat them, I slapped them down so hard that they gave me some of their cities for free within ten turns of their invasion beginning.
In short, everything that was wrong with the coding of Civ 5 is wrong in this game too.  Every.  Single. Thing.
However, now that I'm finished tearing this game a new one for being a blatant cash grab and barely a better mod than some of the user made mods out there, let me say that there are some definite improvements in a few areas for this game.
1.  Your Faction: Instead of picking from a shortlist of decent civs, you now get to customize your own.  Some options are still blatantly better than others, but it's still worthwhile to experiment.
2.  Aliens: Much more interactive than barbs, but still very simplistic.  The uncertainty adds tension, but makes for a random element that will detract from balance in multiplayer games.  Nonetheless, a solid improvement over barbarian mechanics.
3.  Quests and Tech: These allow for a customization of your civ, allowing two different players to enjoy very different styles of game unlike the single path that Civ 5 restricts you to.
What I'm saying is basically this: it's a fun game.  It's interesting, it's enjoyable, and it's ultimately probably worth a $25 expansion cost.  What it isn't is a different game from Civ 5.  Seriously, if you own Civ 5, keep playing that.  If you don't, buy whichever fits your prefered genre.

Infinity Wars tries a lot of bold new things. Some of these succeed, while others do not.
Firstly, and unfortunately most importantly, the game is genuinely free to play. It isn't Heartstone free to play, where non-paying players need to grind for years to accumulate the same quality of cards as someone who spends $1000. IW lives up to its name. A new player has the potential to build a competitive deck from just the cards he receives from the tutorial, and initial booster packs ('soulbound packs'). Those who choose to spend are able to gain platinum cards (just shiny), better artwork, sounds, effects, etc, and more cards to play with, BUT THESE CARDS ARE NOT NECESSARILY ANY BETTER. They are just more options to explore should you get bored of using the same, but highly effective, strategy every game. No cards are locked behind a pay-wall, although if you want to build a deck with 10+ legendaries in it (that is NOT NECESSARILY BETTER THAN A DECK WITH 0 LEGENDARIES), be prepared to pay or grind.
There isn't much to say about the artworks or effects. If you like them, great. If not, you don't. There's no option to turn them off, but then again, we aren't playing Microsoft Excel.
The community is also extremely active, for its size. It is certainly no Heartstone, which has the publishing collosus of Blizzard behind it, nor is it Yugioh, where even in my relatively small town there are frequently 20-30 player tournaments with prizes. The developers, too, are frequently active on the forums, and this game has been patched at once a month since I began to play. I say this with absolute confidence; if this game has a larger player base, it has the potential to lead the market with its innovation and new ideas.
Why, then, do I NOT recommend this game for you?
It's free, so there's no harm trying. But as you progress beyond Puffy the Fish and encounter more and more cards and combinations, you will realise one serious flaw in the game design. The devs have shown they are not a money laundering scheme, and genuinely wish to see this game develop into something for the gamers to enjoy. They design and maintain their game with all the best intentions, but unfortunately in this case it does not equate to results.
Infinity Wars has a unique turn system unlike Heartstone, MTG, Yugioh, etc. I remember something similar in some Marvel DC comic card game ages ago, and that is that both players have their turns at the same time. Not only is this extremely confusing for new players (this, and the copious amount of addon-systems that are needed as a result, to determine things like card resolution order, etc), it is also fundamentally incompatible with their card design, which follows a far more traditional MTG/Yugioh approach.
In short,  the cards for this game do not match the rules for this game. It is like eating Butter Chicken Flavoured Ice Cream, driving to work in a $2999 bottle of wine eating your favourite hamburger while diving into a beautiful coral reef. Oil and water don't mix. Or, for a more contextual example, like throwing a pokemon card into Yugioh. What are energies??? At best, this system leads to frustrating gameplay, where both players are reluctant to do anything out of fear, that they will incorrectly anticipate between two WHOLLY VALID courses of play and thus screw themselves over for the rest of the game. At worst, this creates massive imbalances in the game due to some cards being overpowered in the context in which they are placed. For example, 'draw 3 cards' is a common effect in pokemon. Put that card into yugioh, and it will completely break the game.
The game has a great community, great ambitions and has the potential to change the face of TCG games. However, this is no easy task, and despite the best intentions of the DEVS, clearly indicated by the fact that the game is not pay to win, the gaping flaws in the game's current fundamental design will not allow it to provide a largely positive experience.

I hopped onto the bandwagon of this series a couple of iterations ago - Legends, i think - and i'd been impressed by it from a technical standpoint. I never found the gameplay that immersive, but it was always good to kill a couple of hours when nothing else was entertaining.
The latest installment abandons that.
I bought the game largely for the visual updates, and partly to support the developer, who has done amazing work in creating these games, but i have to say i found this one a disappointment, perhaps/almost to the point of regretting buying it. While the basic controls are the same, the game itself is very much not, from little niggles like "you can no longer safely engage jump from inside a station" (Load last save or accept failure and exit?) to more prominent stuff like "the entire game economy now functions differently, so all you have learned of the franchise thus far is no longer useful"
The mission format always struck me as an interesting introduction to the games mechanics, and later, as a diversion from the games primary play of exploration and/or space combat - being a way to reliably engage in the latter in a relatively safe manner - but this version makes it both central and absolutely required. There is basically no other way (that i have yet found) to qquickly, reliably, and easily make money to fit out your ship and progress to the parts of the game you probably bought it for.
What'smore, it is a LOT grindier. The most lucrative missions almost always take place in/around planetary atmospheres now, and though the speed unit has basically been doubled over Mercenaries, you sure won't feel it when trying to fly around a planet. Never mind that flashy wing system, spacecraft will burn up if they even approach the sound barrier. The most seductive missions - collect 5 samples of aerial creatures for study - appear to pay for a minimal amount of work, but in actuality you could easily spend a half hour fruitlessly chugging around the planetary surface at what feels like crawling speed, attempting to find the wretched things. And if you accidentally collect a unit of biological material from some other source (the trees sparsely littering the planet) you are going to have to destroy that stack and start over.
I really want to like this game but unless there's some hidden mechanic not apparent to a casual player, I just don't think i can.

This is an outstanding metriodvania with heavy dark souls influence.   First of all you have to be on the nosy side. One of those people who enjoys exploring and turning over stones, to really appreciate this gem. One of those completionist. If you are not, you will be robbing yourself of what  this games truly offers. Which is rich rich lore, story, and a since of discovery.   Just like dark souls you can miss a whole lot if you aren't taking time to smell the roses. That includes sections of the game and powerups which can make the game significantly easier. This IS a  metriodvania. And I mean in the classic Metriod vien.  There is a ton of back tracking and there is almost no hand holding. You progress as you see fit using your brain. Sometimes when you discover a new area, you might be doubting that you are ready and won't progress only to find out you were all along.  Which I find amazing in the day of game mechanics that push you along when its safe .There are no waypoints here. Even using the in-game map requires some thought until you get something which makes it easier. And after a while of playing, you won't  use that thing you got anyway.  Why? Because you got gud.  I like it. This game is about getting gud. From map usage to critters you fight  to boss battles, you have to pay attention and learn. There is no praying and  button mashing here to get by. Speaking of which, the controls were tight with my xbox controller. If you mess up, you can only look at yourself. Plenty of times after I died,  I was yelling at myself "why am I jumping?" or "why did I swing again?"  "Take what they give you" Man it was great! As you can see above , the art is top notch. The music is superb and will stick with you well after you are done. I played this game blind and it was a blast to discover. This isn't a game in so much as it is an experience. My GOTY right now.

First review for a Dishonored game, because I trully think this one deserves some love. Of course there's some negative things, but I think this piece is a nice step in the right direction.
Context : I played all Dishonored content to date and really enjoyed the first one and its DLCs, didn't enjoy as much Dishonored 2. I played the game in Hard with objectives markers disabled.
This expansion is an example of less can be more, and I'm talking about the gameplay with Billie Lurk. The fact that Billie only has 3 powers, with an unlimited energy regeneration is a fantastic idea. With this change, the game allows for a lot of experimentation and risk taking on top of having a smart level design making you use all of your powers all the time. The fact that there's Whale bone EVERYWHERE is amazing to experiment with crafting, but there's a lack of interessting bonecharms.
The missions are far more interessting with more meaningful options to tackle the problems at hand (The bank heist is an interessting and challenging puzzle). The addition of contracts forces you to pay attention to the environment from the start and immerse yourself to decript the small clues you start with.
I didn't really mind the fact that two missions were in the same locations because the goal and setting of the missions were so differents. Plus you can see some consequences of your last coming if you complete some contracts/side missions.
Loved the revisit of the conservatory, a level I really didn't like in Dishonored 2. Here the layout is changed and way more limited because of the event of the last game, which makes the level way more controled level design-wise.
Really hated the last mission tho. The layout was messy and unplayable without the objective markers, except if you like running around for an hour. I didn't like it mostly because of the level design.
the fact that we are not going after targets and more about informations/items was really rewarding for me and the surprise in the bank vault if you resolve the puzzle is a great addition, a shame we can't use it in more levels.
Really liked the fact that the chaos system disappeared. The lack of nuance of this system was really annoying and consequences should really be more organic and not just binary like the first two games. Although this game doesn't have consequences in the big picture, you have consequences for your actions case by case and not only because you killed X number of people in this mission. This way the game "shames you" less for playing the game your way.
The story was crazy bad, but hey, I wasn't expecting anything after Dishonored 2. I actually think DotO killed the lore. The narration was kinda cool tho, but Daud and the Outsider were really annoying and non sensical.
Would love more missions and a new game+ with Billie having all her abilities from the start and items/bonecharms (Maybe different bonecharms).
People are complaining about length because you can finish it in 4-5 hours for 30$. Well yeah, you can finish it that fast if you follow the objective markers and going in like a dumb dumb. So maybe that's your playstyle, okay, but you can finish Dishonored 2 in 7-8 hours playing this way, and this was double the price, so I think it's kinda fair for DotO to be 30$.
Bonus point for performances, i5 4670, GTX 1070. 60fps locked 95% of the time in ultra (without adaptive resolution).

Where to begin? This is a one of kind brutal turn base RPG, set in a Ancient Era of the Roman Empire. While there is influences of the Khans, and Egpytians the complex culture that exists in this world. The monsters in this world are the people, and how far everyone is willing to go to stay alive and keep their head out of water. And spare their miserable souls to the heiarchy of the gods.
You will be lied to, you will be cheated, and many times you'll find your "bad♥♥♥♥♥quot; warrior being taken down by four thugs armed with nothing but shivs and pants. However, not every battle is optional. Using your insight to find the lies within their dialogue and making decisions that suit your best interest of survival.
Combat is brutal, as everyone else on these reviews may tell you. While functioning on a map that is color coated based on your mobility the game will help you make "smarter" decisions when battling people. It will not hold your hand as you choose the best options each turn. Similar to the fallout V.A.T.S. where the character may choose a limb and strike at the location to of the enemy to cripple them or an advantage they carry over you.
The dialogue is superb, and the characters all their level of charm. Each offering different dialogue choices on how they feel about you, where you come from and where you stand with other political affilates. There are multiple options, and so many paths that the story will have you wanting to see every side.
I will be honest, the audio and graphics are nothing special to look at, and at times a sense of world interaction seems empty. It would have been cool to interact with the world around you more and utilize it in taking advantges whether it be the height of a tower, or a small doorway to fight enemies one at a time. There are times the game does this but I wish I would have seen more.
Overall, this game is great. It has a free demo, so if anything do what I did and try it. After a while once you truly, "understand the system" you will appreciate the game so much more. Try it out, the money is worth it.

Age of Decadence is an extremely unique RPG experience, The way dialogue works and the high quality writing reminds me of Pillars or Eternity or Baldur's gate, the combat is very difficult (Not Dark Souls difficulty, personally) but you have a selection of non-violent approaches and dialogue options/skills that can help you avoid some extremly hard battles,
If you are a hardcore turn based gamer and enjoy long, difficult battles then the fighting approach is for you.  The Quests seem to be well written and features a few different approaches to every situation.  You won't find the more modern use of waypoints which can make it difficult to locate the more hidden quests but you can easily look up guides or just search around the games main towns and talk to the many characters,
On the subject of characters, they have a ton of personality that makes them each feel like unique individual's, The in-game portraits are very well drawn and really bring out the personality type of the character.
The game certainly isn't for everyone but it's certainly worth trying for the story if nothing else.
I highly recommend the game in its current state and the official release is less then a month away.
Pros/Cons
Training
+ Informative
+ Well Written Dialogue
Main Game
+ 8 Backgrounds to choose (which affect starting parameters)
+ Reputation with factions
+Lots of skills & attributes to choose
+ High-quality portraits

+ Good graphics
+ Varied, well-designed environments

Age of Decadence is one of the longest RPG in the making by a small and dedicated team (Iron Tower Studio). I remember reading about him about 9-10 years ago and since them I've waited for it to release. The game is set in a post apocalyptic roman empire like world and features turn based combat and lots of C&C.
When starting the game you receive a warning that this game isn't some fantasy dragon killer simulator. When I first played the demo this year I died on the first quest, because I was stupid and tried to fight someone instead of running away. In this game, with a badly made build you can die easily. The thing that you have to remember though is that this is an Role Playing Game so that if you choose skills/stats related to the selected class (background) the game will be just fine to play. Sure, if you try to be greedy you will get killed if you are not prepared. This means that a change to the way you play this kind of games is required. Like a said above, a bad build is easily made if you don't think about the way a class is played. A merchant maybe should't get into fights and instead should try to talk his way out of problems or solve quests. Sure, you can try to spread into many skills but this may mean you will be unprepared for some future situations, so specialization I think is key. I would say this game is similar to Neo Scavanger on this part. In both games you have to think  about what you are going to do. Eating uncleaned water or trying to fight a soldier without having some weapon training could be deadly in both games.
Now that the role playing part is described, I think I should write a bit about story. If you read any of the other reviews, you will know this game is full of C&C (Choice & Consequence). Many of the actions you will take will influence the events that you will received in the future and how you will be treated. Kill a guild trader and you may find that an assassin will be sent after you. Believe the words of a shady looking person and you will find yourself dead in a ditch. The C&C part is probably the reason this game took so long to make, since every background should be viable and also different from the others. What this means is that huge ammounts of text are in this game and it's a lot of (great) reading to be made. I don't think there is any game with so much C&C. The only game that has a smaller amount of C&C is maybe the Witcher series, but not even them don't have as many outcomes and ways to deal with situations. Now that I think a bit, maybe Fallout 2 is a bit similar to it. Both are post apocalyptic games, with turn based combat and many skills that unlock different ways to solve the problems. Similar to Fallout New Vegas there is also a reputation system which opens or closes the way you gain access to some quests.
Like I said in the beginning, the combat is turn based, with different type of attacks available for each weapon. Each weapon class also has different uses and special attacks (eg. you can impale with the spear). If you played Fallout 1 or Fallout 2 is should be very similar. You use action points to move, to make attacks, use items (like poison), etc. Related to fight is also a crafting & alchemy mechanic which can be used to turn the balance on your favor in the harder fights. I think that the fights are well made, with enemies trying different tactics to kill you. What is important also to fighting is avoiding damage, which can be made in two ways: dodge or armor (you can't max both since armor decreases dodge chance).
This is a great game and I recommend it to any serious RPG fan. If you only played this kind of games recently, and didn't try older RPGs, this kind of game may seem harder to play but it really is not. It's a game that doesn't treat you like some brain-dead jellyfish. From my part, this should be the game of the year.
TL; DR
Game is great, lots of C&C with classes that play different and turn based combat. GOTY material, now go and buy a copy!

Death of the Outsider is not groundbreaking, but it’s a good lore entry in the series and if you like the void powers you have available it’s quite fun. Unfortunately, if you don’t like them you’re stuck with them. There are no skill trees or different abilities to choose from – only the three main abilities. One is a variant of blink where you put down and then trade places with a doppelganger, the other allows you to remotely scout the area, and the third lets you take the faces of NPCs. Stealing faces is actually pretty fun, and leads to some interesting scenarios. It’s likes the opposite of possession of the previous games: instead of being stuck with a body at the end, you can steal the face of someone already dead or unconscious.
There is some further simplification in the way items and resource management is handled. Bone charms remain and have the same function, but mana potions are gone now. Instead, your abilities are refilled “directly from the void.” This allowed me the freedom to use my abilities all the time instead of saving them for crucial moments as I did in the previous games. I hope this simplification isn’t a trend moving forward, but it works for the not-full-length Death of the Outsider.
It is worth picking up if you want more of the same Dishonored action, but if you’re new to the series, I suggest starting with the first game otherwise you'll be missing out on some story.

Recently bought this game and got really into it. It's definitely not a game for everyone.
+ Character customization. Choosing gender, skin color and the like.
+ Origin, you can choose your character's background story ex. Thief, Drifter, Merchant.
+ Reputation system, which determines how certain people treat you.
+ Skill and attribute allocation.
+ Tactical combat, which challenges you to adapt.
+ Tons of insanely great dialogue.
+ Rare, Roman Post Apocalyptic setting. ( I wish more RPG's had Roman settings/backgrounds).
+ So many paths to choose, that branch out. Making replayability an enjoyable must.
+ Easy save system. Quicksave and quickload makes the game easier, since every choice has an impact on the story.
+ Crafting system, which can be used anywhere
+ Supports high resolutions.
+ Have to use your brain, since you can't fight or talk your way out of every encounter.
+/- So many creative ways to die, I mean one wrong choice in dialogue and you end up getting ambushed by 4 thugs, lose hp points permanently or just end up dead out of nowhere.
- Some glitches, bugs and unfinished quests but that's to be expected.
Overall it's a really great game done with a lot of love. I would recommend it to anyone who loves RPG's and to those casuals who want to challenge themselves.

I won't hold this against the game, though, as I'm probably just trying to convince myself I'm secretly not terrible.

This freaking game... I used to think that I was capable of doing what needed to be done in these sorts of games to at least get through each encounter, even if battered and bruised, but to survive to fight another day... I read the reviews beforehand, I thought these were much the same as those for similar games I've completed with just a little bit of forethought, and I thought that maybe I could make it through most of the game without batting an eyelid... Boy, was I wrong...
You cannot be a jack of all trades and master of none and still hope that your skills will get you through. You cannot hope on blind luck that maybe, just maybe, those guards in the distance will somehow not notice your presence and leave you to your own devices... You cannot enter a potential conflict and think that you'll then be able to talk your way out of it, or that there'll be some saving grace or guardian angel to prevent your inevitable demise... This game is unforgiving... You are useless... You are as if you (yes, you, in the real world sitting there reading this) decided that you would step away from your computer for a few minutes, pick up a dagger, sword, etc., and try to take over the world...
You are not a god. You are not a champion. You are not even in the running to make the finals of a computer game tournament. You are useless: a random person with no particular ability to do anything, trying to make something of themselves in a world where only the strong can become recognised, and the weak do anything to please so they don't offend those in power. You could simply take up a trade, hoping that taxes don't increase too much, your lord won't restrict the rights bestowed upon you for being their loyal citizen, and, above all, that your city won't be raided by a more powerful army where you'll likely need to forego many of the "luxuries" that you've become used to living in an established settlement. You could do this, but where's the fun in that? If that sort of life suits you, try a real life simulator. If you want to be a god, try any other RPG.
If not, and you really want to work (and I really do mean work) towards achieving all that you feel is entitled to you, then, perhaps, this game is for you. You won't be able to finish all the tasks put to you. You won't even finish half (I've yet to try the "god mode" listed in the guides, but it seems that this will restrict the story you develop.) My only suggestion (after numerous failed attempts at living in this unforgiving world) is to focus your development on the character choice you make in the beginning. I've yet to determine if this method will be successful in all situations, because even the most eloquent of speakers runs into trouble in this game, but it seems to be your best bet if you truly wish to survive.
Put simply, you will die... Many times... And often at the most inopportune moment... But... To succeed in these situations makes it all the more worth it. A fantastic game, and a credit to the developers. Your survival is up to you. Your life is yours to lose. The question is, are you willing to risk making that sacrifice?

For those of you who don't know, Civ 5 was famous for being simple, easy, slow, boring, poorly optimized, and almost completely broken.  It took two expansions and more patches than can readily be counted to fix it, and it's still only really worth it for the immersion it grants you in the history of our world.  For the first year it was out almost the entire multiplayer community snubbed it completely in favor of its predecessor, Civ 4.
This is mechanically and spiritually the same game.  The story, the flavor text, the setting, and the appearance of the game are all new(ish).  However, almost everything else in the game is a gussied up version of Civ 5.  Same culture, same resources, same resource management, same global resources, same complete failure to understand the game's mechanics in a balanced and sane manner.
The game is still poorly optimised and will try to crash your computer on every load even if you meet the recommended system requirements.  Load times are long and waits at the end of turn can be excruciating.  Oh, and the AI is flat out dumber than a bag of rocks.  First time I played I set the AI to cheat slightly and still easily doubled the next highest score in the first hundred turns.  Two of them declared war on me at the same time and not only did I defeat them, I slapped them down so hard that they gave me some of their cities for free within ten turns of their invasion beginning.
In short, everything that was wrong with the coding of Civ 5 is wrong in this game too.  Every.  Single. Thing.
However, now that I'm finished tearing this game a new one for being a blatant cash grab and barely a better mod than some of the user made mods out there, let me say that there are some definite improvements in a few areas for this game.
1.  Your Faction: Instead of picking from a shortlist of decent civs, you now get to customize your own.  Some options are still blatantly better than others, but it's still worthwhile to experiment.
2.  Aliens: Much more interactive than barbs, but still very simplistic.  The uncertainty adds tension, but makes for a random element that will detract from balance in multiplayer games.  Nonetheless, a solid improvement over barbarian mechanics.
3.  Quests and Tech: These allow for a customization of your civ, allowing two different players to enjoy very different styles of game unlike the single path that Civ 5 restricts you to.
What I'm saying is basically this: it's a fun game.  It's interesting, it's enjoyable, and it's ultimately probably worth a $25 expansion cost.  What it isn't is a different game from Civ 5.  Seriously, if you own Civ 5, keep playing that.  If you don't, buy whichever fits your prefered genre.

I highly recommend this game, with a few caveats.
If you:
- have ever learned, played, and enjoyed a flight simulator.
- like sandbox and space games in general.
- have ever a played a game like SWG:JTL, where you liked it so much that you mastered all three pilot trees several times over, became a master shipwright, didn't too much mind mining in space for resources, and was proud of having squeezed 64.78 units of mass into a 65 mass ship frame.
- have ever played a game like Elite Dangerous and found yourself absolutely detesting sitting around waiting, or other arbitrary time sinks that have little to no gameplay value whatsoever.
- would prioritize depth of gameplay over graphical appearance if forced to make a choice between the two.
Then, Evochron Legacy is for you.
Unfortunately I find it nearly impossible to review this game without comparing it to Elite Dangerous, so by way of comparison to E:D
Pros:
- More advanced avionics , flight model, and better cockpit controls.
- True singleplayer game. No internet connection required.  Multiplayer? Theres small servers you can join, or run your own server.
-  Persistant world, even in singleplayer.  Your actions directly effect territory control or local market conditions.
- You can mod Evocrhon Legacy. I'm currenly running MasterEffect Reborn to spruce up the graphics,  and some texture and  HUD mods.
- No innane and arbitrary timesinks.  In otherwords, you don't have to spend 15 minutes traveling to a space station after entering a system.  Hyperspace will bring you right to it.
- More freedom.  Example, your top speed is not limited.  You can for instance, keep boosting yourself to ludicrus speeds, turn off flight assist, and just coast doing 5 digits in speed, and you'll keep that way until you decide to slow down (which will cost you fuel), or you collide into something.
- You can construct items, and buildings.  Want to build a base on a planet or a space station? You can do that.
- You can travel to and fly around in every planets atmosphere  in the game.  No extra DLC fee required.
Cons:
- Graphics look dated. I wouldn't say they are absolutely terrible, but if your wanting bleeding cutting edge graphics with all the bells and whistles, your in for a mild amount of disappointment.
- Game has a steep learning curve.  But then so does Elite Dangerous.  It's this learning curve that will be your biggest hurdle to overcome to get the most out of this game.

Some may look at this game as another childish block based "MineCraft" style shooter.
When in reality, it's just an incredibly fun and user friendly multiplayer shooter experience. This game easily gives you a creative outlet, which makes the game so much more personally AND conceptually. Instead of buying $14.99 DLC for a few new maps for your AAA titles, you can find a new server that is hosting brand-new community created and free maps that are incredibly fun. The diversity and variety between the maps creates more memorable and fun moments than you would even hope to experience in games like CounterStrike, or Call of Duty.
The ability to create your own character from the very pixel, allows anyone who desires it to express themselves in anyway they want. There are no limits, or restrictions to your creativity. You don't just have a few different generic military themed outfits to pick like Call of Duty or a few character models like CS:Source, And if we haven't learned anything, it's that You, the player, loves customization. Why else do you buy camos off the market or aim for the head as much as you do in Call of Duty?
The game is currently in early access, and is only going to get better. This game needs a lot of support, and needs to be brought out of the dark. The potential is amazing and it is a shame that more people aren't playing this game. I have a few pretty fancy AAA titles in my library, but this Indie game that isn't even finished yet draws my attention more than anything else in my library of games.
If you are to buy this game, you will enjoy it. It's very fun with friends, and the possibilities are endless with the amount of customization. I bought a 4-pack for my friends and we love to join up in the same server and play.

*Note I've played this game for about 2 weeks now, not via steam, simply bought a cd key here*
This game is a budget elite dangerous (before horizons) which has all the features you wanted to begin with.
And you can play singleplayer. No internet, no problem. There's also a demo available to try before you buy.
Furthermore, the developer chooses a very retro however surprisingly detailed graphics feel, hitting things which other games don't! (which is great for budget and gaming rigs alike) but focuses moreso on gameplay, and is constantly involved with the small community attempting to make the game better and better. Buying the game means you get to be a part of that community, your voice is heard.
If I had a couple wishes, it'd be a little bit more of a campaign / story with characters, maybe more control of the stations you build and how they run and operate on the grand scale of things, some more capital ship assault weapons (like another weapon option for a "very heavy assault" role but have it be almost useless in dogfights) and a direct ability to order and limited docking with capital ships to use as fire support in more intense missions.
all THAT said.
The biggest potential this game has is for multiplayer, dealing with NPCs is fine,...to a point. Humans fly different, act different, talk different. The Major issue is there are not enough players yet to make these "dynamic" universes...dynamic. Even with the few we get (16 at most) it becomes quite dynamic.
That said, if you buy the game, spend some time on multiplayer! You'll help build up the re-playability and enjoy it alot more. That's where the REAL potential lies, the playerbase really just needs to be increased.
You don't have to though, that's a selling point. And do check the game forums, there are rules about multiplayer, so if you are new, there's not only a wealth of info on multiplayer and a great playerbase to help you, but also they won't simply frag you when you haven't a clue what to do.
At least, if you are sticking to friendly space :) Otherwise any battles are initiated by asking.
Don't buy this game if you want the latest that puts your shiny 1080 gtx to the test, it will not.
Buy this game if you want a genuinely interesting sandbox with a little bit of a story and missions thrown in.
It's been a fantastic indie space sim, and very rich, very modable, (there's already some sound, application and ship model mods out). Can't wait to see more of you out there.

*NOTE: This is an Early Access review meaning it will be a lot shorter than a normal review but will still explain what I thought about it. A full review will be published once Blockstorm has released. You can also skip down to the ending to see my final score.

Blockstorm is a voxel FPS game set in a world made of destructible blocks. All maps and characters included in the game are made with the same tools that are available to the public. You can build everything in Blockstorm, and you can destroy it. Blockstorm was developed by GhostShark and published by IndieGala.
After playing Ace of Spades and Guncraft I've been a little skeptical on any voxel first person shooters. But, I was definitely wrong. In its early access state, Blockstorm provides more to do than Guncraft and Ace of Spades combined. You can build maps with the spectacular map editor, create your own skin, or even download other people's skins! The replyability of Blockstorm is definitely there along with a fantastic FPS design. With being able to customize almost anything, you can practically have a new experience everytime you play a match. Each match is quick enough so you won't lose interest while playing as a character.
Blockstorm does lack in game modes with only providing classic deathmatch, team deathmatch, and another mode named "Assault". The game modes all work well and would definitely suffice if those were the only modes, but the more gamemodes the merrier.
Overall, Blockstorm provides an excellent new addition to the FPS community and is definitely worth a playthough if you're interested in Voxel FPS like Ace of Spades or Guncraft.
Final Score: 8.5/10

*This review focuses on lyrical consideration rather than literal assessment. For detailed game information and analysis I recommend
*
Space, the vast tapestry of the night sky, became a personal symbol for me at a young age.  I remember lying in the meadow over the hill behind our house, far enough away from any human activity that I was able to feel truly unanchored, adrift.  It was just me, the stars, and the soft rustle of the wind through the goldenrods.  I soon discovered science fiction novels and video games, through which I experienced clandestine trysts with the stars.  I still see space in this way- a symbol of my desire for true freedom and self-determination, a concept that is both idealized and impossible.
At its best, space simming gives me a chance to immerse myself in a dream, intoxicated by the delirious mixture of total freedom, relentless peril, and unflinching solitude.  I've never been able to get into the more linear, mission-based style of space sims (Wing Commander, Freespace). And frankly, as a youngster, I saw the commercial success of these games as a mark against their integrity and worth.  I played them once and never played them again, resenting the obscurity of the gameplay experience I so loved.  Take as counterpoints Space Rangers or Star Control, games I continue to play every few months, many years after I first encountered them.
The rising Indie Era carries with a glut of new games identifying with any number of formerly niche or fringe markets, with the idea that these new games are made by people who like to play them.  Suddenly those sacred tropes are everywhere: start as a nobody with a tiny ship, trade and fight your way to fame and fortune however you see fit.  Travel from base to base, help or hinder factions, explore the vastness and exploit whatever you find.  I am giddy as I scroll through the many new titles built on this common formula.
But, as we have been forced to learn, the Indie Era has a darkside. For every labor of love built by caring craftsmen, there are five unruly messes abandoned without a second thought.  I know that life happens, and building a game is tough- but unfinished is unfinished.  I've had high hopes for a few- Drifter, Jumpdrive (formerly Paragon), etc. But alas.
Even the multi-million dollar powerhouse Elite:Dangerous often feels half-finished.

My first few hours in E:L were a revelation.  I had the same thought so many times it became a mantra: "One man and a contracted artist achieved in a year what Frontier hasn't in 30!"  Planetary landings even on atmospheric planets, modular ship and utility construction, escort jobs, etc, etc. Elite:Dangerous is an amazing game, no doubt, but the difference between Frontier and StarWraith in terms of intent and delivery is astounding. If ED is the sleek, high-design chair you ordered online from Ikea, then EL is the sturdy, simple chair your nephew made for you in his workshop out back.  StarWraith values craftmanship and community involvement over glamour and the clink of stacking coins.
EL is a loving answer to all the issues we had with its predecessor.  Every system is improved.  The sim physics are tighter.  Missions are more complex, more diverse.  The hired artist designed new and more adept ship and object models.  There are far more items comprising a far wider range of uses.  And, one of my favorite points, the activity of AI entities and regional markets are more responsive to player choices and actions.  he game universe is procedurally generated and expands on demand, allowing for ever greater voyages and adventures that are entirely unique to the individual player's experience.
If you like space sims or space at all, buy it. If you appreciate craftsmanship and community involvement from a game studio, buy it.  If you just want to give a true artist the support he needs to practice his craft, buy it.  History will remember Evochron and StarWraith as major contributors to the space sim genre.
Lovely Game

I had extremely choppy/laggy mouse and keyboard movement which might be due to my weak computer but this game should not as demanding on the cpu as it is. Despite all that Kairo's atmosphere is enjoyable and the much needed hint system helps in teaching you what the level design won't. Towards the later segments of the game the puzzles lose some of their quality and the map design will leave most players wondering around without much enjoyment.
If you enjoy difficult puzzles and open ended mysteries Kairo will give you your money's worth

Evochron is an expansive sandbox space combat simulator that encourages exploration. Don't blow this off as some clone or half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥attempt; this will give everyone who enjoys space sims and exploration plenty of entertainment.
This game has a fairly steep learning curve; it kind of throws you into a universe and sets you free. The controls and GUI are daunting at first, but if you just take the time to learn (look for some tutorials) it starts to become second nature. You WILL need to learn how to properly navigate!! Fuel is limited, and (I'm assuming) your time is limited as well. To save fuel, time, and headache, learn how to navigate! Flying "dead stick" thru space will probably just get you killed, or at the very least waste a lot of time.
The star system is vast, mostly contained within our own Milkyway galaxy...TO SCALE. I'm sure that no person has enough time to completely explore the whole area; as it would take thousands and thousands of hours to do so. While there are plenty of inhabited systems that you access with jump gates; there are many uncharted areas that are left for the player to find on their own. You'll find most of these areas through missions and buying information; or by building survey stations that will search uncharted sectors.
You can purchase\craft base structures to collect fuel, hold cargo, mine asteroid fields, or find uncharted systems in nearby sectors. To get materials and money, you'll need to explore and ask friendlies about any information or missions. Missions range from finding lost cargo, gathering materials, escorting friendlies, or attacking enemies. They're all fairly basic but can lead to rare loot that you can sell or keep. This is where it's best to have a friend or two to team up with so you can complete objectives faster.
There's a fairly robust ship customization mechanic that allows you to change the type, performance, weapons, cargo/crew, and arrange the different sections of the hull. You can customize your vessel almost however you want; from re-arranging the chassis and different sections, to customizing weapon platforms and even your character/crew.
The only cons that I have is the small (but active) community. So few people play that it's rare to see anyone else playing. Graphics aren't the best, but they're definitely not terrible. They actually look better than a lot of other indi games, and are still easily passable by todays standards. And if you add mods or ENB fx, it will look even better.
There's really too much to write about, and I have barely scratched the surface. It's best to support a great and dedicated developer, who is constantly improving the game even years after release. It's cheap, it's fun, and IMO has more content than most AAA titles.

Personally, I do enjoy the game. It is a different approach to the World of Subways franchise. I enjoy the driving aspects and would recommend it to those who enjoy train simulators. However, of course. No game is perfect and there are some glaring problems.
I do not drive a train in real life. However, I can tell that the braking is a little off. There is no way EVER that a train would be able to brake that fast. It just is unheard of so that really needs improvement. Along with this. The train lacks a lot of detail, I have watched many videos about how good the game is and the only reason that it isn't as detailed as World of Subways volume 3 is because they don't have enough information about this type of train. Yes I can understand that it can be hard to do research especially on a game based in the 1990s (I think). However, I guarantee that the information will be out there and doing a little extra research would help the design of the game appear better.
Along with the graphics and detail. The surroundings are extremely weird. The game appears to be set in a city where are the houses are perfect cuboids. I think a little more dynamic views of the surroundings would make the game appear more realistic instead of the cars, when they slow down, appearing to have no suspension what-so ever. I mean seriously, they are bouncing around like a mental bunny. The detail on the track is good (could be better).
The NPCs are a massive problem in this game as well. There are really, and I mean really, unrealistic. You can tell that TML studios rushed the depot and the NPCs in it. First, let's talk about the depot. I think that the depot is an interesting concept and I personally like it (the concept that is). However, I dislike it in this game because it is so poorly made. The depot lacks extreme amounts of detail and just seems like a waste of time. There is nothing to interact with in the depot except the NCPs. It just seems like a waste of time, you could do everything in the depot in a menu to save a ton of time. On your side designing it and the players' side playing the game. The depot lacks a load of detail and just seems thrown together in a mad rush to release the game. Furthermore, TML have put no effort in the NPCs either. If they don't have the effort to make the depot appear some-what good. The NPCs will be terrible as well. Some of the NPCs have the most ridiculous voice tone I have ever heard in a human being. The way they talk dosn't even make them seem human at all. Along with this, TML didn't even have the effort to try and make the mouth movements match with what they are saying. The tutorial was the worst though, you know when Steve shows you around. The camera angles are ridiculously off and you end up right in the face of that non-human character Steve while he talks with the horrific mouth sync.
Speaking of NPCs, you know the director. You can talk to him whenever you want and he tells you how you are doing. I guarentee that 90% of you, when you click him, it will say "I have to say you are doing really bad." I mean I work myself to pieces for an hour and get 90% overall and he thinks that's bad. WHAT? Also, when you go past a red light in the game it sends you back to the cringey depot to talk to the boss. But that only occurs with red lights. So when you derail the train everything is fine but edging past a red light... OOOOOO... What have you done.
Overall, I enjoy this game and is a "interesting" concept compared to the other games in the franchise. However, I do currently see it as a step-down from World of Subways 3 and maybe even 2 and 1. Personally, I enjoy the gameplay but how I see the game visually and the mechanics of the game are definitely, as the director would put it, "in the lower-third." These errors can easily be fixed but I do believe that they will not and I really wanted this game to recieve the credit it deserved. But unfortunately, TML just didn't put enough effort and research to make this game what it should have been.
Thank you for reading.

Hollow Knight is probably one of the best Metroidvania games I've ever played.
A careful balance of intriguing level design, perfectly crafted platforming challenges, fair and challenging bosses, and an incredibly detailed world to explore all make for a game that I won't soon forget.  Not to mention the cost; at $15 full price, the game has a ton of bosses, multiple endings, and 30-40 hours of gameplay, depending on how much optional content you want to complete, or even find (not to mention that there are plans to continue updating the game with additional, free content, the first of which landed last week).  Hollow Knight is simply chock-full of secrets and hidden areas, many of which require you to go to the distant corners of the map to fulfill their conditions for entry.  Some are simply a spectacle, while others have deep lore significance as well as giving you more possibilities for how your game will end.  But never fear; once you beat that last boss, you can continue playing, searching for whatever you may have missed the first time around.
The setting is dark and decrepit, the player arriving to a kingdom long dead and buried, but still filled with hints of lore and history.  Coupled with a corpse run mechanic on death and a cast of charming NPCs with a backstory only given to you through their dialog that you'll occasionally hear as you explore the many caves and nests within, the game has a feel that is reminiscent of Dark Souls, but that's all it is; a vague inspiration taken from a game with a similar atmosphere.  Do not be mistaken: this is a game about exploration, finding power ups to unlock addtional paths and levels, and the occasional boss or platforming challenge.
If you've ever enjoyed a metroidvania game even to a small degree, this game is worth it.  Don't hesitate, unless you really really need to save that money; for the playtime this game gives you, $15 is an outright steal.
Worth the price.

On a side note i found out from the developer i was conned by the amulet dealer so i should have stuck with my gut and thought something was off with a magical amulet. Honestly thats a pretty cool feature i guess but not enough to keep me playing however.
The graphics and art design arent great but in this kind of game, gameplay and combat are more important. I just wanted to mention graphics quality is not on par with the likes of Pillars of Eternity or even Shadowrun. Obviously the budget of these titles is very different but i would like to draw attention to the prices. Shadowrun Hong Kong (19.99). Pillars of Eternity (44.99). Age of Decadence (29.99). Now isnt price and total gameplay (in terms of hours of course) the most important thing to consider? $10.00 more than shadowrun and $15.00 less than Pillars of Eternity is exspensive for an indie game with a shoestring budget compared to the former multi-million dollar games.
The starting town feels empty. You cant talk to anyone but merchants and some quest givers/ quest completers. When you wish to travel to a new area you pull up your map and click on it, fast travel ensues. The game immediately made me think of a visual novel, which isnt a knock by itself as i have played and enjoyed quite a few visual novels. However this game has a steep pricetag for what it offers.
Combat is turn based and in the few battles i was able to particpate in without crashing, tactics were to get up close to the enemy and swing until one of you is dead. Your character has the ability to select different attacks depending on the weapon he is weilding. For example an overhead strike with a broadsword. The different attacks do different levels of damage, consume different levels of AP, or have different chance to hit. There is also the ability to aim at places like your opponents legs to cripple mobility, or do some sort of whirlwind strike that hits multiple opponents. Other tidbits of action like sneaking and stealing are all calculated based on your skills. For example in one quest you can sneak into a ruin, to do so its all skill based you click sneak in the conversation window and sneak past the immediate guards. Than you click sneak again to get into the tunnel, if your sneak skill is high enough again you succeed. Gameplay really seems lackluster as i anticipate random skill checks for almost everything you want to do in this game.
Character creation is pretty bland there are a few options to make your character look different maybe 5 hairstlyes and a  few hair colors and skin colors. Other than that there is a list of skills and attributes which arent sufficiently explained to a new player. There is your average attribute system and a list of combat skills and non combat skills. Investing in combat attributes unlocks combat skill points that you can distribute and so on. The character skill system seemed very deep to me on the surface but because of other parts of the game i was not able to delve into it and enjoy it.
All in all i have played and enjoyed many cRPGs but i cant recommend this one. Many crashes, terrible combat and gameplay, not very good story and the graphics are very indie scene as well, though i would excuse the graphics if the game had anything else fun about it.
I would also just like to note that while some fans of the game believe that in order for me to write a negative review i must slog through 5-10 more hours of boring gameplay that is not reasonable. In the first hour of gameplay after experiencing multiple crashes and encountering other issues i switched to a game i actually enjoyed again.

Dawn of a Soul:
~~~~~~~~~~~~

Mathematics, let’s face it, is a very important part of any life. Some of us are blessed with a skill with numbers, and others (like myself) see mathematics as a curse to be avoided at all costs. Regardless of how you look at it, it’s part of our daily activities. So let’s make it fun, shall we? Let’s have a go at Dawn of a Soul!
Dawn of a Soul is a mathematical puzzle game where you have to connect numbers into a chain in order to reach a specific score and clear a level, collecting all shards to get your soul back.
The game has four different stages and sixty-four levels to clear, the first few being tutorials. In a nutshell, a shape made of nodes will appear on the screen. Some of these nodes might be of different colours, formats (eg. diamond, round) and have numbers in them.  At the bottom of your screen there is a number displayed, which you have to reach by connecting the intersections together using a round marker. Well, it’s fine when you have to reach the number three by connecting three red nodes, each containing the number one. It becomes a little bit harder when the goal is in the hundreds and the shape has different colours of nodes.  You’ll be able to connect nodes of different colours as long as you have connected intersections which give you a minimum equation of six. The value will be displayed around your marker. Each time you do manage to connect to a different colour, you’ll increase the multiplayer by one. Oh, don’t worry about keeping track of the big equation, it will also be displayed at the bottom of your screen.  Most of the time, you’ll have to connect the intersections in one stroke. On some occasions, you’ll have a few more strokes at your disposal in order to reach the displayed number. Each time you clear a level, you’ll be rewarded with one or two shards.
The pixel graphics are well done and the game runs very well. It’s fun and easy to play.
Positives:
~~~~~~~
-	Nice pixel graphics
-	Well designed-levels
-	Easy to play
-	Achievements
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	No trading cards
This is a fun, casual mathematical puzzle game for all ages. Give it a go!
6/10

The Age of Decadence. Where do I even begin to describe this beast of a game?
RPG's nowadays tout having choices. And consequences for said choices. You'll find that most of the times, they're fairly small and maybe not so imaginative and won't affect the story for the most part.
Not in Age of Decadence! While you are still a player in an elaborate play, you are still capable of turning it on its head unlike a lot of other games today, and I speak from experience given my extensive run into the world of rpg's.
Unlike most RPG's today, you can play as a"pacifist" (I use quotes, because you will most likely be the cause of many a people's tragic "accidents" and "mishaps") That in itself in an achievement - you can go through the entirety of the game without ending a life personally and still come out on top. I yearn games which allow me to avoid killing my fellow men, even though it is encouraged or easier if I do so.
Or, you can follow the path of a warrior and cut down anyone who thought it'd be smart to give a psycho a mean look.
Another thing that is very notable about this game, is the almost absolute lack of morality! It's almost black comedy levels (I imagine that was the intent, but I digress). And it's glorius! Whereas in other games, you will be condemned utterly as the worst scum of humanity, or your meanie acts will be considered for the greater good. Not here!
In order to make it, you got to be the baddest badass or the most cunning schemer to ever grace (or profane) the land, and exploit almost any opportunity that comes your way. As told to you by a warning whenever you start a new game -"Look out for yourself, because no one else will". So grab your sword, or prepare your ink and pen, because you are in for a bumpy ride that might end up with you on top of things. Or at the bottom of a ditch after a brawl gone bad.

- Comments on you making effort to avoid the story?

- Makes you feel properly engaged, despite the fact that you do nothing but walk and click?
Trust me, if you aren't sure about it, play the demo. That'll give you an excellent idea of what this game is like.

This mathematical puzzle game has a very creative concept you would maybe expect on mobile platforms, but uses the PC's wider display for deeper in-depths mechanics and levels. It has an original approach on the casual-friendly puzzle genre by finding the optimal chain(s) in combining the numbered nodes and switching the colours on the right spot to increase the multiplier.
You don't need high mathematical skills to solve the puzzles, simply counting to a reasonable degree is all you'll need (the game keeps track of your equation in the bottom) and  the routes are often quite intuitive. The final score you need to reach is given in any level, while often there is a second, lower score to move on to the next level and coming back later. New mechanics are added along the way, but always with very easy to learn tutorials. But make no mistake, the higher levels are very challenging and will need your focus to master them.
Finally, the visuals are beautiful for a little indie game. The pixel look is very well made with shiny particles around the nodes which results in a very satisfying feeling by building the chain while also maintaining a clear overview of the level.
If there is anything negative about the game, it would be the dialog based options menu, which may be casual friendly, but require more clicks (and time) than necessary if you are a savvy PC player. But once you're set, the ingame controls are fine.
I can highly recommend it for anyone who is looking for an original puzzle game.

Having finished one game I can't truly recommend this. It's alright, but just alright. This comes from a veteren of Civ IV and V. If you're new to the Civ franchise I think this one is a fantastic place to start.
The future setting, while the whole premise of the game, is actually its biggest downfall. The histrorical anchors in Civ V serve as a point of reference for what you're researching. Researching the wheel lets you build roads, building the pyramids makes your workers faster and so on. In Beyond Earth you get none of that, you research pseudo-scientific things from a very confusing and dificult to navigate "tech-web" to build pseudo-scientific sounding laboratories and whatnot. None of these technologies or buildings are acompanied by any art beyond minimalist icons which makes telling the difference between a miasmic repulsor and a terrascape incredibly dificult.
Another thing that was really badly done, in my game at least, was the end-game. I went with a "contact" victory which involves decoding a signal for 20 odd turns,  building a becon for 40 odd turns, and then activating it and waiting another 25 turns. This was a whole lot of time which I spent doing next to nothing. I saw little point in engaging in war, my nearest neighbours loved me because we had trade routes, I had already built everything I needed, and nobody looked at the vulnerable giant becon sitting next to my capital broadcasting into deep space and thought "Huh, better destroy that before he wins the game." It was a dull end to a fairly dull game and I was playing on what the game classifies as "hard".
I'll play it again, I think the big red thumbs down is perhaps a little harsh but I can't give it a full thumbs up either.

There ae a lot of questions that come up with this game, so let me keep this introduction brief. If you're like me, you've probably played several of these Early Access/Beta games and have been burned a few times by lack of content and general poor quality. Some I like (Prison Architect, Project Zomboid, Space Engineers), others I've quickly forgotten about. This is a game that makes the former list and will continue to recieve my support.
For some background, you shold familiarize yourself with a couple of other games- Minecraft (everyone knows of); Silent Storm (A tactical 3rd person RTS that has a fully destructable environemnt); The Battlefield games; King Arthur's Gold.
This game combines elements of each of those previous games and does most of it better than similar titles.
The resolution: It's a higher quality than Minecraft and in general, the graphics are a better quality than most Voxel games like it. If you blow up a block, for instance, the block explodes into dozens of smaller ones, that each obey the laws of physics. This lends itself nicely to a realistic feel in a gunfight, as the terrain and environment turn to rubble and dust around you!
Physics: Structures actually obey the laws of physics (mostly); if you blow up the base of a freestanding object, the rest crumbles (In the style of a 3d King Arthur's Gold).
The Editors: This is where the game really shines! Look at the artwork the community has done in regards to characters. There are so many small details you can edit, you can let your imagination run wild!
The map editor is also very detailed, allowing you to create huge structures, or vast fields. Were you a kid that liked playing with Legos and then destroying your masterpieces with as much ingenuity as you were legally allowed? That's the map editor in a nutshell :)
You can then take these creations and share them online with other players in game, or via the forums. Which brings me to....
Community: Small but active. Devs and Admins regularly interact on the forums, answering questions and giving feedback. You get the sense that they really are relying on the players to help them shape the game... unlike soooooo many other games on this Steam list.
And then we get to the bad...
Population: Is depressingly low. I've yet to see more than 10 people on a server. However, when you combine this with all of the above and the Early Access state of the game, there really isn't much you can complain about. IN some cases, playing may even become secondary to creating maps and characters!

I was surprised to hear about this game, it came completely out of nowhere. I didn't even see it on Steam first, someone posted about it on a Star Citizen facebook group. Apparently Steam thinks I'm more interested in seeing 10,000 X Rebirth advertisements. It's sad because this game could really use more exposure.
In terms of gameplay, it's everything Elite aspired to be yet failed to become. But if you value a massive galaxy, play Elite. If you value the most beautiful graphics ever, play Star Citizen. Where this game shines isn't in graphics, or the size of its universe (though its universe is in some ways, ways that I think matter, bigger than Elite), but in its content, in its gameplay, which is simply some of the best I've seen in... ever. It's literally the best I've seen and that's why I'm amazed I haven't heard about this until now.
So let's go over the pros:
+Open to modding. Private servers. Make your own server, your own world, customize it the way you want. I haven't explored this nor seen many examples of it so far, but that's to be expected so soon after release. In the coming months there will hopefully be some good mods available. So far it seems only that graphical changes are possible, perhaps some remodelling and some new missions. Time will tell how much modders can do to this game.
+A truly open world. Go anywhere. Do anything. Land on any planet, attack any vessel, attack any space station or city. It looks like you can even devote resources to researching new weapons and components not normally available.
+A real sandbox. You can build your own space stations and sprawling cities on the surface, and attack them as well.
+Ship customizability. It's simplistic yet refreshingly open. I put it at a step above Elite's ship customization. You can change out weapons, engines, shields, plating, etc., but also change the fundamental capabilities of your frame by changing crew capacity, energy levels, fuel tanks, how many hardpoints you have, etc. You can also customize the appearance of it by moving wings, engines, etc., and choosing between a few (sadly only a few) colors.
+You can form a fleet. It can be NPC's or players. I'm fairly sure it can only be NPC's in single player, and only players in multiplayer, not sure... hopefully a mod changes that eventually, or the dev does.
+Very stable. Haven't crashed once, nor encountered any bugs of any kind. In the days of EARLY ACCESS (even when they don't say early access anymore) a game that legitimately feels like a finished product is a rare thing.
Cons:
-Graphics are pretty poor for this day and age.
-Combat for a newbie, especially during the combat tutorial, is likely to be frustrating. Your ship shakes violently when you take hull damage and it's quite annoying.
-Few people play it, with about 75 average right now according to steamcharts. There are probably a few more who bought it from the developer's website rather than through Steam, but I doubt it's more than 100-125 average. For such a large world spread across many systems and sectors, space might be lonely. For this reason, I highly recommend you play this with a friend if you're the sort who needs the online component.
Update:
-Mission system seems threadbare, and it's often hard finding a mission you want to do.
-Lack of interaction with capital ships. They're shiny juggernauts in space that seemingly hold no purpose.
Both of these things are, from what I've heard, being worked on by modders. They remain cons for the game as it shouldn't be the community's job to flesh a game out.
-Another negative: While you get more "to work with," so to speak, at higher tiers of ship, it does not seem possible to truly expand beyond what the initial ships are capable of. If you are a miner in your beginning ship, you can customize your ship to have the maximum number of cargo holds, giving you room for 250 items. However, even with the largest of ships, it does not seem possible to exceed this limit of 250 items.
Update 2:
-When I got the game, I did so after having asked questions on its forums. Among them was whether or not capital ships were available for player use. The answer was "no, but someone's working on a mod to make them available." It seems I was misled and this is not even possible. The game is open to mods but not as much as I initially thought, and for the most part mod support includes changes to the HUD and graphics, rather than any changes to gameplay (though addition of new missions is possible, it seems).

Well... after a good 6 years of waiting after the amazing Hitman Blood Money, here come's Absolution.
It is not a sequel per say, more like a reboot and keeping a few elements from past games.
Pros:
-David Bateson voice actor for 47, same VA on all previous Hitmans
-Other known actors to do voice acting in this game
-Graphics are impressive
-Great animation on the character models
-High replayability, many ways to get a mission done (Bloodbath, Ghost and Accidental style).
-Cat and mouse playstyle with enemies will never get tiresome
-Contracts Mode adds diversity
Cons:
-Glitchy and poor AI (spots your even through walls!)
-Lame and cliché-ed story (Agent 47 on the run... really? Sure it's different but... yup, weak)
-Bad and broken stealth (so bad that gunning around "à la CoD style" is more satisfying and it actually works better)
-No weapon customizations before each mission unlike Blood Money.
-No Jesper Kyd for the soundtrack (he did all previous Hitman). Though, the OST is not THAT bad but not memorable either.
-BROKEN checkpoints system, that only save your position in the map; everything respawns, including downed/killed enemies if reloading a checkpoint. Why couldn't IO given the Quicksave / Quickload option like Blood Money?
-Pointless and annoying QTE, that DOES NOT BELONG ON ANY PC GAMES!
-Annoying disguise system that is weak.
So did I like Absolution? SO-SO... it's a good game but as a Hitman game, it is VERY DISAPPOINTING and a step down, especially after having played Blood Money which is far superior.
Now that I'm done with the game here's my advice...
DO NOT buy this game at full price. Wait for a deal! Especially if your a fan of the Hitman franchise, you'll be disappointed the same as me so buy on a deal or pricedrop... heck, EVEN IF your new to Hitman franchise, buy on deal!
Better, get Blood Money now and Absolution later once it's cheaper!
7 / 10
PS: It was announced lately that Square Enix Montreal will be developing the next Hitman game so it remains to be seen if this will be good or bad! Also, it seems the franchise will get the CoD treatment, with yearly releases... all rumours for now though.

What do Portal, Antichamber, Quantum Conundrum, and...oh hell, why not...Bad Rats have in common?
They are all puzzle games (in some sense), yet they all have character to them, something that brings charm to an otherwise incredibly dull game.
Kairo, on the other hand, has absolutely no character in its' floating stone architecture. I wandered the halls looking for some storyline or meaning to my progress, yet there's absolutely nothing to keep your interest for longer than 10 minutes (except possibly for the achievements). Not even Kairo's architecture is interesting, resembling the surreal cubic design of Assassin's Creed's Animus with all the life sucked out of them.
The game doesn't even redeem itself on its' puzzles, which are ridiculously simple and generic, and yet are still explained in full within the game's hint menu.
I only spent $0.82, and yet I still feel like I wasted my money. Save up and buy a better puzzle/platformer instead.
